title: Multifunctional ADM hydrogel containing endothelial cell-exosomes for diabetic wound healing
abstract: Non-healing wound, with limited treatment options, remains a prevalent complication of diabetes mellitus. The underlying causes wherein include oxidative stress injury, bacterial infection, cellular dysfunction, and persistent inflammation. Acellular Dermal Matrix (ADM), a wound dressing composed of natural extracellular matrix and abundant bioactive factors, has been successfully developed to treat various wounds, including burns and diabetic ulcers. Protocatechualdehyde (PA) & trivalent iron ion (Fe3+) complex (Fe3+@PA) exhibits potential antioxidant and antibacterial properties. In this study, we developed a dual hydrogel network by combining Fe3+@PA complex-modified ADM with light-cured gelatin (GelMA), supplemented with exosomes derived from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC-Exos), to create an ADM composite hydrogel system (ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA) with antioxidant, antibacterial, and cell-promoting functions for diabetic wound treatment. Through in vitro experiments, we investigated the biosafety, antioxidant and antibacterial properties of ADM composite hydrogel. Furthermore, we examined the protective effects of ADM composite hydrogel on diabetic wound. The above experiments collectively demonstrate that our ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel promotes diabetic wound healing by eliminating bacterial infection, reduced the reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, protecting cells against oxidative stress damage, promotingcollagen deposition and angiogenesis, which provides a promising strategy to optimize ADM for diabetic wound treatment. Keywords: Diabetic wound healing, Acellular dermal matrix, Exosomes, Hydrogel

sections.text: Chronic non-healing wounds, particularly diabetic foot ulcers, impose a significant health and financial burden on millions worldwide [1]. The complex healing process of skin wounds involves hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling [2]. However, chronic wounds in diabetic patients exhibit poor healing due to prolonged inflammation, increased oxidative stress, severe bacterial infection, impaired cellular migration and proliferation, diminished re-epithelialization, and reduced angiogenesis [3]. Although various biomaterials mimicking the extracellular matrix (ECM) have been developed for wound closure and healing, they often fall short of replicating the natural ECM in terms of morphology, biocompatibility, and cellular interaction [4,5]. We propose a novel approach utilizing bioengineered scaffolds derived from native skin tissue, namely native skin-derived acellular dermal matrix (ADM), to accelerate the repair of chronic wounds by mimicking the in situ cellular environment (Fig. 1). ADM possesses inherent bioactive cues, appropriate biocompatibility, and mechanical properties, while its degradation products are non-toxic. Moreover, the ADM comprises essential components such as proteoglycans, growth factors, collagens, elastin, laminin, fibronectin, hyaluronan, heparan, primary fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and thrombospondin, which contribute to the wound healing process [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. Applying ADM to wounds is typically digested using chemical and physical methods, followed by self-assembly to form a hydrogel [[10], [11], [12]]. The dual hydrogel network leverages GelMA to augment the mechanical characteristics of the hydrogel, all the while preserving the innate three-dimensional architecture of ADM and the bioactivity of cytokines. Consequently, this hydrogel demonstrates commendable mechanical properties, an inherent three-dimensional extracellular matrix structure, and cytokines capable of interacting with cells. To further enhance the wound-healing properties of the hydrogel, we incorporated protocatechualdehyde (PA) and Fe3+ to create a complex (Fe3+@PA). PA is a naturally occurring phenolic aldehyde known for its pro-apoptotic and antibacterial properties and good biocompatibility [[13], [14], [15]]. In an alkaline environment, Fe3+ forms complexes with PA through ligand bonding, allowing PA to reduce oxidation of the aldehyde group through physical cross-linking of the catechol moiety with Fe3+. This cross-linking preserves the reducibility of the complexes, resulting in excellent ROS scavenging ability [16]. Exosomes (Exos), small vesicles with 50–150 nm diameters, play a crucial role in regulating cell-to-cell communication by transferring proteins, lipids, DNA, RNA, and other bioactive substances [17,18]. Various studies have demonstrated the potential of stem cell-derived exosomes in promoting wound repair through different mechanisms, such as down-regulating transforming growth factor (TGF-β) expression, activating the AKT/eNOS pathway for angiogenesis, and enhancing cell function while inhibiting apoptosis [[19], [20], [21]]. Human umbilical vein endothelial cell-derived exosomes (HUVEC-Exos) have shown promising results in promoting wound healing by modulating immune responses, reducing inflammation, promoting angiogenesis, accelerating skin proliferation and re-epithelialization, and regulating collagen remodeling to inhibit scar proliferation [22]. Moreover, HUVEC-Exos are cost-effective and readily available. Various factors can influence the prognosis of diabetic trauma patients, and targeting a single etiology may not lead to the desired therapeutic outcomes. We aimed to address three essential factors—elevated oxidative stress levels, susceptibility to bacterial infection, and impaired cellular function—in diabetic wounds by utilizing the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel to promote diabetic wound healing. In this study, we designed a multifunctional hydrogel named ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA, which exhibits good biocompatibility, inhibits bacterial infection, and releases HUVEC-Exos to promote wound healing by reducing oxidative stress levels in diabetic wounds. Integrating ADM, Fe3+@PA complexes, and HUVEC-Exos synergistically enhances the wound healing properties of the hydrogel, offering a promising approach for accelerating diabetic wound repair.

When HUVECs reached 85–90 % confluence, they were cultured in an exosome-free medium. The supernatant was collected. After centrifugation (3,000 g × 25 min, and 13,000 g × 40 min) to eliminate dead cells, debris, and large microvesicles, exosomes were extracted using ultracentrifugation (120,000 g × 70 min). Identifying HUVEC-Exos was conducted through transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and western blot analysis [23].

sections.section: Preparation and characterization of ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel
sections.text: The raw materials including protocatechuic aldehyde (PA), ferric chloride hexahydrate (FeCl3-6H2O), acellular dermal matrix (ADM), light-cured gelatin (GelMA), and HUVEC-Exos were used to form hydrogels through ultrasonic cavitation and photo-crosslinking at room temperature. Specifically, a Fe3+@PA solution was prepared according to a previous study, mixed with ADM particles, and excess Fe3+@PA was removed through centrifugation. Then, GelMA solution containing HUVEC-Exos was added, and gel formation was achieved through ultrasonic shaking under 416 nm blue light [24]. The ADM particles were obtained from Jiangsu Youchuang, and GelMA was purchased from EFL (Jiangsu, China). The physicochemical properties and structures of the hydrogels were evaluated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and a rheometer. The degradation of the hydrogels was assessed using an enzymatic method with 2 U/mL collagenase-I. The degradation rate was calculated based on the weight loss of the hydrogels (degradation rate = (Wi - Wx)/Wi × 100 %, where Wi represents the initial weight of the dry sample, and Wx indicates the weight of the dry sample degraded on day x).

sections.section: Evaluation of biocompatibility, antioxidant, and antibacterial properties in vitro for ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel
sections.text: Cytotoxicity was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assays. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured with a microplate reader. The relative survival rate, defined as 100% in comparison to the control group, was calculated as Cell Viability = (As-Ab)/(Ac-Ab), with As representing the absorbance of different groups, Ac denoting the absorbance of the control group, and Ab signifying the absorbance of the blank.A leaching experiment was conducted using 10 mg of material soaked in 1 mL of DMEM containing 10% FBS for 24 hours to generate the leaching solution. Subsequently, the cells were exposed to this leaching solution for 24 hours (while the control group received treatment with a PBS solution). Following this treatment, the cells were fluorescently stained with LIVE/DEAD staining solution and then examined and photographed using a fluorescence microscope.To assess the hemocompatibility of the ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA (AFG). The collected red blood cells were purified and diluted to a 5% (v/v) concentration. This diluted RBC suspension was blended with the AFG, while ultrapure H2O served as a positive control and PBS as a negative control. Following a 4-hour incubation at 37°C, the mixture underwent centrifugation at 2000 rpm for 10 minutes. Subsequently, the supernatant was transferred and the absorbance at 540 nm was measured using a microplate reader.The DPPH method was employed to measure the scavenging ability of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by AFG hydrogel. Cell viability was assessed using a CCK-8 assay, while enzyme activity was measured using superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) kits. The antimicrobial ability of ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel was evaluated through colony formation assays and bacterial live-dead staining assays. For the antimicrobial ring assay, 100 μL of bacterial suspension (109 CFU/mL) was dropped on an agar plate and spread. Then, the sterilized samples were placed on the agar plate and incubated for 24 h at 37 °C. Finally, the inhibition zone around the hydrogel was analyzed.

The release of HUVEC-Exos from ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel was quantified using the microBCA assay for protein quantification. Hydrogels with or without 50 μg HUVEC-Exos were immersed in 1 mL PBS containing 2 U/mL collagenase-I, and the protein concentration in the liquid supernatant was measured. Exosome release (%) was calculated as (Ce - Ch) × 1 mL/50 μg × 100 %, where Ce represents the protein concentration in the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA supernatant and Ch indicates the protein concentration in the ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel supernatant. HUVEC-Exos were labeled with Dil and co-cultured with HUVECs. The internalization of HUVEC-Exos was observed using laser confocal microscopy. Red fluorescence was observed in the cytoplasm of HUVECs proving that HUVEC-Exos were internalized by HUVECs.

sections.section: In vitro proliferation and migration assays
sections.text: The proliferation of HaCaT and HUVECs was assessed using 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU, Beyotime, China) staining according to the manufacturer's instructions. HaCaT and HUVECs cells were planted in 96-well tissue culture plates. After culturing for 24 h, the cell medium was replaced and 5, 10 or 20 μg/mL of HUVEC-Exos or PBS was added. The migration function of HaCaT and HUVECs was evaluated through a Transwell assay. Cells were seeded in Transwell chambers (Corning, USA). Cell suspension was added to the top compartment and treated with PBS, 5, 10 or 20 μg/mL HUVEC-Exos. After incubation for 24 h, the chambers were removed and the cells migrating to the lower surface were stained with 0.1 % crystal violet. Data were expressed as an average of cells per field that migrated through micropores.

Animal experiments were conducted following the guidelines of the Animal Care Committee of Tongji Medical College. Type I diabetes was induced by intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (STZ, 50 mg/kg) for 5 consecutive days, blood glucose was monitored for 2 weeks thereafter. Mice with blood glucose level >16.7 mmol/L were considered diabetic and maintained for 4 weeks. The full-thickness round cutaneous wound was created on the diabetic mice (diameter: 10 mm). The diabetic mice were divided into five groups (n = 8): control group (100 μL PBS), AG group (100 μL ADM/GelMA), AEG group (100 μL ADM-Exos/GelMA), AFG group (100 μL ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA), and AEFG (100 μL ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA). The normal group mice were none-diabetic control group (n = 8). The procedure was performed under aseptic conditions. The wound area was captured on day 0, 5, 9, and 13. The wound area was measured and analyzed using Image J software. After two weeks, the surrounding tissue was dissected for further analysis. Re-epithelialization and collagen deposition were confirmed through H&E and Masson staining (n = 5). Immunofluorescence staining and immunohistochemical staining were conducted to analyze inflammatory responses, ROS levels, cell proliferation and angiogenesis in the wound area (n = 5).

All statistical data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism (version 8.0) and presented as means ± standard deviations (SD). All experiments were repeated at least three times. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's multiple comparisons test was applied for comparisons involving three or more groups. Statistical significance was accepted at P < 0.05 (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001).

Our hydrogel design aims to confer antioxidant and antimicrobial properties to the acellular dermal matrix (ADM) by preserving its natural three-dimensional extracellular matrix structure and the activity of internal bioactive factor while enabling exosome release for diabetic wound repair. We modified ADM with Fe3+@PA to achieve this and incorporated GelMA to create a double cross-linked network. The formation mechanism of the hydrogel is depicted in the Additional file, Fig. S1. The UV–Vis spectrum of the Fe3+@PA solution was recorded, revealing an absorption peak at approximately 440 nm, indicating successful coordination of Fe3+ with PA [25]. This coordination protects PA from autoxidation at high pH (Additional file, Fig. S2) [26]. The mechanical properties of the hydrogels were evaluated using rheological measurements. The relationship between the energy storage modulus (G′) and the loss modulus (G″) of the AFG20 hydrogel (20 mg/mL ADM in ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA) was investigated using a rheometer (Fig. 2a). The results consistently showed that the energy storage modulus of the hydrogel exceeded the loss modulus, indicating that the hydrogel possess sufficient mechanical strength. The gelation time of the hydrogel is a critical factor for their application as biomaterials. Test results demonstrated that the hydrogel exhibited fast gelation, allowing for rapid in-situ gelation within wounds (Fig. 2b, e). Hydrogel used as dressings are commonly acknowledged for their ability to absorb tissue exudate and maintain a moist environment, which facilitates wound healing. Consequently, we examined the water content and swelling rate of the hydrogel in pH 7.4 phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at 37 °C (Fig. 2c, f). After soaking the hydrogel in PBS until no further change in mass was observed, it was determined that the water content and swelling rate remained approximately 97 % and 3700 %, respectively. These findings indicate that the addition of ADM-Fe3+@PA particles did not significantly affect the hydrogels' water content and swelling rate. Furthermore, material degradability is a crucial feature for biomedical applications. To evaluate the degradation performance of the hydrogel, they were immersed in a PBS solution containing 2 U/mL collagenase-I and incubated under conditions simulating fluid biological environments. The degradation rate decreased with increasing concentrations of ADM-Fe3+@PA particles (Fig. 2d). Notably, the hydrogel containing 20 mg/mL ADM-Fe3+@PA particles exhibited a degradation rate exceeding 70 % within ten days, reaching the desired degradation rate. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was employed to examine the morphology of the hydrogel. The results revealed interconnected multilayer porous structures in the prepared hydrogel. Importantly, no significant differences were observed in the microscopic structures among the three groups of hydrogel, indicating that the addition of ADM or ADM-Fe3+@PA particles did not affect the hydrogels' fundamental structure and pore size (Fig. 2g).

sections.section: Biocompatibility and antioxidant properties of hydrogel
sections.text: Excellent biocompatibility is essential for the application of medical biomaterials. In wound healing, keratin-forming cells and endothelial cells play crucial roles in regenerating the epidermis and vascular networks, respectively. This study investigated the cytotoxicity of hydrogel containing ADM-Fe3+@PA particlesusing HaCaT cells and HUVECs. In cell viability assays, the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) (Fig. 3a, b, d, e) and cell live-dead staining (Fig. S3) was adapted. The CCK-8 assays revealed that the hydrogel maintained high cell viability, with approximately 95 % and 88 % viability after 24 and 48 h of co-incubation, respectively, for concentrations up to 30 mg/mL ADM-Fe3+@PA. Hemocompatibility evaluation demonstrated low hemolysis rates (HR) of 1.50 %, 1.61 %, 1.90 %, and 1.95 % for concentrations ranging from 10 to 40 μg/mL ADM-Fe3+@PA, meeting the ASTM standard for biological materials (HR <5 %)(Fig. 3c,f) [27]. These findings collectively confirm the excellent biocompatibility of the ADM-Fe3+@PA hydrogel. Excessive free radicals at the wound site can induce oxidative stress, leading to cytotoxicity and hindering wound healing [28,29]. It has been reported that MGO, a precursor substance of advanced glycosylation end products (AGE), is involved in diabetic cell damage through the induction of oxidative stress [30]. Therefore, the antioxidant properties of the hydrogel were assessed. We selected methylglyoxal (MGO) for inducing diabetic cell models. The survival rate of HUVECs was approximately 54 % when treated with 400 μmol/L of MGO, whereas the survival rate of HaCaT cells was approximately 66 % when exposed to 250 μmol/L of MGO. Consequently, subsequent experiments utilized MGO concentrations of 400 μmol/L for HUVECs diabetic models and 250 μmol/L for HaCaT diabetic models (Additional file, Fig. S4). Our study demonstrated that treatment with ADM-Fe3+@PA hydrogel extract restored the survival rate of HaCaT and HUVECs to over 85 % following MGO-induced damage (Fig. 3g and h). Generally, the activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione reductase (GSH-Px), crucial intracellular antioxidants, decreased in the presence of elevated oxidative stress induced by MGO. However, treatment with ADM-Fe3+@PA hydrogel extract restored SOD and GSH-Px activity to approximately 78 % and 87 % in both cell types, respectively (Fig. 3j and k) (Additional file, Fig. S5). The hydrogel extracts efficiently scavenged the stable free radical 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH-), suggesting their ability to scavenge extracellular ROS (Fig. 3i, l) [31]. Previous research has shown diabetic wounds exhibit significantly higher levels of local reactive oxygen species (ROS) than non-diabetic wounds [28]. This study confirmed that the ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel possesses potent ROS-scavenging capabilities through DPPH-radical scavenging assays. Furthermore, the ROS-scavenging ability of the hydrogel was independent of the concentration of ADM-Fe3+@PA. In conclude, we demonstrated that the ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel could effectively restore antioxidant enzyme activity, reduce the intracellular ROS level in cells and protect those cells against oxidative stress damage from MGO.

Diabetic wounds are particularly susceptible to bacterial infections, which poses challenges for effective wound healing. Additionally, the formation of bacterial biofilms hampers the exchange of substances within the wounds, further impeding the healing process. Therefore, diabetic wound dressings should possess antimicrobial properties. In this study, we evaluated the antimicrobial efficacy of ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel in vitro against E. coli and S. aureus. The results demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction in bacterial colony count with increasing concentrations of ADM-Fe3+@PA, indicating the good antimicrobial effectiveness of ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel (Fig. 4a and b) [32]. PI dye, which penetrates only dead bacteria with compromised structures and emits red fluorescence upon excitation, revealed a significantly higher percentage of red fluorescence in the ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA group compared to the control group. These findings indicated that ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel effectively killed both E. coli (78.2%) and S. aureus (75.4%) (Fig. 4c and d) [33]. Statistical analysis of the antimicrobial experiments indicated that the antibacterial efficacy of ADM-Fe3+@PA particles did not significantly increase beyond a concentration of 20 mg/mL, suggesting 20 mg/mL as the optimal antibacterial concentration. Moreover, a bacterial inhibition ring formation assay was performed. The resulting ring area devoid of bacterial growth indicated the strength of the antimicrobial activity. The ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel at a concentration of 20 mg/mL exhibited a substantial inhibitory effect on the growth of both E. coli and S. aureus, with the diameter of the inhibitory ring measuring approximately 79 % and 74.1 % of that in the positive control, respectively (Fig. 4e and f). These results further demonstrated the excellent antibacterial activity of 20 μg/mL ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel.

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed the bilayered and nearly circular morphology of HUVEC-Exos (Fig. 5a) [34]. Western blot analysis revealed the expression of the exosomal marker CD31 in HUVEC-Exos, while GM130 was not detected (Fig. 5b), confirming the successful isolation of HUVEC-Exos. To assess the release capability of HUVEC-Exos from ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel, daily exosome release was measured using the microBCA microprotein assay. Approximately 50 % of total exosomes were released within five days, indicating sustained release from the hydrogel (Additional file, Fig. S6). Co-incubation of HUVECs and hydrogel loaded with Dil-labeled exosomes demonstrated the uptake of HUVEC-Exos by HUVECs, as observed by the presence of red fluorescently labeled exosomes near the cell nucleus (Fig. 5c). The effects of HUVEC-Exos on the proliferation and migration functions of HUVECs and HaCaT cells were assessed using the EdU staining assay (Fig. 5d, e, Figs. S7a and b). and cell migration assay (Fig. 5f, g, Figs. S7c and d), respectively. HUVEC-Exos treatment significantly increased the proportion of proliferating cells and the number of migrating cells compared to the control group, showing concentration-dependent effects in both cell types. Furthermore, the restorative effect of HUVEC-Exos on MGO-induced impairment of diabetic cell functionality was investigated (Fig. 5h-k, Figs. S7e–h). While HUVEC-Exos treatment partially restored the proliferation and migration impairment caused by MGO, it could not wholly normalize the cell levels. Subsequently, the treatment effect of ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA on the functional impairment of diabetic cells were evaluated. Compared to the MGO group, treatment with ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA extract resulted in a higher proportion of proliferating cells and a more significant number of migrating cells (Fig. S8). These findings indicated that ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA hydrogel, in synergy with HUVEC-Exos, could effectively reverse the proliferation and migration impairment caused by diabetic cell injury.

sections.section: ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel accelerates diabetic wound healing in vivo
sections.text: In this study, diabetic mice were utilized to evaluate the wound-healing efficacy of a hydrogel formulation. The wound area was measured on days 0, 5, 9, and 13 after creating full-thickness wounds on the mice's dorsal region (Fig. 6a and b). The experimental groups included non-diabetic mice (Normal group), ADM/GelMA group (AG group), ADM-Fe3+@PA/GelMA group (AFG group), ADM-Exos/GelMA group (AEG group), ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA group (AFEG group), and GelMA group (Control group). All hydrogel groups exhibited accelerated diabetic wound repair compared to the Control group. Notably, the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel demonstrated the highest efficiency in promoting wound healing, approaching levels observed in the normal group. HE staining revealed the formation of dermal granulation tissue and migration of epidermal cells to the wound tissues during wound closure (Fig. 6c and d). The length of the granulation gap served as an indicator of wound healing, with the remaining hydrogel groups exhibiting enhanced wound repair compared to the Control group and the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel exhibiting the most significant effect. Additionally, Masson staining demonstrated superior collagen deposition and remodeling in the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA group, indicating improved tissue repair and regeneration (Fig. 6e and f). These findings suggest that ADM-Fe3+@PA and HUVEC-Exos synergistically promote diabetic wound healing in vivo.

To evaluate the impact of hydrogel on neovascularization and mature vessel formation in the wound tissues, we conducted immunostaining of wound tissue for CD31 and α-SMA. CD31 served as an indicator of neovascularization (Fig. 7a and b), while α-SMA acted as a marker for mature blood vessels (Fig. 7c and d) [35]. Remarkably, microvessel density was highest in the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA group, surpassing even the levels observed in the Normal group. Thus, ROS levels in the wound were measured based on DHE staining. The red fluorescence signal was dramatically reduced in the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA group compared to other groups, indicating the potential of the hydrogel to mitigate oxidative damage (Fig. 7e and f) [36,37]. To evaluate the inflammation levels in diabetic wounds, we performed an immunofluorescence staining analysis of IL-1β [38]. The results revealed a significant reduction in inflammation levels within the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA group (Fig. S9). The analysis of Ki67 staining demonstrated a notable increase in mitotic cells in the hydrogel-treated wounds compared to the control group, indicating the hydrogelcolud promote cell proliferation (Fig. S10). In brief, the results demonstrated that ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel could promote wound cell proliferation, efficiently diminishes the inflammatory response and oxidative stress, and thereby enhance angiogenesis and tissue regeneration.

In this study, we developed the ADM-Fe3+@PA-Exos/GelMA hydrogel system to accelerate diabetic wound healing by addressing multiple aspects of the healing process. The hydrogel effectively improved diabetic cell function, inhibited bacterial growth and promoted collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and maturation in diabetic wounds while reducing oxidative stress and inflammation. These findings represent a significant advancement in the application of ADM materials and offer new possibilities for the clinical translation of ADM in diabetic wound.
