title: Biosynthesis of a dual growth factors (GFs) functionalized silk sericin hydrogel to promote chronic wound healing in diabetic mice
abstract: Chronic non-healing wounds, such as diabetic foot, pressure sores and bedsores have seriously affected the life quality of patients worldwide. GFs provide a potential solution to promote chronic wound healing by promoting cell proliferation and differentiation. However, limited resource, high cost, and instability in vivo greatly hindered their clinical applications. In present study, two silk gland bioreactor silkworm stains were generated to successfully synthesize functional silk fibers incorporating high expressions of EGF and PDGF-BB. The two GFs functionalized silk raw materials were used to fabricate a dual GFs sericin hydrogel (E/P-SH) delivering system with tunable material performances for better cell adhesion and biocompatibility, sustainable release of the dual GFs to synergistically promote cell proliferation and migration, which realized the significant healing of chronic full-thickness skin wound in diabetic mice within 12 days with more organized collagen arrangement and better epithelialization degree by reducing inflammatory response and promoting vascularization. These findings demonstrated that the biosynthesized dual GFs-SH delivering system provides an opportunity to broaden the wide utility of GFs in clinical treatment of diabetic wound healing. Image 1 •Transgenic silkworm was engineered for the massive bio-synthesis of growth factors (GFs) functionalized silk fibers.•The GFs achieved a highly-efficient biosynthesis in the sericin layer of silk fiber.•The E/P-SH was fabricated with desirable mechanical, injectability, and sustained release of the GFs.•The E/P-SH synergistically promotes cell proliferation and migration, realizes the significant healing of chronic full-thickness skin wound in diabetic mice. Transgenic silkworm was engineered for the massive bio-synthesis of growth factors (GFs) functionalized silk fibers. The GFs achieved a highly-efficient biosynthesis in the sericin layer of silk fiber. The E/P-SH was fabricated with desirable mechanical, injectability, and sustained release of the GFs. The E/P-SH synergistically promotes cell proliferation and migration, realizes the significant healing of chronic full-thickness skin wound in diabetic mice.

sections.text: Nowadays, there are over 536.6 million people (10.5 %) with diabetes in the world between the ages of 20 and 79, and it is expected to rise to 783.2 million people (12.2 %) in 2045 [1]. Various complications caused by diabetes also seriously threaten the life length of patients [2]. About 25 % of diabetic patients are also affected by poor healing of diabetic wounds. Chronic non-healing wounds [3,4] caused by diabetic feet also seriously affect the quality of life of patients and greatly increase the family and social burden of patients [5]. Skin is a complex tissue and the largest organ in the body [6]. Wound healing is a coordinated, sequential biological process evolving homeostasis, inflammation, proliferation or tissue regeneration, and tissue remodeling. This complex mechanism is regulated by diverse cellular actors and biochemical signals that either promote tissue restoration or delay recovery through multifaceted interactions [7]. An ideal wound dressing should maintain a moist environment for the wound, prevent bacterial infestation, possess good biocompatibility, require a specific biological activity to promote the wound healing [8]. In this case, hydrogels would meet the requires as an ideal dressing due to their unique characteristics [9,10]. Besides, GFs which participate in the regulation of the proliferation, differentiation and development of many types of cells, play an important regulatory functions in the process of wound healing [11]. Among of which, EGF is a small molecule protein composed of 53 amino acids, which was first isolated from the mouse submandibular gland in the early 1960s, which can participate in the regulation of cell proliferation, migration and differentiation [12]. Previous studies have proved that EGF could effectively promote the healing of ulcers in diabetic groups through enhancing the epidermal tissue remodeling [13]. Meanwhile, PDGF-BB is a homodimeric protein formed by PDGF-B monomer protein, and it is also the most clearly characterized member of the PDGF family [14]. Previous studies also proved that PDGF-BB could promote cell proliferation, migration, differentiation and had a great contribution to the repair of diabetic chronic wounds healing by promoting vascularization [15,16]. In the past decades, several U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved GFs-gel drugs such as Regranex® (Becaplermin) [17], Plermingel®, Healace®, and GEM21S® have been developed for clinical treatment of chronic ulcers. However, poor stability, rapid diffusion, uncontrolled signaling, and side effects of the GFs-based therapies remains challenges. Therefore, more efforts are needed to conduct in-depth research on the source safety of growth factors, safe delivery and sustained release of growth factors to prolonged effect and reduce side effects, particularly, the synergetic effect and mechanism of dual or multiple growth factors in promoting diabetic wound healing [11,18]. Silk sericin, which accounts for about 25 % of the composition of Bombyx. mori silk, is currently emerged as a desirable biomaterial with fine mechanical property [19], biocompatibility [20], controllable biodegradation [21], and protection of the protein bioactivities [22,23]. Silk sericin could be fabricated into different material forms such as hydrogel [24,25], film [26], 3D scaffold [27,28], integrated AI electronics [29] for the wide applications in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine [[30], [31], [32], [33]]. Meanwhile, the middle silk gland (MSG) of silkworm, which synthesize and secrete a large amount of the silk sericin proteins [34], has shown great potential as an ideal bioreactors for synthesis of exogenous recombinant proteins [35]. In the past two decades, several expression systems on usages of the promoters from the encoding genes of silk proteins have been constructed to produce exogenous proteins in silk cocoons of the transgenic silkworms [35,36]. In addition, various strategies associated with the introduction of enhancer, transcription regulatory elements, usage of integrase to avoid “position effect” from the chromosome had greatly improved the expression efficiencies of these systems [[37], [38], [39], [40], [41]]. As results, many high-valuable recombinant proteins such as fluorescent proteins [42], human serum albumin [37,43], growth factors [[44], [45], [46], [47]], human lactoferrin [48], human superoxide dismutase [49], and glucose oxidase [50] achieved the successful expressions in the silk cocoons with predicted biological activities [37,39,43,[51], [52], [53], [54], [55]], suggesting the silk gland could be an useful bioreactor system to genetically functionalize the silk by incorporating the recombinant proteins in silk proteins [28,[56], [57], [58]], which could effectively promote the application of silk based biomaterials in the fields of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine [59]. The present study demonstrates the genetical engineering of a transgenic silkworm for synthesizing EGF and PDGF-BB silk fiber, which were subsequently used as raw materials to fabricate a sericin hydrogel based dual GFs delivering system (E/P-SH). Finally, the developed E/P-SH was successfully used to treat the chronic non-healing wounds in diabetic mice with significant therapeutic effects, and the therapeutic mechanisms were comprehensively explored (Scheme 1). The present study provides alternative for the treatment of non-healing wounds in clinical diabetes.Scheme 1The present study illustrates the genetical engineering of transgenic silkworms for synthesizing the EGF and PDGF-BB silk fibers, which were subsequently used as raw materials to fabricate a sericin hydrogel based dual GFs delivering system (E/P-SH). The developed E/P-SH was successfully used to treat the chronic non-healing wounds in diabetic mice within 12 days with significant therapeutic effects by reducing inflammatory response and promoting vascularization.Scheme 1

sections.section: Biological synthesis of the EGF and PDGF-BB silk fibers using the transgenic silkworm strains
sections.text: To realize the cost-effective and large-scale synthesis of the EGF silk fibers by transgenic silkworms, an engineered EGF (eEGF) was firstly designed by fusing a PlGF-2 motif [60] at C-terminus of amino acid sequence of human EGF mature peptide (GenBank: KAI2535564.1) for enhanced ECM binding efficiency. Then, the coding sequence of the eEGF was optimized based on the codon usage preference of silkworm, commercially synthesized (Genscript, Nanjing, China), and sub-cloned into a shuttle vector psL1180[hr3CQ-Ser1sp-DsRed-Ser1PA] by BamH I and NotI restriction enzyme sites to construct the vector psL1180[hr3CQ-Ser1sp-eEGF-Ser1PA], in which the entire expression cassette was cut by AscI and further cloned into the AscI site of the pBac[3 × P3DsRed; af] vector [61] to create the final transgenic expression vector pBac[3 × P3DsRed; hr3CQ-Ser1p-eEGF-Ser1PA], abbreviated as phSeEGFSer1. The ultrapure plasmids of phSeEGFSer1vector and pHSP70-PIG helper vector with continuous expression of piggyBac transposase [49] were extracted using the QIAGEN Plasmid Mini Kit with concentrations of ∼600 ng/μL and mixed together at a 1:1 M ratio. The mixed plasmids were then microinjected into dechorionated silkworm embryos within 1 h of egg-laying through microinjection using an Insect Embryo Auto-MicroInjector (IEAMJ, Chongqing, China), where the piggyBac transposon driven by the transiently expressed transposase would randomly insert the exogenous gene expression frame into the "ATCC" site of the silkworm genome. In order to screen out positive individuals that can be stably inherited, where positive transposition occurs in germ cells. The injected embryos were carefully incubated in an environment at 25 °C with 85 % relative humidity for hatch, the hatched larvae (G0 generation) were then artificially fed to moth stage, intervarietally crossed or backcrossed with wild type silkworm moth to obtain G1 generation silkworm eggs. On the 6th-7th day, the G1 silkworm eggs were exposed under a fluorescence stereomicroscope microscopy (Olympus, Japan) to select positive transgenic moths with 3 × P3DsRed expression in the eyes or nerves, which were named as SeEGF. Another transgenic silkworm stain termed as SePDGF-BB [25] was used for synthesizing ePDGF-BB silk fibers in this study.

sections.section: Expression analysis of the recombinant proteins in the transgenic silk fibers
sections.text: The SeEGF and SePDGF-BB silkworm strains were independently fed with mulberry leaves at large scale (∼100000 larvae per time) in an environment at 25 °C with 85 % relative humidity until spinning for harvesting the eEGF and the ePDGF-BB silk cocoons. The harvested silk cocoons were shattered into powder in a liquid nitrogen environment using a mill (A11 basic, IKA, Germany). Then, the major sericin proteins and exogenous proteins within the silk cocoon powders were subsequently extracted by extraction buffer (50 mM Tris-Cl, 8 M Urea, pH 7.4) at extract ratios of 2.5 % (w/v) cocoon shell, heated in an 85 °C water bath with magnetic stirrer for 30 min. The supernatant was then collected after centrifugation at 12000 rpm, 4 °C, for 10 min. The wild type (WT) silk cocoon extract was used as negative control. The commercially purchased EGF and PDGF-BB recombinant protein standards were used as positive control. Then, the different extracted protein samples and controls were subjected to 12 % SDS-PAGE electrophoresis, stained by Coomassie brilliant blue or transferred to PVDF membranes for Western blot (WB) analysis, followed by the immune reactions using the anti-EGF antibody (Abcam, USA) or the anti-PDGF-BB antibody (Abcam, USA), and the HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody (Beyotime, China), and visualization using ECL (Amersham Biosciences, USA). The images of the WB were recorded by a Chemiscope Series (Clinx Science Instruments). The contents of the eEGF and ePDGF-BB in the silk fibers were quantified by densitometrically comparing the intensity of recombinant proteins on the immunoblot to those of standards with known concentrations using Image J software (http://rsb.info.nih.gov/ij/) according to our previous reports [53,62].

sections.section: Fabrication of sericin hydrogels with desired material performance and customized growth factors
sections.text: The concentration of silk sericin for fabrication of the sericin hydrogel with appropriate material performance to better meet the demand of the non-healing wounds was firstly explored. The natural sericin proteins extracted from the WT silk cocoons at extract ratios of 1 %–6 % (w/v) were prepared following the above extraction method. Then, the sericin supernatants with different concentrations were placed in to a cellulose dialysis bag (MWCO 3500 Da, Spectrum Laboratory, Inc., USA) and dialyzed against deionized water at 4 °C for 3 days with at least 6 changes of the deionized water to thoroughly remove urea and salts [57]. After the dialysis, the supernatants were either remained in the dialysis bag or poured into a specific mold and placed in a 4 °C environment for a continuous 2–3 days to induce gelation of the silk sericins. The obtained sericin hydrogels were then processed into models of different shapes for further usages. To extract bioactive eEGF from the silk fibers, the eEGF silk powder was dissolved (6 %, w/v) in another extraction solution (50 mM Tris-Cl, 2 M Urea, pH7.4), stirred on ice bath for 6 h for extraction. To extract bioactive ePDGF-BB from the silk fibers, the ePDGF-BB silk powders was dissolved (6 %, w/v) in another extraction solution (50 mM Tris-Cl, 4 M Urea, pH7.4), stirred at room temperature for 45 min for extraction. After the thorough extractions, the eEGF and the ePDGF-BB supernatants were independently recovered by centrifuge at 12000 rpm for 30 min at 4 °C and further concentrated using an ultrafiltration tube (Millipore, USA). The contents of the eEGF or ePDGF-BB in the supernatants were further calculated according to the above method. To fabricate the sericin hydrogels with specific concentration of the customized growth factors, the eEGF and the ePDGF-BB extracts were either mixed with the PBS or each other in equal volume, and further mixed with the equal volume of the silk sericin extract prepared by a 5 % extract ratio to create four types of stock solutions: WT-sericin solution, EGF-sericin solution, PDGF-sericin solution, and EGF/PDGF-sericin solution, respectively. These four stock solutions were then subjected to dialysis to remove the urea and salts, and induce the gelation of silk sericin following the above-described method. The obtained four types of sericin hydrogels: WT-sericin hydrogel (WT-SH), the EGF-sericin hydrogel (EGF-SH), the PDGF-sericin hydrogel (PDGF-SH), and the EGF/PDGF-sericin hydrogel (E/P-SH) were then processed into models of different shapes for further usages.

The different dry cocoon silk fibers or the lyophilized hydrogels were fixed in the center of the specimen holder, and placed in a sputter coater (JEOL, NeoCoater MP-19020NCTR, Japan) to gold-coat the surface of the sample. Subsequently, scanning electron microscopy (Hitachi SU3500, Japan) was used to observe and photograph the hydrogel surfaces at an operating voltage of 5.0 kV. Three observations at different positions were photographed for each sample. The diameters of different cocoon silk fibers or pore sizes of each hydrogel were calculated on the SEM images using the Image J software (http://rsb.info.nih.gov/ij/).

The tested sericin hydrogel samples were freeze-dried, weighed and recorded as W1, and placed in ddH2O of known volume V1. After the material is fully absorbed water for 1h, the total volume is recorded as V2 (volume of material and water), and the mass of the material is weighed and recorded as W2. The volume of the remaining ddH2O is denoted as V3, and the porosity and water absorption of the material are calculated according to the following formula:Porosity(%)=v1−v3v2−v3×100%Wateruptake(%)=W2−W1W2×100%

The lyophilized hydrogel was weighted and marked as Wd, then the lyophilized hydrogels were immersed in PBS. At the determine time, the swollen hydrogels were taken out and weighed, marked as Ws. The swelling ratios of sericin hydrogel was calculated as follows:Swelling (%) = (Ws-Wd)/Wd × 100

The rheological measurement was performed on rheometer (Thermo Fisher, USA) under continuous flow mode using a parallel plate (60 mm) under a stable air pressure of 30 psi. The viscosity of each hydrogel was recorded with the change of shear rate (0–8 s−1) at 25 °C.

FTIR analysis was conducted following the procedure as described by a previous report with slight modification [22]. Briefly, the lyophilized sericin hydrogels were analyzed by INVENIO instrument (BRUKER, Germany) over a spectral region of 4000-800 cm−1 in ATR mode at a resolution of 4 cm−1 with 35 scans. The obtained spectrums in the wavelength range 1000 cm−1-1800 cm−1 were analyzed using OMNIC 9 software (Thermo Scientific). Amide I peak-splitting method by Peak-Fit v4.12 software was used to analyze the secondary structure of hydrogels, in which the spectral range of 1615–1630 cm−1 and 1695-1705 cm−1, 1650-1660 cm−1, 1631-1655 cm−1 and 1660-1695 cm−1 represents β-sheet, α-helix, random coil, and β-turn, respectively [63]. Each spectrum represented the mean of separate deconvolutions for 9 separate tests for each sample. Statistical analysis of the data was performed using the software Origin2021.

HaCaT cell line (Human immortalized epidermal cells, bio-73031, Biobw, China), HFF-1 cell lines (Human epidermal fibroblasts, bio-68174, Biobw, China), Raw264.7 (TIB-71, ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA), and HEUVC (Human endothelial cell, PCS-100-013, ATCC, USA) were used in this study. After cell resuscitation at 37 °C, the cells were cultured in a 37 °C cell incubator containing 5 % CO2 using 10 % Gibco serum and Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) with high-sugar.

sections.section: Cell attachment on different fabricated sericin hydrogels
sections.text: The tested hydrogels were directly fabricated in the 96-well cell culture dishes by adding 20 μL of the different liquid sericin extracts in to each well, placing at 4 °C for 2–3 days to induce the sericin gelation, washing by PBS to completely remove the urea and salts, sterilizing by UV radiation for at least 30 min, and conditioning with the DMEM medium for 4 h. HaCaT cell at ∼96 % confluence was suspended in fresh complete culture media with 10 % FBS, and seeded on the surface of the different sericin hydrogels at a density of 1 × 104 cells per well. Meanwhile, the same number of cells were directly seeded onto the surface of 96-well TCP cell culture dishes as positive controls. Six hours after seeding, the culture media was completely removed from the wells and the well were then gently washed twice with PBS (pH 7.4). The number of the cells adhering on the hydrogels or TCP dishes were calculated by the cell counting kit-8 (C0037, Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Briefly, 10 μL of the CCK-8 solution was added to each well of the 96-well plate seeding with cells, incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Thereafter, equal amounts of the supernatants in the wells from the different groups were transferred into fresh wells and subjected to absorbance measurements at 450 nm using a Glomax Multi Detection System (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). The measurements were performed in triplicate and repeated independently three times.

Cell viabilities of HaCaT cell seeding on the surface of different sericin hydrogels for different times were evaluated by a LIVE/DEAD® viability/cytotoxicity kit (Molecular Probes™, Eugene, OR, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol and imaged using a fluorescence microscope (EVOS FL Auto, Life Technologies, USA). Live cells stained by Calcein-AM dye produced the green fluorescence (ex/em ∼495 nm/∼515 nm), while dead cells stained by EthD-1 dye emitted the red fluorescence (ex/em ∼495 nm/∼635 nm).

sections.section: Release behavior of EGF and PDGF-BB from the fabricated sericin hydrogels
sections.text: Each 1 g of the fabricated WT-SH, EGF-SH, PDGF-SH and E/P-SH hydrogels were weighed, and immersed into 1.5 mL tube with 1 mL PBS and placed in a 37 °C incubator. Three parallel experiments were set for each group. At each time points, all PBS in the tube were collected and stored in a −40 °C refrigerator, the remained hydrogels in the tube were weighed, and another fresh 1 mL of PBS was added into the tube. After 28 days, ELISA kit (Thermo fisher, USA) was used to detect the contents of EGF and PDGF-BB in the collected PBS solutions.

1 × 104 cells of macrophages Raw264.7 (TIB-71, ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) with ∼90 % confluence was seeded on the surfaces of the different hydrogels formed directly in the 96-well plate. Meanwhile, equal amounts of RAW264.7 cells were seeded directly into the wells of the 96-well plate with or without lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) at doses of 5 μg/mL as positive or negative controls, respectively. Cells were then cultivated in DMEM with 10 % (w/v) FBS at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. At days 1 post cell seeding, the cytoskeleton and nucleus were stained with ghost pen cyclic peptide and DAPI, and imaged using a fluorescence microscope (EVOS FL Auto, Life Technologies, USA). Meanwhile, the cell medium supernatants were collected for quantitation of early indicators of inflammation, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) using an TNF alpha Mouse ELISA Kit (MM-0132M2, MEIMIAN, China) and IL-1β Mouse Uncoated ELISA Kit (MM-0040M2, MEIMIAN, China).

sections.section: Cell proliferation assays by CCK-8 and EdU incorporation
sections.text: HaCaT cells with ∼90 % confluence suspended in a DMEM medium with 0.5 % FBS, were seeded in 24-well cell plate with transwell device (Thermo Fisher, USA), and starved for 12 h before sample treatments. Thereafter, 10 μL of different sericin hydrogels were added into transwell device, the equivalent commercial EGF and PDGF-BB standards in solution forms were added as positive controls. The cell plates were then cultured in cell incubators for 24 h. Subsequently, cell viability treated by different samples was evaluated using cell counting kit-8 (C0037, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) according to the above method. Cell proliferation was measured using a Click-iT® EdU Imaging Kits (Thermo Fisher, USA). Briefly, cells treated by the different hydrogel samples for 24 h were labeled by the EdU (5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine, a nucleoside analog of thymidine) at a concentration of 2 μM at 37 °C overnight, fixed immediately by 3.7 % formaldehyde, permeabilized by 0.5 % Triton® X-100, followed by EdU detection by Alexa Fluor® 555 azide and cell nucleus dye, and imaged by fluorescence microscopy (EVOS FL Auto, Life Technologies, USA) for proliferating cells (Ex/Em: 555/565 nm) and cell nuclei (Ex/Em: 358/461 nm).

HFF-1 cells with ∼90 % confluence was suspended in DMEM medium with 0.5 % FBS, seeded in 24-well cell plate with transwell device (Thermo Fisher, USA), starved for 12 h, wounded by scratching the surface of HFF-1 cells with a sterile pipet tip, and washed with PBS to remove cellular debris. Wounded cells were then treated without or with mitomycin C (1 μg/mL) for 1 h, washed with PBS, then co-cultivated with the transwell containing different sericin hydrogels for 9 h or 18 h. Initial wounding and the movement of the cells in the scratched area were photographically monitored using a microscope (Nikon). Quantitative analysis of cell number in the scratched area was calculated using Image J software.

20 μL of Matrigel (Sperikon, SP00604-0005, China) with low growth factors was added to a pre-frozen 24-well plate, incubated at 37 °C for 30 min in a cell culture incubator to allow the basement membrane to form a gel. Subsequently, ∼1 × 105 of HUVECs cells within 3rd to 5th generations and with 80 % confluent was mixed with 10 μL of different sericin hydrogels, and then seeded in to each well of the 24-well plate with Matrigel. The HUVECs were further incubated in an incubator and photographed for vascularization at 8 h post cell seeding. Quantitative analysis of parameters evaluating capillary formation, including the number of junctions, number of segments, total length of segments, and number of branches, were conducted using an angiogenesis analyzer (Angiogenesis Analyzer for Image J).

sections.section: Anti-inflammatory analysis by monitoring macrophage polarization of macrophages
sections.text: Raw 264.7 macrophages were cultured in 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 104 cells/well in RPMI 1640 medium with 10 % FBS for 12 h. After cell adherence, the cells were treated by 1 μg/mL LPS for 6 h to induce cellular inflammation. Then, the cell mediums in each well were replaced with fresh mediums with or without the four fabricated sericin hydrogels for additional 24 h cultivation. The cells were then independently immunoblotted with an iNOS (ABclonal, China) antibody and a CD206 (ABclonal, China) antibody, further immunoblotted with a Cy3-labeled goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) (Beyotime, China) or an Alexa Fluor 488-labeled goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) (Beyotime, China). DAPI was used to indicate the nuclei, and the cells were observed and photographed under fluorescence microscopy.

Animal procedures complied with ethical standards were approved by the Animal Management and Use Committee of Southwest University. A 5 mL aliquot of mouse blood from the healthy C57BL/6J mouse anticoagulated with 0.2 mM of EDTA was centrifuged under 3500 rpm at 4 °C for 5 min to collect the erythrocyte precipitates, which were further diluted by 10 times in saline solution. 1 g of different sericin hydrogels were weighed, immersed in 0.9 % saline for 24 h to collect the leachates, further filtered with a 0.22 μm filter head and placed in a refrigerator at 4 °C for later use. The commercial EGF and PDGF standard proteins were dissolved in 0.9 % saline as controls. Subsequently, the different samples were each added into the saline solution with erythrocyte. Meanwhile, the ultra-pure water was set as a positive control, and the saline was set as a negative control, and a blank control without erythrocyte solution was also set (each group had three parallels). All groups were photographed and the OD values at 580 nm were measured. The hemolysis rate was calculated by the formula:Hemolysis rate = (Sample OD value - Negative OD value) / (Positive OD value - Negative OD value) × 100 %.

sections.section: Full-thickness wound model in diabetic mouse
sections.text: The SPF-grade C57BL/6J male mice at six-week-old were acclimated for 7 days, then intraperitoneally injected with streptozotocin (STZ) at a dose of 180 mg/kg. The fasting blood glucose level was measured 72 h after the injection. Mice with blood glucose levels exceeding 11.1 mmol/L were considered to be a successful diabetic mouse model. The diabetic mice were then anesthetized, and a circular full-thickness skin excision wound with a diameter of 8 mm was created on their backs using an 8-mm hole punch according to previous reports [64,65]. Subsequently, the diabetic mice were randomly assigned in to six groups (n = 6): Null (Saline), WT-SH, EGF-SH, PDGF-BB-SH, E/P-SH and EGF-PDGF-STD (E/P-STD), respectively. Subsequently, the wounds of the diabetic mice were covered by the corresponding sericin hydrogels with diameter of 10 mm and thickness of 2 mm or the equivalent E/P-STD, bandaged with breathable gauze. On 0, 3rd, 7th, and 12th day post treatment, the wound sizes of different groups were monitored, digitally photographed and the wound areas on 7th and 12th day were calculated using Image J software. The wound area was calculated using the formula At/A0 (where A0 represents the initial area and At represents the area at different time points thereafter). The wound width was measured by measuring the average diameter in multiple directions on the digital photographs of the wounds healed on day 12 from different groups using ImageJ software.

The mouse wound samples from different groups were embedded in paraffin. Then, longitudinal sections of the mouse wounds at 12th day of treatments by different hydrogels were made into a 4 μm thickness on a paraffin microtomy. After routine deparaffinization and dehydration, the tissue sections were stained with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) for 5 min, differentiated in a 1:1 mixture of alcohol and hydrochloric acid for 5 s, followed by water washing. Then, the sections were counterstained with eosin for 5 min, washed with water, and then subjected to routine dehydration and clearing. Finally, the sections were mounted with neutral resin and observed and photographed using an optical microscope (MDS4, Evident, China).

After routine deparaffinization and rehydration, the sections of the mouse wound at 12th day of treatments by different hydrogels were stained by 1 % acid fuchsin for 10 min, followed by three washes with 1 % acetic acid and rinsing with 1 % phosphomolybdic acid. Subsequently, the sections were stained by 1 % brilliant green for 8 min, followed by three washes using 1 % phosphomolybdic acid and three washes using 1 % acetic acid. After dehydration and clearing, the sections were mounted with neutral resin. Optical microscopy was used for observation and photography. Furthermore, Image J software was employed to measure the percentage of total tissue area occupied by bone content in each image. Three samples were selected from each group.

Mouse skin tissues sections from the center of the wound area at 12th day of treatments by different hydrogels were deparaffinized, rehydrated, incubated with H2O2 for 10 min, incubated with an anti-CD206 antibody (Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA) overnight at 4 °C to reflect the anti-inflammation by analysis of macrophage polarization, or an anti-CD31 (Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA) to evaluate the vascularization in the wound by analysis of angiogenesis [10], washed three times by PBS, and visualized by a phycoerythrin-conjugated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA). Nuclei were stained with 40,6-dia midino-2-phenylindole (Sigma-Aldrich). Images were acquired on an inverted fluorescence microscope (EVOS FL Auto, Life Technologies, USA).

Data are indicated as mean ± S.D. (standard deviation) for at least n = 3. Statistical analyses were calculated by Student's t-test. N.S. was considered not significant, ∗p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant, ∗∗p < 0.01 was considered highly significant, ∗∗∗p < 0.001 was considered extremely significant and ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001 was considered very extremely significant.

sections.section: Design and fabrication of sericin hydrogels to meet the demand of the diabetic non-healing wound
sections.text: A hydrogel system desirable for the diabetic non-healing wound should provide moisture retention to the wound area, suitable mechanical properties, good biocompatibility, swelling behavior and ideal surface structure and components for cell adhesion, which are critical to promote keratinocyte migration, collagen formation, angiogenesis, and reduced scar formation [66,67]. For this purpose, the liquid silk sericins were firstly extracted from the wild type silk fibers with the extraction ratios of 1.0 %, 1.5 %, 2.0 %, 2.5 %, 3.0 %, 4.0 %, 5.0 % and 6.0 % (w/v), respectively. These different sericin feedstocks were subjected for inducting the sericin gelation. The results showed that the sericin liquids with extraction ratios above 1.5 % could successfully form the visible sericin hydrogels with good mechanical properties which could maintain the structural integrity of the material during processing (Fig. 1A). SEM showed that the sericin hydrogels derived from different extraction ratios exhibiting the typical internally connected porous structure (Fig. 1B), in which the porosity and the pore size of the sericin hydrogel became denser and smaller with the increase of extraction ratios (Fig. 1C and D). Remarkably, the pore size of the sericin hydrogel with the extraction ratio from 3 % to 5 % ranged from 160 to 190 μm which could meet the requirements as fine wound dressing to support cell adhesion and growth [67]. The sericin hydrogels from different extraction ratios showed good swelling behaviors of 96.3 % ± 0.9 % (Fig. 1E). Cell adhesion assay showed that considerable HaCaT cells could efficiently adhere, spread out and form the pseudopods on the surface of the sericin hydrogels fabricated from different extraction ratios within 4 h post cell seeding, which are comparable with the HaCaT cells seeded on the surface of the commercial TCP (Fig. 1F and G), indicating that the good surface structure of sericin hydrogels for cell adhesion. Furthermore, rheological mechanics of the different sericin hydrogels were analyzed. The energy storage modulus G′ represents the amount of energy stored by the materials, reflecting the solid properties of the materials. The loss modulus G″ represents the amount of energy lost, reflecting the liquid properties of the materials. When G’ > G″, the material is mainly elastic deformation and behaves as a solid state, when G’ < G″, the material is mainly viscous deformation and behaves as a liquid state. Viscosity measurement assay showed that the viscosity of all the sericin hydrogels decreased with the increase of shear rate. Meanwhile, the viscosity of the sericin hydrogels became higher with the increasing of the sericin extraction ratios (Fig. 1H). Initially, the sericin hydrogels with extraction ratios from 6 % to 1.5 % showed typical solid characteristics and higher energy storage modulus G '. However, their solid states collapsed into a liquid state with the increasing of the shearing strain. Attractively, the curves of the energy storage modulus and the loss modulus of the sericin hydrogels from the 6 % and 5 % extraction ratios almost overlapped, indicating that there was no obvious difference in the solid properties of the two hydrogels, and both have excellent stability (Fig. 1I). Therefore, the silk sericin hydrogel fabricated using a 5 % (w/v) extraction ratio was more suitable for the wound healing due to its stable solid property, easy processing, ideal pore size of 163.3 ± 8.3 μm, good swelling behavior and cell adhesion properties.Fig. 1Design and fabrication of sericin hydrogels with tunable material performances to meet the demand of diabetic non-healing wound. (A) Digital photographs of the silk sericin hydrogels fabricated from different extraction bath ratios, right inset represents the good mechanical properties of the silk sericin hydrogel (5 % extraction ratio) which maintained good structural integrity of material. Scale bar is 1 cm. (B) SEM images of freeze-dried sericin hydrogel materials fabricated using different extraction ratios. Scale bar is 200 μm. (C), (D) and (E) represents the porosity, pore size, and swelling behavior of the lyophilized sericin hydrogels fabricated using different extraction ratios, respectively. (F) Optical microscope images of the cell adhesion on the surfaces of different fabricated sericin hydrogel for 4 h. Scale bar is 200 μm. (G) CCK-8 assay of the cell adhesion on the different hydrogel surfaces after 4 h. Analysis of viscoelasticity (H) and amplitude scanning (I) of silk sericin hydrogels with different extraction ratios. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (n = 3).Fig. 1

sections.section: Generation of transgenic silkworm strains for cost effective synthesis of the EGF and the PDGF-BB silk fibers
sections.text: To realize large-scale and cost-effective production of growth factor functionalized silk fibers, transgenic vectors for bio-synthesizing the EGF and the PDGF-BB were constructed (Fig. 2A–C), utilizing our previously constructed silk sericin expression system [38]. These vectors were then micro-injected into the non-diapause silkworm embryos for intergenerationally screening transgenic silkworm individuals with expression of 3 × P3DsRed genetical screening marker (Fig. 2B–D). As results, two stable transgenic silkworm stains SeEGF and SePDGF-BB synthesizing these growth factors simultaneously with synthesis and secretion of the silk proteins were generated. SDS-Page and Western blot analysis showed that the corresponding EGF and PDGF-BB recombinant protein bands were successfully identified in the respective cocoon silk extracts (Fig. 2E–G). Grayscale comparison with the commercially purchased EGF and PDGF-BB standards based on the Western blot analysis determined that 1 g of the two transgenic cocoon silk contained ∼0.32 mg of EGF recombinant protein and ∼0.24 mg of PDGF recombinant protein, respectively (Fig. 2F–H). SEM analysis showed that the raw cocoon silks from the EGF and the PDGF-BB transgenic silkworms exhibited a similar micro-structure morphology to that of the WT silkworm, with two silk threads glued together by sericin and diameters of ∼15.33 μm for the WT cocoon silk, ∼14.81 μm for the EGF cocoon silk, and ∼13.92 μm for the PDGF-BB cocoon silk, respectively (Fig. 2I).Fig. 2Generation of transgenic silkworm strains for cost effective synthesis of the EGF and the PDGF-BB silk fibers. (A) Schematic of transgenic vector for construction of transgenic EGF silkworm. 3 × P3DsRed represents the genetic marker to screen transgenic silkworms. hr3CQ represents an enhancer from BmNPV to improve the transcriptional activity of the promoter. Ser1P represents the basal promoter region of the Sericin-1 (Ser1) gene. Ser1PA each represents the transcriptional terminal signal isolated from the sericin-1 gene. ITR represents the sequences of the piggyBac left and right arms mediating the integration of transgene into the silkworm genome. (B) Images of the G1 eggs of positive transgenic PDGF-BB silkworm individuals exposed under white light, red fluorescence and EGFP fluorescence, respectively. Scale bar is 200 μm. (E) SDS-Page and western blotting of the EGF expression in the silk fibers of the transgenic silkworm. Black triangle indicates the EGF recombinant protein. (F) Quantitative analysis of the EGF recombinant proteins in the silk fibers through gray-scale comparison of western blotting with commercial EGF standard. Black triangle indicates the EGF recombinant protein. Hollow triangle indicates the commercial EGF protein. (G) SDS-Page and western blotting of the PDGF-BB expression in the silk fibers of the transgenic silkworm. Black triangle indicates the PDGF-BB recombinant protein. (H) Quantitative analysis of the PDGF-BB proteins in the silk fibers through gray-scale comparison of western blotting with commercial PDGF-BB standard. Scale bars are 200 μm for the above images and 50 μm for the below images, respectively. (J) Calculation and comparison of the diameters of the different raw silk fibers. sections.section: Physicochemical characterization of functional GFs sericin hydrogels
sections.text: A processing flow chart was designed to fabricate the functional GFs sericin hydrogels incorporated with single growth factor or dual growth factors using the EGF cocoon silks and the PDGF-BB cocoon silks as raw materials in 3–4 days (Fig. 3A). Firstly, the EGF and the PDGF-BB with bio-activities and sufficient amounts were extracted from their cocoon silks using buffers with lower concentrations of urea (2 M for EGF extraction and 4 M urea for PDGF-BB extraction) and lower temperatures (4 °C for EGF extraction and 25 °C for PDGF-BB extraction) to avoid the deactivation of the GFs during extraction. The concentrations of obtained GFs extracts were estimated to be ∼3.25 μg/mL for the EGF and ∼2.35 μg/mL for the PDGF-BB, respectively. Then, the undissolved cocoon silks were then subjected for the silk sericin extraction using 8 M urea at 85 °C. Finally, the sericin solution extracted by a 5 % (w/v) extraction ratio was mixed with required GF extracts at 1:1 ratio (v:v), dialyzed against deionized water at 4 °C for sericin gelation. Four types of active sericin hydrogels, named as WT-SH, EGF-SH, PDGF-SH, and E/P-SH were successfully fabricated with characteristics of good transparency and easy processing (Fig. 3B). The dosages of the EGF and the PDGF-BB in the fabricated sericin hydrogels were estimated to be ∼1.63 μg/g and ∼1.18 μg/g, respectively, which were in the dosage range that has been reported to be effective in clinical application [13]. It is worth mentioning that the doses of GFs in the sericin hydrogel are arbitrarily tunable for the clinical trial demands by concentrating or diluting the GFs crude extracts. SEM analysis showed that freezing-driedd hydrogels revealing a porous and internally connected structure (Fig. 3C). The pore sizes were estimated to be 173.82 ± 18.99, 130.65 ± 12.07, 128.85 ± 17.15, 94.57 ± 12.01 for the WT-SH, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, and the E/P-SH, respectively, which fit the requirement as fine wound dressing to support cell adhesion and growth [67]. The smaller pore sizes of the GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels might probably be caused by the addition of GFs in sericin solution which induced weak interaction between the sericin pI of sericin is ∼4.0) and the two GFs (pI of eEGF is 9.34 and pI of ePDGF-BB is 10.33) due to ionic forces, which enhanced the structural stability of GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels and eventually lead to small pore size of hydrogels. In vitro degradation curves of the different hydrogels in PBS solution showed the obvious biodegradable characteristics and the total degradation of ∼60 % within 28 days. Meanwhile, there was no significant difference in the degradation rate between the four types of sericin hydrogels (Fig. 3D). The degradation characteristics of sericin hydrogel were consistent with previous reports [24,25,68]. The release behavior of GFs from the sericin hydrogels was analyzed and showed a sustained release pattern (Fig. 3E and F). The cumulative total amounts of the released EGF were approximately 7.4 ng/g from the EGF-SH and 19.8 ng/g from the E/P-SH within 28 days, respectively (Fig. 3E). The cumulative total amounts of the released PDGF were approximately 49.8 ng/g from the PDGF-SH and 117.6 n/g from the E/P-SH within 28 days, respectively (Fig. 3F). The release rates of the EGF from the EGF-SH and the E/P-SH were estimated to be ∼0.45 % and ∼1.21 % within 28 days, respectively. Meanwhile, the release rates of the PDGF-BB from the PDGF-SH and the E/P-SH were estimated to be ∼4.22 % and ∼9.97 % within 28 days, respectively. These results suggested that only a small portion of the GFs were released from the sericin hydrogels, while the vast majority of the GFs remained in the sericin hydrogels. Under this circumstance, the sericin hydrogel together with the loaded GFs would be removed once the wound healing completes, which could effectively prevent the excessive cell proliferation caused by the massive release of growth factors, thereby avoiding other potential risks. Therefore, the slow degradation and slowly sustained release ability of hydrogel was conducive to the subsequent in-situ healing of wound tissue. FTIR characterization of the four sericin hydrogels showed three similar characteristic peaks which represented the amide I (C=O stretching vibrations), the amide II (N-H bending), and the amide III (C-N stretching vibrations) appeared at 1590-1699 cm−1, 1480-1570 cm−1, and 1200-1310 cm−1, respectively (Fig. 3G) [69,70]. Further peak splits of the amide I band region showed that five obvious absorption peaks each representing β-sheet (1610–1625 and 1696-1704 cm−1), random coil (1640-1660 cm−1), α-helix (1650-1660 cm−1), and β-turn (1660-1695 cm−1) were observed in the four fabricated sericin hydrogels (Fig. 3H–K), in which the β-sheet secondary structure was dominated by ∼43.08 % for the WT-SH, ∼43.53 for the EGF-SH, ∼47.73 % for the PDGF-SH, and ∼50.88 % for the E/P-SH, respectively, respectively (Fig. 3L). These results suggested a dense network of intermolecular hydrogen bonds formed in the four types of sericin hydrogels, which contributed to material stability.Fig. 3Physicochemical characterization of functional GFs sericin hydrogels. (A) Preparation process (∼3–4 days) of GFs sericin hydrogel with bioactivity, dose and combination adjustability. (B) Digital photos of the prepared GFs sericin hydrogel material. Scale bar: 1 cm. (C) SEM analysis of the four freeze-dried sericin hydrogel materials. Scale bar: 200 μm. (D) In vitro degradation curves of the four sericin hydrogel materials within 28 days. (E) Release behavior of the EGF from the EGF-SH and the E/P-SH within 28 days. (F) Release behavior of PDGF-BB from the PDGF-SH and the E/P-SH within 28 days. (G) FTIR absorbance curves of the four fabricated sericin hydrogels scanned from 1100 cm−1 to 2000 cm−1. (H–K) each represent the FTIR absorption spectrum of the amide I peak for the WT-SH (H), EGF-SH (I), PDGF-SH (J), and E/P-SH (K), respectively. Wavelength numbers of 1615–1630 cm−1 and 1695-1705 cm−1 as β-sheet structure; 1631-1655 cm−1 as random-coil structure; 1650-1660 cm−1 as α-helix bands; and 1660-1695 cm−1 as β-turn. (L) Chart summarizing the contents of secondary structure of the four types of sericin hydrogels in amide I bands by FTIR.Fig. 3

sections.section: The GFs sericin hydrogels exhibited excellent cell adhesion, biocompatibility and caused no cellular inflammatory
sections.text: Cell adhesive performances of the four fabricated sericin hydrogels were evaluated by seeding the HaCaT cells on the surfaces of the hydrogels for duration of 4 h, the results showed that the cells effectively adhered on the hydrogel surface and rapidly formed pseudopods (Fig. 4A), suggesting the good adhesive performances of the four fabricated hydrogels. An enhanced CCK-8 assay further confirmed cell numbers by measuring absorbance at 450 nm. No significant difference in cell adhesion was observed between hydrogels with different growth factors, consistent with commercial TCP plates (Fig. 4C). This indicated that the four sericin hydrogels were comparable to commercial TCP plates in promoting cell adhesion. HaCaT cells seeding on the hydrogel surface for 24 h co-cultivation was stained with the Live & Dead kit, in which the green signal indicated the living cells, while the red signal indicated the dead cells. The result showed the dominated green signal indicated that living cells were pronounced than the dead cells, indicating the fabricated hydrogels had none cytotoxicity. Attractively, the HaCaT cells seeding on the sericin hydrogels with growth factors exhibited better growth conditions comparing to these seeding on the WT-SH and TCP (Fig. 4B). Cellular inflammatory response assay of the fabricated four hydrogels on the Raw264.7 cells were conducted. The results showed that the LPS-induced Raw264.7 cells showed obvious differentiation, with irregular edges extending filopodia, enlarged size and a trend of nuclear enlargement. By contrast, the cell morphology in the Null, WT-SH, EGF-SH, PDGF-SH, and E/P-SH groups exhibited with full and round cytoskeletons and nuclei similar to normal cells (Fig. 4D). Measurements of cell diameter and area revealed no significant difference between the blank control and the four hydrogel groups, but the LPS-treated group showed significant cell enlargement compared to others (Fig. 4E and F). ELISA analysis showed that the releases of the proinflammatory factors, the TNF-α and the IL-1β from the macrophages post treatments by different sericin hydrogels for 1 day showed similar levels to these macrophages seeded on the TCP plates, while significantly lower compared to the LPS treatment (Fig. 4G and H). These results suggested the four fabricated sericin hydrogels did not induce significant cellular inflammation. In vitro hemolysis assay showed that the fabricated four GFs sericin hydrogels didn't cause the significant erythrocyte rupture comparing to the positive control (ddH2O) (Fig. 4I and J). Supernatants from each group were further measured at 580 nm (Fig. 4K), which showed hemolysis rates of 100 % for the positive control group, 0 % for the negative control group, 3.51 % for the WT-SH, 2.45 % for the EGF-SH, 1.01 % for the PDGF-SH, 4.57 % for the E/P-SH, and 2.65 % for the E/P-STD, indicating good hemocompatibility of the four fabricated GFs sericin hydrogels.Fig. 4Biocompatibility and inflammation analysis of the GFS sericin hydrogels. (A) White light images of HaCaT cells seeding on the surface of different sericin hydrogels after 4 h to reflect the adhesion assay of the GFs sericin hydrogel. Scale bar is 400 μm. (B) Live/Dead cell staining assay to analyze the in vitro toxicity of the four fabricated sericin hydrogels. Live cells are stained by green fluorescence; the dead cells are stained by red fluorescence. Scale bars are 200 μm. (C) CCK-8 assay of the cell adhesion on the four different hydrogel surfaces after 4 h. (D) The morphology of Raw264.7 cells after coculturing with different hydrogels and LPS for 24 h. Cytoskeleton and nucleus were stained with red fluorescence and blue fluorescence, respectively. Scale bars are 100 μm. (E) Diameters of Raw264.7 cells post co-cultivation with the different sericin hydrogels and LPS for 24 h. (F) Cell areas of the Raw264.7 cells post co-cultivation with the different sericin hydrogels and LPS for 24 h. ELISA analysis of the proinflammatory factors, TNF-α (G) and IL-1β (H) released from the RAW264.7 cells post treatment by different samples for 1 day. (I) Digital photo of the in vitro hemolysis assay without the blood cells. (J) Digital photo of the in vitro hemolysis assay with the blood cells. (K) Hemolysis rates of different fabricated sericin hydrogels. P.C. represents the positive control. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (n = 6) on a scale of 100 μm.Fig. 4

sections.section: The GFs sericin hydrogels promoted significant cell proliferation, cell migration, angiogenesis and anti-inflammation
sections.text: HaCaT cells for testing the cell proliferation were independently co-cultured with the four types of fabricated GFs sericin hydrogels for 24 h and stained with an EdU kit, where blue fluorescence indicates the nuclei and red fluorescence indicates proliferative cell. The results showed that the EGF-SH and the PDGF-SH with single GF achieved a stronger effect on promoting cell proliferation comparing to these from the WH-SH. By contrast, the E/P-SH with dual GFs achieved the strongest effect on promoting cell proliferation (Fig. 5A). CCK-8 analysis further confirmed that, compared with the Null control and the WT-SH, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, and the E/P-SH along with their corresponding commercial standards in solution forms significantly promoted the cell proliferation (Fig. 5B). Notably, the dual GFs functionalized sericin hydrogel was more effective than the single GF functionalized sericin hydrogel. Cell scratch test was used to evaluate the effect of different GFs-loading sericin hydrogels in promoting cell migration. The results showed that significant differences in cell migration among different treatments could be observed after 9 h in absence of mitomycin C. Among of which, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, and the E/P-SH treatments were significantly superior in promoting cell migration comparing to the Null and the WT-SH treatments, and E/P-SH achieved the best effect in promoting cell migration (Fig. 5C and D). In presence of the mitomycin C which could inhibit cell proliferation, significant differences in cell migration also could be observed after 18 h among different treatment groups. Similarly, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, and the E/P-SH treatments were significantly superior in promoting cell migration comparing to the Null and the WT-SH treatments, and the E/P-SH achieved the best effect in promoting cell migration (Fig. 5E and F). These results indicated that the synergy of EGF and PDGF-BB dual growth factors had a better effect in promoting cell migration. In vitro vascularization by co-culturing HUVECs with different sericin hydrogels was conducted. The results showed that both the EGF-SH and the PDGF-SH with single GF, could promote cell tube formation to a certain extent, while E/P-SH with dual-GFs could significantly promote cell tube formation (Fig. 5G). Quantitative analysis further confirmed that the GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels achieved significant promotions in number of junctions (Fig. 5H), number of segments (Fig. 5I), total tube length (Fig. 5J), and number of branches (Fig. 5K) in HUVECs compared to the control group. Among of which, the E/P-SH treatment achieved the greater effect in promoting the angiogenesis. These results suggested that the GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels might possess the potential to promote the blood vessel formation.Fig. 5Effects of the GFs sericin hydrogel on promoting cell proliferation and migration. (A) Cell proliferation was detected by EdU incorporation after 24 h co-culture of different sericin hydrogels with HaCaT cells. The nucleus and proliferating cells are stained with blue and red fluorescence, respectively. Scale bar is 200 μm. (B) CCK-8 assay of the cell growth conditions in the presence of different sericin hydrogels. (C) Cell scratch tests for evaluating the cell migration promoted by different sericin hydrogels in absence of mitomycin C. Blue dotted line indicates the initial wound edge, red line indicates the migrated cell area. The scale bars are 300 μm. (D) Quantitative and statistics analysis of migrated cell areas after treatments of different sericin hydrogels in absence of mitomycin C. (E) Cell scratch tests for evaluating the cell migration promoted by different sericin hydrogels in presence of mitomycin C. Blue dotted line indicates the initial wound edge, red line indicates the migrated cell area. The scale bars are 1000 μm. (F) Quantitative and statistics analysis of migrated cell areas after treatments of different sericin hydrogels in presence of mitomycin C. (G) In vitro vascularization by co-culturing HUVECs with different sericin hydrogels on Matrigel at different magnifications. The scale bars are 400 μm and 1 mm, respectively. (H–K) Quantitative and statistics analysis of total tube length, number of reticular pores, number of junctions, and number of segments in HUVECs compared to the control group. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (n = 3). Significance differences are indicated as ns, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, and ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001.Fig. 5 The anti-inflammation effects of the GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels were further analyzed. Immunofluorescence analysis of iNOS and CD206 expressions which indicate the M1-type macrophages and the M2-type macrophages, respectively [71,72] showed that treatments by both the WT-SH and the other three types of GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels significantly decreased the iNOS expression (Fig. 6A) and increased the CD206 expression (Fig. 6B) in the LPS-induced macrophages, suggesting that both the WT-SH and GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels transformed M1-type macrophages into M2-type macrophages to function the anti-inflammatory effect. It was worth noting that there was no significant difference in the anti-inflammation effects among the WT-SH and the GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels, suggesting that the anti-inflammatory effect was not attributed to growth factors but to sericin protein, which had been proven with anti-inflammatory effects [73,74].Fig. 6In vitro anti-inflammatory activity of the GFs-loaded sericin hydrogels. Immunofluorescence of the iNOS (A) and the CD206 (B) in the LPS-induced Raw 264.7 macrophages treated with different WT-SH and GFs-sericin hydrogels for 24 h. Scale bars are 200 μm.Fig. 6

sections.section: The GFs sericin hydrogels promoted the healing of full-thickness wound in diabetic mice
sections.text: The full-thickness healing wound model in diabetic mouse was constructed following the flowchart (Fig. 7A). By the 3rd and 7th day of wounding, the wounds of mice treated by the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, and the E/P-SH showed significant healing effect compared with the WT-SH and the CK treatments (Fig. 7B). By the 12th day of wound healing, the wounds of mice treated with EGF-SH, PDGF-SH and E/P-SH were basically all healed compared with CK group and WT-SH group. Among of which, the E/P-SH treatment achieved the best healing effect on the diabetic mice wound, which was comparable to that of E/P-STD. By the 3rd day, the wound healing rates of mice from the CK, the WT-SH, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD groups were calculated to be 20.33 ± 6.88 %, 25.43 ± 6.48 %, 40.39 ± 7.13 %, 43.72 ± 1.03 %, 58.04 ± 5.53 % and 53.71 ± 11.95 %, respectively. By the 7th day, the wound healing rates of mice from the CK, the WT-SH, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD groups increased to 48.07 ± 8.46 %, 53.74 ± 16.41 %, 69.55 ± 3.09 %, 68.98 ± 0.91 %, 69.07 ± 4.62 % and 76.27 ± 3.99 %, respectively. By the 12th day, the wound healing rates of mice from the CK, the WT-SH, the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD groups further increased to 64.45 ± 13.32 %, 72.79 ± 8.86 %, 85.78 ± 6.55 %, 86.97 ± 1.67 %, 91.65 ± 1.27 % and 91.06 ± 0.42 %, respectively (Fig. 7C). Statistically, by day 12 of wound healing, there was no significant difference in wound healing and wound width between the WT-SH treatment group and the CK treatment group. In contrast, EGF-SH, PDGF-SH, E/P-SH treatments showed significant effects on promoting the wound healing and reducing the wound width, where the E/P-SH treatment group had the best effects which was comparable to the E/P-STD positive control (Fig. 7D and E). The long-term effects of the hydrogels on wound healing, including scar formation and tissue regeneration were further evaluated. The results showed that the wounds from all of the groups completely healed on the 22nd day with thickened epidermis associated with hypertrophic scarring in groups of the WT-SH, the EGF-SH, and the PDGF-SH compared to the none treatment group (N.T.) (Fig. 7F). Notably, the epidermal thickness of mice from the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD groups was similar with that of the N.T. group (Fig. 7G), indicating that the synergistic effect of EGF and PDGF-BB in the E/P-SH was more effective in promoting full-size wound healing of diabetic mice and showed better effect in reducing scar formation.Fig. 7The GFs sericin hydrogels promoted the healing of full-thickness wound in diabetic mice. (A) Schedule to generate a diabetic mouse model for the wound healing analysis of the GFs sericin hydrogels. (B–C) Representative pictures of mouse wounds in different treatment groups on days 0, 3, 7, and 12. Scale bar is 0.5 cm. Statistics of wound healing areas (D) and wound width (E) in different treatment groups on the 12th days. (F) H&E staining of completely healed tissue of diabetic mouse treated by different hydrogels on the 22nd day. Epidermal thickness is indicated by the blue arrows. Scale bar: 200 μm. (G) Statistical analysis of the epidermal thickness after complete healing. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (n = 3), scale bar is 200 μm.Fig. 7

H&E staining of the wounds on the 12th day where the nuclei, cytoplasm and neutrophils were indicated by blue, red and black arrow showed that the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD treated mice exhibited more hair follicles and sweat glands compared to the CK and the WT-SH treatments. Notably, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD treated mice exhibited optimal epithelialization and dermal development. In addition, the mice from the CK and WT-SH groups revealed more neutrophils, indicated a stronger inflammatory response which delayed the wound healing. By contrast, the mice from the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD groups exhibited reduced neutrophils and inflammation which benefited to the wound healing (Fig. 8A). Masson staining of the mice wounds healing to the 12th day were conducted, where collagen fibers were stained by blue, muscle fibers, cytoplasm, erythrocyte were stained by red, and nucleus was stained by black blue. The results showed that the better epithelialization with shorter wound widths were observed in mice treated by the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD comparing to these mice treated by the CK and the WT-SH. Among of which, mice wounds treated by the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD showed the smallest wound widths (Fig. 8B). In addition, more ordered collagen depositions (stained by blue) were observed in the mice from the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD groups compared to these mice with the disordered collagen depositions from the CK and the WT-SH groups, suggesting the promotions of the GFs on the wound healing. It was worth mentioning that the mice wounds treated by the EGF-SH exhibited better collagen depositions and epithelialization (stained by blue) while the PDGF-SH treatment resulted better angiogenesis and less inflammation (stained by red), suggesting the different mechanisms of EGF and PDGF-BB in promoting wound healing. Overall, the mice wounds treated by the E/P-SH and the E/P-STD showed the highest contents of collagen deposition compared to these with less collagen depositions in the mice wounds treated by the EGF-SH and the PDGF-SH, suggesting a synergistic effect of the PDGF-BB and EGF on promoting the diabetic wound healing [60,75]. Furthermore, immunofluorescence analysis showed that signals of the angiogenesis marker (CD31) and the M2 marker (CD206) of macrophages were significantly enhanced in the mice treated by the EGF-SH, the PDGF-SH, the E/P-SH, and the E/P-STD, indicating accelerated angiogenesis and effective repolarization of macrophages from M1 phenotype to M2 phenotype (Fig. 9A–C). Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensities further confirmed that the CD31 and the CD206 in the E/P-SH treated mice achieved the highest expressions among all the groups (Fig. 9B–D). These results suggested that synergy of EGF and PDGF-BB in sericin hydrogels realized promotion of vascularization by accelerating angiogenesis and effective anti-inflammation by regulating macrophage polarization, thus achieved better development of epithelial and dermal tissues, more organized arrangement of collagen, and finally promoted the wound healing in diabetic wounds. The possible synergistic mechanism is speculated that EGF promotes the migration and proliferation of keratinocytes by activating the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway and dominating early epidermal repair, while PDGF-BB stimulates fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis and enhances matrix remodeling by activating the PI3K-Akt and LAS-MAPK pathways.Fig. 8Histological and immunofluorescence analysis of wound healing on the 12th day. (A) H&E staining of the healing tissues of diabetic mouse treated by different hydrogels on the 12th day. The black dashed lines indicated the new epidermal tissue. Black arrows indicated the segmented neutrophil. Scale bar: 0.5 cm. (B) Masson staining of the healing tissues of diabetic mouse treated by different hydrogels on the 12th day. The white dashed lines indicated the newly formed epidermal tissues. Scale bar: 0.5 cm.Fig. 8Fig. 9Immunofluorescence analysis of the diabetic mice wound tissue healed on the 12th day. (A) Representative immunofluorescent images of CD31 staining in the wound tissue of mice treated by different samples. Blue: DAPI; Red: CD31. Scale bar: 200 μm. (B) Quantitative analysis of the CD31 expression according to the positive-stained areas in (A). (C) Representative immunofluorescent images of CD201 staining in the wound tissues of mice treated by different samples. Blue: DAPI; Green: CD206. Scale bar: 200 μm. (D) Quantitative analysis of the CD206 expression according to the positive-stained areas in (C). Significance differences are indicated as ns, ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, and ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001, respectively.Fig. 9 In summary, the present study successfully demonstrated the feasibility of creating GFs-functional silk fibers such as EGF and PDGF-BB through silk gland biosynthesis system for developing the dual-GFs sericin hydrogel system to promote full-size wound healing in diabetic mice, this strategy not only verified the previous strategy of promoting the healing of diabetic wounds by multiple growth factors [60,75], but also ingeniously overcame the source and stability of the growth factors by silk gland biosynthesis and sericin hydrogel delivery. It is also worthy of noting that more efforts are still needed to determine the appropriate clinical dosages of the GFs in the sericin hydrogel to reduce the potential risk for increased malignancies at sites distant from the wound area to well fulfill the demands of clinical trials and guarantee the safety of clinical applications in the future.

In this study, a series of GFs functionalized sericin hydrogels were successfully generated using the genetically engineered silk fibers which were cost effectively and massively spun by two transgenic silkworm strains. The strategy for extracting GFs with bioactivities and adjustable dose and combination from the silk fibers was designed to fabricate the active GFs sericin hydrogels with desirable stability, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and sustainable release of the GFs to promote cell proliferation and migration. This system further achieved the significant healing of full-thickness wound in diabetic mice within 12 days with more organized collagen arrangement and better epithelialization degree by reducing inflammatory response and promoting vascularization. These findings suggest that the genetically fabricated dual GFs sericin hydrogel delivering system provides an opportunity for chronic diabetic wound healing treatment to broaden the wide utility of GFs in clinic.

title: Regenerative potential of PRP-based scaffolds in chronic wound healing: Mechanisms, advances, and therapeutic insights
abstract: Chronic wounds such as diabetic foot ulcers, venous leg ulcers, and pressure ulcers often remain trapped in the inflammatory phase due to oxidative stress, protease overactivity, and impaired cellular responses, particularly in diabetic conditions. These wounds require advanced therapeutic strategies beyond conventional care. Regenerative medicine—especially platelet-rich plasma (PRP)-based interventions—has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing wound repair. This review examines recent developments in PRP-loaded scaffolds, focusing on their biological mechanisms, structural advantages, and clinical applications. It synthesizes findings from key studies that integrate PRP with natural and synthetic biomaterials, often combined with bioactive agents like adipose-derived stem cell exosomes. PRP-containing scaffolds promote wound healing through multiple pathways: enhancing cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodeling; reducing inflammation via M2 macrophage polarization; and facilitating collagen deposition. Their antibacterial properties and controlled release of growth factors such as VEGF and TGF-β1 further support tissue regeneration. Additionally, scaffold composition improves mechanical strength, elasticity, and growth factor bioavailability. Innovations such as GelMA/SFMA hydrogels and COL/PRP-ADSC-exos composites have shown superior outcomes in preclinical models. PRP-based scaffolds offer a multifunctional platform for chronic wound treatment by combining biological activity with structural support. Despite existing challenges such as variability in PRP preparation and limited clinical data, ongoing research and emerging technologies hold strong potential to standardize and enhance these therapies for future clinical translation.
