sections.text: Wound healing is a multifaceted biological process that occurs in four overlapping stages: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling [1]. The initial phase, hemostasis, plays a crucial role in stopping blood loss through vasoconstriction and the formation of a clot, which also serves as a scaffold for subsequent cell migration. This process is followed by inflammation, where neutrophils and macrophages clear pathogens and debris from the wound site while simultaneously releasing various growth factors that stimulate tissue repair. In the proliferative phase, new tissue, blood vessels, and epithelial layers are formed, aiding in the regeneration of the wound. The final phase, remodeling, involves the reorganization of collagen to form scar tissue, a process that can take up to two years or more to complete [2,3]. Chronic wounds, however, present a significant challenge as they fail to progress through these stages in a timely manner, often stalling during the inflammation phase. This prolonged inflammatory state is typically characterized by an overabundance of proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and the presence of senescent cells, all of which disrupt the healing process. These factors impair the extracellular matrix (ECM), preventing the wound from advancing to the proliferative phase [4,5]. In addition, dysfunctional mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and other cellular deficiencies exacerbate the issue, particularly in conditions like diabetes, where the natural healing response is often compromised [6,7]. Addressing chronic wounds requires not only identifying and managing these underlying issues but also restoring the balance of cytokines, growth factors, and functional cells necessary for proper healing. The management of chronic wounds involves a comprehensive patient and wound assessment to identify contributing factors such as infection, vascular issues, and comorbid conditions [8]. Chronic wounds, including diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), venous leg ulcers (VLUs), and pressure ulcers (PUs), necessitate a careful evaluation that includes factors such as wound size, depth, and appearance, along with tests for neuropathy and arterial insufficiency. A multidisciplinary approach is essential, incorporating treatments such as infection control, debridement, and revascularization, with compression therapy often recommended for VLUs [9]. In the case of DFUs, offloading pressure is crucial to prevent further damage and facilitate healing [10]. Topical wound therapies range from simple saline dressings to more specialized treatments like honey, collagenase, and antimicrobial agents, though these should always be used in conjunction with the basic principles of debridement and infection management [11]. More advanced therapies, such as negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT), hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), and electrical stimulation, have demonstrated promising results in treating chronic DFUs and VLUs, although additional research is necessary to confirm their long-term efficacy [8]. In addition to these traditional methods, biological and bioengineered therapies have garnered increasing attention as effective tools in chronic wound management. Autologous PRP, recombinant growth factors, and cellular treatments are emerging as promising therapies for accelerating wound healing [12]. PRP, for example, promotes healing by enhancing the release of growth factors from platelets, while recombinant human growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (rhPDGF) have shown improvements in healing outcomes for DFUs [13]. Cellular therapies, including those based on stem cells derived from bone marrow or placental tissues, present exciting opportunities to enhance tissue repair and promote wound closure by stimulating the regeneration of damaged tissues [14]. Despite the promising results from these therapies, challenges remain in standardizing treatment methods and ensuring consistent outcomes, necessitating further research to optimize protocols for chronic wound care [12]. Regenerative medicine has proven to be pivotal in managing chronic wounds that fail to advance through the typical stages of healing [15]. Chronic wounds, such as DFUs, VLUs, and PUs, often become stalled in the inflammatory phase, which is characterized by an imbalance of cytokines, growth factors, and dysfunctional cells. This prolonged inflammation, coupled with impaired cellular function, disrupts tissue regeneration and further damages the ECM [16]. One of the key challenges in chronic wound healing is the dysfunction of stem cells, particularly MSCs, which are essential for tissue repair and regeneration. In conditions such as diabetes, MSCs are often deficient or impaired, contributing to the delayed healing process [17]. Regenerative therapies aim to restore cellular function and stimulate tissue regeneration by addressing stem cell deficiencies. By restoring the balance of growth factors, cytokines, and other molecular signals, regenerative medicine can help break the cycle of chronic inflammation, facilitating the transition to the proliferative and remodeling phases of healing [18]. Stem cell therapies, in particular, have shown significant promise in enhancing wound healing. Stem cells derived from bone marrow (BMSCs) and placental tissues, including the amnion and umbilical cord, offer substantial advantages in treating chronic wounds. These cells secrete growth factors and cytokines that promote cell migration, angiogenesis, and tissue regeneration [19]. Studies have demonstrated particularly favorable outcomes for chronic DFUs, with improvements in healing rates and reductions in complications such as infections and amputations [20]. In addition to stem cell therapies, biological treatments such as PRP and recombinant growth factors (e.g., rhPDGF, rhEGF) play crucial roles in accelerating wound healing by enhancing cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and collagen formation [12]. PRP, in particular, derived from the patient's own blood, has been shown to be effective in chronic lower extremity wounds, including DFUs, due to its ability to promote tissue regeneration [21]. Acellular and bioengineered tissue-based therapies have also gained attention in the field of wound healing. These treatments use decellularized tissues, such as amniotic membranes, collagen matrices, and dermal allografts, as scaffolds to support cellular migration and tissue repair [22]. These therapies are especially valuable in chronic wounds where native tissue regeneration is insufficient. For example, dehydrated human amnion/chorion membranes (dHACM) have shown promising results in DFUs by enhancing wound closure and reducing infection rates [23]. Alongside advanced therapies like NPWT, HBOT, and electrical stimulation, regenerative medicine offers a comprehensive approach to chronic wound care. These therapies, when combined with appropriate wound management and assessment, hold the potential to significantly improve healing outcomes, particularly in complex cases where traditional treatments have failed [12,24]. By incorporating regenerative approaches, clinicians can address the underlying causes of delayed wound healing, enhance tissue regeneration, and ultimately improve the quality of life for patients suffering from chronic wounds. While the evidence continues to evolve, the future of wound care increasingly relies on regenerative medicine to promote faster and more effective healing, particularly for patients with underlying conditions such as diabetes and venous insufficiency [12,25]. PRP is a biological therapy that has garnered significant attention for its potential to accelerate wound healing, particularly in chronic wounds. Derived from the patient's own blood, PRP is rich in platelets that, when activated, release growth factors essential for tissue repair and regeneration [26]. The biological significance of PRP lies in its ability to enhance the natural wound healing process by supporting the four overlapping phases of healing: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling. In the early stages of healing, platelets release growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which attract and activate the cells needed for tissue repair. These growth factors stimulate the proliferation of endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and keratinocytes, facilitating angiogenesis, collagen synthesis, and re-epithelialization [27,28]. Chronic wounds often experience delays in the healing process due to prolonged inflammation, excessive protease activity, and dysfunctional cells such as senescent fibroblasts. PRP helps address these issues by providing a concentrated source of bioactive molecules that support cellular functions and restore the wound environment [29]. Studies have demonstrated that PRP therapy accelerates wound closure, particularly in conditions like DFUs and VLUs, which are typically resistant to conventional treatments [26]. By promoting tissue regeneration, reducing bacterial load, and stimulating angiogenesis, PRP enhances the wound healing process [30]. Moreover, PRP's ability to modulate the inflammatory response and reduce oxidative stress is particularly beneficial in chronic wounds, where inflammation and oxidative damage often impede healing [31]. Traditionally, PRP is injected directly at the injury site, but sustaining its presence over time has proven challenging, often necessitating multiple injections that cause fluctuations in growth factor levels, reduce therapeutic predictability, and increase patient discomfort [27]. To address these issues, PRP-based scaffolds have been developed to enable controlled, sustained release of bioactive molecules, enhancing wound healing and tissue repair. Acting as three-dimensional (3D) matrices, PRP scaffolds support key cellular processes such as attachment, proliferation, and differentiation. By mixing PRP with activators like thrombin or calcium salts, PRP gels are formed, creating fibrin networks that foster MSC growth. However, conventional PRP gels face limitations, including rapid GF release, which can reduce their therapeutic duration and increase the risk of tissue hyperplasia, as well as insufficient mechanical stability for surgical applications [32,33]. Incorporating PRP into synthetic, natural, or composite scaffolds improves biocompatibility, bioactivity, and mechanical strength, while advanced strategies like chemical cross-linking further enhance scaffold stability and sustained growth factor delivery. These innovations enable PRP-based scaffolds to create a more effective bioactive environment, provide better mechanical support, and deliver prolonged therapeutic benefits, making them valuable in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [34]. Despite the promising potential of PRP-containing scaffolds in wound healing, there remains a critical gap in understanding how scaffold composition and PRP formulation influence therapeutic efficacy. While existing studies highlight improvements in mechanical properties, bioactivity, and growth factor release, the lack of standardized methodologies and clinical protocols limits their widespread application. Furthermore, the precise mechanisms through which PRP modulates inflammation, ECM remodeling, and cellular interactions within scaffolds require further investigation. This review aims to bridge these gaps by synthesizing recent advancements in PRP-based scaffolds, analyzing their biological and mechanical properties, and identifying key challenges that must be addressed for clinical translation. Through this comprehensive evaluation, we seek to provide a clearer understanding of the role of PRP-containing scaffolds in regenerative medicine and their potential to enhance wound healing outcomes.

Wound healing is a highly organized and dynamic biological process that enables the body to repair tissue damage, restore its integrity, and regain normal functionality. This process occurs in four distinct stages: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and maturation, with each phase characterized by specific cellular and molecular events that contribute to the overall restoration of the wounded tissue [25], as illustrated in Fig. 1.Fig. 1Phases of wound healing. The process begins with hemostasis, during which blood loss is controlled through the formation of a platelet plug and a fibrin matrix. This is followed by the inflammatory phase, where neutrophils, recruited by histamine release from mast cells, help eliminate dead cells and prevent infection. Monocytes then differentiate into macrophages, aiding in the clearance of cellular debris and neutrophils in the wound area. In the proliferative phase, multiple processes occur, including keratinocyte migration to close the wound, angiogenesis for new blood vessel formation, and fibroblast activation, which stimulates granulation tissue formation. Finally, during tissue remodeling, fibroblasts, MSCs, myofibroblasts, and blood vessels collaborate to reshape the wound site, ultimately leading to complete wound closure (Figure reprinted from Ref. [61], licensed under CC BY 4.0.).Fig. 1 The first stage, hemostasis, begins immediately after tissue injury and aims to prevent excessive blood loss through a series of rapid and coordinated steps. Initially, blood vessels constrict in a process known as vascular spasm, which reduces blood flow to the injured site [25]. This is followed by platelet activation and the formation of a temporary plug at the wound site. Platelets adhere to the exposed collagen with the help of von Willebrand factor (vWF) and glycoprotein receptors. Once activated, they undergo structural changes and release granules containing adenosine diphosphate (ADP), serotonin, and thromboxane A2. ADP attracts additional platelets, serotonin acts as a vasoconstrictor, and thromboxane A2 enhances both platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, reinforcing the plug in a positive feedback loop. To further stabilize the clot, fibrin threads form through a coagulation cascade, solidifying the platelet plug and creating a protective barrier that prevents additional blood loss [35]. The inflammatory phase follows hemostasis and is critical for clearing debris, pathogens, and damaged tissue while establishing an environment conducive to repair. During this phase, blood vessels dilate, and their permeability increases, enabling immune cells, such as neutrophils and macrophages, to migrate to the wound. Neutrophils, the first immune responders, work to eliminate pathogens and cellular debris while also releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines that amplify the inflammatory response. Macrophages, which replace neutrophils later in the phase, play a dual role by continuing debris clearance and releasing growth factors like VEGF and TGF-β, which stimulate tissue regeneration. This inflammation must be tightly regulated, as excessive or prolonged inflammatory responses may hinder healing or lead to chronic wounds [2,36]. After inflammation subsides, the proliferative phase begins, characterized by active tissue repair and regeneration. During this phase, fibroblasts migrate to the wound site and begin producing collagen, particularly type IIIcollagen, to form a new ECM that provides structural support [37]. Another essential process in this phase is angiogenesis, where new blood vessels form to restore oxygen and nutrient supply to the regenerating tissue. This process is driven by VEGF, which promotes endothelial cell proliferation and migration. As granulation tissue, rich in fibroblasts and endothelial cells, fills the wound gap, epithelial cells at the wound margins multiply and migrate across the wound bed, forming a protective layer that seals the wound [38]. These cellular processes work in coordination to close the wound and prepare the tissue for the final stage of healing. The maturation or remodeling phase follows the proliferative stage and can continue for weeks, months, or even years, depending on the severity of the injury. During this phase, the newly formed tissue undergoes structural refinement to improve its strength, functionality, and durability. Initially, the wound contains type III collagen, which is less organized and more elastic. Over time, this is replaced by type I collagen, which is stronger and forms cross-linked, organized fibers, increasing the tensile strength of the repaired tissue. Despite these changes, scar tissue typically retains only about 70–80 % of the original skin's strength [39]. Excess fibroblasts and endothelial cells are removed through apoptosis, or programmed cell death, helping refine the wound and prevent excessive tissue buildup. As the collagen matrix is remodeled and aligned along tension lines, the tissue becomes better adapted to withstand mechanical forces. Proper wound care during this phase, including hydration, protection from infection, and minimizing tension on the wound, can improve outcomes by reducing scarring and enhancing the quality of the healed tissue [40].

Several patient-related factors significantly influence wound healing. Age, particularly in individuals over 60, is one such factor, as older adults often experience delayed healing despite maintaining the quality of tissue repair. This delay is attributed to changes in the inflammatory response, such as slower T-cell infiltration, altered chemokine production, and reduced macrophage function [41]. Aged individuals tend to show slower re-epithelialization, collagen synthesis, and angiogenesis [42]. However, exercise can improve wound healing in older adults by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines through an anti-inflammatory response [43]. Sex hormones also play a role, with aged males experiencing slower healing compared to females. Estrogen, for example, regulates genes involved in regeneration and matrix production, whereas androgens tend to negatively impact wound healing [44]. Stress is another significant factor, as it disrupts the neuroendocrine-immune balance through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system (SNS) [45]. Psychological stress increases the release of glucocorticoids, such as cortisol, which suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines necessary for the initial inflammatory phase of wound healing. This impairment of immune cell function and reduced cell adhesion further hinders the healing process [46]. Additionally, unhealthy habits associated with stress, such as poor sleep, inadequate nutrition, and substance abuse, also negatively impact wound recovery [47]. Diabetes has a well-established effect on wound healing, with individuals being especially prone to chronic diabetic foot ulcers, which are a major cause of amputations. The delayed healing in diabetes is due to multiple factors, including hypoxia, hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and high levels of metalloproteases. These factors lead to impaired tissue repair and reduced angiogenesis, as well as defects in immune function and cell activity [48]. Neuropathy, common in diabetic patients, further hampers the healing process due to impaired neuropeptide levels [49]. Medications also affect wound healing, with glucocorticoid steroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and chemotherapeutic drugs being particularly influential. Glucocorticoid steroids, although effective in reducing inflammation, hinder wound repair by suppressing fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis [50]. NSAIDs, particularly when used long-term, reduce fibroblast function and delay epithelialization [51]. Chemotherapeutic drugs, which inhibit cellular metabolism and protein synthesis, impair immune responses and collagen production, making wounds more susceptible to infection and delayed healing [52]. Obesity is another patient-related factor that compromises wound healing. Obese individuals face a higher risk of infections, wound dehiscence, and pressure ulcers due to factors such as hypoperfusion and ischemia in subcutaneous adipose tissue. These complications are further exacerbated by poor tissue perfusion, pressure-induced injuries, and microbial accumulation in skin folds [53]. Obesity also alters immune function through bioactive substances known as adipokines, which contribute to delayed healing [54]. However, weight loss has been shown to improve immune function and support better healing outcomes [47]. Alcohol consumption, whether acute or chronic, significantly impairs wound healing. Alcohol suppresses the immune response, disrupts several key processes like re-epithelialization and angiogenesis, and increases the risk of infection [55]. Both acute and chronic alcohol exposure reduce collagen production, impair wound closure, and contribute to hypoxia and oxidative stress at the wound site [56]. Smoking is another environmental factor that severely affects wound healing. It increases the risk of complications such as infection, wound rupture, and delayed recovery. Smoking impairs immune function, reduces blood flow to the wound site through vasoconstriction, and hinders several cellular functions crucial for tissue repair. The toxic substances in tobacco smoke, particularly nicotine, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen cyanide, interfere with the body's ability to heal effectively [57]. Smoking cessation can improve wound healing, but nicotine replacement therapies may also offer some benefit by promoting collagen synthesis [58]. Environmental factors, particularly nutrition, play a pivotal role in wound healing. Nutrient deficiencies, including those in proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals, can delay recovery and increase the risk of complications. Carbohydrates provide essential energy for tissue repair, while proteins and amino acids like arginine and glutamine support collagen synthesis and immune function [59]. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), particularly omega-3, enhance immune function and may reduce infections [60]. Vitamins such as C, A, and E help with tissue repair by promoting collagen synthesis and reducing inflammation [47]. Micronutrients like magnesium, copper, zinc, and iron are crucial for collagen production and overall wound healing [47]. A balanced, nutrient-enriched supplement can significantly improve healing, especially in chronic conditions, highlighting the importance of proper nutrition for optimal recovery.

PRP, a biological derivative of autologous blood, is defined by its elevated platelet concentration relative to baseline levels prior to centrifugation and is distinguished by its retention of normal physiological levels of clotting factors along with an enrichment of various bioactive molecules, including growth factors, chemokines, cytokines, and plasma proteins [27]. The process of obtaining PRP involves centrifuging whole blood, which separates its components—red blood cells, PRP, and platelet-poor plasma (PPP)—according to their density gradients [62]. Notably, PRP formulations may differ not only in platelet concentration but also in terms of leukocyte content and activation status, distinctions that give rise to the different types of PRP employed for therapeutic purposes [63]. While commercial devices designed to prepare PRP typically achieve platelet concentrations that range from two to five times the baseline level, scientific investigations have suggested that excessively elevated platelet concentrations do not necessarily translate into improved therapeutic efficacy and may, in some cases, exert inhibitory effects on the healing process [64]. Historically, PRP was first utilized in blood transfusion medicine and later as a fibrin tissue adhesive aimed at enhancing fibrin polymerization to improve tissue sealing [65]. Over the years, however, PRP has evolved into a regenerative therapeutic modality intended to stimulate tissue healing through the localized delivery of growth factors that activate the healing cascade at injury sites. The biological complexity of PRP extends well beyond PDGFs alone, as its diverse content—including cytokines, leukocytes, fibrin, and other bioactive proteins—interacts dynamically with the local microenvironment to modulate tissue repair processes [66]. Despite the early enthusiasm surrounding PRP-based interventions, the clinical application of this technology has been impeded by the absence of standardization, inconsistent scientific data, and a lack of consensus regarding classification systems, all of which have contributed to variable and, at times, unpredictable clinical outcomes [67]. The variability in PRP formulations arises from differences in preparation protocols, compositional elements, and activation methods, a heterogeneity that has prompted researchers to propose various classification systems in an effort to standardize the terminology and facilitate clearer distinctions between different PRP products. One of the earliest and most influential classification frameworks was introduced by Ehrenfest in 2009, which categorized PRP formulations based on leukocyte content and fibrin network density [68]. This classification distinguished between pure PRP (P-PRP), which is devoid of leukocytes and forms a low-density fibrin network upon activation, and leukocyte-rich PRP (LR-PRP), which contains leukocytes and also forms a low-density fibrin network. Additionally, Ehrenfest's system included pure platelet-rich fibrin (P-PRF), characterized by its absence of leukocytes and the formation of a high-density fibrin network that cannot be injected, as well as leukocyte-rich PRF (L-PRF), which contains leukocytes and forms a high-density fibrin network [68]. Building upon this foundational classification, the PAW system, proposed by Delong et al. categorized PRP according to three key parameters: platelet concentration, activation status, and white blood cell (WBC) content [69]. This system not only defined platelet concentration in terms of four distinct ranges but also determined whether PRP was activated with exogenous agents and whether leukocytes, specifically neutrophils, were present or absent in the formulation [69]. The PAW classification was further refined by Mautner et al. who developed the PLRA system, which added layers of specificity by incorporating absolute platelet counts, the percentage and presence of leukocytes and neutrophils, red blood cell (RBC) content, and the use of exogenous activators [27]. In 2016, Magalon et al. introduced yet another classification framework, the DEPA system, which evaluated PRP based on four critical parameters: the dose of injected platelets, categorized into low, medium, high, and very high doses; the efficiency of platelet recovery, which could range from poor to high efficiency; the purity of PRP, assessed by the relative proportion of platelets to RBCs and leukocytes; and the activation process, specifically considering the use of exogenous clotting factors such as thrombin or calcium chloride [70]. Around the same time, the MARSPILL classification system was proposed by Lana et al. which sought to emphasize the significance of peripheral blood mononuclear cells in PRP formulations and thereby added another dimension to PRP characterization [71]. Despite the introduction of these various classification systems, the field has yet to adopt a universally accepted framework for PRP standardization, a challenge that continues to hinder the reproducibility of research findings and the consistent application of PRP in clinical practice. Given the inherent heterogeneity of PRP bioformulations and the continuously expanding range of its clinical applications, achieving consensus on a unified classification system remains an ongoing challenge. Nevertheless, future research efforts are likely to focus on refining PRP preparation techniques with the goal of optimizing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing variability and enhancing reproducibility across clinical studies. The establishment of a standardized classification system for PRP would not only improve data interpretation and facilitate cross-study comparisons but also contribute to enhanced patient care by ensuring that regenerative medicine applications are guided by evidence-based protocols and scientifically validated best practices [27].

PRP is an autologous concentration of human platelets that exceeds the physiological baseline found in whole blood, typically achieving platelet concentrations three to five times higher than normal. In healthy individuals, the standard platelet count ranges from 150,000 to 350,000 cells per microliter of blood, with platelets serving as small, discoid, non-nucleated cells derived from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow and possessing a lifespan of approximately seven to ten days [72]. Their primary physiological function is closely tied to hemostasis and coagulation, particularly during vascular injury, where they adhere to the damaged endothelium and activate the coagulation cascade [73]. Upon activation, platelets undergo shape change and release the contents of their granules, initiating a biochemical cascade that contributes not only to clot formation but also to tissue healing and repair. Central to PRP's regenerative properties is its bioactive composition, including growth factors, cytokines, and other molecules that interact with the local cellular environment to stimulate wound healing and tissue regeneration [26]. Platelets contain three distinct types of granules—alpha, delta, and lambda—each with a specialized function. Alpha granules are the most abundant, comprising approximately 10 % of the platelet's volume, and each platelet contains between 50 and 80 alpha granules [74]. These granules house a wide variety of soluble and membrane-bound proteins, including integrins, platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecules, glycoproteins, and leucine-rich repeat family receptors, which contribute to cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation during tissue repair [35]. Importantly, alpha granules release over 300 bioactive molecules, including growth factors that play critical roles in clotting, inflammation, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Delta granules, also known as dense bodies, primarily store clotting stimulators such as calcium, magnesium, adenosine, serotonin, and histamine, which enhance platelet aggregation and vascular contraction. In contrast, lambda granules, which function similarly to lysosomes, contain enzymes that degrade proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates, thereby facilitating the removal of cellular debris and pathogens from damaged tissues [75]. The therapeutic potential of PRP is largely dependent on the release of these bioactive molecules following platelet activation. Once activated, the platelets release growth factors that initiate and regulate key cellular processes, including chemotaxis, mitogenesis, angiogenesis, and differentiation. These processes collectively stimulate local mesenchymal and epithelial cells to migrate, proliferate, and increase collagen synthesis, ultimately leading to the formation of fibrous tissue, extracellular matrix remodeling, and, in some cases, scar tissue formation [76]. Many of the growth factors released by platelets exhibit synergistic effects, interacting through complex intracellular signaling pathways that enhance wound healing. Among the most critical growth factors in PRP are PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, epidermal growth factor (EGF), insulin-like growth factor (IGF), and fibroblast growth factor (FGF). PDGF, initially discovered in platelets, is also secreted by monocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells, and consists of A and B subunits that form three isoforms: PDGF-AA, PDGF-BB, and PDGF-AB. PDGF plays a key role in promoting fibroblast chemotaxis and mitosis, stimulating collagen synthesis, and enhancing extracellular matrix remodeling. In addition, PDGF recruits macrophages and neutrophils to the injury site, where they further amplify the inflammatory response by releasing TGF-β and other cytokines [77,78]. TGF-β belongs to the TGF-β superfamily, which also includes bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). This multifunctional cytokine exists in three isoforms—TGF-β1, TGF-β2, and TGF-β3—and plays a central role in regulating cellular proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [79]. Upon injury, platelets secrete the active form of TGF-β1, which promotes collagen production, inhibits collagen degradation, and facilitates angiogenesis, connective tissue regeneration, and immune cell recruitment. In bone injuries, TGF-β1 enhances osteoblast proliferation while simultaneously inhibiting osteoclast differentiation, thereby promoting bone formation and reducing bone resorption [79]. VEGF, another key growth factor secreted by activated platelets and macrophages in response to tissue damage, is essential for angiogenesis. It stimulates endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and the formation of new blood vessels, thereby improving nutrient supply and oxygen delivery to the injury site [80]. The angiogenic effects of VEGF are further amplified by the presence of PDGF, TGF-β, and EGF, which together enhance blood vessel maturation and stability [81]. EGF, in particular, plays a pivotal role in promoting endothelial cell chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and mesenchymal cell mitosis, and research has shown that it accelerates epithelialization, thereby significantly reducing wound healing time. EGF also increases cytokine secretion from mesenchymal and epithelial cells, further promoting tissue repair [82]. IGF-1 is a 70-amino acid polypeptide hormone that is normally found in plasma and transported into platelets via IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs) [83]. Upon platelet activation, IGF-1 stimulates mesenchymal cell differentiation and mitogenesis, with a particular impact on bone healing, where it promotes osteoblast proliferation and differentiation [84]. FGF, which is among the most potent mitogens affecting mesenchymal cells, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts, also plays a critical role in bone and cartilage repair. By stimulating chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation, FGF enhances the regeneration of cartilage tissue, while its angiogenic effects, in conjunction with VEGF, contribute to improved blood supply to damaged tissues [85]. The combined action of these growth factors underscores the complexity and versatility of PRP's therapeutic potential. Together, they influence numerous biological processes, including cell proliferation, extracellular matrix remodeling, angiogenesis, and immune cell recruitment, all of which are essential for effective tissue repair and regeneration. Understanding the complex interplay of PRP's bioactive components and their downstream signaling effects is critical for optimizing PRP's clinical applications and maximizing its therapeutic efficacy in regenerative medicine [84,86]. By tailoring PRP formulations to specific injury types and patient populations, clinicians may be able to enhance its therapeutic outcomes, ultimately improving the efficacy of PRP-based interventions in various fields, including orthopedics, dermatology, and dentistry.

The development of PRP-based scaffolds has emerged as a pivotal advancement in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine due to their capacity to enhance wound healing and tissue regeneration by providing a sustained release of bioactive factors at the injury site. As illustrated in Fig. 2, PRP can be incorporated into scaffolds through various strategies, including lyophilization, gel formation, and protein cross-linking, to enhance its mechanical stability, bioactivity, and regenerative efficiency. Traditionally, PRP has been administered via direct injection to accelerate the healing process, as its high concentration of growth factors promotes cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. However, maintaining PRP at the target site over an extended period has proven challenging, as the rapid diffusion and degradation of growth factors necessitate multiple injections to achieve sustained therapeutic effects [27]. This practice not only introduces variability in GF levels but also increases patient discomfort and diminishes clinical predictability, prompting researchers to explore scaffold-based systems as an alternative means of PRP delivery. These systems aim to enhance the bioavailability of PRP's bioactive components while simultaneously addressing the limitations associated with rapid GF depletion, poor mechanical stability, and weak adhesion to tissue defects [27].Fig. 2Strategies for PRP incorporation in scaffolds for tissue engineering applications. PRP is either lyophilized to enhance shelf life and bioactivity before scaffold preparation (resulting in lyophilized PRP-loaded scaffolds) or directly incorporated into scaffolds through various methods. These methods include PRP gel formation via thrombin and CaCl2 activation, leading to PRP gel-loaded scaffolds, and protein cross-linking, resulting in PRP-based scaffolds with improved mechanical properties and sustained growth factor release. The use of synthetic, natural, or composite scaffolds enhances biocompatibility, mechanical stability, and regenerative efficiency, facilitating wound healing, osteogenesis, and tissue repair (Figure reprinted from Ref. [33], licensed under CC BY 4.0.).Fig. 2 One promising strategy involves the formation of solid PRP gels by mixing liquid PRP with exogenous activators such as thrombin, calcium salts, ascorbic acid, batroxobin, or collagen [87]. This process catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen into a fibrin network while activating platelets, thereby transforming PRP into a 3D scaffold capable of promoting wound healing and providing structural support for cells. For example, adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) have been successfully encapsulated in fibrin gel networks by adding thrombin and/or CaCl2 to PRP-cell solutions, creating a microenvironment conducive to cellular proliferation, migration, and differentiation [88]. Despite these benefits, PRP gels are hindered by uncontrolled GF release, limited mechanical stability, and suboptimal adhesion to tissue defects, which collectively reduce their regenerative efficiency and clinical applicability. To address these challenges, researchers have sought to enhance PRP's functional properties by incorporating it into synthetic, natural, or composite scaffolds, thereby improving the biocompatibility, bioactivity, and mechanical performance of the resulting biomaterials. PRP-loaded scaffolds facilitate a more controlled and sustained release of Growth factors and cytokines, mitigating the rapid depletion observed in conventional PRP gels and enhancing their therapeutic efficacy. Preclinical studies have demonstrated the utility of PRP-loaded composite films and hydrogels in promoting nerve regeneration and functional recovery, particularly in animal models of sciatic nerve injury and diabetic wound healing [89,90]. In parallel, the use of lyophilized PRP has garnered considerable interest due to its ability to extend PRP's shelf life while preserving its bioactivity. The freeze-drying process removes water from PRP, rendering it more stable for long-term storage without compromising its regenerative potential [91,92]. Comparative studies on 3D-printed Ti6Al4V scaffolds coated with either fresh or lyophilized PRP have revealed superior bone regeneration and osseointegration with the lyophilized PRP coating, underscoring the benefits of this preservation technique in bone tissue engineering [93]. Another innovative approach to enhancing PRP-based scaffold performance involves chemical cross-linking, wherein PRP proteins are stabilized through covalent cross-linking reactions to form hydrogels with improved mechanical strength and controlled GF release [94]. For instance, photo-crosslinkable PRP hydrogels synthesized using o-nitrobenzyl alcohol (NB)-modified hyaluronic acid (HA-NB) exhibit enhanced tissue adhesion and sustained GF release upon light exposure, making them particularly effective in cartilage tissue engineering [95]. Similarly, oxidized dextran (OD) has been employed as a cross-linking agent for platelet lysate (PL) proteins, resulting in cryogel scaffolds with interconnected macroporous structures that support stem cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation [96]. Recent advancements in PRP-based scaffold technology have further expanded the potential applications of these biomaterials in regenerative medicine. Biomineralized PL/OD cryogels, which mimic the biochemical and mechanical properties of the bone extracellular matrix, have demonstrated the ability to enhance osteogenic differentiation and angiogenesis, thereby promoting bone tissue regeneration [87]. In parallel, natural cross-linking agents such as genipin have been utilized to develop hybrid PL/HA-NH2 scaffolds, which facilitate MSCs attachment and proliferation while minimizing cytotoxicity [97]. Other innovative fabrication methods include the production of PRP-derived microbeads through fibrinogen polymerization and ionotropic gelation of alginate, which have shown potential in modular muscle tissue engineering due to their high surface area and tunable mechanical properties [98,99]. Photopolymerization techniques have also expanded the versatility of PRP-based scaffolds, as evidenced by the development of human methacryloyl platelet lysate (PLMA) hydrogels. These hydrogels, synthesized through ultraviolet (UV) light exposure, exhibit tunable mechanical characteristics and support in vivo-like cell invasion, making them suitable for diverse applications, including osteosarcoma modeling, bone tissue engineering, and 3D bioprinting [100,101]. The continuous evolution of PRP incorporation strategies in scaffold design underscores the growing potential of these biomaterials in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering. By optimizing scaffold composition, fabrication methods, and cross-linking strategies, researchers aim to enhance the bioactivity, mechanical properties, and clinical efficacy of PRP-based scaffolds. Such innovations have the potential to overcome the limitations of conventional PRP therapies, ultimately improving patient outcomes in a wide range of clinical contexts, from musculoskeletal and dental regeneration to wound healing and soft tissue repair. As the field advances, further research into the molecular mechanisms underlying PRP's regenerative effects and its interactions with various scaffold materials will be essential for the development of next-generation PRP-based delivery systems tailored to specific injury types and patient populations [33,102].

sections.section: Case studies: mechanism of PRP-containing scaffolds in wound healing
sections.text: In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of scaffolds for tissue engineering, particularly those incorporating platelet-rich plasma (PRP) to enhance wound healing and tissue regeneration. PRP-containing scaffolds have gained attention due to their ability to influence a variety of cellular processes essential for tissue repair, including cell proliferation, migration, adhesion, and apoptosis regulation. Additionally, these scaffolds have shown promise in promoting angiogenesis, modulating inflammation, and improving collagen deposition, all of which contribute to more effective wound healing. The controlled release of growth factors and optimization of mechanical properties are also critical factors in ensuring the efficacy of PRP-containing scaffolds. Fig. 3 illustrates the key cellular and biological processes influenced by PRP-containing scaffolds in wound healing, while Table 1 summarizes various PRP-integrated scaffolds, their compositions, experimental models, and key findings, highlighting their diverse applications in tissue engineering. PRP-containing scaffolds have emerged as a promising approach to enhance wound healing by promoting cell proliferation, migration, and adhesion. These scaffolds leverage the bioactive components of PRP to stimulate cellular processes crucial for tissue regeneration. Numerous studies have investigated the effects of PRP on different scaffold compositions, demonstrating its ability to enhance cell viability, modulate gene expression, and support extracellular matrix formation. This section synthesizes recent findings on the role of PRP-containing scaffolds in cellular behavior and their potential application in regenerative medicine.

The incorporation of PRP within collagen-glycosaminoglycan (GAG) scaffolds effectively promoted cell proliferation across various cell types involved in wound healing, often matching or surpassing proliferation observed in fetal bovine serum (FBS)-supplemented controls. Specifically, PRP-loaded composite scaffolds enhanced the proliferation of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) and BJ fibroblasts, while also supporting the proliferation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) in basal conditions. Additionally, PRP combined with gelatin-based scaffolds significantly increased mitochondrial activity over time, particularly when paired with photostimulation, leading to statistically significant increases in cell proliferation [103,104]. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analyses confirmed successful cell attachment, spreading, and increased extracellular matrix deposition, particularly in PRP-treated groups. Gene expression studies further supported these findings, revealing elevated expression levels of extracellular matrix-related genes, including collagen type IV (COL4), VEGF, and PDGF, all of which contribute to fibroblast proliferation and enhanced cellular activity [104]. PRP-containing scaffolds demonstrated significantly higher levels of Ki67-positive cells, indicating increased cell division and regenerative potential compared to unmodified scaffolds [105] (Fig. 4).Fig. 4Ki67 Staining of Proliferating Cells. High-magnification images are presented with corresponding colored frames following the overall morphological view. (II) Quantification of proliferating cells in the full-thickness skin graft layer. Cell migration, a critical factor in effective wound healing, has been evaluated using 3D core-and-shell models and in vitro scratch assays. PRP-containing scaffolds promoted greater cell migration, particularly in conjunction with photostimulation, facilitating the movement of fibroblasts into the scaffold structure. This effect was attributed to increased laminin expression and enhanced extracellular matrix formation, both of which support cell movement and integration [104]. In a separate study, PRP-integrated poly(glycerol sebacate)/polylactic acid (PGS/PLA) scaffolds significantly improved fibroblast (L929) migration, accelerating wound closure within 12–24 h. The enhanced migration was primarily driven by the release of key growth factors, including PDGF and VEGF, which play central roles in cell motility and tissue regeneration [106]. Notably, while PRP-containing scaffolds improved HaCaT and HUVEC migration, the impact on hMSCs and HACAT cell migration was minimal, suggesting that scaffold composition and PRP concentration influence migratory responses [103,105].

Beyond proliferation and migration, PRP-containing scaffolds have demonstrated excellent biocompatibility by enhancing cell adhesion. Fibroblasts exhibited strong adhesion to hydrogel surfaces, maintaining high viability and forming interconnected networks. Confocal microscopy confirmed that cells adhered along the macroporous scaffold structures, creating an environment conducive to effective tissue regeneration [107]. PRP-modified scaffolds also promoted better cell attachment by upregulating adhesion molecules and extracellular matrix components, further strengthening cellular integration within the scaffold [105].

sections.section: Mechanisms of PRP-induced proliferation and anti-apoptotic effects
sections.text: PRP-containing scaffolds enhance fibroblast proliferation by stimulating cell cycle progression and upregulating proliferation-associated genes. Fibroblasts treated with PRP exhibited a concentration-dependent increase in proliferation, with an optimal PRP concentration of 50 %. This effect was attributed to the upregulation of cyclin D1 and cyclin D3, which facilitate the transition from the G1 phase to the S phase of the cell cycle [108]. Additionally, PRP plays a crucial role in suppressing fibroblast apoptosis, thereby enhancing cell survival. Flow cytometry analysis revealed a significant reduction in apoptotic cells in PRP-treated groups, correlated with decreased expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax and increased levels of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. Moreover, adenosine, a key PRP component, contributed to fibroblast survival by activating the A2A receptor. Inhibition of this receptor impaired PRP's proliferative effects and increased apoptosis, highlighting the importance of adenosine signaling in PRP-mediated cellular protection [108]. PRP-containing scaffolds offer significant advantages for wound healing by enhancing cell proliferation, migration, and adhesion while simultaneously preventing apoptosis. These effects are mediated through the release of bioactive growth factors, modulation of gene expression, and the creation of a biomimetic extracellular matrix. The integration of PRP with various scaffold compositions, combined with external stimulatory strategies such as photostimulation, further optimizes these regenerative outcomes. Future research should focus on refining scaffold designs and optimizing PRP concentrations to maximize their clinical potential in wound healing applications.

Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, is a critical process in tissue regeneration and wound healing. PRP has emerged as a promising biomaterial for enhancing angiogenesis due to its rich reservoir of growth factors that promote vascularization. In recent years, various scaffold materials have been developed to incorporate PRP, aiming to optimize its bioactivity and therapeutic potential. This analysis explores the angiogenic efficacy of PRP-containing scaffolds across different material compositions, highlighting their impact on endothelial cell organization, neovascularization, and vascular stability. The incorporation of PRP into collagen-glycosaminoglycan (GAG) scaffolds demonstrated significant angiogenic potential, particularly at later time points. While initial endothelial tubular formation was lower than in controls, the composite scaffolds eventually developed well-structured and interconnected vascular networks. This delayed but enhanced angiogenesis underscores the role of PRP in sustained vascular growth, as confirmed by in vivo studies that showed significantly increased vascularization in surrounding tissues [103]. PRP-containing polydopamine-coated chitosan-silk fibroin (pDA-CSS@PRP) scaffolds also exhibited superior angiogenic performance. These scaffolds facilitated robust neovascularization under full-thickness skin grafts, evidenced by a greater number of newly formed blood vessels with extensive branching. Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed a significantly higher density of CD31-positive vascular structures, indicating improved blood supply to regenerating tissues. These results suggest that the sustained release of growth factors from PRP plays a crucial role in enhancing vascularization and accelerating wound healing [105] (Fig. 5). Similarly, PRP-loaded poly(glycerol sebacate)/polylactic acid (PGS/PLA) scaffolds significantly enhanced endothelial tube formation, branching, and total tube length in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Compared to control and PGS/PLA scaffolds alone, the PRP-containing version exhibited a markedly higher number of vascular loops and branching points. This suggests that the bioactive factors in PRP play a pivotal role in endothelial cell organization and neovascularization, essential for effective tissue regeneration [106]. Another notable scaffold, CBPGCTS-SF@PRP, outperformed PRP gel in promoting angiogenesis. This scaffold facilitated neovascularization with well-developed large-lumen structures and a stable blood vessel network. In contrast, the PRP gel degraded rapidly, leading to reduced bioactivity and less organized vascular growth. The increased angiogenic response observed with CBPGCTS-SF@PRP highlights its potential in soft tissue reconstruction, emphasizing the importance of scaffold stability for sustained growth factor release [109].Fig. 5In Vivo Angiogenesis Assessment.
