In summary, we designed and fabricated a copper single‐atom nanozyme‐based therapeutic nanoplatform, CBPV, by strategically integrating multifunctional components to achieve spatiotemporally controlled antimicrobial and tissue‐regenerative effects. The hierarchically porous carbon matrix of CBPV, derived from Cu/DA/F127 self‐assembly and pyrolysis, achieves two significant breakthroughs: it maintains 100% atomic dispersion of Cu‐N3 catalytic sites and exhibits superior photothermal conversion efficiency (η = 43.9%) under NIR‐II irradiation. This nanoarchitecture, featuring coordinatively unsaturated active copper sites, facilitates potent dual‐enzyme mimetic activity (POD and OXD), which drives the simultaneous generation of ROS, NO, and RNS through thermally amplified cascade reactions. By synergizing Van‐mediated targeting with NIR‐II‐responsive PTT, CDT, and NO therapy, the CBPV platform demonstrates complete biofilm eradication via ONOO−/hyperthermia dual attack mechanism, accelerated diabetic wound closure by modulating the inflammatory microenvironment and promoting NO‐mediated angiogenesis, and deep‐tissue sterilization capability enabled by superior NIR‐II laser penetration depth. The combination of multi‐modal sterilization methods in the CBPV nanoplatform effectively overcomes the limitations of traditional single‐modal antimicrobial methods. Significantly, the demonstrated spatiotemporal control of biocatalysis, photothermal, and gas therapeutics provides a blueprint for developing intelligent nanozyme‐based systems in precision medicine. Overall, this work not only advances the fundamental understanding of multi‐enzyme mimicking nanomaterials but also establishes a versatile therapeutic platform for managing complex infections, with immediate implications for diabetic wound care and deep‐seated biofilm eradication.

Experimental details, including materials, instruments, photothermal performance, and photothermal stability experiments, bacterial culture, bacterial ROS level detection, biocompatibility assessment of nanomaterials, and statistical analysis, are listed in the Supporting Information.

First, 1.0 g of Pluronic F127 and 0.5 g of DA were added to a 100 mL mixture of water and ethanol (water: ethanol = 1: 1) under ultrasound to ensure thorough dissolution. Then, 1.3 mg (0.005 mmol) of Cu(C5H7O2)2 was added and dissolved completely. Under stirring conditions, 2 mL of MES was slowly added to the solution, and the reaction took 30 min to obtain an emulsion. Next, 5 mL of NH3·H2O was added slowly, and the mixture was stirred for 60 min. The resultant product, Cu/PDA/F127, was collected by centrifugation at 10 000 rpm for 10 min and washed three times with anhydrous ethanol. The product was then placed in a vacuum‐drying oven and heated at 60 °C overnight. Following this, the dried Cu/PDA/F127 was transferred to a tubular furnace and heated under nitrogen flow at 350 °C for 3 h with a heating rate of 1 °C per min, followed by calcination at 800 °C for 2 h with the same heating rate. After cooling, the calcinated sample was added to the hydrochloric acid (0.5 M), and the mixture was stirred in an oil bath at 60 °C for 24 h to obtain mCu‐SAE after filtration. To prepare the CBPV, Van (30 mg, 0.02 mmol), EDC (80 mg, 0.4 mmol), and NHS (60 mg, 0.5 mmol) were dissolved in 1 mL of ultrapure water. The mixture was allowed to activate for 1 h. Subsequently, MPEG5000‐NH2 (60 mg, 0.01 mmol) was introduced, and the mixture was stirred for 6 h. Afterward, the mixture underwent dialysis for 3 days to purify PEG‐Van. BNN6 was subsequently loaded into mCu‐SAE via the anti‐solvent crystallization method. Specifically, 10 mg BNN6 was dissolved in 0.5 mL ethanol, followed by a dropwise addition of 10 mL mCu‐SAE (0.5 mg mL−1) aqueous solution under continuous stirring. The mixture was equilibrated for 12 h to facilitate efficient drug loading through controlled crystalline deposition. The synthesized PEG‐Van was then added to the mixture and stirred overnight. Excess reactants were removed by centrifugation at 10 000 rpm for 10 min. The product was then washed three times with ethanol and ultrapure water to yield pure CBPV.

this study utilized MB and TMB to evaluate the •OH generation capacity of NPs. For the TMB assay, solutions with a gradient of NP concentrations (0, 25, 50, 100, and 200 µg mL−1) were prepared. Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) at a concentration of 1 mMM and TMB at 0.02 M were added to these solutions, and the mixtures were incubated for a specified period. The changes in absorbance were measured using a UV–vis spectrophotometer. Additionally, the effect of different concentrations of H2O2 (0, 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 mm) on the generation of •OH was assessed using the same method. To further validate the photothermal promotion of •OH production, TMB colorimetric reactions were conducted both with and without laser irradiation. For the MB experiment, solutions with a similar concentration gradient of NPs (0, 25, 50, 100, and 200 µg mL−1) were prepared. H2O2 at 1 mM and MB at 15.6 µM were added to these solutions, followed by a brief incubation period. The changes in absorbance were again detected using a UV–vis spectrophotometer.
The Michaelis–Menten constant (Km) and maximum velocity (Vmax) were determined based on the Michaelis–Menten saturation curve.

This study used BQ and a superoxide anion detection kit to measure •O2 − production. Two identical test tubes were prepared, each containing CBPV, H2O2, and MB. BQ was added to one of the test tubes, and both tubes were then incubated at 37 °C for a specified period. The changes in absorbance for both tubes were subsequently measured using a UV–vis spectrophotometer. Additionally, the •O2 − detection kit was employed to quantify •O2 − production. A series of samples with varying concentrations of CBPV (12.5, 25, 50, 100, and 200 µg mL−1) were prepared. The experimental protocol provided by the kit was followed, and the absorbance of each sample was measured at 530 nm using a UV–vis spectrophotometer. The •O2 − content for each concentration was determined by using a standard curve generated from standard solutions.

CBPV were dispersed in deionized water at various concentrations (25, 50, 100, 150, and 200 µg mL−1). The samples were then irradiated with a NIR laser (1064 nm, 1.25 W cm−2) for 10 min, followed by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 10 min. Subsequently, 50 µL of the supernatant was collected, and the NO release under laser irradiation for each concentration was detected using the Griess assay kit. Similarly, the effects of various incubation intervals (0, 10, 20, 40, 60, 120, 240, and 360 min) at 37 °C and different laser irradiation durations (0, 1, 3, 5, 7, and 10 min) on NO release were evaluated. Additionally, the impact of different laser power settings (0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, and 2 W cm−2) on NO release was assessed, as well as the changes in NO release at room temperature over varying incubation intervals (0, 1, 3, 5, 7, and 10 min). Additionally, the DAF‐FM DA fluorescent probe was employed to investigate the NO release properties. DAF‐FM DA (5 µL, 5 µM) was mixed with varying concentrations of CBPV (0, 25, 50, 100, 150, and 200 µg mL−1), and NO production was analyzed using a fluorescence spectrophotometer after laser irradiation for a consistent duration.

Dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR123) serves as a fluorescent probe exhibiting preferential oxidation kinetics toward ONOO− over other ROS, generating rhodamine 123 with significantly enhanced quantum yield. For quantitative analysis, DHR123 (5 µM) was reacted with test materials and H2O2 (100 µL, 1 mM) at 37 °C for 60 min, followed by spectrofluorometric quantification. Complementarily, spatiotemporal ONOO− generation during bactericidal activity was monitored by co‐incubating DHR123 with H2O2, nanomaterials, and bacteria for a specified period before the confocal imaging using a Leica STELLARIS 8 STED system with 63 × oil immersion objective.

The fluorescent dye Rhodamine B (RhB) was used to label various NPs. By stirring RhB (5 mg) with 5 mL of the mCu‐SAE (1 mg mL−1), CB@PEG (1 mg mL−1), or CBPV (1 mg mL−1) aqueous solution for 12 h and then washing with deionized water until the supernatant is colorless, NPs with fluorescent emission capabilities are obtained. The RhB‐labeled NPs (1 mg mL−1, 200 µL) were then added to 100 µL of a bacterial suspension and 700 µL of PBS in a 1 mL centrifuge tube and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. After incubation, the mixture was centrifuged at 8,000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was removed. The pellet was treated with 400 µL of DAPI and incubated at room temperature for 2 h. Following this, the sample was washed three times with PBS. Finally, the pellet was resuspended in 20 µL of PBS, and 10 µL of the resuspended sample was placed on a microscope slide for observation using a Leica‐CS‐SP8‐STED LSCM.

The in vitro antibacterial activity of CBPV was evaluated using the agar plate method. E. coli or MRSA (1 mL, 1 × 10⁷ CFU mL−1) cell suspension and NPs (1 mL, 50 µg mL−1) were mixed. The experiment was conducted using twelve different treatment methods, as follows: 1) PBS treatment alone, 2) 1064 nm laser irradiation (1.25 W cm−2) of PBS‐treated bacteria, 3) 250 µM H2O2 treatment, 4) 1064 nm laser irradiation (1.25 W cm−2) of H2O2‐treated bacteria, 5) co‐treatment with 50 µg mL−1 mCu‐SAE and 250 µM H2O2, 6) 1064 nm laser irradiation (1.25 W cm−2) of mCu‐SAE and H2O2 co‐treated bacteria, 7) co‐treatment with 50 µg mL−1 NMCNPs@BNN6 NPs and 250 µM H2O2, 8) 1064 nm laser irradiation (1.25 W cm−2) of NMCNPs@BNN6 NPs and H2O2 co‐treated bacteria, 9) co‐treatment with 50 µg mL−1 CB NPs and 250 µM H2O2, 10) 1064 nm laser irradiation (1.25 W cm−2) of CB NPs and H2O2 co‐treated bacteria, 11) co‐treatment with 50 µg mL−1 CBPV and 250 µM H2O2, and 12) 1064 nm laser irradiation (1.25 W cm−2) of CBPV and H2O2 co‐treated bacteria. After treatment, each group was incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. Subsequently, the cell suspensions were diluted with PBS, and 40 µL of the diluted suspension was evenly spread on solid LB agar plates. The plates were inverted, sealed, and incubated at 37 °C overnight. The following day, the agar plates were photographed, and colony counts were recorded.

After grouping and treating the samples using the agar plate method, they were incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. The samples were then centrifuged at 8,000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded. Following this, 10 µL of SYTO‐9 and 10 µL of PI were added, and the mixture was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. SYTO‐9 stains both live and dead bacteria green, while PI specifically stains only dead bacteria red. The samples were washed three times with PBS, and 10 µL of the stained bacterial suspension was transferred onto a glass slide. Finally, the staining was observed using LSCM to assess the antibacterial activity of the different functions of CBPV.

One milliliter of E. coli or MRSA (1 × 108 CFU mL−1) was added to the confocal dish and incubated at 37 °C for 48 h, with the LB liquid medium being changed every 12 h. The biofilm was then washed three times with sterile PBS. Following this, the samples were grouped and treated according to the agar plate method and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. The live and dead bacteria on the biofilm were stained using SYTO‐9 and PI. After a 30‐min incubation at 37 °C, the excess dye was washed away with sterile PBS. Finally, LSCM was used to observe the extent of biofilm disruption in each group.

First, E. coli or MRSA was diluted in a liquid LB medium to achieve the appropriate concentration. The samples were grouped and treated using the agar plate method, then incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. Next, 500 µL of the treated bacterial suspension was added to poly‐L‐lysine‐coated cell coverslips. After incubating at 37 °C for 12 h, the supernatant was removed. The bacteria were then fixed by adding 200 µL of 2.5% glutaraldehyde and incubating for at least 6 h. Following fixation, gradient dehydration was carried out using ethanol at various concentrations. Finally, SEM was used to observe the bacterial morphology in each group.

We investigated the impact of CBPV on the migratory behavior of vascular cells using in vitro scratch assays and Transwell migration assays. Initially, a cell scratch assay was performed. L929 cells were cultured in 12‐well plates until they reached 90% confluence. Subsequently, a cell‐free wound was generated in each well using a 200 µL sterile pipette tip. Following multiple washes with PBS, mCu‐SAE, CB, and CBPV (1 mL, 25 µg mL−1) were added to the respective groups. Cell migration was subsequently monitored at predetermined time intervals using an inverted fluorescence microscope. To further assess the impact of NO released from CBPV on the migratory behavior of vascular cells, Transwell migration assays were conducted. HUVECs (1 × 104 cells well−1) were suspended in 100 µL of DMEM medium containing 25 µg mL−1 NPs and 1% FBS. Subsequently, the cells were seeded in the upper chamber of the Transwell, while DMEM (1 mL, containing 20% FBS) was added to the lower chamber. Following a 24‐h incubation at 37 °C and 5% CO2, non‐migrated cells remaining on the upper layer were gently removed with a cotton swab. The cells that migrated to the lower surface of the Transwell were then stained with a 1% crystal violet solution and visualized using an inverted fluorescence microscope.

Matrigel was coated onto 12‐well plates and allowed to solidify for 30 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, HUVECs (2 × 104 cells well−1) were seeded in each well and cultured in serum‐free DMEM supplemented with 25 µg mL−1 NPs. After incubation for 6 h in an incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2, the cells were imaged using an inverted fluorescence microscope.

All animal experiments were carried out with the permission of the Institutional Animal Protection and Utilization Committee of Wuhan University in China (Approval Number: WQ20210366). All procedures followed the animal ethical standards.

A type 1 diabetes mouse model was established using 4‐5‐week‐old, 18–20 g female Kunming mice (Henan Skobes Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China). First, the mice, which had been fasted overnight, were injected with alloxan (10 mg mL−1) at a dosage of 150 mg kg−1 for three consecutive days. After the three‐day injection period, blood glucose levels were measured. Successful establishment of the type 1 diabetes mouse model is indicated by fasting blood glucose levels >11 mmol L−1 within one week.

An epidermal wound infection model was established in mice with successfully induced diabetes. A full‐thickness circular wound with a diameter of 8 mm was created on the back of each mouse. Following this, 100 µL of MRSA (1 × 107 CFU mL−1) was inoculated onto the wound to establish the epidermal wound infection model, with day 0 designated as the establishment day. The diabetic mice were randomly divided into six groups (n = 10): Group 1 (PBS treatment), Group 2 (PBS + laser treatment), Group 3 (mCu‐SAE treatment), Group 4 (mCu‐SAE + laser treatment), Group 5 (CBPV treatment), and Group 6 (CBPV + laser treatment). Treatments were administered on days 1 and 3, and wound temperature changes were recorded using a photothermal imaging system. Mouse body weight and infection wound status were monitored on days 1, 3, 7, 9, and 13. On day 3 after treatment, exudates from the wounds in each group were plated to observe bacterial growth at the wound sites. Epidermal tissue samples were collected on days 3, 7, and 13 for H&E staining, Masson staining, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence experiments to evaluate wound healing. To assess the toxicity of the treatments, major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys) along with whole blood and serum were collected on day 13 for H&E staining, complete blood count, and liver and kidney function tests.

A subcutaneous cyst infection model was established in mice with successfully induced diabetes. The diabetic mice were randomly divided into six groups (n = 10): Group 1 (PBS treatment), Group 2 (PBS + laser treatment), Group 3 (mCu‐SAE treatment), Group 4 (mCu‐SAE + laser treatment), Group 5 (CBPV treatment), and Group 6 (CBPV + laser treatment). A 100 µL mixture of bacteria and mineral oil (1:1) was injected into the backs of the mice in each group to establish the subcutaneous cyst infection model, with day 0 designated as the establishment day. Treatments were administered on days 1 and 3, and changes in cyst temperature were recorded using a photothermal imaging system. Mouse body weight and changes in subcutaneous cyst size were monitored on days 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11. On day 11, bacteria from the cyst site were plated to observe the residual bacterial count. On days 7 and 11, skin tissue surrounding the cyst was collected for H&E staining, Masson staining, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence assays to evaluate the skin recovery around the cyst. On the final day, the main organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys), as well as whole blood and serum, were collected. H&E staining, complete blood count, and liver and kidney function tests were performed to evaluate the biosafety of the entire treatment process.

All data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD) and were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 8 software. Each experiment was performed with at least three replicates, and t‐tests were used to determine statistical differences between groups. A p < 0.05 is considered indicative of a significant difference, with significance levels denoted as *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, and ***p < 0.001.

title: Lactobacillus extracellular vesicle-driven oxygen-releasing photothermal hydrogel reprograms macrophages and promotes angiogenesis to accelerate diabetic wound healing
abstract: Chronic wound healing remains clinically challenging due to insufficient angiogenesis coupled with persistent inflammatory microenvironments. Macrophage M2 polarization plays a pivotal role in resolving inflammation and promoting angiogenesis. Capitalizing on scalability and translational advantages, extracellular vesicles derived from Lactobacillus bulgaricus (Lac-EVs) were employed to activate this mechanism. The anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic efficacy of Lac-EVs was initially confirmed through in vitro experiments. To support their delivery and function within the hostile diabetic wound microenvironment, a chitosan (CS)-based hydrogel incorporating haemoglobin (Hb)-polydopamine (PDA) complexes was engineered via Schiff base crosslinking with aldehyde-functionalised polyethylene glycol (CHO-PEG-CHO). This platform enabled stable delivery of Lac-EVs, supplemental oxygen release, and NIR-triggered photothermal functionality. In vitro studies demonstrated that the Lac-EVs-laden hydrogel (PCPH@Lac-EVs) effectively induced M2 macrophage polarization, enhanced endothelial cell migration, and promoted angiogenesis. In murine full-thickness diabetic wounds, PCPH@Lac-EVs combined with NIR irradiation achieved 99.3 % wound closure within 13 days, significantly outperforming untreated controls (72.3 %). Mechanistic analysis indicated that the accelerated healing resulted from synergistic enhancement of Lac-EV-mediated inflammation modulation and functional angiogenesis via oxygen release and mild photothermal stimulation. This study highlights the potential of Lac-EVs, delivered via a functional hydrogel, as a promising therapeutic strategy for diabetic wound treatment. sections.text: Diabetes has emerged as a global health crisis, with chronic hyperglycaemia leading to systemic physiological damage [1,2]. Among its complications, impaired wound healing is particularly severe, significantly affecting patients' quality of life [3]. A key barrier is disrupted angiogenesis driven by persistent inflammation [4], where hyperglycaemia inhibits M2 macrophage polarization, sustaining a pro-inflammatory microenvironment. Current evidence suggests that reprogramming macrophages toward the M2 phenotype can mitigate inflammation, promote angiogenesis, and accelerate wound closure [5]. This macrophage-focused strategy forms a strong therapeutic basis for diabetic wound healing. While extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from mammalian cells (e.g., bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, M2 macrophages) show promise in promoting M2 polarization and angiogenesis [6,7], their application is limited by ethical concerns, complex extraction processes, and scalability issues [8]. In contrast, EVs derived from Lactobacillus bulgaricus (Lac-EVs) offer a promising alternative, with advantages in terms of mass production via cost-effective fermentation and standardized purification protocols. Functionally, Lac-EVs have demonstrated potential to enhance angiogenesis and accelerate wound healing [9]. Notably, Lactobacillus bulgaricus itself promotes M2 polarization, a mechanism validated in models such as colitis [[10], [11], [12]]. This suggests that Lac-EVs, as carriers of the bacterium's biological activity, may similarly modulate immune responses. Thus, exploring the capacity of Lac-EVs to reprogram macrophages in the context of diabetic wound inflammation is well-justified. Harnessing Lac-EVs for macrophage modulation presents a promising strategy for immune regulation and wound therapy, leveraging both their therapeutic function and production feasibility. However, the low bioavailability of EVs in vivo highlights the need for an efficient delivery system. Hydrogels are promising candidates owing to their ability to encapsulate bioactive agents and maintain a moist healing environment [13]. Chitosan (CS), a naturally derived polysaccharide, has been widely studied for hydrogel wound dressings because of its excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability [14,15]. The cationic nature of CS supports electrostatic loading of EVs [2,16], and its abundant amino groups allow for chemical modification and dynamic crosslinking via reversible Schiff base reactions with aldehyde-functionalised compounds. These reactions enable hydrogel formation under mild conditions without external initiators. The resulting hydrogels possess self-healing properties and can conform to irregular wound surfaces, making them suitable for sustained Lac-EV delivery [17,18]. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of Lac-EV therapy is further challenged by chronic hypoxia in diabetic wounds. This hostile environment impairs angiogenesis and macrophage activity, ultimately hindering inflammation resolution and tissue regeneration [19]. Therefore, co-delivering oxygen is essential to support the full therapeutic potential of Lac-EVs. Various oxygen carriers have been developed to address hypoxia [20,21], among which haemoglobin (Hb)—a natural oxygen transporter—stands out because of its high oxygen-binding affinity and biocompatibility [22]. However, integrating Hb into CS hydrogels remains difficult owing to weak physical interactions, which lead to rapid Hb leakage and reduced efficacy. Polydopamine (PDA), rich in catechol and amine groups, can form stable interactions with Hb through π–π stacking and hydrogen bonding, enabling effective incorporation into hydrogel networks. This stabilizes Hb, supports sustained oxygen release, and enhances Lac-EV function [23,24]. PDA also possesses strong photothermal conversion under 808 nm near-infrared (NIR) light, inducing mild hyperthermia (∼42 °C) that promotes endothelial cell proliferation and neovascularization [[25], [26], [27], [28]]. Additionally, the localized heat enhances circulation, accelerates metabolic waste clearance, suppresses excessive inflammation, and facilitates tissue repair [29]. PDA's intrinsic immunomodulatory properties, including promotion of M2 polarization and mesenchymal stem cell paracrine activity, further contribute to wound healing. Its catechol groups also confer strong tissue adhesion, ensuring long-lasting hydrogel retention and local Lac-EV delivery [[30], [31], [32], [33]]. Hence, to synergistically enhance the delivery, microenvironmental support, and efficacy of the therapeutic agent Lac-EVs in the challenging diabetic wound, we developed an injectable chitosan-based hydrogel PEG-CS-PDA-Hb@Lac-EV (PCPH@Lac-EVs) for co-delivery of Lac-EVs and oxygen (Scheme 1). The hydrogel was fabricated in two steps: (1) formation of a CS-PDA-Hb precursor via Schiff base and Michael addition reactions, with Hb complexed by PDA; (2) mixing with CHO-PEG-CHO and Lac-EVs to achieve final crosslinking. PDA provided tissue adhesion and photothermal responsiveness, while dynamic Schiff base bonds endowed the hydrogel with self-healing ability. Functionally, sustained Lac-EVs release induced M2 macrophage polarization, supported by oxygen and NIR-stimulated angiogenesis, collectively promoting tissue remodeling. This multifunctional platform, centered on Lac-EVs-mediated macrophage reprogramming and enhanced by oxygen delivery and mild photothermal therapy, shows strong potential for clinical translation in diabetic wound treatment.Scheme 1(a) Synthesis diagram of injectable PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (b) Physical properties illustration of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (c) Diabetic wound healing mechanism of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel through supplying O2, slowly releasing Lac-EVs and producing mild photothermal to promote angiogenesis.Scheme 1

sections.section: Extraction and functional evaluation of Lac-EVs
sections.text: The bacterial strain was first identified by observing typical circular colonies with smooth, entire margins and moist surfaces on MRS agar plates (Fig. 1a). This morphological profile, together with Gram staining that revealed short, rod-shaped, Gram-positive bacilli consistent with the Lactobacillus genus (Fig. 1b), confirmed the identity of the strain as Lactobacillus. Lac-EVs were subsequently extracted from Lactobacillus bulgaricus. Microscopic examination revealed vesicles exhibiting characteristic bilayer membrane structures (Fig. 1c). Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) demonstrated a single-peak size distribution (Fig. 1d), indicating excellent vesicle uniformity. Collectively, the morphological features, Gram staining, bilayer membrane integrity, and monodisperse size distribution conclusively verified the identity and purity of the extracted Lac-EVs, with no significant contaminants detected.Fig. 1Characterization biological properties of Lac-EVs. (a) Growth of colonies on MRS agar medium; (b) Gram staining results. Scale bar, 50 μm. (c) Micrograph of obtained Lac-EVs by TEM. Scale bar, 100 μm. (d) Particle size distribution as measured by NTA. (e) Photographs of HUVECs cells migration by scratch test after 36 h incubation at different Lac-EVs treatments concentration (3.5 μg/mL, 7 μg/mL, 10.5 μg/mL). Scale bar, 300 μm. (f) Tube formation results of HUVECs at different Lac-EVs treatments concentration (3.5 μg/mL, 7 μg/mL, 10.5 μg/mL). Scale bar, 150 μm. (g) Quantitative analysis for migration ratio of HUVECs cells after 36 h incubation (n = 3). (h) Quantification of nodes number, and (i) Total capillary length of HUVEC (n = 3). The levels of (j) pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α) and (k) anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10) in Raw264.7 macrophages treated with Lac-EVs at different concentrations. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analysis: ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001.Fig. 1 The pro-angiogenic effects of Lac-EVs were evaluated in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Migration assays revealed that Lac-EVs enhanced cell motility in a concentration-dependent manner, with a 10.5 μg/mL treatment producing the most pronounced pro-migratory effect (Fig. 1e). Similarly, in vitro tube formation assays showed that Lac-EVs promoted vascular network complexity in a dose-dependent fashion (Fig. 1f). Quantitative analysis also showed that at 10.5 μg/mL, Lac-EVs have the best effect on promoting migration and vascularization (Fig. 1g–i). To assess the immunomodulatory activity of Lac-EVs, macrophages were treated with increasing concentrations (3.5, 7.5, and 10.5 μg/mL). Cytokine level revealed that TNF-α was significantly suppressed and IL-10 expression was markedly elevated across these concentrations, demonstrating a robust immunomodulatory effect. (Fig. 1j and k). Next, The TLR-4/NF-κB pathway, a central regulator of macrophage polarization [34], was investigated to elucidate the molecular basis of these functional changes. The qRT-PCR results showed that LPS stimulation significantly increased the gene expression of TLR-4 and NF-κB in macrophages. Following Lac-EVs intervention, both genes exhibited concentration-dependent suppression, with the most pronounced inhibitory effect observed at the concentration of 10.5 μg/ml (Fig. S1a and S1b). Western blot quantification demonstrated decreased p-NF-κB/NF-κB ratio in Lac-EVs-treated macrophages (0.07) compared to control (0.09) and LPS-stimulated groups (0.10), indicating attenuated phosphorylation of NF-κB following 10.5 μg/ml Lac-EVs intervention (Fig. S1c). These findings demonstrate that Lac-EVs possess potent pro-angiogenic and immunomodulatory capabilities, both of which display concentration-dependent efficacy. Therefore, 10.5 μg/mL was selected as the optimal working concentration for subsequent experiments.

sections.section: Synthesis and characterization of PCPH@Lac-EVs Hydrogel
sections.text: To fabricate a Lac-EVs delivery hydrogel, the precursor CS-PDA-Hb was first synthesized through dopamine self-polymerization, Michael addition between chitosan and polydopamine, and Hb complexation with PDA. This precursor was then crosslinked with CHO-PEG-CHO via Schiff base chemistry to yield PEG-CS-PDA-Hb (PCPH) hydrogels. Infrared (IR) spectroscopy of PCPH revealed distinct peaks for the amide bond (1541 cm−1, from Hb), CH2 (1693 cm−1, from CHO-PEG-CHO), and the Schiff base bond (1655 cm−1), confirming successful hydrogel synthesis (Fig. 2a). UV–Vis spectra of both CS-PDA-Hb and PCPH displayed the characteristic Hb absorbance peak at 406 nm, further validating Hb encapsulation (Fig. S2a). In the 1H NMR spectrum of CS-PDA-Hb (red line, Fig. S2b), peaks at 6.6–6.9 ppm were attributed to aromatic (Ar) protons from the PDA benzene ring and Hb porphyrin rings, while signals at 3.1 ppm and 2.8 ppm were assigned to methylene groups on the PDA side chain, confirming covalent PDA incorporation. For PCPH (blue line, Fig. S2b), new peaks emerged at 8.0 ppm (Schiff base proton, –N=CH–), 4.0 ppm (adjacent –CH2–N = ), and 3.5 ppm (–O–CH2– from PEG), while the aromatic protons shifted to 6.5–6.8 ppm, reflecting microenvironmental changes from PEG crosslinking. These NMR and UV–Vis findings collectively verified successful hydrogel formation. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) further supported this: nitrogen content increased from 8.96 % in CS to 12.52 % in CS-PDA-Hb owing to PDA and Hb incorporation, then dropped to 2.58 % in PCPH owing to dilution by PEG (Fig. S2c and S2d). High-resolution C 1s spectra showed peaks at 284.8 eV (C-C/C-H), 286.2 eV (C-O/C-N), and 287.1 eV (C=O/C=N). N 1s spectra displayed peaks at 399.6 eV (-NH-/C-N) and 400.2 eV (C=N), the latter confirming Schiff base formation (Fig. S2e and S2f).Fig. 2(a) Infrared (IR) spectrometry of CS, CS-PDA-Hb and PCPH. (b) Photograph of gel-sol transition process from PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (c) Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of PCPH hydrogel (i-iii) and PCPH@Lac-EVs (iv-vi) hydrogel at different magnifications. (d) Fluorescence microscope photographs of PCPH hydrogel (i) and PCPH hydrogel contained Lac-EVs labeled with PKH26 (ii). (e) The injectability demonstration of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (f) Swelling ratio of PCPH hydrogel and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (g) Degradation behavior of PCPH hydrogel and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel.Fig. 2 The PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogels were obtained by incorporating Lac-EVs during gelation (Fig. 2b). Fluorescence spectrophotometry determined encapsulation efficiency to be 74.9 %. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of both PCPH and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogels showed a porous 3D architecture (Fig. 2c). PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogels had rougher surfaces, likely due to the loading of Lac-EVs. Fluorescence imaging of PKH26-labeled Lac-EVs further confirmed uniform vesicle distribution throughout the matrix (Fig. 2d), demonstrating successful encapsulation. Additionally, the hydrogel demonstrated excellent injectability and could be extruded to form a distinct “NIN” pattern using a syringe, illustrating its adaptability to irregular wound surfaces (Fig. 2e). Swelling studies showed that both PCPH and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogels followed similar trends and reached equilibrium within 40 min (Fig. 2f), indicating their ability to absorb wound exudate and enable sustained Lac-EVs release. Given that biodegradability is crucial for wound healing applications, hydrogel degradation was evaluated under simulated physiological conditions over 14 days. As shown in Fig. 2g, both hydrogels displayed clear degradability. Interestingly, Lac-EVs-loaded hydrogels degraded faster during the initial phase, likely due to partial disruption of crosslinks by Lac-EVs incorporation.

Self-healing property is crucial for a hydrogel's structural stability under mechanical stress and normal peristaltic movements during wound repair. This property is endowed by dynamic Schiff base bonds, as verified through cyclic strain tests and macroscopic observations. Strain scanning analysis of PCPH and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogels showed that the incorporation of Lac-EVs had no significant adverse effect on the rheological behaviour of the hydrogels. The intersection point (G′ = G″, critical strain) was observed at 1276 % for PCPH and 994 % for PCPH@Lac-EVs (Fig. 3a), beyond which the hydrogel network disintegrated into a fluid state. Based on this, cyclic strain tests were conducted at 5 % and 1500 %. Results showed that both PCPH and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogels transitioned into a liquid-like sol state (G′ < G″) under high strain (1500 %) and quickly recovered into a solid-like gel state (G′ > G″) at low strain (5 %) across multiple cycles (Fig. 3b and c).This reversible behaviour is attributed to the dynamic nature of Schiff base bonds—these bonds dissociate under high shear strain, causing network disintegration, and rapidly reform under low strain to restore structure (Fig. 3d). Visual observations further confirmed that the hydrogels could self-heal after physical damage (Fig. 3e). These findings indicate that the hydrogels possess strong self-healing ability, and that Lac-EVs incorporation does not compromise this function.Fig. 3(a) Strain scanning of PCPH and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel in the range of 5 % ∼ 1500 %. (b–c) Rheological time sweep under cyclic low-high shear strain of PCPH (b) and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel (c) during five cycles between 5 % and 1500 % strain. (d) Illustration of the self-healing process of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (e) Macroscopic observation of the self-healing effect of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel. (f) Adhesion mechanism of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel on tissue surface. (g) Photographs of the PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel onto porcine tissue, which remains adhered to the tissue after bending, distorting, squeezing, stretching, and rinsing with PBS. (h) Lac-EVs release curves of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel via photothermal treatment in simulated physiological conditions. (i) Oxygen-supply ability of pure Hb, PCP@Lac-EVs, PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel and PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel after NIR irradiation determined by the enhancement of oxygen concentration in oxygen-presaturated PBS after corresponding treatments with equivalent amount of Hb. (j) Temperature change curves with time as well as the corresponding photothermal images of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel and PBS under NIR irradiation. (k) Temperature change curves with time of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel under different power NIR irradiation. (l) Photothermal stability of PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel after five times on-off cycles of NIR irradiation.Fig. 3 In addition, adhesive properties are critical for wound applications. The catechol and quinone groups in PDA facilitate strong adhesion by forming non-covalent (hydrogen bonding) and covalent interactions with nucleophilic groups (e.g., amino and sulfhydryl) present in tissues, resulting in stable anchoring (Fig. 3f). This tissue adhesion was demonstrated by in situ gelation of the hydrogel on porcine muscle tissue. As shown in Fig. 3g, the hydrogel remained firmly adhered despite bending, twisting, compressing, stretching, and PBS washing. Such robust adhesion ensures close contact with the wound surface, helping maintain a moist environment and preventing bacterial invasion. To reduce local inflammation and promote angiogenesis in diabetic wounds, the PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel must retain and steadily release Lac-EVs. Therefore, the release kinetics were assessed under both NIR and non-NIR conditions in a simulated physiological setting. As shown in Fig. 3h, Lac-EVs were released continuously for about 7 days in both conditions, with final release efficiencies exceeding 80 %, and no notable difference between groups, suggesting that NIR does not alter the release profile. Next, the oxygen-release capacity of the hydrogel was studied by monitoring dissolved oxygen in deoxygenated PBS (Fig. 3i). Pure Hb served as a positive control, and PBS or PEG-CS-PDA (PCP) hydrogel without Hb as negative controls. Oxygen concentration in the PCPH@Lac-EVs group steadily increased to ∼5 mg/L, closely matching the value from pure Hb, while PBS and PCP showed no increase. These findings confirm that Hb retains its oxygen-carrying capacity when encapsulated in the hydrogel. Moreover, the oxygen concentrations in NIR-irradiated samples were comparable to non-irradiated ones, indicating that NIR exposure does not compromise oxygen delivery capacity. Because of the excellent photothermal conversion capacity of PDA, the hydrogel heats up under 808 nm NIR irradiation. After 5 min of NIR exposure, the hydrogel temperature rose by ∼10 °C, while PBS showed no change (Fig. 3j). Thermal imaging (inset, Fig. 3j) further confirmed effective photothermal conversion. Increasing laser power from 0.7 W/cm2 to 1.2 W/cm2 elevated the temperature from 8.1 °C to 21.8 °C, demonstrating tuneable photothermal behaviour (Fig. 3k). Based on these findings and the risk of thermal injury to skin, 0.7 W/cm2 was chosen as the optimal NIR power. Additionally, the hydrogel maintained consistent heating across five on/off cycles, demonstrating reliable and repeatable photothermal performance (Fig. 3l).

sections.section: In vitro regenerative and anti-inflammatory effects evaluation of PCPH@Lac-EVs Hydrogel
sections.text: First, the safety of NIR treatment was verified. As shown in Fig. S3, NIR alone exhibited no significant cytotoxicity toward HUVECs, RAW 264.7 macrophages, or HFB fibroblasts. Likewise, the PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group (with temperature elevation to ∼42 °C) showed no cytotoxicity but significantly enhanced cell proliferation compared to PBS, confirming that the NIR conditions used were safe. Next, hydrogel cytocompatibility was evaluated. CCK-8 results (Fig. 4a) confirmed that all hydrogel formulations promoted HUVEC proliferation. Additional testing with degradation products (Fig. S4) further confirmed hydrogel biosafety.Fig. 4(a) The cell viability of HUVEC cells were measured in each group after 24 h and 48 h of cell culture (n = 3). (b) PKH26 labeled Lac-EVs loaded on the hydrogel taken up by HaCat cells. (c) Photographs of HUVECs cells migration by scratch test after 36 h incubation. Scale bar, 300 μm. (d) In vitro tube formation results of HUVECs with different treatments. Scale bar, 150 μm. (e) Quantitative analysis for migration ratio of HUVECs cells after 36 h incubation (n = 3). (f) Quantification of nodes number, and (g) Total capillary length of HUVEC (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analysis: ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001. I: PBS, II: PCP, III: PCPH, IV: PCPH@Lac-EVs, V: PCPH@Lac-EVs with 808 nm NIR irradiation.Fig. 4 With biosafety established, Lac-EVs delivery efficacy was examined. Fluorescence imaging of HaCaT cells treated with PKH26-labeled Lac-EVs-loaded hydrogels revealed successful cellular uptake, even under NIR (Fig. 4b), confirming that the hydrogel system effectively delivered Lac-EVs. Cell migration assays showed that the Hb-functionalised PCPH hydrogel significantly enhanced cell migration (P < 0.1 vs PBS), while PCPH@Lac-EVs further amplified this effect (P < 0.01). PCPH@Lac-EVs under NIR irradiation yielded the strongest migration response (P < 0.001), indicating that photothermal therapy synergises with Lac-EVs and oxygen to optimise the wound microenvironment (Fig. 4c). In vitro angiogenesis assays revealed that PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR significantly increased vascular network formation (Fig. 4d). Quantitative analysis supported this, showing 90.8 % enhanced migration (Fig. 4e), a 3.2-fold increase in vascular node density, and a 1.7-fold increase in branching complexity over PBS (Fig. 4f and g). These results demonstrated that Lac-EVs synergistically potentiate tissue regeneration when combined with oxygenation and mild photothermal stimulation. The immunomodulatory function of the hydrogel was systematically assessed. Biocompatibility of different hydrogels with macrophages was verified via CCK-8 assay (Fig. S5). To delineate the role of Lac-EVs release kinetics, it was found that sustained release profiles directly induced macrophage phenotypic switching through dose-accumulation (Fig. S6). Subsequent immunofluorescence analysis revealed that Lac-EVs release synergized with mild photothermal to amplify the M2-polarizing capacity of Hb-loaded PCPH. As shown in Fig. 5a–d, the PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group exhibited the strongest immunoregulatory effect. For M1, CD86 dropped to 84.4 % with PCPH, 71.4 % with added Lac-EVs, and 61.0 % with additional photothermal stimulation (p < 0.0001 vs LPS). For M2, CD206 expression rose to 120 % with Lac-EVs + oxygen, and to 130 % with NIR augmentation (p < 0.0001 vs LPS). Flow cytometry also showed an optimal M2 polarization from oxygen-photothermal synergized Lac-EVs therapy (Fig. S7). Cytokine assays corroborated these findings: PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR significantly downregulated TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, while upregulating IL-10 and Arg-1 (Fig. 5e–j). Overall, the synergy of oxygen and photothermal therapy enhances Lac-EVs-driven immunomodulation to support effective diabetic wound healing.Fig. 5Immunomodulatory properties of hydrogels. sections.section: PCPH@Lac-EVs Hydrogel accelerated wound healing in diabetic mouse
sections.text: The biosafety of NIR on intact murine skin tissues was primarily evaluated in vivo (Fig. S8). Murine skin subjected to either NIR irradiation alone or hydrogel-mediated NIR treatment (temperature maintained at ∼42 °C) were histologically assessed. H&E analysis demonstrated preserved histoarchitecture in both experimental groups, with tissue morphology features comparable to untreated controls, confirming the biocompatibility of the implemented photothermal parameters. Given that efficient retention of Lac-EVs is prerequisite for wound healing, we next evaluated the delivery efficiency of Lac-EVs. DiR-labeled free Lac-EVs and DiR-labeled Lac-EVs-loaded PCPH hydrogel were applied to full-thickness skin defect wounds in mice (Fig. S9). After 48h, fluorescence was detected using in vivo imaging. The results revealed a significantly weaker fluorescence signal at the wound site in the free Lac-EVs group compared to the hydrogel group. This indicates that unprotected free Lac-EVs exhibit low targeting efficiency due to rapid clearance or diffusion, whereas the hydrogel enables passive targeting enrichment and prolonged retention of Lac-EVs at the wound site through physical encapsulation and sustained release. Capitalizing on this enhanced retention capability, the therapeutic efficacy of Lac-EVs-loaded hydrogel in diabetic wounds was further assessed. To this end, five different groups (PBS control, PCP, PCPH, PCPH@Lac-EVs and PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR) were evaluated using a diabetic mouse model with full-thickness skin defects (1 cm diameter). Samples were collected at the corresponding time points illustrated in Fig. 6a. Firstly, the photothermal conversion performance of the PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel on the wound surface was examined using thermal imaging (Fig. 6b). The results confirmed effective photothermal behaviour, with wound temperatures maintained at approximately 42 °C.Fig. 6Effects of the hydrogels in promoting diabetic wound healing in mice. (a) Schematic illustration of the timeline of animal experiments to test the therapeutic effect of hydrogels. (b) The photothermal images of mice wound treated with PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel after being exposed to 808 nm irradiation. (c) Photographs of the wounds in different groups at 0 d, 3 d, 7 d, 10 d, 13 d. (d) Traces of wound-bed closure at 0 d, 3 d, 7 d, 10 d, 13 d. (e) Wound area curves over time in different groups (n = 3). (f) H&E staining of the wound in different groups at day 13. Scale bar, 4X: 500 μm; 10X: 500 μm. (g–i) Relative quantitative analysis of dermal gap (g), epidermal thickness (h) and numbers of hair follicles (i) at day 13 (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analysis: ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001. I: PBS, II: PCP, III: PCPH, IV: PCPH@Lac-EVs, V: PCPH@Lac-EVs with 808 nm NIR irradiation.Fig. 6 The effect of the hydrogel on macroscopic wounds healing was systematically assessed by capturing representative wounds photographs from different treatment groups at various stages, tracing the healing trajectories, and quantifying wound areas (Fig. 6c–e). The PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group—where oxygen delivery and mild photothermal therapy synergistically enhanced Lac-EVs efficacy, achieved near-complete wound closure (99.3 %) by day 13. This demonstrated optimal therapeutic efficiency, surpassing the PBS control (72.3 % closure) and intermediate groups including PCP (82.8 %), PCPH (90.1 %), and PCPH@Lac-EVs (95.9 %). Progressive improvement in the PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group was observed through dynamic monitoring, with significant wound closure as early as day 3 (68.0 % closure vs 22.6 % in PBS). These findings confirm that the oxygen-photothermal synergistic Lac-EVs hydrogel system delivers rapid and sustained efficacy in diabetic wound treatment. Hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining on day 13 revealed that the PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel group with NIR irradiation exhibited fully regenerated skin architecture, characterized by a dense epidermis and well-structured dermis (Fig. 6f). Quantitative analysis confirmed optimal regenerative outcomes in the oxygen-photothermal enhanced-Lac-EVs group, which achieved a minimal dermal gap of 1.9 mm—significantly narrower than PBS (4.2 mm), PCP (3.9 mm), PCPH (3.4 mm), and PCPH@Lac-EVs without NIR (2.9 mm) (Fig. 6g). The epidermal thickness in the NIR-treated PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel group was thinner, more uniform and superior to the other groups (Fig. 6h). As hair follicles reflect skin regenerative capacity, their number was also evaluated. The NIR-treated PCPH@Lac-EVs group showed 66 regenerated follicles—tripling that of the PBS control (22) and outperforming PCP (27), PCPH (41), and PCPH@Lac-EVs (49) groups (Fig. 6i). These results were attributed to Lac-EVs in conjunction with oxygen delivery and photothermal enhancement, promoting re-epithelialisation, dermal reconstruction, and appendage regeneration. Collagen, the main extracellular matrix component in the dermis, plays a crucial role in wound repair. Masson's trichrome staining revealed that the oxygen-photothermal enhanced Lac-EVs synergistic group (PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR) achieved the highest collagen deposition (33.3 %), significantly exceeding the PBS control (10.7 %), PCP hydrogel (17.1 %), PCPH (20.0 %), and PCPH@Lac-EVs without NIR (28.1 %) (Fig. 7a and b). Immunofluorescence analysis further demonstrated that this synergistic approach promoted Lac-EVs-driven collagen remodeling, with the highest levels of collagen I—indicating accelerated tissue maturation—and reduced collagen III compared to PBS controls, suggesting reduced scarring risk (Fig. 7c–e). Together, these results highlight that oxygen and photothermal enhancement of Lac-EVs accelerates collagen synthesis, improves matrix quality, and minimises scar formation—culminating in regenerative healing of chronic diabetic wounds.Fig. 7Histological and immunological analysis of the wound tissues. (a) Masson staining of the wound in different groups at day 13. Scale bar, 4X: 500 μm; 10X: 500 μm. (b) Relative quantitative analysis of collagen volume fraction at day 13 (n = 3). (c) Immunofluorescence staining of collagen I (red) and collagen III (green) at the 14th day. Scale bar, 50 μm. (d–e) Relative quantitative analysis of collagen I (d) and collagen III (e) at day 13 (n = 3). (f) Blood vessels stained with α-SMA (green) and DAPI (blue) in different groups at day 7. Scale bar, 4X: 500 μm; 10X: 500 μm. (g) Relative quantitative analysis of vessels density pre field at the seventh day corresponding to α-SMA staining (n = 3). (h) The HIF-1α expression of the skin tissues obtained from different groups at day 13, HIF-1α: green, DAPI: blue. Scale bar, 25 μm. (i) Relative quantitative analysis of HIF-1α at day 13 (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM Statistical analysis: ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001. I: PBS, II: PCP, III: PCPH, IV: PCPH@Lac-EVs, V: PCPH@Lac-EVs with 808 nm NIR irradiation.Fig. 7 As tissue regeneration depends on vascular supply, angiogenesis is essential in diabetic wound healing. Immunofluorescence analysis of α-SMA on day 7 revealed that the PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group showed the most robust neovascularization, outperforming all other groups (Fig. 7f and g). This vascular advantage corresponded with improved wound closure rates, indicating that oxygen-photothermal synergistically boosts the regenerative capacity of Lac-EVs through enhanced angiogenesis. Hypoxia is a key obstacle to angiogenesis in diabetic wounds. Under hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) expression is elevated. Immunofluorescence staining of HIF-1α showed significantly lower expression in the PCPH, PCPH@Lac-EVs, and NIR-treated PCPH@Lac-EVs groups compared to PBS and PCP controls (Fig. 7h and i). These results indicate that Hb-incorporated hydrogels alleviate wound hypoxia by delivering oxygen and thereby reduce HIF-1α expression. This in turn enhances Lac-EVs efficacy by promoting anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage polarization [35]. The importance of macrophage M2 polarization in reducing inflammation and promoting angiogenesis was confirmed through CD86/CD206 immunofluorescence analysis (Fig. 8a–c). The PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group exhibited the highest CD206 expression and lowest CD86 expression, indicating strong immunomodulatory effects compared to PBS. This was corroborated by cytokine profiling, where the same group showed the lowest TNF-α and highest TGF-β levels, consistent with effective inflammation resolution (Fig. 8d–f). These results demonstrate that oxygen and photothermal synergistically enhance Lac-EVs-mediated immunomodulation, suppressing inflammation and accelerating healing through angiogenesis.Fig. 8Immunological analysis of the wound tissues. (a) Immunofluorescence staining of CD86 and CD206 in different groups at day 7, DAPI: blue, CD86: green, CD206: red. Scale bar, 25 μm. (b–c) Relative quantitative analysis of CD86 (b) and CD206 (c) at day 7 (n = 3). (d) Representative image of TNF-α and TGF-β immunostaining in wound tissue from different groups at day 7, DAPI: blue, TNF-α: green, TGF-β: red. Scale bar, 25 μm. (e–f) Relative quantitative analysis of TNF-α (e) and TGF-β (f) at day 7 (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical analysis: ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001. I: PBS, II: PCP, III: PCPH, IV: PCPH@Lac-EVs, V: PCPH@Lac-EVs with 808 nm NIR irradiation.Fig. 8 Finally, H&E staining of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys) on day 13 showed no significant pathological alterations in any treatment groups compared to controls (Fig. S10), confirming the long-term biocompatibility of the hydrogel system.

This study addresses the dual challenges of impaired angiogenesis and persistent inflammation in diabetic wounds by developing an integrated therapeutic platform (PCPH@Lac-EVs) that combines Lac-EVs as the core immunomodulator with oxygen-releasing and photothermal hydrogels. The dynamically cross-linked hydrogel enables a Lac-EVs-centric therapeutic strategy, synergistically enhanced by Hb-mediated oxygenation and PDA-derived photothermal stimulation. Specifically, oxygen and photothermal effects amplify Lac-EVs-mediated macrophage reprogramming, suppressing pro-inflammatory M1 polarization while promoting anti-inflammatory M2 polarization. As a result, pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) decreased, while anti-inflammatory factors (IL-10, Arg1) increased, reshaping the immune microenvironment to accelerate angiogenesis. In diabetic mice, the Lac-EVs-centric synergy—with oxygen and photothermal augmentation—achieved 99.3 % wound closure by day 13, significantly outperforming PBS controls (72.3 %). By positioning Lac-EVs as the central therapeutic agent and leveraging oxygen-photothermal assistance, this study offers a promising strategy for chronic wound management.

Chitosan (CS, Degree of deacetylation ≥95 %, viscosity 100–200 mpa.s) was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Dopamine hydrochloride (DOPA, 99 %), Hemoglobin (Hb, from bovine) and Acetic acid were obtained from Sinopharm group Co., Ltd. Disaldehyde polyethylene glycol (CHO-PEG-CHO, Mw 2000) was purchased from Shanghai yuanye Bio-Technology Co., Ltd. Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) was purchased from Shanghai Diyi Biological Co., Ltd. Micro bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit was purchased from MiShu (Xi'an) Biotechnology Co., Ltd. High Glucose Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) was purchased from Gibco. Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was purchased from Zhejiang Tianhang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) was purchased from Beijing Solarbio Science &Technology Co., Ltd. Basement Membrane Matrix, Cy3-conjugated AffiniPure Goat Anti-Mouse IgG H&L and Alexa Fluor® 488-conjugated AffiniPure Goat Anti-Mouse IgG H&L were purchased from MedChemExpress. CD86 Polyclonal antibody and CD206 Polyclonal antibody were purchased from Wuhan Sanying Biotechnology Co., Ltd. RNA EASY FAST Total RNA Extraction Kit was obtained from Tiangen Biotech (Beijing) Co., Ltd. Prime Script TMRT Master Mix and TB Green® premix ExTaq TMⅡ were purchased from Takara Bio Inc. Hoechst 33342 was purchased from Shanghai Beyotime Biotechnology Co., Ltd. PKH26 was purchased from Umibio (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. QuantiCyto® Mouse TNF-α ELISA kit and QuantiCyto® Mouse IL-10 ELISA kit were purchased from Neobioscience Technology Co., Ltd. All reagents were analytically pure and used directly. Cell culture: RAW264.7 cell line and HaCat cell line were purchased from Wuhan Pricella Biotechnology Co., Ltd. HUVEC cell line was obtained from Xi'an Institute of Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine. RAW264.7 and HUVECs were incubated in high glucose DMEM, which consist of 10 %FBS, 1 % penicillin and streptomycin. HcCat cells were incubated in DMEM, which consist of 10 %FBS, 1 % penicillin and streptomycin. All kinds of cells were cultured in the incubator of 37 °C, 5 % CO2. Bacterial culture: Lactobacillus bulgaricus was purchased from BeiJing Scitop Bio-Tech Co., Ltd. Lactobacillus bulgaricus cultured in the inchbator of 37 °C under anaerobic conditions with MRS medium.

Synthesis of CS-PDA-Hb: The hydrogel precursor CS-PDA-Hb was synthesized by complexing Hb, DOPA and CS via dopamine oxidation polymerization and hydrogen bond interaction. In brief, CS (300 mg) and acetic acid (95 μL) were dissolved in 15 mL deionized water under stirring. After, DOPA (125 mg) and Hb (125 mg) were added in the CS solution and then stirred 24 h at 40 °C. The obtained CS-PDA-Hb was freeze-dried and set aside at 4 °C. Preparation of hydrogel PEG-CS-PDA-Hb (PCPH): The hydrogel was prepared by Schiff base reaction between amine from CS-PDA-Hb and aldehyde group from CHO-PEG-CHO. Specifically, CS-PDA-Hb (37 mg) was dissolved in 1 mL deionized water and then CHO-PEG-CHO (100 mg) was mixed in the CS-PDA-Hb solution. After standing for a few minutes, the mixture changed from the sol state to the gel state. Finally, the hydrogel PEG-CS-PDA-Hb (PCPH) was obtained after rinsing with deionized water several times to remove unreacted substance. Extraction and Characterization of Lac-EVs: The MRS medium was used for the culture of Lactobacillus bulgaricus at 37 °C under anaerobic conditions. When the bacterial density reached 108 CFU/mL, the supernatant was collected by centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant was then further centrifuged at 10,000g for 30 min, and the resulting precipitate was discarded. The next centrifugation step at 150,000g for 90 min was performed to collect the precipitate. Subsequently, resuspend the precipitate with PBS and repeat the above step. Lac-EVs were finally obtained. The microscopic morphology of Lac-EVs was observed using a transmission electron microscope, and the particle size and potential were determined using a nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA). Preparation of hydrogel PCPH@Lac-EVs: To prepare the PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel dressing, CS-PDA-Hb (37 mg) was dissolved in the PBS (1 mL) containing Lac-EVs from Lactobacillus bulgaricus and then CHO-PEG-CHO (100 mg) was added in the mixed solution. After standing for a few minutes, the hydrogel containing Lac-EVs (PEG-CS-PDA-Hb@Lac-EVs, PCPH@Lac-EVs) was prepared after rinsing with PBS several times to remove unreacted substance.

Self-healing evaluation: To evaluate the self-healing capability, the hydrogel sheet of 500 μL was cut into two pieces and then brought into contact with each other. Subsequently, the whole was observed after 1 min and take photos to record the process. Adhesive Properties of Hydrogels: Fresh porcine skin was obtained from markets and cut into sheets of 5 × 2 cm. Then, excessive fat in the sheet was shed off and then the sheets were immersed in PBS solution to ensure the tissues were moist. Next, the skin sheets were taken out from PBS and the residual liquid on the surface was removed with filter papers. The 300 μL of hydrogel precursor solution were then evenly spread onto the porcine skin, followed by the addition of crosslinking agent CHO-PEG-CHO to initiate the hydrogel formation. The states of the hydrogel-porcine skin complex was carefully observed and photographed after undergoing various external forces, including bending, twisting, extrusion, stretching, and PBS washing, to evaluate the adhesion of the hydrogel under complex external force. Injectable and Swelling property: Injectability was checked by injecting hydrogel from needle into water and drawing the word "NIN". The above process was recorded in photo and the injectability of the hydrogel and its morphology after injection was analyzed. To determine swelling capacity, the hydrogel was placed in a sealed tube containing PBS (pH 7.4) maintained at 37 °C to simulate wound exudate conditions. Subsequently, the hydrogel was weighed in wet state at designated time points. Finally, the swelling ratios of the hydrogel were determined using the following formula:SR = (Wt − W0)/W0 × 100 %where SR denotes swelling ratio, Wt denotes the weight of the hydrogel after swelling for a specific time, and W0 denotes the weight of the hydrogel in wet state before swelling. Rheological Properties of the Hydrogels: The rheological properties of the hydrogels were evaluated using a Haake Mars40 rheometer. The storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) of the hydrogels were investigated by positioning it between parallel plates with a diameter of 8 mm. The experiment was conducted using a time sweep test at a temperature of 37 °C, with a frequency of 10 rad s−1 and strain of 1 %. Strain amplitude sweep tests were employed to detect the critical strain point of the hydrogels. Moreover, G′ and G″ were measured during five cycles of oscillation strain at 37 °C, ranging from 5 % to 1500 %. Photothermal and Oxygen Release Property: Temperature-time profiles of PBS and the hydrogels were measured using an 808 nm laser. The photothermal conversion efficiency of the hydrogels was investigated under varying power settings, and the photothermal stability was also assessed through five laser on-off cycles. A dissolved oxygen meter was used to measure the oxygen-carrying capacity of PCPH hydrogel before and after 808 nm laser irradiation, with PBS, Hb, and PCP hydrogel serving as control samples for comparison. Lac-EVs release: The Lac-EVs release profile from the prepared PCPH@Lac-EVs hydrogel was detected by fluorescence spectrophotometer. After washing, 500 μL hydrogel loaded with PKH26-labeled Lac-EVs was immersed in 5 ml PBS. At designated time points, 3 ml of the solution was withdrawn to measure the fluorescence spectrum of the supernatant. The loaded amount and cumulative release were calculated based on the standard curve.

Cell viability: HUVEC and RAW264.7 cells were selected for evaluating the biocompatibility and cell proliferation of the hydrogel. To determine cell survival rate, cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 103 cells/well and incubated for 24 h to allow the cells to adhere to the walls. Subsequently, cells were co-cultured with different hydrogel formulations, and viability was quantified at 24-h and 48-h using the CCK-8 assay. In the PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR group, cells were irradiated with an 808 nm NIR laser at 0.7 W for 5 min, while real-time thermal imaging maintained the culture temperature at 41–42 °C throughout irradiation. Uptake of Lac-EVs by Cells: After being labeled with the fluorescent molecule PKH26, PKH26-labeled Lac-EVs were used to prepare the hydrogel. Subsequently, the hydrogel was cocultured with HaCaT cells for 16 h. Following fixation and nuclear staining, the uptake of Lac-EVs by the cells was documented through photography by inverted fluorescence microscope. The microscope parameters were configured with a 20 × objective lens magnification, an exposure time of 300 ms for the DAPI fluorescence channel, and 800 ms for the PKH26 fluorescence channel. HUVEC Migration and Tube Formation Assays: HUVECs were seeded into a 6-well plate at a density of 3.5 × 105 cells/well and cultured in high glucose DMEM medium containing 10 % FBS at 37 °C, 5 %CO2, allowing the cells to proliferate and coalesce into a contiguous monolayer. Subsequently, after removing the cell culture medium, equal-distance scratches were made on the monolayer of cells using a sterile pipette tip of 10 ml. Then, the cells were gently washed with PBS buffer to remove loose cell debris. Simultaneously, a DMEM culture medium containing different kinds of hydrogel group was prepared as the migration culture medium and adjust the cultivation conditions (1 %O2, 37 °C). At certain time points, the scratch width was accurately measured via inverted microscopy, and corresponding images were captured using an integrated digital camera for detailed analysis. Then, the scratch closure degree was calculated using ImageJ software based on the acellular regions in the captured images, to evaluate the cell migration efficiency after hydrogel treatment. For tube formation assay, Matrigel was dispensed into a 96-well plate and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. HUVECs cells (2 × 104 cells/well) were then seeded into the Matrigel-coated wells and grouped based on the specific material treatments. The tubes were observed using inverted microscope after incubation at 1 %O2, 37 °C for 6 h, and the quantitative statistics of angiogenesis were conducted using ImageJ software. Immunofluorescent staining: The anti-inflammatory capacity was evaluated in an LPS-stimulated macrophage model. RAW264.7 macrophages were stimulated with LPS under hypoxic microenvironment for 2 h and then cultured in different hydrogel formulations. After 20 h, the macrophages were fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde, and then immunofluorescence staining for the M2 marker CD206 (1:400) was conducted to assess the macrophage regulation ability of the hydrogels. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA): Cell processing method is the same as immunofluorescent staining. ELISA kits were prepared per manufacturer's instructions. Using a co-culture system of RAW264.7 macrophages and different hydrogel formulations, the cell supernatant on 24h was collected for measuring anti-inflammatory (IL-10) factors content according to the instructions of the ELISA kit. qRT-PCR: Cell processing method is the same as immunofluorescent staining. After exposure of 24h,qRT-PCR was used to detect the expression of anti-inflammatory cytokine genes (Arg-1, IL-10). Briefly, the collected RAW264.7 macrophages were used to extract total RNA with Total RNA Extraction Kit, and cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit. qRT-PCR was conducted by TB Green® premix ExTaq TMⅡ. The 2−ΔΔCt method was used to analyze the relative gene expression. The primer sequences are shown in Table S1.

Animal Model Production: All animals were purchased from the Animal Centre of Xi'an Jiaotong University, China. The animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTUAE2024-2566). Kunming mice were treated with streptozotocin (STZ) through intraperitoneal injection to establish a model of diabetic mice. When the fasting blood glucose concentration of mice exceeded 11.5 mmol/L, full-thickness wounds (diameter: 1.0 cm) were created on the backs of the mice. The diabetic wounding mice were randomly divided into five groups (PBS control, PCP, PCPH, PCPH@Lac-EVs and PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR) (n = 6). The PCPH@Lac-EVs and PCPH@Lac-EVs + NIR groups received 125 μg Lac-EVs per wound. The wound areas were record with a camera at certain time points. The wound closure rate was measured using ImageJ software. Histological analysis: Wound tissues were collected at day 7 and 13, respectively. Next, the collected samples were fixed with 4 % formaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. Finally, 7 μm-thick sections were prepared for H&E, Masson staining and immunofluorescent staining. The obtained slices were observed and photographed using fluorescence microscope, and the resulting images were semi-quantitatively analyzed using Image software.

The infrared (IR) spectra were measured by Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS20 FT-IR using KBr pellets. Scanning electron microscope images were recorded by ZEISS GeminiSEM 300 operated at 5 kV voltage. Rheological properties were determined using a Haake Mars40 rheometer equipped with an 8 mm parallel plate. Photothermal performance was tested using an 808 nm near infrared light source (MDL-III-808). Oxygen carrying capacity was measured by a dissolved oxygen meter (Leici JPSJ-605). Fluorescence photograph was captured by a MShot MI52 inverted fluorescent microscope.

All acquired data were processed using GraphPad Prism v8.0. Student's t-test was used for comparison between two groups, while analysis of variance (ANOVA) model was employed for comparison among multiple groups. The data are presented as mean ± Standard Error of the Mean (SEM) of the measured values (∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, ∗∗∗P < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗P < 0.0001).
