title: Microenvironment self-adaptive multifunctional hydrogels elicit immunomodulation mediated wound healing
abstract: Herein, we report a microenvironment self-adaptive multifunctional hydrogel (GBOD-PF) dressing with intrinsic hemostasis, antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties that promotes collagen deposition, activates the immune response, and angiogenesis, accelerates large-scale chronic wound healing. To address these needs, aldehyde-functionalized dextran (ODT) was first synthesized through oxidation, and an injectable hydrogel was prepared by mixing Gel and ODT solutions in the presence of borax and paeoniflorin (PF) through the formation of dynamic Schiff base bonds (GBOD-PF). This multifunctional hydrogel exhibits remodeling and self-healing properties, enhanced adhesion strength and biocompatibility. Moreover, it possesses broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and superior hemostasis, providing early-stage protection for complex wounds. Notably, GBOD-PF targets the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway, a core mediator of inflammation, thereby dampening the inflammatory cascade. The results demonstrate the application of the GBOD-PF hydrogel in an infection wound and diabetic model wound healing model, which enhanced immune response, induced M1-to-M2 macrophage repolarization to establish anti-inflammatory microenvironment, regulated MMP-9, promoted angiogenesis, thereby inducing a pro-regenerative response. Therefore, this work provides an effective strategy for the treatment of chronic wound repair and tissue regeneration. Keywords: Multifunctional hydrogels, Hemostasis, Inflammation-responsive, Bacterial infection, Diabetic chronic wound closure

sections.text: The normal wound healing process typically involves four stages: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and maturation [1]. The disruption of healing and impairment of chronic wounds are multifactorial; however, they manifest as persistent inflammation and long-term microcirculatory deficits [2]. Chronic wounds include various ulcer types, such as diabetic foot ulcers, pressure ulcers, infected ulcers, venous ulcer, arterial ulcers and radiation ulcers [3]. Chronic wounds remain a significant clinical, social, and economic challenge in light of an aging population and the ongoing threats of diabetes, obesity, and infection [4,5]. However, several treatment strategies are limited by the complexity of the pathogenesis of chronic wounds. Strategies such as aggressive debridement, surgical angiogenesis, antimicrobial therapy, and use of tissue alternatives have limitations [6]. Thus, finding an effective treatment to improve hard-to-heal chronic wounds and reduce the disease burden is a critical focus in various fields. Notably, conventional wound dressings fail to promote the closure of chronic wounds, which remain stuck in persistent inflammation that hinders healing [7]. Recent investigations of chronic wound tissues have indicated that an imbalance between the classically activated M1 phenotype macrophages with pro-inflammatory properties and the alternatively activated M2 phenotype macrophages with anti-inflammatory properties, prevents normal wound healing [8]. Due to persistent inflammation, macrophages exhibit a reduced ability to induce the M1 to M2 phenotypic transition, leading to an accumulation of M1 macrophages that may damage the microenvironment of the wound and activate latent extracellular proteases, such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and inflammatory cytokines [9]. In severe cases, programmed cell death (e.g., apoptosis and iron apoptosis) occurs within and adjacent to the wound bed. This necessitates drastic measures like tissue debridement, amputation, or more severe interventions to save the patient's life. Hydrogels based on natural components have attracted considerable attentions because of their excellent biocompatibility, flexible design, and a suitable modulus that matches that of soft tissue [10]. In recent years, hydrogels with various functions such as scavenging reactive oxygen species and antimicrobials, modulating immune cells, and promoting angiogenesis, have been designed to modulate the wound microenvironment [11]. However, the integrity of hydrogels is easily disrupted under normal and localized pressure [12]. Injectable self-healing hydrogels are particularly attractive because they can fill deep or irregularly shaped wounds without difficulty and maintain their structure and therapeutic effect even after injury [13]. Therefore, the self-healing ability and injectability are key factors that must be considered during the design of hydrogel dressings. Although injectable self-healing hydrogel therapies are effective, their efficacy largely depends on the incorporation of nanoparticles, cytokines anti-inflammatory drugs, cellular therapies, and nanozymes [[14], [15], [16], [17], [18]]. For example, Liu et al. prepared a Chinese herbal hydrogel whose antibacterial rate was more than 95 % and the wound closure rate was twice that of the control group [19]. Zhao et al., developed a therapeutic wound dressing, called, MnCoO@PDA/CPH, using a biomimetic hydrogel system and modified nanozymes [20]. Shi et al., prepared a hybrid hydrogel based on gelatin methacrylate and lipopeptide-surfactin, that could accelerate wound healing by inducing macrophage polarization and angiogenesis in full-thickness skin [21]. However, the current multifunctional hydrogel designs are unsustainable because hydrogels only act as carriers and do not fully participate in the healing process. Gelatin (Gel) is a well-known natural macromolecule that is biocompatible, biodegradable, and non-immunogenic. Gel offers unique properties such as the hemostasis, biodegradability, contributes to cell adhesion and proliferation, and moisture maintenance, and is a nonirritant; these characteristics render Gel beneficial for use in wound healing-related applications [22,23]. Natural products, compared to traditional anti-inflammatory medicine, offer a wider range of advantages and functions [24,25]. They have been used to treat complex diseases such as pneumonia and enteritis, because they usually comprise mixed compositions rich in antibacterial and antiviral monomers [26]. However, although herbs have considerable therapeutic effects, their complex targeting makes effective and specific therapies difficult [27]. Additionally, large doses can cause organ toxicity, including liver toxicity [28,29]. Researchers are now focusing on single components of natural products to mitigate these issues. Although these monomers have limitations such as poor water solubility and short in vivo half-life, they also offer accurate dosage, low side effects, and stable efficacy [30,31]. Paeoniflorin (PF), the main bioactive constituent of total paeoniflorin, possesses high immunomodulatory, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activities, making it valuable in biomedical applications [32,33]. For example, PF can regulate the polarization of macrophages in wound, inhibit the expression of inflammatory factors, and promote the production of anti-inflammatory/pro-healing factors, thus further promoting wound healing [34,35]. In this study, we developed a wound microenvironment-self-adaptive multifunctional hydrogel with encapsulated active PF, called GBOD-PF. Aldehyde-functionalized dextran (ODT) was first synthesized through oxidation, and an injectable hydrogel was prepared by mixing Gel and ODT solutions in the presence of borax through the formation of dynamic Schiff base bonds (GBOD). Based on the biopolymer Gel and ODT backbone, the hydrogel can conform to any asymmetrical wound, significantly possess broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, and superior hemostasis, providing early-stage protection for complex wounds. Ultimately, via physical doping, PF, a traditional Chinese medicine monomer with anti-inflammatory properties, was uniformly distributed into the GBOD hydrogel (GBOD-PF). Notably, GBOD-PF targets the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway, a core mediator of inflammation, thereby dampening the inflammatory cascade. The special structures and physicochemical properties of the hydrogel disrupt the bacterial charge balance, inhibiting the growth of bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) and Escherichia coli (E. coli). Additionally, the results in vivo showed that GBOD-PF modulated the phenotype of the macrophages from M1 to M2, promoted collagen regeneration, contributing to accelerated wounds closure in infected and diabetic chronic wounds. In addition, we found that GBOD-PF hydrogels significantly downregulated the expression of inflammatory cytokines and the levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9), which degrade a variety of growth factors and matrix proteins required for wound healing [36]. Besides, GBOD-PF hydrogels further accelerated angiogenesis, thereby exerting significant therapeutic effects on chronic diabetic wounds. In summary, the GBOD-PF hydrogel could accelerate the healing of chronic wounds by (i) conforming to irregular wounds, (ii) exhibiting hemostatic ability, (iii) exerting antimicrobial effects, (iv) exhibiting anti-inflammatory effects, (v) decreasing the expression of MMP-9 in wounds, and (vi) promoting the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). These microenvironment-adaptive multifunctional hydrogels, with their simple fabrication and low cost, have promising applications in chronic wound dressing.

sections.section: Synthesis and characterization of borax complexation of dextran aldehyde prepolymer
sections.text: DT was dissolved in water at a concentration of 10 % (w/v), and sodium periodate was added to the DT solution in dark with vigorous stirring for 12 h at room temperature. Afterwards, ethylene glycol was added to neutralize any unreacted periodate for 2 h. The DT aldehyde (ODT) was purified in water with a dialysis tube (Mw 3500 kDa) for 3 days and then lyophilized. Herein, the oxidization degree of ODT was quantified by measuring the number of aldehyde groups in polysaccharide chains according to a standard protocol [37]. Hydroxylamine hydrochloride titration quantified the oxidation degree of ODT at 22.9 %. The chemical structure of the ODT was verified via 1H NMR spectroscopy (Avanc III 600 MHz Digital NMR Spectrometer, BRUKER, Germany) and FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Nicolet iS50, Thermo Fisher Scientific Co., Ltd., USA). Then, the obtained ODT (5 %, w/v) was dissolved in 0.1 M borax aqueous solution through stirring for 30 min. The mixed solution was purified by dialysis and then lyophilization to obtain the borax complexation of dextran aldehyde prepolymer (BODT). The chemical structure of the final product was verified by 1B-NMR spectroscopy (Bruker Avance NEO 400 MHz, Switzerland).

sections.section: Synthesis and characterization of GxBODy hydrogels
sections.text: Gel solutions were first prepared by dissolving gelatin powder (5 %, 10 %, and 15 %) in deionized water and stirring at 50 °C for 30 min. Then, BODT solution (5 %, 10 %, and 15 %) was mixed with gel solution in equal volume ratios to form a cross-linked Gel-BODT hydrogels. To facilitate further discussion, we named the Gel-BODT hydrogels as GxBODy, where x and y represent the original concentrations of the Gel and BODT solutions, respectively. In addition, we designated G15BOD15 hydrogel as GBOD hydrogels. The chemical composition and microstructure of these hydrogels were characterized via XPS spectroscopy (XPS, K-Alpha, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha, USA), FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Nicolet iS50, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and a Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FE-SEM, SU8010, Hitachi Limited, Japan).

sections.section: Synthesis and characterization of paeoniflorin-loaded hydrogels (GBOD-PF)
sections.text: PF (50 mM) was dissolved in 15 % BODT solution, mixed with 15 % Gel solution, after a few seconds, the GBOD-PF hydrogel was formed. The chemical composition and microstructure of the hydrogels were then assessed by FE-SEM and 1H NMR.

The mechanical properties of the hydrogels were carried out on a Rheometer ARES-G2 (TA-Waters, USA) in a time sweep mode. The strain scanning was performed at a frequency of 1.0 rad/s with 5.0 % strain amplitude at 25 °C to determine the dynamic storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″). The strain amplitude scanning test was performed to obtain the critical strain point. An alternate step strain scanning test was performed at a constant frequency of 10 rad/s at 37 °C to evaluate the self-healing ability of hydrogels. The oscillatory strain switches between a small strain (γ = 5.0 %) and a large strain (γ = 200 %), ensuring that the duration of each strain value is 200 s.

The GBOD-PF hydrogel (0.2 g) was extracted using a 5 mL syringe and injected into 5 mL of pH 5.8 or 7.4 PBS buffers. All of the supernatant was removed at different intervals and an equal amount of PBS was added to keep the volume of the released mixture constant. Each group was measured at least three times. PF releases were assessed by a UV–visible spectrophotometer (SHIMADZU UV-2550, Shimadzu Instrument, China) with a characteristic wavelength of 360 nm. And the cumulative amounts of PF released from the GBOD-PF hydrogel were calculated.

M1/M2 macrophage proportion changes following GBOD treatment were analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSCalibur; Becton Dickinson). Peritoneal exudate macrophages (5 × 105 cells/well) in 48-well plates were pretreated with GBOD-PF leachate (0.3 mg/mL, 2 h), followed by co-stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 24 h). Cells were detached using trypsin/EDTA, harvested, and resuspended in 100 μL FACS buffer (PBS containing 2 % fetal bovine serum). To reduce nonspecific binding, samples were incubated with Mouse BD Fc Block™ (553142, BD Biosciences) for 5 min in darkness. Subsequently, cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies: anti-CD86 (560582), anti-F4/80 (565480), anti-CD206 (552850), and anti-CD11b (557396; all BD Biosciences, USA). Antibody incubation proceeded for 30 min at 4 °C under light-protected conditions. After two washes with FACS buffer, cells were acquired on a FACS Canto II flow cytometer (BD Biosciences).

sections.section: Infected rat model induced by E. coli
sections.text: Prior to operation, all the animals were domesticated for 1 week. In detail, 8 mm circular wound was created on the back of rats, E. coli solution (108 CFU, 10 μL) was added into the wounds. The wounds were distributed into four groups (control group, E. coli group, and E. coli/GBOD hydrogel group, and E. coli/GBOD-PF hydrogel group), with 6 rats in each group. The wounds were photographed at 4, 7, and 10 days. Tissues from mice at 10 days were taken for subsequent experiments. The wound area was quantified by Image J software. At the 4th and 7th day, all materials were replaced by fresh ones. The relative wound area for each group was calculated as follows: The relative wound area (%) = Wound area dayn/Wound area day0 × 100 %.

sections.section: In vivo wound healing assay in diabetic rat
sections.text: STZ was dissolved in pH 4.5 citrate buffer, and SD rats were intraperitoneally injected with STZ solution (60 mg/kg) once a day for 5 consecutive times. The rats whose fasting blood glucose value greater than 15.0 mmol/L for continuous two detections were defined as the diabetic model. The in vivo wound healing induced by the hydrogel was performed in diabetic model [38]. Firstly, a full-thickness skin wound in 8 mm diameter was made on the back of each rat. Then, the wounds were randomly allotted into four groups (n = 6): Control group, URGO group, GBOD group and GBOD-PF group. A Tegaderm dressing served as the Control group. The URGO hydrogel, which demonstrated optimal performance in commercial assessments, was selected as a representative. The wounds were observed at 4, 7, 10, and 14 days, and analyzed by Image J software. Besides, all materials were replaced by fresh ones at the 4th, 7th, and 10th day. The relative wound area for each group was calculated as follows: The relative wound area (%) = Wound area dayn/Wound area day0 × 100 %.

Herein, the adjacent hydroxyls on the DT polysaccharide backbone are partially oxidized to form aldehyde groups using sodium periodate as the oxidizing agent (Fig. 1b and c). The chemical structure of the aldehyde groups was confirmed through FTIR spectroscopy and 1H NMR. A new peak at 1725 cm−1 was observed in ODT (Fig. 1b), this is the characteristic peak of the aldehyde group. The reference peak at 8.28 ppm contributing to the aldehyde group in the ODT was clearly visible in the spectrum (Fig. 1d) but absent in unmodified DT. Besides, the active groups in borax can react with the aldehyde groups of ODT to form cross-linked modifications, which was confirmed via 11B NMR spectroscopy. The peaks at 9 and 13 ppm are characteristic of borax, but these peaks are shifted in the BODT complexation (Fig. 1e); this may be attributed to the complexation of borax with diols of DT to form mono- and di-complexes, respectively. The gelation time of GBOD was faster than that of borax un-incorporated hydrogel (GOD) (6.2 ± 1.6s) (Fig. S1), which may be because borax exhibits the ability to form boron ester bonds with hydroxyl compounds [39]. Because of incorporation of borax into the ODT solution, the linkages of DT chains at multiple points remained soluble, there by accelerating hydrogel gelation.

sections.section: Preparation and characterization of GxBODy hydrogels
sections.text: The ODT aldehyde self-crosslinked with the Gel in the presence of borax, forming a Schiff base between the free amino groups of Gel and the aldehyde groups of BODT, aided by boronic-diol complexation of ODT (Fig. 1a). GxBODy hydrogels were rapidly formed by mixing equal volumes of Gel solution (15 %) with BODT solution (5, 10, or 15 %) using a double-tube syringe. We designated the G15BOD15 hydrogels as GBOD. The gel formation time correlated with the aldehyde group content, as indicated by the Schiff base reaction between free aldehyde groups of ODT and primary amines in tissue proteins (Fig. S1, Supporting Information) [40]. Fig. 1f showed images of G15BOD5, G15BOD10, and G15BOD15. The morphology and structure of the hydrogels were examined using FE-SEM. As shown in Fig. 1g, all samples exhibited a porous structure that facilitates O2 and medicine transportation. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was widely used to observe changes in surface properties during modification [41]. The XPS spectra revealed the main signal at 400 eV, corresponding to the N 1s, which was founded in Gel and GBOD. For the XPS C 1s fine spectra, GBOD showed a characteristic peak at 287.5 eV corresponding to the C=C/C-N bonds, confirming the formation of dynamic amido bonds between BODT and Gel [42] (Fig. S2, Supporting Information). Furthermore, the FTIR spectroscopic analysis of BODT, Gel, and GBOD hydrogels revealed a characteristic imine (-C=N) stretching vibration at 1657.5 cm−1, confirming the formation of Schiff base linkages between -CHO groups of BODT and -NH2 groups of Gel (Fig. S3, Supporting Information) [43]. To evaluate the microenvironment adaptation behavior of GBOD, we measured the swelling rate of the hydrogel at different pH values [44]. The swelling of hydrogels was evaluated at 37 °C; the hydrogels rapidly expanded in the initial 4 h and reached equilibrium at 12 h. The swelling rates of hydrogel in each group were about 317.2 % (pH 7.4) and 305.7 % (pH 5.8), respectively (Fig. S4, Supporting Information). Besides, the hydrogels incubated in PBS 7.4 and PBS 5.8 exhibited initial average pore diameters of 56.3 ± 2.7 and 59.1 ± 3.9 μm, respectively, which significantly increased to 71.0 ± 5.8 and 102.9 ± 25.6 μm after 12 h (Fig. S5b, Supporting Information). However, the highly swollen hydrogel exhibits extremely thin and distorted pore walls (Fig. S5a, Supporting Information). These results indicate that GBOD hydrogels possess good water absorption capacity and can be used as wound dressings.

The mechanical properties of hydrogels are crucial for their application as tissue adhesives; therefore, dynamic time-sweep rheological experiments were performed. The storage modulus (G′) increased from 49.8 to 6959.8 Pa as the concentration of BODT increased from 5 % to 15 % at the angular frequency of 6 rad/s in 1500 s (Fig. 1h). This was attributed to the elasticity-strengthening effect of the aldehyde groups that interpenetrated the hydrogel network. In particular, when the BODT concentration was 15 %, the crossover of G′ and G″ was not observed at the early stage of hydrogel formation, while the gelation time of G15BOD5 hydrogels was 30 s. We further assessed the bonding strength of the hydrogels to the tissues surrounding the wound. The adhesion properties were related to the concentration of Gel; a fiber-like structure (black arrow) was observed in the Gel hydrogel (15 %, Fig. S6, Supporting Information) [45]. Porcine skin was used as a representative tissue because it is biologically similar to human dermis. Shear adhesion tests of the hydrogels were performed using the test setup shown in Fig. 2a and b. The average bonding strength of G15BOD15 hydrogels was 151.3 ± 25.4 kPa, which was significantly higher than that of Gel (75.0 ± 5.8 kPa), G5BOD15 (92.0 ± 17.7 kPa), G10BOD15 (120.0 ± 19.1 kPa) and positive control (URGO, 4.9 ± 2.1 kPa) (Fig. 2c and d). This was probably because the NH2 groups in the Gel strengthened the interactions between the tissue and the hydrogels. To test this hypothesis, we conducted dynamic time-sweep rheological experiments to measure the storage (G′) and loss moduli (G″). The storage modulus of G5BOD15 (187.8 Pa) was lower than that of the G10BOD15 (921.8 Pa), URGO (712.4 Pa) and G15BOD15 hydrogels (7136.0 Pa) (Fig. 2e). The viscosity of the hydrogels increased with an increase in the Gel concentration from 5 % to 15 %, aligning with the significant increase in bond strength (Fig. 2f). Importantly, the viscosity of URGO was also lower than that of G15BOD15 hydrogels. URGO, a commercial hydrogel, were used as controls. These results demonstrated that the bonding strength and mechanical properties of GxBODy hydrogels could be adjusted by varying the concentration of Gel and BODT. Considering its superior performance, the G15BOD15 (GBOD) hydrogel was selected for subsequent studies. The GBOD hydrogel attached to all major organs including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys and did not fall off (Fig. 2g). The dyed GBOD hydrogels remained intact and tightly adhered to the porcine skin without detachment after stretching, twisting, or water immersion for 24 h (Fig. 2h), indicating that the GBOD hydrogel had considerable tissue-binding strength.

sections.section: Injectability and of self-healing ability GBOD hydrogels
sections.text: Dyed GBOD hydrogels could be continuously injected into water using a 1 mL syringe, where they maintained a gel state without dissolving, indicating that the physical cross-links in the GBOD hydrogel can temporarily dissociate under external shear force and quickly re-form, ensuring excellent shape stability after agitation (Fig. S7, Supporting Information). Because hydrogels may encounter external mechanical forces post-application, their self-healing ability can significantly extend their lifespan [46]. The macroscopic self-healing properties of the GBOD hydrogels were further demonstrated in Fig. 2i. A disc-shaped GBOD hydrogel, was cut into half-moon pieces, merged back together without external intervention and maintained integrity even under external force. We conducted continuous cyclic strain tests (5 % strain → 200 % strain → 5 % strain) at a constant angular frequency (10 rad/s) to evaluate the self-healing properties of GBOD hydrogels. As presented in Fig. 2j, the hydrogels transitioned to a sol state (G′ < G″) when the critical strain exceeded 200 %. Subsequently, the G′ of GBOD hydrogels returned to their original G′ level immediately after transitioning from high strain (200 %) to low strain (5 %). This result demonstrated that the rapid sol-gel transition behavior of the GBOD hydrogel is fully reversible and reproducible, which is critical for wound applications. These results suggest that the GBOD hydrogels can reversibly re-establish hydrogen bonding and dynamic covalent Schiff base networks to ensure self-healing and injectability (Fig. 2k).

sections.section: Hemostasis in vitro and in vivo
sections.text: Rapid and effective wound hemostasis in the early stages of hemorrhage can result in prolonged rescue time, and can reduce the high mortality rate due to excessive bleeding [47,48]. In this work, the blood-clotting capability of GBOD was evaluated in vitro using the blood clot index (BCI). Gauze and gelatin sponges (KK), two different types of commercial hemostats, were used as controls. As presented in Fig. 3a, the color of the rinse water in GBOD remained largely unchanged even after shaking, indicating that blood-clotting may automatically occur within 3 min. In addition, the BCI of GBOD (17.4 ± 2.4 %) was considerably lower than that of KK (51.4 ± 2.2 %) and Gauze (85.7 ± 3.5 %), thereby demonstrating that GBOD hydrogels exhibited effective blood-clotting capacities (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, the hemostatic performance of the hydrogel was evaluated using a mouse model of liver injury (Fig. 3c). The Control group and Gauze groups presented the most blood loss (0.12 ± 0.016 g and 0.15 ± 0.008 g, respectively) and the longest hemostatic times (44.33 ± 8.14 s and 37.33 ± 2.52 s, respectively). When applying GBOD hydrogels, the blood loss and hemostatic time were significantly reduced to 0.069 ± 0.001 g and 25.00 ± 3 s, respectively (Fig. 3d and e). The improved hemostatic effect was attributed to the hemostatic components of the Gel and aldehyde-modified poly DT aldehyde, which accelerated blood coagulation [49]. As shown in Fig. 3f, there were numerous RBCs were adhered and aggregated on the GBOD surface, which showed powerful blood cell binding ability, which related to rapid blood clotting [50]. Additionally, GBOD exhibited superior absorption capacity for whole blood and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) (Fig. 3g and h), highlighting its rapid aggregation and concentration abilities.

sections.section: Paeoniflorin (PF)-loaded hydrogels (GBOD-PF) and drug release in vitro
sections.text: Recently, the anti-inflammatory function of PF has been widely recognized, leading to its application beyond that of a purely anti-inflammatory agent [35,51]. Considering the characteristics of chronic wounds and the excellent properties of the GBOD hydrogel, we designed a PF-loaded hydrogel (GBOD-PF). PF exhibits excellent hydrophilic properties owing to the large number of hydrophilic groups such as hydroxyl (-OH) and carboxyl (-COOH) groups on its surface (Fig. 4a). In this study, PF-loaded GBOD hydrogels were quickly formed by combining GBOD hydrogels with PF via hydrogen bond (Fig. 4b). The formation of a PF-load BODT solution (BODT-PF) was confirmed using 1H NMR spectroscopy. The characteristic peaks of PF at 3.2, 4.9, and 7.4 ppm were presented in the BODT-PF spectra (Fig. 4c). Additionally, the microstructure of GBOD-PF was evaluated, and the results suggested that the addition of PF did not alter the hydrogel network or properties (Fig. 4d). Considering the sensitive pH responsiveness of the borate ester bond and hydrogen, the response of the hydrogel to pH variations was investigated [52]. With the alteration in pH 7.4, 45 % of PF was released after 72 h (Fig. 4e). In the simulated wound inflammatory microenvironment (pH 5.8), about 53 % of the PF were rapidly released at 72 h. This fulfilled a principal requirement of the drug delivery system. GBOD-PF exhibited a constant drug release over 3 days consistent with first-order drug release kinetics.

For antibacterial evaluation, S. aureus and E. coli. were used as the representative strains as they are the most common species isolated from chronic wound biofilms [53]. As shown in Fig. 4f, ODT, BODT, GBOD, and GBOD-PF completely inhibited the growth of bacterial colonies in culture medium including gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria compared with DT and Gel, indicating the excellent antibacterial property of hydrogels was attributed to aldehyde groups form ODT. Furthermore, we evaluated the antibacterial efficacy of GBOD and GBOD-PF against Gram-positive S. aureus and Gram-negative E. coli using a standardized agar plate counting assay (Fig. 4g). Results revealed maximal antibacterial activity in those two groups. The excellent bacterial abilities of these samples were attributed to the aldehyde groups present in the hydrogels [54,55]. Therefore, GBOD-PF plays a key role in the antibacterial process and exhibits great potential in reducing the risk of wound infection.

The biocompatibility of the GBOD-PF hydrogels on NIH 3t3 cells and macrophage cells was tested by the live/dead assay and Cell Counting Kit 8 (CCK-8). Cell images obtained after live/dead staining are shown in Fig. 4h, which shows that the GBOD-PF hydrogel had no obvious cytotoxic effects on NIH 3t3 cells within 3 d. Similarly, CCK-8 (Fig. 4i) showed that the GBOD-PF hydrogels did not cause significant cell death in NIH 3T3 cells and macrophage cells within 3 days, comparable to the control group. Blood compatibility is an important consideration when hydrogels are applied in vivo. In this study, GBOD-PF showed excellent hemocompatibility, with a hemolytic activity of 3.0 %, compared to the hemolysis in the positive control (water; nearly 100 %) (Fig. S8, Supporting Information). All the above results demonstrate the biocompatibility of GBOD-PF, indicating no adverse effects on cells or erythrocytes, making it a promising material for wound healing potential applications.

sections.section: Anti-inflammatory activity and immunoregulatory mechanisms of the GBOD-PF hydrogel
sections.text: Macrophages are categorized into pro-inflammatory (M1) and anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotypes. Dysregulation of the M1/M2 phenotype ratio is one of the main causes of non-healable chronic wounds [56,57]. Herein, we investigated the anti-inflammatory activity of GBOD-PF hydrogels and their effect on the expression of genes related to the M1/M2 phenotype of macrophages induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The M1-related genes (IL-1β) sharply increased after LPS stimulation (Fig. 4j). The GBOD-PF group showed significantly inhibited levels of IL-1β expression in the inflammatory condition. Besides, the GBOD-PF group showed an increased expression of M2-related genes (TGF-β) compared to the LPS groups (Fig. 4j). Furthermore, the changes in mucosal macrophage polarization condition were further evaluated by quantitative flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. 5a–d, we found that LPS-treated group showed elevated CD86 and F4/80, which was the phenotypic markers of for M1 macrophages. However, the trend in the relative abundance of CD86 and F4/80 expressing cells was significantly reduced after treated with GBOD-PF. In contrast, the number of cells with the expression of CD206 and F4/80 was increased in GBOD-PF groups. Interestingly, although GBOD also exhibited anti-inflammatory effects, the combination of PF with GBOD gels maximized its therapeutic effectiveness. All these results suggest that GBOD-PF hydrogels could substantially induced M1-to-M2 macrophage repolarization to establish anti-inflammatory microenvironment. The anti-inflammatory effect of GBOD-PF hydrogel prompted us to further explore the underlying immunomodulatory mechanisms. In the pathogenesis of wound healing, the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway plays a crucial role [58,59]. TLR4 (Toll-like receptor 4) is a pattern recognition receptor that identify molecular patterns associated with pathogens, such as bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) [60]. Once TLR4 is activated, it can initiate a series of signal transduction processes, including the activation of NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-B). In patients with chronic wound, the abnormal activation of the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway may lead to an overamplification of the inflammatory response, thereby exacerbating the damage and dysfunction of skin tissue [61]. Herein, western blot analysis revealed that LPS significantly stimulated the TLR4-NF-κB signaling axis in macrophages and promoted the expression of TLR4, p-IκBα, and p-p65 (Fig. 5e–h). However, the trend in the relative abundance of TLR4, p-IκBα, and p-p65 expressing cells was significantly reduced after treated with GBOD-PF. This indicates that GBOD-PF primarily suppresses M1 macrophage-mediated immune responses by blocking the TLR4-NF-κB signaling pathway. Pipeline experiments were conducted to investigate the effect of GBOD-PF on the healing of HUVECs. Herein, a cell damage model was first established using H2O2 and high sugar conditions [62]. The angiogenic capacity of GBOD-PF was evaluated by counting the number of capillary-like structures of HUVECs on matrix gel. As shown in Fig. 5i and j, compared with the oxidative-stress damage induced by H2O2, the GBOD-PF group effectively enhanced the angiogenic capacity of HUVECs. The advantage in tube-forming performance further proved that GBOD-PF are promising for chronic wound as wound dressing materials.

sections.section: Therapeutic effects on the infection chronic wound healing
sections.text: To further evaluate the repair effect of GBOD-PF hydrogel on infected wounds, a full-thickness wound healing model was established in SD rats infected with E. coli (Fig. 6a). As shown in the macroscopic observations (Fig. 6b and c) and quantitative data of wound healing (Fig. 6d), the relative wound areas in the GBOD-PF group were observed to be the smallest throughout the entire treatment period, showing the most rapid healing. On the 4th day, the wound closure area ratio of the GBOD-PF group (45.9 ± 9.1 %) was significantly higher than that in the model group ((E. coli + control, 68.7 ± 6.5 %). We also observed no obvious weight decreases in any groups during the entire treatment process (Fig. 6e).

To further illustrate the effect of the hydrogels on tissue regeneration, the wound tissue was evaluated using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining on day 10 (Fig. 6f). The results revealed that wounds treated with GBOD-PF exhibited the narrowest granulation tissue gap, suggesting faster recovery of wounds (Fig. 6h). Additionally, the GBOD-PF group (0.74 ± 0.15 mm) exhibited the shortest scar length, fewest inflammatory cells, and complete re-epithelialization on day 10, compared to the model group (1.51 ± 0.07 mm). Furthermore, collagen was secreted and accumulated to form mature restored skin as wound healing progressed. Thick collagen bundles with a deeper blue color appeared in the wounds treated with GBOD-PF (Fig. 6g and i), indicating more mature skin recovery. The data indicate that GBOD-PF can effectively improve wound healing at the tissue level.

Subsequently, to assess for bacterial residues in vivo, bacteria were collected from the wound and plated for observation. On day 4, E. coli colonies were isolated from wound tissues for bacterial load analysis, where the GBOD and GBOD-PF hydrogel-treated groups exhibited markedly reduced bacterial counts, confirming superior in vivo antibacterial efficacy (Fig. S9, Supporting Information). Next, gram staining was performed to evaluate the degree of infection in wound tissues. Fig. 6j reveals that wounds in the model group exhibited a widely distributed and concentrated dark red color, indicating severe infection. In contrast, the GBOD and GBOD-PF groups displayed significantly reduced wound infections, with much less dark red coloration in the wound tissues. These data demonstrate that GBOD-PF can effectively inhibit bacteria in wound tissue. In addition, no significant histological changes were observed in major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney) of the rats treated with the hydrogels, which indicates that the hydrogel exhibited good biocompatibility (Fig. S10, Supporting information).

sections.section: Therapeutic effects on diabetic chronic wound healing
sections.text: Full-thickness wound healing was established in a diabetic model using SD rats (Fig. 7a) to investigate the wound healing ability of the GBOD-PF hydrogel and explore the relationship between immunity and macrophage polarization throughout the treatment period. Initially, rats with STZ-induced diabetes were injected intraperitoneally for 5 consecutive days, and blood glucose levels were monitored to confirm model establishment [63]. Subsequently, we established the following treatment groups: Control (I), URGO (II, a commercial hydrogel wound dressing), GBOD hydrogel (III), and GBOD-PF hydrogel (IV). Wound observations and photographs were conducted on days 0, 4, 7, 10, and 14 (Fig. 7b and c). Notably, wounds were observed at the determined time for 14 d; GBOD and GBOD-PF hydrogels showed a remarkable decrease in wound size, whereas the control groups exhibited a smaller decrease in wound size. The quantitative data for wound closure, showed that the GBOD-PF group achieved 96.8 % closure, compared to that in the control group (53.2 %) and URGO group (94.1 %) (Fig. 7d). In addition, no obvious weight reduction was observed in any of the groups (Fig. 7e) during the entire treatment process. H&E staining of wound samples were collected on day 14 revealed that the GBOD-PF group had the shortest length of the wound area, followed by the URGO, GBOD and Control groups, which was consistent with the results from direct observation of the wounds (Fig. 7f and g). A histological examination of the healed wound was performed using Masson's trichrome staining (Fig. 7h and i). On day 14, all groups exhibited collagen deposition; however, the collagen in the GBOD-PF group exhibited a more intense blue color than the other groups, and there was a statistically significant difference in their densities (Fig. 7i). This highlights the positive effect of GBOD-PF on diabetic wound healing, which was consistent with the wound healing rates of the other groups. In addition, H&E staining showed none aggregation of inflammatory cells at the tissue interface after implanting hydrogels in rat for two weeks (Fig. S11, supporting information). Notably, no remarkable pathological abnormalities were noticed in the sections of the major organs, indicating that the GBOD-PF hydrogel exhibited excellent biocompatibility (the heart, liver, spleen, lungs and kidneys) (Fig. S12, Supporting Information).

sections.section: In vivo regulation of macrophage polarization
sections.text: Macrophages play a critical role in diabetic chronic wound healing. M2 macrophages inhibit inflammation and promote tissue regeneration [38]. Therefore, immunofluorescence staining was performed to measure the M1 macrophage markers TNF-α at the wound site to assess macrophage polarization. The fluorescence intensity of TNF-α was significantly decreased in the GBOD-PF group (Fig. 8a), whereas that of M2 macrophage markers, IL-10, increased, confirming the anti-inflammation capacity of the hydrogels for effective wound treatment (Fig. 8b). Besides, we further examined the M1 macrophages and M2 macrophages with CD86 and CD206 in wound by immunofluorescent staining, respectively. The GBOD-PF groups had large positive expression of CD206. Additionally, the fluorescence intensity of CD86, an M1 marker, was markedly reduced in GBOD-PF groups relative to the Control group (Fig. 8c and d). Additionally, consistent with the treatment-induced shift in M1/M2 macrophage ratios, wound tissues in the GBOD-PF group showed significantly lower protein levels of IL-6, whereas the protein levels of IL-10 increased, confirming the anti-inflammation capacity of the hydrogels for effective diabetic chronic wound treatment (Fig. 8e–g). The high concentration of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in the wound microenvironment can hinder the healing of chronic diabetic wounds. The excessive MMP-9 degrades essential growth factors and extracellular matrix components, impeding wound healing [36,64]. A lower concentration of MMP-9 was detected in the wounds in the GBOD-PF group, as indicated by the western blot assays (Fig. 8e–h). This significant reduction in MMP-9, compared to the control group, likely resulted from the effective release of PF by the hydrogel. These findings suggested that the hydrogel could enhance M2 polarization and suppress M1 polarization, and mitigate inflammatory responses.

Angiogenesis plays a crucial role in wound healing. M2 macrophages secrete VEGF, increase the proliferation of vascular endothelial cells and promote trabecular angiogenesis [65]. We evaluated the neovascularization via double immunofluorescent labeling of CD31 (cluster of differentiation 31) and α-SMA (α-smooth muscle actin), two widely used markers for blood vessels. The fluorescent images revealed that the GBOD-PF significantly enhanced the generation of new blood vessels in the wound areas, while other groups, especially control group, only trigger sparse blood vessels (Fig. 9a). Besides, western blotting and quantitative analysis of VEGF expression in the skin tissues showed similar results, quantitatively confirming that GBOD-PF induced the most prominent increase in VEGF expression among all the treatment (Fig. 9b and c). This further implied that GBOD-PF accelerates the maturation of blood vessels to accommodate the urgent demand of oxygen and nutrients for wound regeneration. These results indicated that the GBOD-PF hydrogel promoted chronic diabetic wound healing by inhibiting inflammation, modulating M2 macrophage polarization, preventing MMP-9 over-secretion, upregulating VEGF secretion, and promoting angiogenesis (Fig. 9d).

Collectively, we successfully design and validate an injectable, adhesive, hemostatic, antimicrobial, and macrophage polarization regulation that comprehensively promotes the rapid healing of bacterially infection and chronic diabetic wounds. This multifunctional hydrogel exhibits remodeling and self-healing properties, enhanced adhesion strength and biocompatibility. Moreover, it possesses broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and superior hemostasis, providing early-stage protection for complex wounds. Our results showed that PF was uniformly distributed in the GBOD hydrogel via physical doping, which can be achieved by responding to the inflammatory environment. Notably, optimized GBOD-PF targets the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway, a core mediator of inflammation, thereby dampening the inflammatory cascade. Notably, we demonstrated that the GBOD-PF gel accelerated large-scale complex chronic wound healing (infected chronic wounds/diabetic chronic wounds). Mechanistically, our results revealed that the GBOD-PF hydrogels significantly downregulated the expression of inflammatory cytokines and MMP9, and accelerated angiogenesis, thus having significant therapeutic effects on chronic diabetic wounds. In summary, this novel anti-inflammatory microenvironment-self-adaptive hydrogel, which simultaneously regulates biochemical and wound microenvironments to promote angiogenesis, has the potential to serve as a powerful tool for enhancing wound healing.

title: 4′-hydroxychalcone nanofiber hydrogel dressing promotes diabetic chronic wound healing by regulating macrophage polarization via the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway
abstract: The activation and polarization of macrophages play a crucial role in the inflammatory response in chronic diabetic wound healing. Modulating macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype can facilitate wound healing. 4′-Hydroxychalcone (4HC) possesses antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and the preparation of novel drugs through electrospun nanofibers and hydrogels can enhance its therapeutic effects. However, the effects of the 4′-hydroxychalcone nanofiber hydrogel dressing (P-4HC) prepared in this study on macrophage polarization and its potential mechanisms in the treatment of diabetic chronic wounds have not yet been elucidated. This study aimed to investigate the effect of P-4HC on macrophage polarization in diabetic chronic wounds and to elucidate its potential mechanisms of action. In vitro, cell compatibility tests were conducted using L929, HUVECs, and RAW264.7, along with ROS, scratch assays, tube formation assays, immunofluorescence tests for macrophage phenotypes, flow cytometry, and Western blotting (WB). In vivo, a diabetic mouse skin wound model was established, and HE and Masson staining, immunohistochemical staining of COL3A1, HIF-1a, and VEGF, immunofluorescence staining of CD31, CD86, and CD206, WB, RT-qPCR, and ELISA were conducted. In vitro and in vivo, P-4HC exhibited good cell compatibility, improved tissue hypoxia, and promoted angiogenesis and collagen deposition. It promoted the transition of macrophages from M1 to M2 type, downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, and upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines and pro-angiogenic cytokines, thereby promoting the healing of diabetic chronic wounds. Transcriptome analysis indicated that the TLR/IL-17/TNF pathway was the main pathway mediating the effects of P-4HC. P-4HC promoted macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype and enhanced wound healing by inhibiting the expression of TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1, thereby suppressing the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway. P-4HC promotes the polarization of macrophages from M1 to M2 phenotype by inhibiting the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway, thereby suppressing inflammation and mitigating tissue damage. These findings provide a scientific basis for the treatment of chronic diabetic wounds and lay a foundation for exploring new therapeutic strategies for diabetes-induced inflammation based on macrophage polarization. sections.text: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder that poses a significant threat to individuals' physical and mental health. Recent studies have indicated that approximately 537 million people worldwide are living with diabetes, and its prevalence is projected to increase by 46 % by 2045 [1]. Diabetic wounds, as one of the most common complications of diabetes, have always been challenging in clinical practice due to their long treatment duration, high medical costs, and high recurrence rates [2]. Generally, the normal wound healing process has typical overlapping stages, including hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and tissue remodeling [3]; however, diabetic wound healing lasts longer due to chronic inflammation, infection, abnormal neovascularization, and reduced collagen deposition [4,5]. Prolonged inflammatory response is a hallmark of difficult healing in diabetic wounds, characterized by significant infiltration of inflammatory cells, such as M1 macrophages [6,7], finally leading to delayed transition from inflammation to remodeling [8]. Therefore, how to suppress excessive inflammation in diabetic wounds is a significant issue that needs further research. Macrophages are immune effector cells used to maintain balance and resist invasive pathogens, playing a critical role in tissue homeostasis and injury [9]. Macrophages can be roughly divided into two categories based on their functions: classically activated macrophages (M1), representing a highly pro-inflammatory state, and alternatively activated macrophages (M2), representing an anti-inflammatory state. In normal wound healing, M1 macrophages dominate from day 1 to day 3, followed by a transition to M2 macrophages, which peak around the 7th day of wound healing. However, in diabetic wounds, the dominant macrophage phenotype remains M1, regardless of the stage of wound healing. This is a key factor in the chronic nature of diabetic wounds, reflecting an impaired transition from M1 macrophages to M2 macrophages in diabetic wounds [4]. Accumulating evidence suggests that macrophage polarization is closely associated with inflammation and diabetic wound healing [10,11]. Excessive abundance of M1 macrophages leads to chronic inflammation; therefore, inducing M2 polarization of macrophages is believed to suppress the inflammatory response and enhance proliferation and diabetic wound healing [12]. Studies have reported that plant extracts and hydrogel dressings can promote the polarization of macrophages from M1 type to M2 type, thereby reducing inflammation and promoting wound healing [[13], [14], [15]]. Wound dressings with immunomodulatory and angiogenic properties have become a critical measure for diabetic wound healing [[16], [17], [18]]. This has led to the rise of many new treatment methods or dressings, such as various wet dressings and peptide therapy [[19], [20], [21], [22], [23]], but none of these methods are perfect, each has its own focus. The electrospinning technique can produce nanofibers with diameters similar to those of the natural extracellular matrix (ECM). These electrospun nanofibers possess a large surface area and high scaffold porosity, which facilitate cell adhesion, proliferation, migration, and differentiation [24]. Additionally, they can promote diabetic wound healing by delivering active agents in a controlled manner [25]. However, in addition to excellent biological properties, an ideal wound dressing should also possess favorable mechanical properties [26]. Hydrogels are highly hydrophilic [27], biocompatible [28], and feature a three-dimensional porous structure resembling the ECM [29]. They demonstrate superior water absorption and high gas permeability, which can prevent bacterial invasion [30]. Their adhesive properties enable sustained drug release in the wound [31], while their sufficient compressibility and recovery capabilities prevent mechanical rupture [26]. Studies have shown that the combination of hydrogels and nanofibers to form novel dressings can significantly enhance wound healing [32,33]. Conventional antibiotics often lead to drug resistance. Therefore, this study incorporated traditional Chinese medicine monomers into the wound dressing to more effectively promote wound healing. 4HC, an α-β unsaturated ketone, has a core structure of chalcone (1,3-diphenyl-2-propenone) [34]. It possesses antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, reducing IL-6 and TNF-α levels while increasing IL-10 levels, thereby alleviating inflammation [35]. Chalcones, aromatic ketones belonging to polyphenolic compounds, are natural antioxidants and precursors for the synthesis of flavonoids. Chalcones exhibit antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer properties. The main advantage of natural medicines is the lack of toxicity, along with their specific bioactivity and bioavailability. Therefore, this study employed the electrospinning method to prepare 4′-hydroxychalcone-loaded nanofibers, which were then incorporated into a hydrogel to develop a wound dressing with anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic properties. The therapeutic effects of this dressing on diabetic chronic wounds were investigated, and transcriptomic analysis was conducted to explore its underlying mechanisms.

Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), mouse fibroblast L929 cells, and mouse monocyte macrophage leukemia RAW 264.7 cells were purchased from BNCC. Both L929 and RAW 264.7 cells were cultured in DMEM medium, while HUVECs were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium containing 10 % FBS and 1 % penicillin-streptomycin. The cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5 % CO2, and other experiments should be carried out after the cells were exposed to high glucose (33 mM) to simulate the microenvironment of diabetes. Male db/db mice and C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old) were purchased from Hangzhou Ziyuan Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. All animal experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of Jilin University. The animal facility was equipped with air filtration systems, and the temperature was maintained at 22–24 °C with 40 %–70 % humidity. The animals had access to standard food and water ad libitum.

First, polylactic acid (PLA) was mixed with 4HC and processed into PLA/4HC composite nanofibers via electrospinning. The resulting fibers were homogenized into short fibers and then dispersed into a PVA/HHA hydrogel solution to prepare 4HC-loaded nanofiber hydrogels at two concentrations: low-dose (1.5 mg/mL) and high-dose (3 mg/mL). The solutions were transferred into molds, such as 96-well plates (0.1 mL/well), 24-well plates (1 mL/well), 12-well plates (1 mL/well), and 6-well plates (2 mL/well), sealed with parafilm to prevent moisture loss, and subjected to freeze-thaw cycles (−20 °C for 22 h followed by 25 °C for 2 h). After 6 cycles, the following hydrogels were obtained: low-dose 4HC nanofiber hydrogel (P-4HC-L), high-dose 4HC nanofiber hydrogel (P-4HC-H), and without 4HC (P-4HC-0).

The P-4HC hydrogel was fully immersed in PBS with pH = 7.4 and shaken at a constant temperature of 37 °C. 1 mL of release medium was taken out at the set times of 6h, 12h, 24h, 48h, 72h, etc., and the same volume of fresh release medium was added. The concentration of 4HC was detected by high performance liquid chromatography.

Dried hydrogels submerged in PBS at 37 °C. At 6, 12, 24, 48, and 72 h, the hydrogels were removed from the PBS, thoroughly cleaned with filter paper, and then weighed right away. The weights of the initial hydrogels and the swelling hydrogels at different times are denoted by Wd and Ws. The swelling ratio of the hydrogels was calculated as follows: Swelling ratio (%)= (Ws-Wd)/Wd × 100.

The samples that have reached the swelling equilibrium are placed in the centrifuge tube (the weight is Ws). Centrifuge at 3000 g for 20 min at room temperature. After centrifugation, the sample was immediately removed, the surface liquid was gently absorbed with filter paper, and the sample was quickly weighed. This weight was the remaining weight after centrifugation (Wᵣ). The following formula was used to calculate the water retention rate: Water retention rate (%) = (Wᵣ/Ws) × 100.

The hemolysis assay was used to assess the hydrogels' hemolytic qualities. Mouse blood was centrifuged for 10 min at 2000 rpm in order to extract the RBCs. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H were extracted for 24 h using PBS in order to get extracts. The diluted RBC solution was mixed with 1 mL PBS as a negative control, 1 mL P-4HC-0 extract, 1 mL P-4HC-L extract, and 1 mL P-4HC-H extract, along with 1 mL deionized water as a positive control. After 2 h of incubation at 37 °C, the mixtures were centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant was then collected so that the absorbance at 540 nm could be measured by the microplate reader. Hemolysis (%) = [(A sample – A PBS)/(A DW – A PBS)] × 100.

HUVECs, L929, and Raw 264.7 cells were passaged at 5 × 10^3 cells/well into 96-well plates containing P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H, respectively (200 μL/well), with 6 replicates per group. The blank control group was cultured without hydrogel for 24 h. Then, CCK-8 was added to the aforementioned 96-well plates (20 μL/well) and incubation continued in the incubator for 2–4 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of the culture medium from each well was transferred to the corresponding well in a new 96-well plate. The new 96-well plate was placed on the microplate reader and the absorbance (OD value) of each well was measured at 450 nm. The highest and lowest values were discarded, and the average OD value of the four replicate wells was calculated as the OD value for each sample. Then, the relative cell viability was calculated.

L929 cells were seeded in 12-well plates (2.5 × 105 cells/ml) and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H were soaked in DMEM (10 % FBS) at 37 °C for 24 h in advance. The medium in the cell culture wells was discarded, and the above hydrogel extract was added. After 24 h of culture, Calcein-AM and PI were added to stain the cells. The live cells were stained green, and the dead cells were stained red.

We used L929 to study the ability of P-4HC to scavenge intracellular ROS. L929 cells were seeded in a six-well plate (5 × 10^5 cells/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Rosup reagent (1 μL/mL) was added to the wells and incubated for 7 h to induce ROS production. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H were soaked in DMEM medium containing 10 % FBS at 37 °C for 24 h in advance. The culture medium was removed from the cell culture wells, the aforementioned hydrogel extract was added, and incubated for 12 h. Cells treated solely with Rosup were used as the positive control, and cells receiving no treatment were regarded as the negative control. The medium was discarded and gently washed twice with PBS 7.4. Subsequently, serum-free DMEM containing DCFH-DA (1 μL/mL) was added. After incubating for 20 min, the cell fluorescence images were observed using a confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM).

We used HUVECs to investigate the effect of P-4HC on angiogenesis. The migration of HUVECs was assessed through an in vitro scratch assay. HUVECs were seeded into a 12-well plate (2.5 × 10^5 cells/well) and cultured at 37 °C for 24 h. A p200 pipette tip was used to make a horizontal scratch and gently rinse with PBS (1 mL, pH = 7.4), thereby removing suspended cells and cell debris. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H were soaked in RPMI-1640 medium at 37 °C for 24 h in advance. The hydrogel extract was added to the above-mentioned wells, and cultured at 37 °C, and photographs were taken under a microscope at 0 h, 24 h, and 48 h. Image J software was employed to calculate the relative scratch area: relative scratch area (%) = (A#/A0) × 100 %. A# and A0 represent the scratch area after # hours of incubation and the initial scratch area, respectively. The formation of tubules on HUVECs was evaluated using Matrigel to assess the effects of P-4HC. Different groups of hydrogels were soaked in RPMI-1640 medium at 37 °C for 24 h. Matrigel was added to the 12-well plate (1 mL/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Then, HUVECs were seeded onto the Matrigel-coated 12-well plates (2.5 × 10^5 cells/well) and incubated for 24 h. Thereafter, the respective extracts were added to each group and incubation continued for another 24 h. Tube formation was observed and statistical analysis was performed using Image J software.

Raw 264.7 cells were diluted to 2.5 × 10^5 cells/mL. The diluted cell suspension was inoculated into a 12-well plate with sterile coverslips at the bottom (1 mL/well) and incubated for 24 h. LPS (1 μg/mL) or IL-4 (40 ng/mL) were dissolved in serum-free DMEM. The cell culture medium was discarded in the above 12-well plate and gently washed twice with PBS. Then, LPS or IL-4 solution was added, and culture continued for 12 h to induce macrophage polarization to M1 or M2 phenotypes. LPS or IL-4 solution was aspirated and gently washed twice with PBS. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H extracts were added. The extract of the anhydrous gel was used for the control group, and the culture continued for 48 h. The culture medium was removed and washed with PBS three times. 4 % paraformaldehyde (500 μL/well) was added and fixed at room temperature for 20 min. Paraformaldehyde was removed and washed with PBS three times. The cells were treated with 0.1 % Triton X-100 for 20 min to enhance membrane permeability. 5 % bovine serum albumin (500 μL/well) was added and blocked at room temperature for 1.5 h. Bovine serum albumin was removed and washed three times with PBS. Primary antibody against CD206 was added and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The primary antibody was discarded and washed three times with PBS. The secondary antibody was added and dark incubated at room temperature for 1.5 h. The secondary antibody was discarded and washed three times with PBS. DAPI was added to stain the nuclei, which was incubated at room temperature for 10 min. The sample was washed with PBS three times. A drop of glycerol solution (glycerol: water = 1:1) was dropped onto the slide. Then, the stained coverslip was transferred onto the slide, and sealed with clear nail polish. Finally, the fluorescence images were observed and recorded using CLSM.

Raw 264.7 cells were cultured in a 12-well plate for 24 h, LPS (1 μg/mL) was dissolved in serum-free DMEM, and Raw 264.7 was polarized to M1. The LPS solution was aspirated and gently washed twice with PBS. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H extracts were added. There was no hydrogel extract for the control group. Culture continued for 48 h. The culture medium was discarded, and 1 mL of PBS was added to each well. A pipette was used to detach the adherent cells and collect them in an EP tube. The tube was centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was discarded, and 500 μL of PBS and 10 μL of F4/80, CD86, and CD206 fluorescent antibodies were added and dark incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The cells were centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 5 min, the supernatant was discarded, and the cells were resuspended in 500 μL of PBS. The cells were analyzed using a flow cytometer (BD C6 Plus).

The cells were seeded at a density of 5 × 10^5 cells per well in a 6-well plate and incubated for 24 h. The culture medium was discarded. We added P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H extracts that had been soaked in the medium for 24 h. The cells were cultured for 48 h. Then, the medium was discarded and the cells were collected. Animal skin tissue was prepared into a homogenate. RIPA lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was used to extract proteins. The proteins were quantified using the BCA protein assay kit. 12.5 % or 10 % polyacrylamide gel was used to separate 30 μg of protein extract per well. The protein sample was then transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane, blocked with skim milk at room temperature for 2 h, and incubated with the primary antibody at 4 °C overnight. The membrane was washed with TBST three times, incubated with the secondary antibody at room temperature for 45 min, and washed with TBST three times. The bands were observed using a chemiluminescent solution.

db/db mice were randomly divided into 5 groups: diabetes model group, P-4HC-0 group, P-4HC-L group, P-4HC-H group, and positive drug group, with 8 mice in each group. An additional 8 wild-type C57BL/6 mice were used as the non-diabetic control group (wild mice). Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane. The back of mice was shaved, and disinfected with medical alcohol. Subsequently, a full-thickness circular wound with a diameter of 8 mm was established in the depilated area on the back of mice using a punch. P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, P-4HC-H, and the positive drug (the trade name is Beifuxin, and the generic name is bovine basic fibroblast factor gel) were applied to the wound surface. The diabetic model group and the non-diabetic control group were treated with saline. Tegaderm transparent dressings were used as secondary dressings to prevent the hydrogel from falling off. On days 0, 3, 6, 9, and 12 after the injury, photos of the wound site were captured and Image J software was used to measure the wound area. Compared to the original wound, the percentage of the wound area on the indicated days compared to the initial area was calculated using the following formula: wound area# (%) = (Wound area#/Wound area0) × 100 %. Wound area# and wound area0 represent the wound area on day # and day 0, respectively.

The wound and surrounding skin tissue samples were harvested on the 12th day after surgery. The tissue samples were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. The tissue samples were cut into 2-μm to 4-μm thick sections. Hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining, Masson trichrome staining (MTS), and COL3A1 staining were conducted to observe the degree of wound healing and collagen deposition. Immunohistochemical staining for hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α) was performed to determine the degree of tissue hypoxia. Immunohistochemical staining for VEGF and immunofluorescence assay for CD31 were conducted to determine the degree of neovascularization. Immunofluorescence assays for F4/80, CD86, and CD206 were conducted to measure the expression of macrophage marker proteins.

The wound skin tissue was obtained on the 12th day after surgery. Wound tissue proteins were isolated and quantitative analysis of the following proteins was performed using ELISA kits: (IL-1β (PI301), IL-6 (PI326), TNF-α (PT512), iNOS (S0025), MDA (S0131S), SOD (S0101S), IL-4 (PI612), IL-10 (PI522), and VEGF (PV957)).

Following the manufacturer's protocol, total RNA was isolated from samples, and cDNA was obtained through reverse transcription. Then, quantitative PCR detection. The comparative threshold cycle (2-ΔΔCt) method was employed to quantify the mRNA expression levels of these genes.
