Transcriptomic analysis was conducted to determine the transcriptional characteristics associated with diabetic chronic wounds treated with P-4HC and explore the potential mechanisms by which P-4HC promotes wound healing. We performed transcriptomic comparisons on the tissues of db/db mice 12 days after wound modeling. The criteria for screening differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were log2 fold change ≥2 and P < 0.05. Their relative abundances were plotted as heatmaps and volcano plots to simplify the visualization of DEGs. GO enrichment and KEGG signaling pathway enrichment analysis were conducted.

Data are presented as mean ± SD. We used GraphPad Prism 9 (Graph Pad Software, USA) for data analysis and visualization. ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01, and ∗∗∗P < 0.001 indicated statistically significant difference.

sections.section: The representation of P-4HC and its biocompatibility and antioxidant properties
sections.text: First, PLA was mixed with 4HC and electrospun into PLA/4HC fibers (Fig. 1A). The fibers were then homogenized into short fibers. Finally, the short fibers were dissolved in a hydrogel solution to prepare P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H (Fig. 1C). The morphology of the fibers and P-4HC was observed by SEM. The fibers had a uniform diameter, no beads, and no adhesion (Fig. 1B). Each hydrogel had a three-dimensional network structure, and short fibers were interspersed in the mesh structure of the hydrogel (Fig. 1D). According to the SEM results, P-4HC had a porous network structure that allowed for adequate drug permeability. In Fig. 1E the release curves of 4HC in P-4HC-L and P-4HC-H are similar. About 70 % of 4HC can be released in the first 24 h, and then it is gradually and slowly released to achieve the effect of sustained drug release. P-4HC's swelling rate rose over time, and all of the hydrogels reached a swelling equilibrium condition after 24 h (Fig. 1F). They then maintained a steady swelling rate, demonstrating their exceptional stability. The P-4HC can offer a favorable milieu for wound healing because of its swelling capacity, which facilitated the absorption of exudate. The water absorption rate of P-4HC at swelling equilibrium reflects its maximum water absorption capacity (Fig. 1G). The water retention rate of P-4HC can reach about 95 %, which can prevent the overflow of exudate and thus facilitate wound healing (Fig. 1H).Fig. 1P-4HC exhibited excellent water absorption capacity, biocompatibility, and antioxidant capacity. (A, C) Images of nanofibers and different hydrogels. (B, D) SEM image of nanofiber and different hydrogels (The scale bars are 5 μm and 10 μm, respectively). (E) Cumulative release curve of 4HC from P-4HC-L and P-4HC-H. (F–H) Swelling ratio, water absorption ratio, and water retention rate of P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H. (I) Hemolysis rate of P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H. RBC supernatant imaging in several hydrogel groups is shown in the inset. (J) Cell viability curve of L929 cells seeded on different hydrogels at 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h. (K) Live/dead cell staining of L929 cells after co-culture with P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H for 24 h (Live cells are indicated by green fluorescence from Calcein-AM, whereas dead cells are indicated by red fluorescence from PI.) (L) After treating L929 cells with Rosup, they were co-cultured with different groups of hydrogels, followed by DCFH-DA fluorescence staining. Cells treated solely with Rosup were regarded as the positive control group, and untreated cells were regarded as a negative control; scale bar = 100 μm. (M) Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity. (n = 3, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001.). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)Fig. 1 P-4HC, as a wound dressing, possesses good biocompatibility, which is very important. We investigated P-4HC's blood compatibility in order to assess its biocompatibility. The supernatant was comparable to PBS, following collection of the supernatants for quantitative investigation, it was discovered that the hemolysis ratios at various hydrogels were less than 5 %, indicating good hemocompatibility as a wound dressing (Fig. 1I). We also employed the CCK-8 method to detect the survival rate of L929 cells, throughout the entire experimental period, cells grew and proliferated well (Fig. 1J). In the live/dead cell staining assay, Fig. 1K shows that the cells in each group were normal in morphology, and almost all were green live cells. Therefore, the biocompatibility of P-4HC was verified again. In Fig. 1L, after stimulating cells to produce a large amount of ROS, P-4HC significantly reduced the cell fluorescence intensity, with the P-4HC-H group showing the weakest fluorescence intensity, almost approaching the negative control group. The above findings indicate that P-4HC has good biocompatibility and antioxidant properties.

sections.section: P-4HC promoted angiogenesis and M2 macrophage polarization
sections.text: P-4HC exhibited good biocompatibility in HUVECs (Fig. 2A). Moreover, P-4HC promoted angiogenesis. The scratch assay in HUVECs revealed that the addition of P-4HC-H significantly accelerated the wound healing rate, with nearly complete healing at 48 h. This finding suggests that P-4HC can enhance the migration of HUVECs (Fig. 2B). In vitro tube formation assay with HUVECs revealed that the tubular network in the P-4HC-H group had the highest density, and the length of the tubes was longer than that in the other two groups (p < 0.01) (Fig. 2D–F). Western blotting also demonstrated that P-4HC promoted angiogenesis, and its effect increased with the increase in the concentration of 4HC (Fig. 2G). P-4HC also exhibited good compatibility with RAW264.7 cells (Fig. 2I). Subsequently, we measured the effect of P-4HC on macrophage polarization in RAW 264.7 cells using flow cytometry. After treatment with P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, and P-4HC-H, the proportion of M1 macrophages (F4/80+CD86+) decreased, while the proportion of M2 macrophages (F4/80+CD206+) increased (Fig. 2J and K). Immunofluorescence staining revealed that P-4HC can increase the fluorescence intensity of CD206. We used LPS and IL-4 to polarize macrophages into M1 and M2. After LPS-induced polarization, the control group showed almost no fluorescence for the CD206 protein. The control group was then incubated with fresh DMEM (10 % FBS) for 72 h, the fluorescence intensity of the CD206 protein was very weak, and almost not detectable. However, after LPS-induced polarization and P-4HC treatment, the fluorescence intensity of the CD206 protein significantly increased, and P-4HC-H was significantly superior to P-4HC-L (p < 0.001). However, after IL-4-induced polarization, the control group cultured with fresh DMEM (10 % FBS) for 72 h showed a significant decrease in the fluorescence intensity of the CD206 protein (p < 0.001). However, when P-4HC was added to macrophages treated with IL-4, the fluorescence intensity of the CD206 protein changed little and remained strong (Fig. 2L–N). This finding indicates that P-4HC can maintain the M2 phenotype of macrophages. Moreover, Western blotting indicated that P-4HC can promote the transition of macrophages to M2 phenotype, with the P-4HC group showing high expression of M2 markers, CD206 and Arg-1 (Fig. 2O and P). Once again, these findings demonstrated that P-4HC promoted the transition of macrophages to the M2 phenotype, and the P-4HC-H group more effectively promoted and maintained this transition compared to the P-4HC-L group.Fig. 2P-4HC promoted angiogenesis and induced and maintained M2 polarization. (A) Survival curves of HUVECs seeded on different groups of hydrogels at 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h. (B) Treatment of HUVECs with different hydrogel extracts in the scratch assay. Scale bar = 100 μm. (C) Quantitative analysis of the relative scratch area at 24 h and 48 h in the scratch test. (D) Representative images of HUVECs forming tubes when seeded on matrigel and treated with different hydrogel extracts, scale bar = 100 μm. (E, F) Using Image J software to measure the relative values of branch point and tube length in tube formation assay. (G, H) Western blotting and quantification of CD31 and VEGF-A expression in HUVECs in different groups. (I) Cell survival curves of Raw 264.7 cells inoculated on different hydrogels at designated times. (J, K) Flow cytometry analysis of CD86 and CD206 expression in Raw 264.7 cells in different groups. Histogram showing the ratio of M1 (CD86+) or M2 (CD206+) macrophages. (L) LPS served as the negative control group, while IL-4 served as the positive control group. Images of Raw 264.7 cells treated with LPS or IL-4, followed by treatment with different groups of hydrogels for 72 h. (M, N) Quantitative analysis of CD206 fluorescence intensity in (L). (O, P) M0 was pure Raw 264.7 cells, while the other groups were stimulated with LPS and then subjected to different treatments. Western blotting and quantification results of CD206, Arg-1, CD86, and iNOS in different groups. β-actin was used as the internal reference. (n = 3, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001.)Fig. 2

sections.section: P-4HC enhanced the healing of chronic diabetic wounds
sections.text: Diabetes chronic wound healing experiments were conducted on db/db mice. The mice were divided into diabetes, P-4HC-0, P-4HC-L, P-4HC-H, positive, and wild-type groups. Saline was administered to the wounds in the diabetes and wild-type groups. These groups served as the diabetes model group and the non-diabetes control group, respectively. Based on the wound photos and closure curves of different groups on days 3, 6, 9, and 12 (Fig. 3A and B), the wound area in other groups showed significant contraction throughout the wound regeneration phase compared to the diabetic model group. The wound area in the diabetes model group showed almost no reduction in the first 6 days, confirming the significant prolongation of the inflammatory phase in the diabetes model group. P-4HC increased the rate of wound healing and significantly decreased wound size compared to the diabetes model group. Moreover, the wound healing speed was accelerated in the P-4HC-H group, which was comparable to that of the positive group.Fig. 3P-4HC enhanced the healing effect of the diabetic chronic wound model. (A) Representative images of wounds in different groups on the indicated days. (B) Quantitative analysis of wound area at the indicated days compared to the original wound (n = 8). (C) Representative images of wound tissues stained with H&E and Masson trichrome staining at day 12, scale bar = 100 μm (up) and 20 μm (down). (D) IHC staining of COL3A1, HIF-1α, VEGF, and representative images of CD31 (green). Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue) at day 12, scale bar = 20 μm. (E–I) Quantitative analysis of collagen area, COL3A1, HIF-1a, VEGF, and CD31 expression in wound tissue. (J, K) The protein levels of CD31, VEGF-A, HIF-1a, and COL3A1 at day 12 were measured by Western blotting and quantified using Image J software. (n = 3, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001.). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)Fig. 3 H&E staining revealed (Fig. 3 C) that newly formed hair follicles, squamous epithelium, and stratum corneum were clearly observed in the P-4HC-H group, and the repair effect was similar to that of the positive and wild-type groups. Collagen deposition is a key factor determining the appearance and strength of the skin; therefore, we employed Masson trichrome staining to measure the extent of collagen deposition in each group. There was a significant difference in terms of collagen deposition between the groups (Fig. 3 C). Collagen deposition in the P-4HC-H group was similar to that in the positive drug group. COL3A1 staining revealed that the amount of collagen in the P-4HC-H group was significantly higher than that in the diabetic model group, P-4HC-0 group, and P-4HC-L group (Fig. 3 D). P-4HC-H accelerated granulation tissue formation, re-epithelialization, and collagen deposition, enhancing chronic diabetic wound healing. At the same time, HIF-1a staining indicated that P-4HC-H improved hypoxia similar to the positive drug, and was superior to P-4HC-L and P-4HC-0 (Fig. 3 D). In addition, VEGF and CD31 staining in the wound tissue on the 12th day after surgery (Fig. 3 D) revealed that the number of new blood vessels in each group was significantly different on the 12th day. The expression level of VEGF and the protein fluorescence intensity of CD31 in the P-4HC-H group were comparable to those in the positive drug group, suggesting that neovascularization in this group was stronger than that in the P-4HC-L, P-4HC-0, and model groups. Western blotting of skin tissues demonstrated that P-4HC-H more effectively promoted angiogenesis, antioxidant capacity, and collagen deposition (Fig. 3 J). Since new blood vessels provide nutrients and oxygen to metabolically active wounds, they can promote the formation of granulation tissue, thus P-4HC-H more effectively promotes the healing of chronic diabetic wounds. The phenotype of macrophages in the wound tissue was analyzed based on immunofluorescence staining. The wound tissue in the P-4HC-H group contained a large number of M2 macrophages (F4/80+CD206+), while most macrophages in the model group had M1 (F4/80+CD86+) phenotype (Fig. 4A–D). Western blotting showed that P-4HC-H can upregulate M2 macrophage markers CD206 and Arg-1. In contrast, the diabetic model group expressed more M1 macrophage markers CD86 and iNOS (Fig. 4E and F).Fig. 4P-4HC promoted M2 polarization, reduced the inflammatory response, and facilitated wound healing in diabetes. (A, B) Immunofluorescence co-staining for F4/80 (green) and CD86 (red) or CD206 (red) in diabetic wound sections on day 12 after receiving different treatments. The cell nucleus was stained with DAPI (blue). Scale bar = 20 μm. (C, D) Quantitative analysis of the mean fluorescence intensity of CD86 and CD206. (E, F) Western blotting of CD206, Arg-1, CD86, and iNOS in wound tissues on day 12. (G–I) The concentration of cytokines in the wound tissue was measured by ELISA on day 12. (J–L) RT-qPCR of wound tissue sections in different groups on day 12. (M, N) Western blotting of IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α in wound tissues. (n = 3, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)Fig. 4 We measured the levels of chemokines in the wound tissue through ELISA experiments to assess the effect of P-4HC on immune function (Fig. 4G–I). Compared to the diabetic model group, the P-4HC group showed reduced levels of pro-inflammatory chemokines IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, lower levels of oxidative stress markers iNOS and MDA, and increased levels of SOD. Additionally, anti-inflammatory factors IL-4, IL-10, and VEGF were all upregulated. At the same time, the expression of inflammatory factors IL-6 and TNF-α was decreased in the wound tissue, while the expression of the anti-inflammatory factor IL-10 was increased (Fig. 4M and N). RT-qPCR demonstrated that P-4HC significantly reduced the expression of inflammatory factors. Compared to other groups, CD206 expression significantly increased in the P-4HC group while CD86 expression significantly decreased in this group (Fig. 4J–L). These results indicate that P-4HC possesses anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects and promotes M2 polarization of macrophages. The above results show that the therapeutic effect of the P-4HC-H group is comparable to that of the positive drug group. However, the positive drug has the risk of allergic reaction and abnormal proliferation leading to scars and promoting tumors, and P-4HC has better stability, better transdermal permeability, a stronger sustained release effect, and a lower cost. It is safer and more economical while playing a role in multiple targets.

We conducted transcriptomic analysis to analyze the mechanism by which P-4HC promotes M2 polarization of macrophages. The BP classification in the GO enrichment analysis indicated that DEPs are mainly involved in immune response, inflammatory response, and defense response (Fig. 5C,G). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis found that the TLR, IL-17, and TNF signaling pathways were downregulated in db/db mice treated with P-4HC. These pathways were more strongly enriched in the P-4HC-H group compared to the P-4HC-L group (Fig. 5D,H). Among these three pathways, the key genes TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1 were significantly down-regulated in the treatment group. Thus, P-4HC may promote the transition of macrophages from the M1 phenotype to the M2 phenotype and enhanced chronic wound healing in diabetes via the TLR/IL-17/TNF pathway. Subsequently, RT-qPCR and Western blotting revealed significant differences in the expression levels of proteins related to the aforementioned pathways in the wound tissue (Fig. 5I–K). The key proteins associated with these pathways, such as TLR9, IL-17A, IL-17RA, IL-17RC, and TRAF1, were significantly upregulated in the diabetic model control group compared to the P-4HC group. The expression of these proteins in the P-4HC-H group was significantly lower than that in the P-4HC-L and P-4HC-0 groups. This is consistent with the changes in the expression levels of TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1 in transcriptomic analysis.Fig. 5Transcriptomic analysis of db/db diabetic control group compared to P-4HC-L and P-4HC-H groups. (A) Heatmap of differentially expressed proteins in the P-4HC-L group compared to the db/db control group. (B) The volcano plot of differentially expressed proteins in the P-4HC-L group compared to the db/db control group. (C) GO annotation of differentially expressed proteins, which were classified into BP. (D) Enrichment analysis of the top 20 signaling pathways in KEGG. (E–H) db/db control group and the P-4HC-H group underwent the same transcriptomic analysis as the P-4HC-L group. (I) RT-qPCR was used to determine the expression levels of key proteins in wound tissues from different groups. (J, K) Western blotting was conducted to detect the expression levels of key proteins. (n = 3, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001.)Fig. 5

sections.section: Elucidating the mechanism by which P-4HC promotes diabetic chronic wound healing
sections.text: In vivo validation experiments were conducted using the activators of TLR, IL-17, and TNF signaling pathways, namely ODN, SR, and RSQ, to verify the role of the aforementioned signaling pathways in P-4HC-mediated M2 polarization. Activation of TLR, IL-17, and TNF by ODN (5 mg/kg), SR (5 mg/kg), and RSQ (3 mg/kg) neutralized the effect of P-4HC (3 mg/mL) on diabetic chronic wound healing. For the healing of chronic diabetic wounds, the combination of P-4HC with each one of the activators (the P-4HC + ODN group, P-4HC + SR group, and P-4HC + RSQ group) decreased wound healing speed compared to the P-4HC group (Fig. 6A and B). In HE, Masson trichrome staining, and COL3A1 staining, the combination of P-4HC with each one of the activators lowered the number of new hair follicles and epidermal layers and decelerated granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition compared to the P-4HC group. However, these groups still exhibited better outcomes compared to the diabetic model group (Fig. 6C and D). At the same time, HIF-1a, VEGF, and CD31 staining (Fig. 6 D) showed that the combined use of P-4HC with ODN, SR, and RSQ neutralized the effects of P-4HC in improving hypoxia and promoting angiogenesis.Fig. 6Verification of P-4HC-mediated healing of the diabetic chronic wound. (A) Representative images of wounds on the indicated days with different treatments. (B) Quantitative analysis of the wound area on the indicated days compared to the original wound, n = 8. (C) Representative images of wound tissues stained with H&E and Masson trichrome staining at day 12, scale bar = 100 μm (up) and 20 μm (down). (D) IHC staining of COL3A1, HIF-1α, VEGF, and representative images of CD31 (green) at day 12. Cell nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). Scale bar = 20 μm. (E–I) Quantitative analysis of collagen area, COL3A1, HIF-1a, VEGF, and CD31 expression in wound tissue. (n = 3, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001.). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the Web version of this article.)Fig. 6 Immunofluorescence staining of CD206 and CD86 indicated that the combination of P-4HC with ODN, SR, and RSQ attenuated P-4HC-mediated M2 polarization of macrophages (Fig. 7A–D). After LPS stimulation, RAW 264.7 cells treated with P-4HC combined with ODN (2 μM), SR (2 μM), and TRAF1 overexpression plasmid had reduced ability to achieve M2 polarization (Fig. 7E and F). ELISA and RT-qPCR (Fig. 7G–K) revealed consistent changes in the levels of inflammatory factors and macrophage markers in wound tissue. Adding ODN, SR, and RSQ reduced the M2 polarization of macrophages and suppressed the anti-inflammatory effects of P-4HC. At the same time, RT-qPCR showed that the expression of TLR9, IL-17A, IL-17RA, IL-17RC, and TRAF1 in the wound tissue of the P-4HC group was significantly lower than that in the diabetic model group. However, the combined use of ODN, SR, and RSQ significantly increased the expression of the aforementioned genes. This finding indicates that P-4HC inhibited the TLR//IL-17/TNF signaling pathway, thereby promoting collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization of macrophages, thereby enhancing diabetic chronic wound healing.Fig. 7P-4HC inhibited the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway, promoted M2 polarization, reduced the inflammatory response, and enhanced diabetic wound healing. We performed Western blotting using both HUVECs and RAW264.7 cells. We used ODN (2 μM), SR (2 μM), and TRAF1 overexpression plasmids to activate TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1 in cultured HUVECs and RAW 264.7 cells and clarify the function of TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1 in wound healing. After separately activating TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1, it was found that CD31 and VEGF-A were significantly downregulated in HUVECs (Fig. 8A–F). In RAW264.7 cells that were treated with LPS(1 μg/mL) in advance, activation of TLR9 using ODN was found to significantly increase the expression of IL-17A, IL-17RA, IL-17RC, and TRAF1, while significantly inhibiting the expression of CD206 and Arg-1. Conversely, it significantly increased the expression of CD86 and iNOS (Fig. 8G–J). Activation of IL-17A with SR significantly increased the expression of TRAF1, TNF-α, CD86, and iNOS, while inhibiting the expression of CD206 and Arg-1 (Fig. 8K–N). Once again, it has been confirmed that P-4HC exerts its effects by inhibiting the activation of the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway and relies on TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1 to promote angiogenesis and the polarization of macrophages to the M2 phenotype, thereby reducing inflammation.Fig. 8Western blotting showed that P-4HC inhibited the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway, promoted angiogenesis, enhanced M2 polarization, reduced the inflammatory response, and promoted diabetic wound healing. Approximately 25 % of diabetes patients will develop diabetic foot ulcers (DFU), which impose a significant burden on patients and society [25,36]. Among patients with DFU, 68 % have a life expectancy of less than 5 years, and their mortality rate is higher than that of most patients with cancer [37,38]. DFU are one of the most common and difficult-to-treat complications of diabetes [39]. Although various types of wound dressings have been used for wound healing, they all have certain limitations. Electrospun nanofibers are promising biomaterials. The porous structure of nanofibers increases their specific surface area, allowing for liquid and gas exchange, which promotes wound healing [40,41]. Moreover, studies have shown that combining hydrogels with nanofibers to form new auxiliary materials can significantly promote wound healing [32,33]. Therefore, this study incorporated the traditional Chinese medicine monomer compound 4HC into the dressing. 4HC has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, which can reduce IL-6 and TNF-α levels, and increase IL-10 levels, thereby alleviating inflammation [35]. However, the specific mechanisms by which dressings containing 4HC hydrogels treat chronic wound healing in diabetes have not yet been elucidated. Therefore, by measuring the markers of M1 and M2 macrophages and the changes in inflammatory cytokines, we explored the regulatory effect of P-4HC on macrophage polarization. Combined with transcriptome analysis, experimental studies helped identify the potential mechanisms by which P-4HC regulates macrophage polarization. In the inflammatory phase, the plasticity of macrophages is crucial for wound healing and remodeling. Macrophages induce the inflammatory response and tissue damage in the early stages of inflammation, characterized by increased levels of inflammatory cytokines and pathogen-killing capabilities. In the late phase of inflammation, macrophages differentiate into the M2 phenotype and enter the proliferative phase, producing anti-inflammatory cytokines [42]. Different phenotypes of macrophages dominate at specific time points during wound healing. After skin injury, the macrophages infiltrating the wound initially polarize to the M1 phenotype, exhibiting pro-inflammatory characteristics. They can phagocytose all cellular fragments of microorganisms, matrix, and platelets, and secrete pro-inflammatory factors [43]. In the later stage, they polarize into M2 macrophages, secreting anti-inflammatory factors. They also release angiogenic factors, which promote the formation of new blood vessels and granulation tissue, and activate fibroblasts to promote collagen deposition and tissue repair, thereby facilitating wound healing [44,45]. Studies have shown that chronic inflammation can lead to the accumulation of ROS and inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6 and TNF-α [46]. A hyperglycemic environment upregulates pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn increases the polarization of M1 macrophages, forming a vicious cycle that hinders the transition of inflammation to proliferation [10]. Therefore, promoting the M2 polarization of macrophages is of great significance for regulating the immune microenvironment of diabetic wounds and promoting wound healing. Our study indicated that P-4HC reduces the proportion of M1 macrophages, enhances M2 macrophage polarization, and lowers the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in chronic diabetic wounds, thereby alleviating the inflammatory response and expediting chronic wound healing. The molecular mechanisms by which P-4HC regulates macrophage polarization and promotes chronic wound healing in diabetes remain unclear. Therefore, we conducted a transcriptomic analysis, which indicated that P-4HC may affect macrophage polarization through the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway. TLRs are a family of signaling receptors on the cell membrane that play a crucial role in innate immunity, particularly in tissue inflammation [47]. TLR9 is a pro-inflammatory receptor that dose-dependently inhibits M2 polarization of macrophages in RAW264.7 cells. TLR9 deficiency suppresses inflammatory and fibrotic signaling pathways [48,49]. The IL-17 cytokine family includes six structurally related cytokines, IL-17A to IL-17F, five receptors (IL-17RA to E), and one cytoplasmic adapter (CIKS). CIKS contains various functional motifs, particularly in its long N-terminal region, including RNA-binding sites, tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor (TRAF) binding sites, and a U-box with TRAFs E3 ubiquitin ligase activity [50]. By inducing pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, IL-17A is associated with various diseases, including autoimmunity, inflammation, tumors, and infections [51]. Recently, researchers have reported the role of IL-17A in macrophage differentiation. For example, in a mouse model of chronic wound healing, IL-17A-deficient mice showed a significant increase in the abundance of M2 macrophages compared to wild-type mice. Antibody-mediated inhibition of IL-17A improved wound closure 14 days after wound healing, which was associated with an increased abundance of M2 macrophages [52]. Studies have also indicated that macrophages significantly overexpress IL-17RA and IL-17RC in the lesional skin of patients with inflammatory diseases [53]. IL-17RA pairs with IL-17RC to bind IL-17A as a covalent homodimer induction signal [54], suggesting that the pro-inflammatory response of IL-17A relies on IL-17RA and IL-17RC [55]. TRAF1 is associated with Th differentiation in the TNF signaling pathway [56]. Studies have shown that the absence of TRAF1 affects inflammatory cell infiltration, the expression of inflammatory cytokines, and inflammatory signaling pathways [57]. In the myocardium of the TRAF1-KO group, M1 markers and TNF-α were significantly downregulated, and M2 markers were significantly upregulated. In contrast, TRAF1 overexpression upregulated inflammatory factors, indicating that TRAF1 inhibits M2 polarization of macrophages [57]. Studies have shown that TLR9 activators can promote the production of IL-17A, and TLR9 knockout can significantly reduce the plasma levels of IL-17A. Blockade of the IL-17A pathway is beneficial for alleviating excessive inflammation, thereby mitigating organ damage [58]. In the TNF signaling pathway, TRAF1 can bind to IL-17A, forming a strong synergistic effect that amplifies the inflammatory response [59]. Therefore, reducing the expression of TLR9 can inhibit the expression of IL-17A and TRAF1, promote M2 polarization of macrophages, reduce the expression of the inflammatory factor TNF-α, and ameliorate tissue damage. In this study, RT-qPCR and Western blotting showed that P-4HC reduced the expression of TLR9, IL-17A, IL-17RA, IL-17RC, TRAF1, CD86, and iNOS in the wound tissue of db/db mice, while increasing the expression of CD206 and Arg-1. In RAW264.7 cells, activation of either TLR, IL-17, or TNF signaling pathway attenuated the therapeutic effects of P-4HC. Notably, TLR activation upregulated the expression of proteins related to both IL-17 and TNF pathways, while IL-17 activation enhanced the expression of TNF pathway-related proteins. These findings indicate that P-4HC exerts its effects by inhibiting the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway. These results strongly suggest that P-4HC enhances the M2 polarization of macrophages by inhibiting the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway, highlighting the potential mechanisms by which P-4HC regulates the inflammatory response in chronic diabetic wounds.

In summary, our P-4HC hydrogel targets TLR9, IL-17A, and TRAF1 to suppress the TLR/IL-17/TNF signaling pathway, thereby shifting macrophage polarization from the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype (Fig. 9). This phenotypic shift facilitates the transition from the inflammatory phase to the proliferative and remodeling phases, finally enhancing the healing of chronic diabetic wounds. This study not only presents a novel wound dressing that significantly improves diabetic wound healing but also provides new possibilities for developing effective and safe wound management strategies.Fig. 9P-4HC improved wound healing by promoting M2 polarization via the inhibition of the TLR/IL-17/TNF pathways.Fig. 9
