title: Multiple dynamic crosslinked multifunctional hydrogels with glucose/pH dual-responsive adipose-derived stem cells-exosomes-releasing for diabetic wound healing
abstract: Diabetic wounds feature a high-glucose and acidic microenvironment that impairs macrophage polarization and healing. Adipose-derived stem cell-derived exosomes (ADSC-exos) show therapeutic potential but suffer from rapid clearance. This study aimed to develop a smart hydrogel for glucose/pH-responsive ADSC-exos release. A dual-responsive hydrogel (HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E) was fabricated via dynamic triple cross-linking. Characterization included rheometry, mechanical tests, and microscopy. In vitro macrophage polarization was assessed via flow cytometry and Western blot. A diabetic mouse wound model evaluated healing rates, histology, angiogenesis, and inflammation. Proteomics and pathway inhibition studies explored mechanisms. Statistical analysis used t-tests and ANOVA. The hydrogel exhibited excellent self-healing, adhesion, and controlled ADSC-exos release under high-glucose/acidic conditions. It promoted M2 macrophage polarization, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), and accelerated wound healing with enhanced angiogenesis and collagen deposition. Mechanistically, the hydrogel suppressed the Notch/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling pathway.  The smart hydrogel facilitates diabetic wound healing through microenvironment-responsive ADSC-exos release and Notch/NF-κB/NLRP3 pathway inhibition, offering a promising strategy for chronic wound treatment.

sections.text: Diabetic wounds, which are commonly located in the extremities, are often difficult to treat. These wounds are the most common non-traumatic cause of extremity amputation [1, 2], with a toe amputation ratio of ~14%–24% [3, 4]. How to effectively promote the healing of diabetic wounds is a major challenge that must be urgently addressed in medical research [5–7]. The high-glucose microenvironment of diabetic wounds impairs the conversion of macrophages from the M1 to M2 phenotype, and M1 macrophages continue to infiltrate and secrete large amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines [8, 9]. The hyperinflammatory state in the surrounding tissues attracts many activated neutrophils, whose phagocytosis and degranulation functions become activated. These neutrophils secrete additional myeloperoxidase into the extracellular space, which leads to the production of hypohalous acids, especially hypochlorous acid, resulting in the formation of a low-pH microenvironment at the wound site [1, 10]. Moreover, the high-glucose environment associated with diabetic wounds favors bacterial outgrowth, with lactic and acetic acids production during wound-related metabolism, further exacerbating the acidic environment in these wounds [11, 12]. The high-glucose and low-pH microenvironment associated with diabetic wounds leads to impaired proliferation, differentiation, and migration of repair-related cells; hinders local angiogenesis and circulation; and impedes extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, ultimately resulting in suboptimal healing of these wounds [13, 14]. Multiple reports support the beneficial role of exosomes from mesenchymal stem cells (MSC-exos) in tissue repair [15–17]. They are nanometers in size and immune-tolerated, exerting various biological functions through transferring messenger ribonucleic acids (mRNAs), and micro RNAs (miRNAs), and other molecules to recipient cells [17, 18]. MSC-exos ameliorate bronchial dysplasia and restore lung function by inhibiting proinflammatory M1 macrophages and enhancing the effects of anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages [19]. Wang et al. reported that MSC-exos also exert inhibitory effects on the inflammation-related Notch pathway [20]. Our study [21] showed that ADSC-exos, a subtype of MSC-exos in cutaneous tissue, increased M2 polarization of macrophages and reduced the release of inflammatory cytokines in a high-glucose environment in vitro. However, when ADSC-exos were injected into diabetic wounds in vivo, their anti-inflammatory effects were limited because of rapid clearance of the body, moreover, prolonged diabetic wound healing further limited the potential therapeutic benefit of ADSC-exos [22–24]. In recent years, hydrogels have attracted researchers’ interest owing to their excellent hydrophilicity, biocompatibility, and 3D porous structure [25–27], whose structure is similar to that of the ECM, enabling optimization of the wound microenvironment to promote healing [28, 29]. Moreover, the use of hydrogels as delivery systems for exosomes is expected to enable MSC-exos to efficiently exert long-lasting biological effects through controlled-release delivery [26, 30–33]. However, hydrogel dressings that can intelligently release MSC-exos in response to the pathological wound microenvironment while exhibiting multifunctional properties to promote diabetic wound healing has barely been reported. In this study, we designed a multiple dynamic crosslinked multifunctional hydrogels with glucose/pH dual-responsive ADSC-exosomes-releasing for diabetic wound healing. The hydrogel was engineered through dynamic triple cross-linking involving Schiff base, phenylboronic ester, and thiol-Ag+ interactions, integrating antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, tissue-adhesive, and self-healing properties. Hyaluronic acid was modified with adipic dihydrazide and 3-aminophenylboronic acid to yield hyaluronic acid-phenylboronic acid conjugate (HAP), enabling pH/glucose-responsive crosslinking via Schiff base and phenylboronic ester bonds. Oxidized chondroitin sulfate (OCS) introduced aldehyde groups for additional Schiff base crosslinking, while its ortho-dihydroxy groups facilitated borate ester formation with HAP. This dual dynamic network selectively dissociates in the hyperglycemic and acidic diabetic wound microenvironment, triggering hydrogel swelling for controlled ADSC-exos release. However, hydrogel dressings based on dynamic dual cross-linking between a Schiff base and phenyl borate ester are extremely prone to structural collapse. Furthermore, the strong susceptibility to bacterial infection is another characteristic of diabetic wounds. Therefore, we introduced 4-arm PEG-thiol to generate a dynamic Ag+-based triple cross-linking network in the hydrogel, which conferred long-term stability, along with antibacterial properties and superior mechanical performance (Figure 1a). The hydrogel exhibited excellent self-healing capability, injectability, adhesion, and biocompatibility properties. Moreover, it was shown to accelerate wound healing in a mouse model of diabetic wounds by reducing the inflammatory response, promoting vascular reconstruction, and enhancing re-epithelialization and collagen deposition. Mechanistic findings revealed that the hydrogel promoted the polarization of macrophages to the M2 phenotype by releasing exosomes that inhibit Notch/NF-κb/NLRP3 signaling to ameliorate the inflammatory response in diabetic wounds (Figure 1b). This study demonstrated the potential application of this multifunctional hydrogel with smart release of ADSC-exos as a novel highly promising strategy for the clinical treatment of chronic diabetic wounds.

sections.section: Evaluation of the dual responsiveness of the hydrogels to pH and glucose
sections.text: The fluorescent dye rhodamine was used as a model drug for the preliminary evaluation of the dual responsiveness of the hydrogels to pH and glucose. Specifically, the PEG/Ag and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogels were first loaded with equal concentrations of rhodamine and then placed in low-pH (pH = 5.5) and high-glucose (33 mM glucose) solutions. The hydrogel solutions were then placed in a shaking incubator at 37°C for 1 h, and hydrogel structural integrity and rhodamine release from the hydrogel were observed. A camera was used to record the aforementioned process.

Label-free LC–MS/MS was used for proteomic analysis of the control group and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel group (n = 5). After protein extraction and trypsin digestion, liquid chromatography mobile phase A was used to dissolve the peptides; then, the peptides were separated by a NanoElute ultra-performance liquid chromatography system and injected into the capillary ion source for ionization analyses by tims-TOF Pro mass spectrometry. The MaxQuant search engine (v.1.5.2.8) was used to process the MS/MS data. KEGG online tools were used to annotate the differentially expressed proteins, which were subsequently matched with annotations in the database using KEGG Mapper. The GO annotation proteome was screened with the UniProt-GOA database (http://www.ebi.ac.Uk/GOA/). P-values <.05 were considered to indicate statistical significance.

All the data were analysed using SPSS 17.0 software, and the results are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Student’s t-test was used for comparisons between two groups, and statistical significance was analysed via one-way variance (ANOVA) one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test. P < .05 was considered to indicate statistically significant results.

In this study, a dual pH/glucose-responsive hydrogel dressing (HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag) was constructed by dynamic dual cross-linking via Schiff base and phenyl borate ester bonds in HAP and OCS, respectively, supplemented by a third dynamic cross-linking network involving 4-arm PEG-thiol and Ag+. Exosomes (E) were then loaded onto the hydrogel to obtain the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel dressing. The characterization results of ADSCs and ADSC-Exos are presented in Figure S1a–e and Figure S2a–c. To assess how the pH/glucose dual-responsive release of exosomes affects diabetic wound healing, we fabricated a non-responsive PEG/Ag hydrogel dressing using 4-arm PEG-thiol and Ag+. Subsequently, exosomes (E) were loaded into this hydrogel to prepare the PEG/Ag-E hydrogel dressing. As observed via laser confocal microscopy, the exosomes were encapsulated within the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel (Figure S2d). The compositions of all four hydrogels are shown in Figure 2a.

sections.section: Rheological and swelling properties of the hydrogels
sections.text: We evaluated the rheological properties of the four hydrogels (Figure 2b). The storage modulus (G′) of all hydrogels was significantly higher than the loss modulus (G″), confirming their elastic nature. Compared to the PEG/Ag hydrogel (G′ of ~600 Pa), the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel had a higher modulus (G′ > 1500 Pa) due to the introduction of the second cross-linking network. Notably, the introduction of exosomes did not affect the rheological properties of these two hydrogels. The PEG/Ag-series hydrogels have favorable water absorption capacity and can thus maintain a moist microenvironment, absorb wound exudate, and prevent infections in the wound. As depicted in Figure 2c, the incorporation of hydrophilic polysaccharides—for instance, HA and CS—led to the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel exhibiting a higher equilibrium swelling ratio (~400%) and a longer equilibrium swelling period (>100 h) compared with the PEG/Ag hydrogel. The latter has an equilibrium swelling ratio of 200% and an equilibrium swelling period of <10 h. This helps maintain a moist microenvironment and facilitates exudate absorption during the early stage of wound healing. Importantly, exosomes loading did not affect the swelling properties of either hydrogel.

sections.section: Evaluation of tissue adhesion, mechanical performance, and microstructure of the hydrogels
sections.text: Sufficient tissue adhesiveness is essential for hydrogel wound dressings to maintain adherence to wound surfaces. A swine skin lap shear test was used to evaluate the tissue adhesiveness of the four hydrogel types (Figure 2d). As shown in Figure 2e, the strength of adhesiveness between the PEG/Ag -series hydrogels and skin was ~5 kPa, attributable to the hydrophilicity of PEG, covalent cross-linking between thiol groups in the hydrogel and tissue extracellular proteins during in situ gelation, and the entanglement of polymer chains. After introducing the dual cross-linking secondary network involving the Schiff base and the phenyl borate ester in HAP and OCS, respectively, to the hydrogel, the tissue adhesiveness of the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogels increased to 11–12 kPa. This increase was mainly due to the formation of dynamic Schiff base interactions between aldehyde groups in the hydrogel and amino groups on the tissue surface. HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E showed greater tissue adhesiveness than commercially available fibrin glue (~5 kPa), making it suitable for chronic diabetic wounds. Frequent movement and stretching of the skin necessitate greater extensibility and mechanical performance of hydrogel dressings. Therefore, we evaluated the tensile properties of the hydrogels through macroscopic observations of stretching and quantitative tensile. First, the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel was highly stretchable (Figure 2f). Further quantitative stretch tests showed that the stretch ratios of HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E exceeded 80%, while the PEG/Ag-series hydrogels had poor tensile properties (stretch ratio <30%, Figure 2g). The stretchability of the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogels significantly exceeded human skin (50%), suggesting that the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel wound dressing can satisfy wound healing requirements in terms of stretchability. Interconnected large-pore structures within the hydrogel can support cellular penetration, facilitating wound healing. We characterized the microscopic appearance of the four hydrogels. The PEG/Ag-series hydrogels showed uniform but incomplete large pore structures, likely due to the low cross-linking density of the polymer network (Figure 2h). After the introduction of the dual cross-linking secondary network involving the Schiff base and the phenylboronic ester in HAP and OCS, respectively, the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogels demonstrated complete and dense large pore structures capable of enhancing cellular infiltration and material exchange. In addition, the microscopic appearance of the hydrogels was consistent with the modulus results.

sections.section: Evaluation of hydrogel self-healing and dual responsiveness to pH and glucose
sections.text: Skin stretching, frequent movement, and infiltration of external environmental factors can physically damage hydrogel dressings. Therefore, effective self-healing is necessary to maintain an intact barrier, thereby prolonging dressing lifespan. The four hydrogels’ dynamic cross-linking networks enable self-healing through single/multiple reversible bonds. Under alternating step strains (600% to 1%), the G′ of the PEG/Ag hydrogel decreased from ~600 Pa to ~170 Pa. This led to G″ being greater than G′, indicating network disruption (Figure 3a). However, switching to low strain (1%) allowed the rapid recovery of the hydrogel to its original modulus, with G′ being greater than G″. This demonstrated that the dynamic cross-linking between thiol-Ag+ in the hydrogel could quickly restore the network structure to achieve rapid self-healing. Three consecutive strain cycles showed consistent G′/G″ recovery, confirming repeatable self-healing. After incorporating dynamic dual cross-linking-encompassing both Schiff base and phenyl borate ester linkages-into the hydrogel, the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel exhibited a more stable G′ value under low strain. This indicates that it has superior self-healing capabilities compared to the PEG/Ag hydrogel (Figure 3b). Building on these findings, we further assessed the macroscopic self-healing performance of the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel (Figure 3c). This was done by bisecting both rhodamine-stained and unstained hydrogel samples, then bringing the cut surfaces into contact without external intervention for 1 min. Healed hydrogels retained >65% strain capacity, nearing the original 80% (Figure 3d). This efficiency stems from synergistic thiol-Ag+ coordination, Schiff base, and phenyl borate ester networks (Figure 3e). Dual responsiveness to glucose and pH, attributed to dynamic dual cross-linking involving Schiff base and phenyl borate ester in HAP and OCS respectively, allows the hydrogel to intelligently respond to high-glucose and low-pH microenvironment associated with chronic diabetic wounds, achieving on-demand exosome release. Rhodamine-loaded PEG/Ag and HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogels were respectively placed in high-glucose and low-pH environments (Figure 3f). The PEG/Ag hydrogel maintained structural integrity over an extended period, and the rhodamine payload was not released to a significant degree. In the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag hydrogel, destruction of the internal dynamic cross-linking network collapsed under high glucose and low pH (Figure 3g), triggering rapid swelling and even partial dissolution. Under these conditions, the hydrogel’s rhodamine payload was rapidly released into the external environment. Furthermore, we measured the concentration of released ADSC-exos in different environments. ADSC-exos release quantification showed both hydrogels exhibited sustained release in PBS (pH 7.4, glucose-free) with comparable cumulative concentrations (Figure 3h). Acidic conditions (pH 5.5) significantly enhanced exosome release versus physiological pH (Figure 3i), due to pH-triggered phenyl borate ester cleavage. This pH-responsive behavior correlates with enhanced drug release in diabetic wounds (Figure 3i), highlighting HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel’s therapeutic potential. Hyperglycemic conditions (33 mM glucose) induced glucose-dependent release kinetics (Figure 3j): Schiff base-mediated structural changes in HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogels progressively amplified ADSC-exos release. These results validate the hydrogel’s dual pH/glucose responsiveness for enhanced diabetic wound repair.

sections.section: Hemocompatibility and cytocompatibility of the hydrogel
sections.text: Hemostasis, the first stage of wound healing, requires hemocompatible wound dressings. In this study, a hemolysis assay was used to evaluate the hemocompatibility of the four hydrogels. The four hydrogels were incubated with mouse red blood cells (RBCs) at 37°C for 1 h (Figure S3a and b), all hydrogels produced pale-yellow supernatants similar to PBS controls, with intact RBC morphology. In contrast, Triton X-100 caused bright red supernatant due to complete hemolysis and erythrocyte rupture. Quantitative analysis showed hydrogel hemolysis ratios <3% (vs. PBS 0% and Triton X-100100%), confirming excellent hemocompatibility (Figure S3c). Hydrogel wound dressings must be biocompatible, and cytocompatibility testing is the most commonly used method to evaluate the biocompatibility of biomaterials in vitro. Fibroblasts are important cellular components of the wound healing process. Therefore, in this study, fibroblasts (L929 cells) were placed in direct contact with the four hydrogels to evaluate their cytocompatibility. After 1 day of direct contact with the hydrogel, the viability of L929 cells in the four hydrogel groups was greater than 90% (Figure S3d). Further dead/live staining showed that the cell density of L929 cells in contact with the four hydrogels was similar to that of the control group and the high glucose group, and most L929 cells maintained a spindle shape (Figure S3e). The Ki67 immunofluorescence (IF) assay showed that the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group contained the largest number of Ki67-positive cells (Figure S3f). This finding confirms that the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group has a strong ability to promote cell proliferation.

sections.section: Effects of the hydrogels on macrophages
sections.text: Macrophages are highly plastic cells. During the wound healing process, they play a crucial role in resolving inflammation throughout the repair process via M1/M2 phenotypic transition [34–36]. Macrophage responses to hydrogels were assessed using Transwell chambers (Figure 4a and c). Exosomes exert their biological effects upon internalization by the recipient cell [37, 38]; accordingly, ADSC-exos labeled with the fluorescent dye PKH26 and macrophages labeled with phalloidin were cocultured for 24 h, after which exosome uptake by macrophages was investigated (Figure 4b). To simulate a diabetic environment in vitro [39], we cultured the macrophages under normal conditions as controls, while under high-glucose conditions as high-glucose controls, and the macrophages with different hydrogels under the high-glucose conditions as the experimental groups. After 3 days of culture, we assessed the viability of the macrophages [40]. The results showed that minimal dead cells were present in each group, with no differences in cell viability among groups (Figure 4d). Dual immunohistochemistry for CD86+ (M1)/CD206+ (M2) revealed significantly lower CD86+/CD206+ ratios in the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group versus others (Figure 4e). Flow cytometry confirmed this group had fewer M1 (CD86+) macrophages than high-glucose controls and more M2 (CD206+) macrophages than the other experimental groups (Figure S4). Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and arginase 1 (Arg-1) serve as markers for M1 and M2 macrophages, respectively [41, 42]. Western blot results showed that, compared with the high-glucose control group, the exosome-loaded group exhibited reduced iNOS expression and increased Arg-1 levels. The HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group showed the lowest iNOS and highest Arg-1 levels (Figure 4f), confirmed by quantitative analyses (Figure 4g and h). IL-1β is a proinflammatory cytokine secreted by M1 macrophages [43], whereas IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine from M2 macrophages [44]. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed that compared with the PEG/Ag-E, the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group had significantly lower concentrations of IL-1β in the cell supernatant and markedly greater protein expression of IL-10 (Figure 4i and j). These results indicate that both the PEG/Ag-E and the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogels promote macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype and reduce inflammatory cytokine release. This can be attributed to the strong anti-inflammatory effects of ADSC-exos in the hydrogel. The glucose/pH-responsive group’s enhanced M2 polarization and anti-inflammatory efficacy stem from Schiff base/phenylboronic ester dual cross-linking, enabling microenvironment-responsive ADSC-exos release. This mechanism ensures optimal exosome bioactivity in diabetic conditions.

sections.section: The hydrogels promote diabetic wound healing
sections.text: Next, the in vivo efficacy of the hydrogels was assessed. Streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice [45] with fasting blood glucose exceeding 16.7 mmol/L via tail vein puncture [46] received 1 cm-diameter full-thickness dorsal wounds. Control mice used Tegaderm dressings, while experimental groups received PEG/Ag-series hydrogels. Ten days after treatment with PKH67-labeled HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E, exosome fluorescence remained detectable in the wound tissues (Figure S2e). As shown in the wound images (Figure 5a), the wound area gradually decreased in all groups. By day 7, the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group exhibited significantly faster healing versus others, achieving near-complete closure by day 10 (Figure 5a and i). Non-responsive exosome hydrogels promoted healing, but environment-responsive hydrogels enhanced efficacy through increased ADSC-exos release. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained day 14 wounds revealed the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group had shortest wound length and most complete epithelialization (Figure 5b), confirming superior healing capacity. The formation and arrangement of collagen stand as key indicators for assessing wound healing. Sufficient collagen deposition facilitates repair processes, while excessive deposition alongside disorganized collagen fibers can lead to scar hypertrophy, thereby hindering healing. In comparison with other groups, the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group exhibited the most orderly collagen arrangement and the highest collagen content (Figure 5c). Both H&E and Masson staining validated the effectiveness of the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel in wound healing. Blood vessels support healing by providing nutrients and oxygen [47, 48]. Blood perfusion analysis using imaging devices [49] revealed gradual perfusion increase across groups over time (Figure 5d and k). The exosome-loaded hydrogel groups exhibited superior angiogenesis, with HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group showing the highest vascularization due to microenvironment-responsive exosome release.α-SMA/CD31 [50, 51] co-IF at day 7 post-injury demonstrated that environmentally responsive hydrogels induced more intact vascular lumens with significantly higher density than those in other groups (Figure 5e–h and j).

sections.section: Anti-inflammatory effects of hydrogels on diabetic wounds
sections.text: Previous studies confirm that after tissue injury, M1 macrophages are initially recruited to wounds, attracting inflammatory cells to clear necrotic tissue and pathogens. During later healing stages, macrophages transition predominantly to the M2 phenotype, promoting tissue repair [52–54]. However, in chronic diabetic wounds, M1/M2 transition is impaired, leading to prolonged inflammation [8, 55, 56]. Persistent inflammation inhibits angiogenesis, resulting in poor granulation tissue development, delayed epithelialization, and slower wound healing [57–59]. We analysed macrophage polarization and inflammation in vivo. Day 3 wound specimens were subjected to IF staining for macrophage markers: F4/80 (pan-macrophage), CD86 (M1), and CD206 (M2). Diabetic controls showed abundant CD86+F4/80+ M1 macrophages. The HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group exhibited significantly fewer M1 macrophages (Figure 6a and h) and predominant M2 polarization (Figure S5a and b) versus other groups. IL-6 and TNF-α levels were assessed via immunohistochemistry on day 3. All exosome-loaded hydrogels reduced inflammatory cytokine expression versus controls (Figure 6b), confirming exosome-mediated anti-inflammatory effects. Furthermore, wounds treated with the environmentally responsive hydrogel exhibited significantly lower levels of inflammatory cytokines compared to other groups. Quantitative analyses confirmed that this group had the lowest IL-6 and TNF-α expression (Figure 6b–d). These findings indicate that the hydrogel efficiently releases exosomes in response to the wound’s high-glucose/low-pH microenvironment, thereby exerting potent anti-inflammatory effects in diabetic wounds. Western blot analysis demonstrated that the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E group more effectively reduced iNOS expression in M1 macrophages and enhanced Arg-1 expression in M2 macrophages versus other treatments (Figure 6e–g). Collectively, these data demonstrate that the environmentally responsive hydrogel substantially ameliorates the wound’s inflammatory microenvironment and promotes M2 macrophage polarization, primarily due to ADSC-exos’ efficient release.

sections.section: Proteomic analysis validates adipose-derived stem cells exosomes anti-inflammatory effects
sections.text: Day 7 post-injury skin tissues underwent LC–MS/MS proteomics [60, 61] (n = 5/group: control vs. HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E). Quality control ensured data reliability (Figure 7a and b). Analysis of 4445 proteins identified 479 differentially expressed (272↑;207↓), visualized via volcano plot (Figure 7d). Cytoplasmic (35.46%) and extracellular (14.79%) localization suggested exosome involvement (Figure 7c). Heatmaps [62] revealed HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E-mediated suppression of inflammatory proteins during remodeling (Figure 7f). GO/KEGG analysis [63, 64] highlighted enrichment in immune defense pathways, including NF-κB signaling and sugar metabolism (Figure 7e and h). These findings collectively demonstrate ADSC-exos’ potent anti-inflammatory bioactivity through targeted pathway modulation. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis [65] revealed correlations between NF-κB-related proteins and four others, with NLRP3 emerging as a key player (Figure 7g). Previous studies demonstrate upregulated NLRP3 inflammasome expression in chronic diabetic wounds, co-occurring with elevated IL-1β/IL-18 levels [66–68]. We propose that macrophage activation triggers NF-κB signaling, subsequently activating the NLRP3 inflammasome complex and amplifying proinflammatory cytokine production, thereby exacerbating the wound’s inflammatory microenvironment. The HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel likely exerts anti-inflammatory effects via suppression of this NF-κB/NLRP3 axis, as validated in subsequent mechanistic studies. As a classic upstream regulatory pathway of NF-κB, Notch signaling exerts detrimental effects on late-stage diabetic wound healing. Proteomics revealed that the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel suppressed NF-κB pathway activity and exhibited NF-κB/NLRP3 interactions. We subsequently validated the Notch/NF-κB/NLRP3 axis. Notch signaling was activated under high glucose, while the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel suppressed Notch-related proteins (NICD, Hes-1, Hey-1), confirming Notch pathway inhibition (Figure 7i and j). Using RBPJ−/− myeloid cells (Notch−/− group) and wild-type controls, we observed that both HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E and Notch−/− groups exhibited reduced NF-κB activation (p-IκBα, p-P65) and NLRP3/Caspase-1 expression versus controls (Figure 7k–n). NF-κB inhibitor (BAY11-7082) controls further demonstrated that the hydrogel decreased NLRP3/Caspase-1 levels (Figure 7o and p) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6; Figure 7q–s), while elevating anti-inflammatory IL-10 (Figure 7t). These data conclusively demonstrate that the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel alleviates inflammation through Notch signaling blockade, thereby suppressing NF-κB/NLRP3 activation and inflammatory cytokine release.

At present, there are >537 million diabetic patients worldwide, and the incidence of diabetic wounds is ~8.1%. Due to the high-glucose and low-pH microenvironment associated with diabetic wounds, repair-related cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration are impaired, thereby hindering local angiogenesis and circulation and impeding ECM synthesis, ultimately resulting in the suboptimal healing of these wounds [13, 14]. This places a heavy burden on families and society. As key components of the innate immune system, macrophages are abnormally activated and mediate inflammation and oxidative stress in diabetic wounds [3]. Studies have confirmed that the number of M1 macrophages in diabetic wounds is significantly increased, and these cells release proinflammatory factors, which modulate angiogenesis and reduce ECM deposition. This abnormal inflammatory environment weakens the ability of M2-polarized macrophages to exert anti-inflammatory effects and promote wound repair. Reduced secretion of anti-inflammatory factors further exacerbates the inflammatory imbalance, ultimately leading to impaired wound healing [4]. Therefore, promoting M2-type polarization and functional recovery of macrophages is critical for the healing of diabetic wounds. ADSC-exos can promote M2 phenotypic transformation of macrophages in high-glucose environments in vitro and reduce inflammatory factor release. However, their therapeutic efficacy upon injection into diabetic wounds remains limited. The reason for this finding is that, on the one hand, prolongation of the healing process limits the function of exosomes with a short half-life; on the other hand, hostile high-glucose/low-pH microenvironments impairing exosome bioactivity, ultimately hindering diabetic wound treatment. In this study, an intelligent dual-responsive exosome delivery system based on a dynamic triple cross-linking network of Schiff bases, phenylboronic esters, and 4-arm PEG-thiol with Ag+ was prepared for the treatment of chronic diabetic wounds. This system specifically responds to pathological high-glucose and acidic microenvironments via Schiff base/phenylboronic ester dual-crosslinking, enabling controlled ADSC-exos release under diabetic conditions. Compared to non-responsive hydrogels, the microenvironment-responsive hydrogel achieves localized exosome enrichment, thereby exerting enhanced anti-inflammatory effects and accelerating diabetic wound healing. Concretely speaking: this intelligent dual-loaded hydrogel is constructed based on a dual dynamic crosslinked network formed by HAP and OCS: On one hand, the Schiff base bonds (-C=N-) confer pH responsiveness, exhibiting significantly accelerated hydrolysis rates in the acidic microenvironment (pH 5.0–6.5) of diabetic wounds; on the other hand, the phenylboronate ester bonds (B-O-C) provide glucose sensitivity, undergoing competitive dissociation when wound glucose concentration exceeds 7 mM. The synergistic action of these dual bonds reduces crosslinking density, triggering hydrogel network hydrolysis and subsequent exosome release. Thereby significantly elevating the local exosome concentration at the wound site to effectively modulate the inflammatory response, accelerate wound healing, and synergistically promote vascularization, collagen remodeling, and inflammation regulation, ultimately improving the healing quality of diabetic wounds. The importance of the Notch signaling pathway in cell fate determination and development is well established. Studies demonstrate that macrophage-specific Notch signaling blockade improves late-stage wound repair in type II diabetes. Our group previously elucidated Notch signaling’s role in burn-induced oxidative stress, sepsis, and inflammation. In this study, we explored the HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel’s regulatory effects on macrophage function at molecular, cellular, and systemic levels, revealing its suppression of Notch signaling-related proteins. GO analysis identified enriched differentially expressed proteins involved in immune defense and inflammatory processes, while KEGG pathway analysis highlighted NF-κB signaling as a key inflammatory pathway. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis revealed NF-κB-NLRP3 correlations (Figure 7g). Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex triggers IL-1β cleavage/release, which amplifies TNF-α, IL-8, and IL-18 production, exacerbating the inflammatory cascade-a hallmark of chronic refractory wounds. Supporting this, NLRP3-deficient mice exhibit reduced M1-associated cytokines (e.g. TNF-α) and elevated M2-associated IL-10. NLRP3 pathway inhibition enhances VEGF, chemokines, and angiogenesis factors, promoting neovascularization and granulation tissue formation. Our findings confirm that the microenvironment-responsive hydrogel accelerates diabetic wound healing via Notch/NF-κB/NLRP3 axis suppression, alleviating inflammation and stimulating angiogenesis. This system optimizes ADSC-exos’ therapeutic potential, offering novel strategies for clinical management of chronic diabetic wounds. Although this hydrogel demonstrates promising therapeutic potential, its clinical translation still faces challenges in scalable production stability (e.g. dynamic crosslinking quality control) and cost-effectiveness. Integrating 3D printing technology to fabricate customized dressings or employing nanoengineering to optimize material composition may serve as effective strategies to overcome current limitations. Future research could explore: combining microfluidics to precisely regulate exosome loading efficiency; incorporating artificial intelligence predictive models to optimize dynamic crosslinking parameters, and developing biodegradable alternatives to mitigate long-term risks. These directions will advance smart hydrogels toward clinical utility.

We successfully developed a dual-responsive hydrogel delivery system that efficiently responds to the high-glucose and acidic microenvironment of chronic diabetic wounds. The HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel effectively promotes diabetic wound healing through controlled ADSC-exos release. This hydrogel demonstrates optimized self-healing properties, injectability, and tissue adhesion—critical characteristics for clinical wound management. Notably, the hydrogel exhibits antimicrobial activity and high biocompatibility. Within a diabetic full-thickness cutaneous wound model, the dual-responsive HAP/OCS/PEG/Ag-E hydrogel notably promoted the M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization shift, mitigating tissue inflammation, fostering angiogenesis, and speeding up wound healing. At the mechanistic level, the hydrogel inhibited the release of inflammatory cytokines through the Notch/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling pathway-this was confirmed by the decreased expression of pathway-related proteins and the weakened inflammatory cascades.

title: Curcumin-loaded copper/iron bimetallic nanoparticle-incorporated hydrogel scaffold: a sequential microenvironment reprogramming platform for accelerated chronic wound healing
abstract: Diabetic wound management represents a substantial clinical challenge owing to the deteriorative tissue microenvironment including the excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), persistent inflammation, and potential bacterial infection. To address these issues, herein, a hybrid hydrogel scaffold (SF@NP-Cur) capable of sequentially reprogramming the wound microenvironment was developed through microfluidic 3D printing technique for infected chronic wound healing. Such scaffold incorporates curcumin-loaded copper/iron bimetallic nanoparticles (NP-Cur), which confers not only the oxidase- and peroxidase-like activities for efficient ROS scavenging, but also enables the multimodal antibacterial behavior via copper release and photothermal effects of NP-Cur. Simultaneously, the release NP-Cur contribute to the pro-migration effect on fibroblasts, accelerating wound healing by promoting collagen deposition and angiogenesis. Furthermore, the loaded curcumin within NP-Cur enables the polarization of M1 macrophages toward the pro-regenerative M2 phenotype. Benefitting from these properties, such hydrogel scaffold potently accelerates the reconstruction of infected diabetic wounds by reprogramming the wound microenvironment indicated by the reduced ROS, attenuated inflammation, plentiful M2-type macrophages, and enhanced neovascularization. Collectively, this immunomodulatory scaffold represents a promising dressing for reconstruction of impaired chronic tissue environments, offering a robust therapeutic strategy for chronic wound repair and regeneration. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12951-026-04139-1. Keywords: SF@NP-Cur scaffold, Multimodal antibacterial, Copper/iron bimetallic nanoparticles, ROS-scavenging, Diabetic wound healing

sections.text: The treatment of non-healing cutaneous chronic wounds following trauma and surgical procedures remains a formidable clinical challenge, bringing about tremendous economic burden for diabetic patients and significantly impairing their life quality [1, 2]. In diabetic wounds, inflammation persists during the remodeling phase, thereby compromising the proper wound healing [3]. The continuing inflammation in diabetic wounds is significantly linked to the bacterial infections and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which result in the occurrence, development, and prognosis of chronic wounds [4]. Bacterial infections are a primary concern in the early stages of wound healing owing to the lack of inherent protective function of skin, which facilitate the release the various of inflammatory factors and significantly alter the microenvironment around the wound due to an increase in certain enzymes secreted by bacteria [5, 6]. Moreover, as a subsequent symptom of pathogen infections, the generated inflammatory cytokines usually initiate the production ROS and further cause tissue damage [7–9]. Such increased oxidative stress consequently compromises key wound healing events, including angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and tissue regeneration, resulting in a significant delay in wound healing efficacy [10, 11]. To address these tissue repair challenges, various materials with antibacterial, antioxidant, and repair-promoting properties have been developed, including hydrogels, films, sponges, and nanomaterials [12–17]. Among them, hydrogels stand out owing to their high compatibility, porous structure, and shape customizability [18, 19]. In particular, the advanced 3D printing technique has propelled the progression of hydrogels in wound healing by enabling the fabrication of intricate hydrogel scaffolds, which can adapt to the different irregular wound shapes and is conductive to cell migration [20–22]. Despite extensive progress, hydrogel scaffold-based therapy for diabetic wounds remains significant challenges, which require them to effectively eliminate pathogen and scavenge superfluous ROS, and meanwhile, possess the capability to reprogram the erratic inflammatory microenvironment to further facilitate tissue growth [23, 24]. Therefore, the development of versatile hydrogel scaffolds that can potently reprogram the chronic wound microenvironment including inflammation, cell behaviors, angiogenesis, and bacterial infection for promoted skin regeneration is still highly anticipated. Here, we present a silk fibroin (SF)-based hydrogel scaffold integrated with curcumin-loaded copper-iron bimetallic nanoparticles (NP-Cur) through microfluidic 3D printing technique for reprogramming the deteriorative wound microenvironment, as illustrated in Scheme 1. SF, derived from natural silk, has garnered significant interest in the biomedical field owing to the exceptional biocompatibility, tunable biodegradability, and large-scale production [25, 26]. Besides, through the chemical modification, SF can be also engineered as 3D printing inks to construct bioactive and customized 3D scaffolds, conforming to the irregular defect geometries and promoting tissue regeneration [27–29]. Despite many successes, the pure SF-based hydrogel scaffolds often exhibit limited antibacterial activity, making them insufficient to address the intricate pathological microenvironment of diabetic wounds. In contrast, Cur, a natural polyphenol, has demonstrated remarkable biological activities including anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects that can alleviate chronic inflammation and remodel the wound microenvironment [30, 31]. While, its clinical application is substantially limited by the poor aqueous solubility, low bioavailability, and chemical instability. As a result, the direct incorporation of Cur into hydrophilic hydrogels often results in the inadequate therapeutic efficacy [32, 33]. To address these limitations, diverse drug delivery carriers have been developed. Metal-phenolic coordination-driven self-assembly, in particular, has emerged as a promising strategy for constructing nanocarriers [34, 35]. Nanoparticles based on metal ions such as silver, iron, and copper ion can not only serve as the effective drug vehicles but also exhibit the enhanced antibacterial properties [36, 37]. Furthermore, the low dose of copper also offers an additional therapeutic benefit by promoting cell migration, whereas iron-polyphenol coordination complexes can be facilely engineered to possess the obvious photothermal conversion capability, enabling the efficient bacterial elimination while minimizing the risk of antimicrobial resistance [38–41]. Thus, it is conceived that, the construction of Cur-loaded iron/copper-based nanoparticles followed by the integration into SF hydrogel systems can not only boost the Cur loading efficiency, but also achieve the enhanced antibacterial and anti-inflammation effects, consequently promoting the tissue microenvironment reprogramming. In this research, we fabricated a SF-based immunomodulatory hydrogel scaffold via microfluidic-assisted 3D printing and applied for the treatment of infected diabetic wound healing. By incorporating Cur-loaded copper/iron bimetallic nanoparticles (NP-Cur), the obtained SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold conferred not only the oxidase- and peroxidase-like activities for efficient ROS scavenging, but also enabled the multimodal antibacterial behavior via copper release and photothermal effects of NP-Cur. Simultaneously, the temperature sensitivity of SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold allowed the continuous release NP-Cur in the infected microenvironment and enabled the pro-migration effect on fibroblasts, which was conducive to tissue repair. Furthermore, the macrophages within the wound bed had a high transformation from M1 to pro-regenerative M2 phenotype, resulting in the enhanced anti-inflammatory effect. In vivo experiments indicated that the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold accelerated infected chronic wound healing by reprogramming the intricate wound microenvironment indicated by the reduced oxidative stress, attenuated inflammation, multimodal antibacterial activity, and further enhanced neovascularization. Thus, it is believed that the proposed strategy presents an effective personalized therapeutic platform for refractory diabetic wounds and provides insights for clinical applications.

sections.section: Preparation and characterization of NP-Cur and SF@NP-Cur
sections.text: The fabrication of the Cur-loaded bimetallic phenolic assembled nanoparticles (NP-Cur) is illustrated in Fig. 1a. In detail, Fe3+ was first added to the TA solution to form the TA-Fe complex via the coordination of the catechol-Fe3+, with the subsequent addition of Cu2+ under vigorous stirring to form the Cu-TA-Fe complex. Then, Cur was added dropwise to the Cu-TA-Fe complex solution to obtain the final NP-Cur. As a control, the nanoparticles without incorporating Cur (denoted as NP1) were also prepared. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and dynamic light scattering (DLS) results in Fig. 1b and c revealed that the NP-Cur possessed a spherical-like morphology and were well-dispersed, with an average particle size of about 400 nm. Besides, with increasing the Fe3+ contents during the preparation of NP-Cur, the color of the resulting NP-Cur solution became deeper (Figure S1). To improve the applicability of NP-Cur, the silk fibroin methacrylate (SFMA) was prepared and the NP-Cur-loaded SFMA solution was used as the 3D printing ink. Thus, by using the photocuring 3D printing technique, the NP-Cur-integrated SF hydrogel scaffolds (denoted as SF@NP-Cur) can be fabricated (Fig. 1d). The presence of characteristic Cur peaks (e.g., hydroxyl and aromatic rings) in the FTIR spectrum of the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel suggested the successful loading of the NP-Cur nanoparticles (Figure S2). Optical images demonstrated the successful fabrication of a cubic lattice scaffold, and the filaments of the scaffold exhibited a regular cylindrical shape (Fig. 1e and f). SEM results revealed that the 3D-printed scaffold possessed a vertically staggered network structure as it was printed and the filaments showed the porous surface from the top and side view. Moreover, the NP-Cur scattered within the scaffold matrix can be clearly observed (Fig. 1g-l). Furthermore, the typical elements, such as C, N, O, Fe, and Cu, were also uniformly distributed within the scaffold from the elemental mapping images (Fig. 1m).

sections.section: Characterization of SF@NP-Cur and its ROS scavenging ability
sections.text: The mechanical strength is critical for their use in the biomedical field. To confirm the mechanical strength of the constructed SF-based hydrogels, the rheological analysis was performed. As shown in Fig. 2a, the storage moduli (G′) and loss moduli (G′′) showed slight changes over the entire frequency range. Besides, G′ of hydrogels increased with raising the SFMA concentrations from 5% to 15%, and the incorporation of NP-Cur showed no influence to the G′. Moreover, the hydrogels maintained a stable G′ across the applied strains of 1% to 100%, and particularly, for the 10% hydrogel, it can achieve a higher fracture strain (~ 788%) than that of 15% hydrogel (~ 298%) (Fig. 2b and S3), suggesting the reduced brittleness and enhanced fracture resistance of the 10% SF hydrogel. Thus, the 10% SFMA formulation was selected as the optimal composition for the scaffold fabrication, and further the printed 10% scaffolds were employed for the subsequent studies. The swelling and degradation ability of hydrogels are also the important properties for the biomedical use. The results showed that the hydrogel scaffold exhibited excellent swelling properties with time, demonstrated the high water-retention ability. In particular, the initial rapid water-swelling ability conferred the hydrogel with the ability to absorb the superfluous exudate (Fig. 2c). Besides, the correlation between NIR-induced heating and hydrogel swelling behavior was elucidated by irradiating the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel for 1, 3, and 5 min, respectively. The results demonstrated that the swelling rates decreased with prolonged irradiation time (Figure S4), which can be attributed to the contraction behavior of the hydrogel’s network under NIR irradiation, leading to the expulsion of internal water molecules. This NIR-triggered deswelling behavior provides the driving force for accelerating the release of encapsulated Cur. Besides, the hydrogel weight remained 80% after 10 days in vitro (Figure S5), suggesting its high stability under the physiological environment. Furthermore, Cur release behavior was evaluated by using Rhodamine B (RB) as the model drug owing to its stable fluorescence. Figure 2d shows that the scaffold’s fluorescence intensity gradually declined over time and completely disappeared after 7 days. To further confirm the drug release behavior of the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold, the drug loading capacity (LC) and encapsulation efficiency (EE) were firstly confirmed to be 2.3% and 90.3%, respectively. The quantitative release curve in Fig. 2e indicates ~ 68% of the drug remained after 7 days, with NIR irradiation (2.5 W/cm²) facilitating drug release likely due to the photothermal conversion ability of incorporated NP-Cur. At day 12, ~ 42% of Cur was released with NIR irradiation for 10 min on day 5, while ~ 35% of Cur was released under physiological conditions. Furthermore, the Fe/Cu ions release from NP-Cur was also assessed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (Figure S6). For NP-Cur incubated under physiological conditions, the supernatants were collected at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 days, and the results showed that Fe³⁺ and Cu²⁺ exhibited a slightly released behavior over the 15-day period. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the generated scaffold remains stable under physiological conditions and exhibits a sustained and controlled drug release performance. In diabetic wounds, the hyperglycemic microenvironment often leads to excessive levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can induce the oxidative stress and impair the healing process. Therefore, the ROS-scavenging ability of the hydrogel prepared in this work was confirmed. Firstly, the H2O2-scavenging ability of hydrogel scaffolds was investigated. As shown in Fig. 2f, the absorbance of pure SF scaffolds with the addition of NP-Cur showed an obvious decreased trend with increasing their concentrations compared to that of pure SF scaffolds, demonstrating the excellent H2O2-scavenging capacity of SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffolds. Also, the ·OH eliminating capacity was assessed by using the 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) (Fig. 2g and h). The results showed that the absorbance exhibited an obvious concentration-dependent behavior, and the colorless TMB could be turned into blue oxide TMB in the presence of ·OH, indicating that the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffolds could effectively scavenge the superfluous ·OH. To determine whether the observed ROS scavenging ability originated from the intrinsic antioxidant properties of the NP-Cur or from their catalytic activity as nanozymes, substrate cycling experiments were conducted. The results demonstrated that the scavenging efficiency of NP-Cur significantly declined after 3 cycles (Figure S7), demonstrating that the ROS scavenging capability of NP-Cur primarily relies on the intrinsic antioxidant effects of TA and Cur. Collectively, the generated SF@NP-Cur hydrogels can effectively ameliorate the oxidative stress microenvironment in diabetic wounds, and further create a favorable condition for the cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and tissue regeneration.

sections.section: Antibacterial ability and NIR-responsive capability of SF@NP-Cur
sections.text: Owing to the formation of Cu-TA-Fe complex within NP-Cur, it is anticipated that the formed SF@ NP-Cur scaffold may possess photothermal conversion capacity. Thus, the photothermal behavior of NP-Cur under NIR irradiation was firstly investigated (Fig. 3a and S8). Notably, the temperature increase exhibited a close correlation with the concentration of Fe³⁺ in the NP-Cur. Specifically, with increasing the Fe³⁺ concentration from 0.1% to 1.2%, the final reached temperature of the hydrogel scaffold showed a corresponding gradual elevation, demonstrating the excellent photothermal conversion capacity of NP-Cur. When incorporation of the nanoparticles into SF hydrogel, the hydrogel can be also imparted the photothermal performance. As shown in Fig. 3b, a clear dependence of the scaffold temperature on the NIR laser irradiation intensity was observed. Furthermore, the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold retained its photothermal performance over the five on/off NIR irradiation cycles (Fig. 3c), demonstrating the excellent photothermal stability. Since the temperature of NP-Cur with 0.3% Fe³⁺ can reach approximately 55 °C, which is suitable for photothermal antibacterial therapy without causing tissue damage. Therefore, SF@NP-Cur scaffold with a 0.3% Fe³⁺ concentration was selected for all subsequent experiments. Benefiting from the superior photothermal conversion capacity and the intrinsic antibacterial performance of the Cu2+ within the NP-Cur, the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold was expected to show the enhanced antibacterial behavior. Firstly, considering the toxicity of Cu2+, the NP-Cur with different Cu2+ contents was prepared and their antibacterial behavior were evaluated by using Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) as the model bacterial (Figure S9). With increasing the Cu2+ concentrations from 0.5% to 1.5%, the antibacterial activity of NP-Cur was comparable. Thus, to mitigate the potential cytotoxicity associated with Cu2+ levels, NP-Cur prepared from 0.5% Cu²⁺ was selected for the fabrication of the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold. As a comparison, the NP1-loaded SF hydrogel scaffold (SF@NP1) was also constructed. Whereafter, the antibacterial abilities following the treatments of SF@NP1 hydrogel scaffolds and SF@NP-Cur scaffolds (SF@NP2 group) in vitro were thoroughly investigated. As displayed in Fig. 3d, the bacterial viability in SF@NP1 group was significantly reduced when compared with the control group, which can be attributed to the bactericidal effect of Cu2+ within the nanoparticles. While, the bacterial in SF@NP2 group showed the similar viability to that in SF@NP1 group. Notably, compared with other groups, the bacterial colonies in the SF@NP2 hydrogel scaffold with NIR irradiation (SF@NP2 + NIR) were the fewest in the agar plate, which can be contributed to the synergetic effect of photothermal antibacterial and intrinsic antibacterial. The bacterial survival ratio after treated differently was assessed through measuring the absorbance of bacterial suspension, and the SF@NP2 + NIR treatment achieved the better inhibitory effects on both bacteria growth (Fig. 3e and g). Furthermore, SEM images in Fig. 3f revealed that compared to the bacteria in control group that maintained their structural integrity, the bacteria in SF@NP2 + NIR group exhibited the severe disruption. This damage can be attributed to the synergetic effect of NIR-induced photothermal effect that destroyed membrane structures and the intrinsic antibacterial effects of NP-Cur nanoparticles that suppressed metabolic activity. Taken together, these results showed that the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold exhibited the enhanced sterilization ability with the exposure to NIR laser irradiation.

sections.section: Biocompatibility of SF@NP-Cur and its protective effect on cells
sections.text: The biocompatibility of materials is the primary consideration for their use in the biomedical field. To examine the biocompatibility of the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold, the cell cytotoxicity test was firstly carried out by coculturing NIH 3T3 cells and Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) with the hydrogel scaffolds. The Live/Dead staining assay demonstrated that the cells showed the high viability following different treatments, which was comparable to the control group. Besides, the obvious proliferation can be observed in all treatment groups after 3 days of incubation (Fig. 4a and b). The CCK-8 results in Fig. 4d also displayed that the cells remained high viability after treatments with the scaffolds, indicating that the scaffolds showed no damage to the cells. Hemocompatibility tests demonstrated that the hemolysis rate in the hydrogel group was significantly lower than that in the H2O group and comparable to the PBS group, highlighting its favorable hemocompatibility and potential to reduce the hemolytic risk during wound bleeding (Fig. 4e). The diabetic wound microenvironment is often characterized by the high glucose, and the generated high glucose (HG) microenvironment has been demonstrated to increase the intracellular ROS levels to impede cell growth and proliferation, thereby further hindering wound healing [42]. Thus, the protective effect of the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold on cells under HG conditions was investigated (Fig. 4c and f). It was found that there were more dead cells in HG group without any treatments, whereas the cells in SF@NP2 group showed the relatively few dead cells. Notably, the SF@NP2 + NIR group exhibited the highest cell viability among all the treated groups. The result indicated that the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold can effectively protect cells from high-glucose stress and suppresses apoptosis, which may be derived from the ROS-scavenging ability of the incorporated NP-Cur. To further confirm this, the ROS-scavenging ability of SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold for cells was evaluated. The H₂O₂-induced cells were treated with the various hydrogel scaffolds, followed by the detection of intracellular ROS levels by using a DCFH-DA probe. The results showed that the SF@NP1 group displayed the relatively weak fluorescence compared to the Rosup group, and in contrast, the SF@NP2+ NIR group exhibited the lowest fluorescence intensity among all the groups (Fig. 4g). Quantitative analysis further confirmed the superior ROS-scavenging efficiency of SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold (Fig. 4h). This potent ROS-scavenging ability may stem from the synergistic mechanism of the bimetallic nanoparticle-catalyzed ROS decomposition and the intrinsic antioxidant properties of Cur. Furthermore, the high-glucose milieu often disrupted the multi-cellular processes such as angiogenesis, cell migration, and proliferation, consequently delayed wound healing. To further elucidate the therapeutic capacity of SF@NP-Cur, the in vitro scratch assay was firstly conducted. The result in Fig. 4i and j revealed that the cells in SF@NP2 group exhibited the significant wound closure after 24 h, and the NIR irradiation can obviously promote wound closure owing to the NIR-triggered Cur release, indicating a potent enhancement of cell migration, which is crucial for re-epithelialization. Furthermore, the tube formation assay demonstrated that the cells subjected to SF@NP2 + NIR treatments showed the significant tube length and numbers than the other groups, highlighting the robust pro-angiogenic activity (Fig. 4k and l). This result is primarily attributed to the effect of the released Cu²⁺ ions, which can act as the essential cofactors for key angiogenic enzymes, thereby activating vascular endothelial growth signaling pathways [14]. Therefore, by effectively eliminating the intracellular ROS and improving Cu²⁺ release under NIR, SF@NP-Cur can significantly alleviate oxidative stress damage and facilitate cell migration and angiogenesis, thereby protecting cells and remolding the tissue microenvironment that are conducive to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression and new blood vessel formation.

sections.section: Anti-inflammatory and pro-proliferative effects of SF@NP-Cur
sections.text: To further demonstrate the efficacy of the hydrogel scaffolds, the tissue remolding and anti-inflammatory ability was evaluated by the immunofluorescence staining. Firstly, the effect of hydrogel scaffolds on tissue remolding was evaluated by staining the representative cell proliferation markers of Ki-67 and the angiogenesis markers of VEGF. As shown in Fig. 5a and e, the HUVECs treated by SF@NP2 exhibited a significantly higher expression levels of Ki-67 compared to the Control and SF@NP1 group, whereas the SF@NP2 + NIR group displayed the highest Ki-67 expression, indicating that the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold can effectively activate cell proliferation pathway under NIR irradiation. The facilitated cell proliferation can be attributed to the synergistic enhancement effect of the released Cu2+ and Cur under NIR. Besides, for the SF@NP2 + NIR group, the expression of VEGF, an angiogenesis-related marker, was also higher than the other treated groups (Fig. 5b and f), demonstrating the efficacy of SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffolds under NIR irradiation to up-regulate VEGF expressions. Thus, the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold with NIR can significantly accelerate wound remolding by promoting cell proliferation/migration and inducing angiogenesis, and further foster a conducive microenvironment for tissue regeneration. Furthermore, macrophages, which primarily polarize into the pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages and the anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages, play a pivotal role in wound healing by modulating inflammation phase. During the initial phase of skin tissue repair, M1 macrophages promote immune responses to eliminate pathogens and bacteria. In contrast, M2 macrophages contribute to the anti-inflammation effect and facilitate tissue regeneration at the later stages of wound repair. CD86 and CD206 have identified to be the typical markers of M1 and M2 macrophages, respectively. As shown in Fig. 5c and g, RAW 264.7 macrophages after LPS treatment exhibited a significant upregulation of CD86 expression compared to other groups, while this elevation can be effectively mitigated by SF@NP2 treatment and notably, the combination of SF@NP2 hydrogel scaffolds with NIR irradiation resulted in the most substantial reduction of CD86 content. Moreover, RAW 264.7 after the LPS treatment can significantly reduce the CD206 expression, and SF@NP2 with NIR treatment was more effective for up-regulation of CD206 expression (Fig. 5d and h), indicating that the RAW 264.7 treated with SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffolds under NIR can promote M1 to M2 macrophage polarization.

The therapeutic efficiency of the SF@NP-Cur scaffold on the wound healing in vivo was further studied by using an infected diabetic chronic wound model. The SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffolds were applied to a mixed infection of E. coli and S. aureus full-thickness wounds in SD rat, and the model fabrication of diabetic mice and detailed therapeutic process was illustrated in Fig. 6a. In particular, following the successful E. coli and S. aureus infection, the wounds created on the dorsum of rats were treated as below: Control, SF@NP1 scaffold (SF@NP1), SF@NP-Cur scaffold (SF@NP2), and SF@NP-Cur scaffold with NIR (SF@NP2 + NIR). For the SF@NP2 + NIR group, the scaffold underwent the NIR irradiation (2.5 W/cm2) for 10 min. Firstly, the in vivo photothermal conversion ability was confirmed. When the NIR was applied onto the scaffold within wounds, the scaffold displayed obvious temperature rise from 26 to 58 ℃ after irradiation for 5 min (Fig. 6b and f), indicating the excellent in vivo photothermal capability of the scaffolds. Besides, it has been demonstrated that the temperature of 50 ℃ displayed negligible damage to tissues but can effectively kill bacteria [8]. The temperature in SF@NP2 group falls within the optimal bactericidal range under NIR irradiation, making it ideal for effective sterilization. During the healing process, typical pictures of the wounds treated differently are also recorded (Fig. 6c). Macroscopically, the wounds in SF@NP2 + NIR group showed significantly accelerated wound healing after a 12-day treatment, whereas there were still obvious wounds observed in the Control, SF@NP1, and SF@NP2 groups. Also, the quantitative wound areas were obtained from these wound pictures (Fig. 6d). After treatment for 12 days, the wound area in SF@NP2 + NIR group was about 4%, which was much lower than that in the Control (23 ± 2.4%), SF@NP1 (17 ± 1.8%), and SF@NP2 (11 ± 2.5%) groups. The superior wound healing efficacy of the SF@NP-Cur with NIR can be attributed to the efficient eradication of bacteria and scavenging of excess ROS at the wound site. Re-epithelialization and collagen deposition are the critical characteristics of wound healing. Thus, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson staining were carried out to demonstrate the diabetic wound healing ability of SF@NP-Cur scaffolds. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) results in Fig. 6e showed that a layer of well-differentiated epidermis and thicker regenerated tissue was formed in SF@NP2 + NIR group after treatment for 12 days, whereas there was partial epidermis generated in control and SF@NP1 groups. Besides, SF@NP2 + NIR group exhibited the smallest wound width when compared to the other groups, and the H&E staining results of wound surrounding skin tissue showed the intact structure with no inflammation or necrosis (Fig. 6g, S10), further confirming the safety of SF@NP-Cur scaffold under NIR laser. Masson staining showed that the SF@NP2 + NIR group presented the higher degree of collagen deposition than the other treated groups. The quantitative results in Fig. 6h also showed that the collagen content in SF@NP2 + NIR group was the highest among all these treated groups, suggesting that the SF@NP2 + NIR treatment can significantly accelerate the tissue regeneration and wound healing by the promotion of collagen deposition. Furthermore, to elucidate whether the re-epithelialization and collagen deposition was derived from the high-energy-consuming processes, carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP), a specific inhibitor of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), was used. In particular, diabetic rats with full-thickness wounds were received treatments of Control, CCCP, CCCP + SF@NP2 + NIR, and SF@NP2 + NIR. The result showed that the wound closure rate in Control group was higher than that in CCPC group, indicating the OXPHOS process was blocked by CCCP, which may force cells to rely on the inefficient glycolysis for energy production, impeding re-epithelialization and collagen deposition. Notably, the SF@NP2 + NIR treatment can achieve the better healing effects than CCPC + SF@NP2 + NIR and CCPC group, suggesting the scaffold can reprogram the microenvironment, shifting the cellular energy metabolism from inefficient glycolysis to OXPHOS, providing sufficient energy to facilitate tissue repair (Figure S11). Moreover, the H&E staining of major organs also demonstrated that there was negligible damage observed in SF@NP2 + NIR group after 12 days of treatment (Figure S12). The potential systemic accumulation of Fe3+ and Cu2+ from NP-Cur in the main organs was evaluated. Specifically, liver and kidney collected from the rats after 12 days of SF@NP2 + NIR treatment were homogenized and then analyzed by ICP-MS. No significant difference in Fe/Cu content was observed between the Control and SF@NP2 + NIR group, indicating no systemic metal accumulation in these key metabolic organs (Figure S13a and S13b). Additionally, the potential bioaccumulation of Cu/Fe bimetallic nanoparticles were also evaluated by the fluorescence imaging through the use of DID-labeled SF@NP-Cur hydrogels. Ex vivo imaging of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) harvested after 12 days of treatments showed no significant fluorescence signals (Figure S14), indicating that the nanoparticles did not accumulate in these organs. Furthermore, the wound healing mechanism of SF@NP-Cur scaffolds was evaluated. Firstly, to exclude the potential regulatory effect of glucose oxidation on wounds, the pH within wounds in the control and SF@NP2 + NIR group were detected on day 6 post-treatment. The results showed that the pH of wounds in SF@NP2 + NIR group ranged from 7.2 to 7.5, with no significant difference compared with the healthy wounds (Figure S15), indicating that the therapeutic effect had nothing to do with the pH regulation caused by glucose oxidation, but mainly depended on the synergistic effects of photothermal antibacterial activity, immunomodulation, and metabolic reprogramming. Then, the balance of T cell subsets in wound beds were evaluated. Because CD4 and CD8 are the typical markers of CD4 + and CD8 + cells, respectively, CD4 and CD8 immunohistochemical staining of wound sections from different groups were supplemented (Figure S16). The results revealed that the SF@NP2 + NIR group exhibited higher CD4 and CD8 levels, indicating that the SF@NP-Cur scaffold with NIR can enhance wound healing by regulating the immune microenvironment. Collectively, these findings demonstrated that the SF@NP-Cur scaffolds with NIR irradiation exhibited the most superior wound healing outcomes among all treatment groups.

sections.section: SF@NP-Cur promotes diabetic wound healing by reducing inflammatory responses, enhancing angiogenesis, and reprogramming the microenvironment
sections.text: Furthermore, regulation of inflammatory factors and promotion of angiogenesis are critical for chronic wound regeneration. In the initial phase of wound healing, the wounds produce abundant pro-inflammatory factors such as IL-6 and TNF-α to initiate repair. While, the prolonged inflammatory response may disrupt the healing cascade, ultimately delaying tissue regeneration. For this purpose, the immunohistochemical staining was performed to evaluate the expressions of anti-inflammatory factors (e.g., IL-6 and TNF-α), and angiogenesis-related makers (e.g., the endothelial cell marker CD31 and smooth muscle α-SMA) on the wounds. Figure 7a revealed that the cells treated by SF@NP2 + NIR showed the lowest expression of IL-6 and TNF-α compared to the that in SF@NP1 group, which can be due to the existence of Cur within the nanoparticles and the robust release of NP-Cur under NIR irradiation. The quantitative results in Fig. 7b and c demonstrated the same results. CD31 and α-SMA are the representative markers to be applied for evaluating angiogenesis of the tissue. Thus, the blood vessel levels in the wound tissues were determined, and the SF@NP2 + NIR group exhibited the highest expression levels of CD31 and α-SMA (Fig. 7a and d), suggesting the greatest degree of vascularization for wounds treated by SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffolds with NIR. Notably, the reprogramming of the wound microenvironment by SF@NP-Cur is a tightly synchronized biological feedback loop (Figure S17). The excessive ROS and bacterial infection can initiate the pathological cascade, and the SF@NP-Cur with NIR intervention triggers interconnected effects. Firstly, the SF@NP-Cur scaffold scavenges the excessive ROS, which attenuates inflammation and drives M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization. Then, polarized M2 macrophages can effectively promote angiogenesis and collagen deposition, further accelerating re-epithelialization. Ultimately, the enhanced tissue repair reduces wound exudate and bacterial growth, further reducing ROS generation. All these therapeutic effects form a synchronized biological feedback loop, demonstrating their mutually reinforced abilities. Collectively, these findings suggested that the SF@NP-Cur scaffold with NIR presents an effective strategy for infected chronic wound healing by facilitating tissue remodeling, suppressing inflammatory responses, and promoting angiogenesis.

In summary, we have presented a SF-based immunomodulatory hydrogel scaffold integrated with the Cur-loaded copper/iron bimetallic phenolic assembled nanoparticles (NP-Cur) for infected diabetic wound healing. The prepared SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold showed dual antibacterial and ROS-scavenging performance owing to the incorporation of NP-Cur. Moreover, the high loading of Cur offers the scaffold with the pro-migration on fibroblasts and angiogenesis effects on HUVECs, facilitating wound tissue remolding. Furthermore, the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold enables the polarization of macrophages toward the M2 phenotype, and thus, suppressed the inflammatory response. In a diabetic rat wound model, the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold can effectively facilitate wound healing following bacterial infection by reprogramming the hostile microenvironment indicated by attenuated inflammation, facilitated cell migration, enhanced angiogenesis, and improved collagen deposition. These features demonstrate that the proposed SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold provide a highly promising platform for precision management of various diabetic wounds. Unlike Cur-based hydrogels limited by the poor solubility and weak antibacterial activity, metal ion-based hydrogels relying solely on ion release, or other antioxidant hydrogels that only alleviates oxidative stress, the SF@NP-Cur scaffolds integrate multimodal synergistic effects and sequential microenvironment reprogramming capabilities, thereby promoting fibroblast migration, angiogenesis, and collagen deposition (Table S1). Additionally, the microfluidic 3D-printed porous scaffold adapts to the irregular wounds, facilitating nutrient exchange and cell infiltration. With these integrated properties, the SF@NP-Cur hydrogel scaffold significantly accelerates the repair process of diabetic infected wounds by reshaping the harmful microenvironment, offering a promising solution for the precise management of diabetic wounds. Notably, the SF@NP-Cur scaffolds show more translational merits owing to the existence of NP-Cur nanoparticles and the utilization of microfluidic 3D printing strategy. Specifically, the bimetallic nanoparticles integrate multiple therapeutic functions (antibacterial, ROS scavenging, immunomodulation) into a single platform, avoiding the limitations of single-component systems. In addition, the microfluidic 3D printing enables on-demand customization of scaffolds adapted to irregular diabetic wounds, while the scalable fabrication process and uniform nanoparticle dispersion ensure reproducible performance. These features collectively enhance the scaffold’s clinical applicability, bridging the gap between the laboratory research and practical wound management.
