sections.section: Biosafety considerations and long-term risk assessment
sections.text: A comprehensive and rigorous biosafety assessment is a prerequisite for the clinical translation of EVH systems, an area currently overshadowed by a predominant focus on efficacy in research [115, 132, 144, 171]. While preliminary studies frequently report an absence of significant acute toxicity or major organ damage in animal models [112, 115, 121], these findings are insufficient to guarantee comprehensive safety. Safety risks must be examined at multiple levels: firstly, the EVs themselves, It is imperative that potential risks be evaluated at multiple levels. The potential risks associated with EVs include the possibility of immune responses triggered by allogeneic or xenogeneic sources, engineering modifications, or repeated high-dose administration [27, 123, 132, 229, 230]. The risks associated with hydrogel carriers are contingent on material degradability; slow-degrading synthetic or composite materials have the potential to induce chronic inflammation, while incorporated nanomaterials (e.g., silver nanoparticles) can introduce concerns regarding toxicity and long-term accumulation [153, 155, 165, 196, 231, 232]. The risks associated with complex systems are amplified in engineered designs, such as genetically modified EVs, which pose genotoxic risks [119, 217, 233], or hybrid systems, which exhibit unpredictable in vivo behaviour [121, 213, 234]. Furthermore, ‘smart’ release systems reliant on microenvironmental responses may become uncontrolled within complex, dynamic wound environments, leading to unintended release [16, 149]. Collectively, these factors heighten the uncertainty and risk profile of EVs-based therapeutic systems. The most critical knowledge gap pertains to long-term systemic safety. The biodistribution, off-target effects, and potential impact of EVs on distant organs or pre-existing conditions (e.g., stimulating dormant tumour cells) remain poorly understood [27, 114, 123, 128]. The prevailing evaluation models are inadequate for the purposes of assessing chronic toxicity, immunogenicity, or carcinogenic potential [235, 236]. A paradigm shift towards a “safety-first” approach is imperative, necessitating long-term toxicology studies, advanced in vivo tracking, and the establishment of standardized safety and quality control thresholds [27, 134–136, 166, 221, 237].

sections.section: Limitations of preclinical models and standardization hurdles
sections.text: The preclinical basis for EVH therapy is considerably constrained by the absence of standardisation and the clinical inadequacy of animal models. However, the extensive utilisation of streptozotocin-induced type 1 diabetic rodent models has proven to be inadequate in accurately replicating the multifaceted pathophysiology of human type 2 diabetic wounds, which frequently encompass components such as ischemia and neuropathy [134, 165, 238]. The heterogeneity of wound parameters, in conjunction with a predominant focus on short-term histological endpoints, further diminishes the clinical predictive value of these studies [115, 152, 238–241]. A significant translational barrier pertains to the absence of unified pharmacological standards for EVs. Inconsistent reporting of dosage metrics (e.g. mass, particle count, volume) and a paucity of systematic dose-response studies are pervasive [115, 119, 242, 243]. It is important to note that there is no standard bioassay to quantify EV “potency,” which prevents meaningful comparison between EVs from different sources or preparations [111, 161, 244, 245]. EVs) are frequently regarded as a homogeneous black box, with inadequate analysis of functionally critical subpopulations and specific cargo, resulting in an underdefinition of their structure-function relationship [119, 134, 138, 246]. The mechanistic understanding of the EV-hydrogel-wound microenvironment interplay is underdeveloped. While the sustained release of hydrogels has been characterised in vitro [115, 116, 177], the release kinetics under pathologically relevant wound conditions and the real-time in vivo bioavailability of EVs remain a subject of investigation [138, 221, 238]. The impact of encapsulation on EVs integrity and the deeper synergistic mechanisms by which hydrogels modulate the local microenvironment to enhance EVs function remain largely unexplored [65, 144, 216, 238].

The process of translating EVH from a laboratory prototype to a marketable product gives rise to systemic industrial challenges. The primary bottleneck is the establishment of scalable, cost-effective, and GMP-compliant manufacturing processes for both biological (EVs) and material (hydrogel) components, and their subsequent combination [115, 151, 175]. The complexity of the process has been demonstrated to directly impact cost, thus rendering treatment affordability a pivotal factor in determining commercial viability [134, 247, 248]. The establishment of a comprehensive quality control (QC) system is imperative for the attainment of regulatory approval. In the context of EVH, QC must encompass the entire product life cycle, from raw materials to the final product, necessitating meticulous characterisation of EVs attributes, hydrogel properties, and composite performance [116, 221]. Furthermore, the overcoming of logistical hurdles related to EVs stability is critical for distribution. Such hurdles may be overcome through the development of stable formulations (e.g., lyophilized powders) and a reliable cold chain [221, 249, 250]. The concept of successful commercialisation extends beyond the realm of manufacturing. In order to achieve this, it is necessary to navigate the complex landscape of intellectual property and formulate clear market access strategies. These strategies must include targeting high-need indications, designing viable pricing and reimbursement models, and utilising expedited regulatory pathways [134, 247, 248]. In view of the multifaceted challenges, strategic collaborations across industry, academia, and healthcare are imperative in order to share risks and accelerate the translation of EVH from a promising platform to an accessible clinical therapy.

The integration of hydrogels and EVs represents a promising regenerative strategy, effectively overcoming key limitations of EVs monotherapy—such as rapid clearance and enzymatic degradation—by providing localized, sustained, and microenvironment-responsive release. This synergistic system has demonstrated significant potential in enhancing angiogenesis, immunomodulation, and tissue repair in chronic wound models. Moving forward, efforts should focus on standardizing EVs production, improving hydrogels tunability for spatiotemporally controlled release, and elucidating underlying molecular mechanisms to facilitate clinical translation.

title: Intelligent-responsive hydrogel synergistically mediates immune remodel-antibacterial-angiogenesis cascade for diabetic foot ulcer repair
abstract: The healing of diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) is severely hindered by dysregulated immune microenvironment, recurrent infections, and insufficient angiogenesis. The persistent and resistant nature, coupled with elevated morbidity and amputation rates, has driven the scientific community to pursue the development of novel therapies. Current wound dressings mostly target a singular aspect and fail to achieve systematic regulation of these dynamically related factors, highlighting the urgent need for dressings capable of accurate sense and response to the complex pathological process of wound and precise repair. Herein, an intelligent treatment strategy of "intelligent response - synergistic regulation" was proposed. We designed a desferrioxamine-loaded Mn-doped zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (DFO@Mn-ZIF-8), which exhibits dual enzyme-mimetic activity to scavenge excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) and, upon disintegration, combats infection and promotes angiogenesis. Subsequently, a glucose- and ROS-responsive chitosan-based hydrogel loaded with DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosome was fabricated (Exo/MOF@CPH). In a validated S. aureus-infected diabetic wound model, Exo/MOF@CPH continuously senses and responds to the dynamic wound microenvironment, simultaneously achieving bacterial clearance, immune reconstitution, and angiogenesis promotion, thereby fostering a healing-friendly microenvironment. This multifunctional single-platform therapy offers a promising translational strategy for DFU repair, advancing smart biomaterial design for complex pathological microenvironment. Image 1 •A novel multifunctional platform (Exo/MOF@CPH) is developed for intervening multiple critical pathological processes of DFU.•Exo/MOF@CPH synergistically regulates macrophage polarization to remodel immune, clears bacteria, and promotes angiogenesis.•The hydrogel accelerates healing via HIF-1α-VEGF, PI3K-Akt, and JAK-STAT pathways, enhancing robust tissue regeneration. A novel multifunctional platform (Exo/MOF@CPH) is developed for intervening multiple critical pathological processes of DFU. Exo/MOF@CPH synergistically regulates macrophage polarization to remodel immune, clears bacteria, and promotes angiogenesis. The hydrogel accelerates healing via HIF-1α-VEGF, PI3K-Akt, and JAK-STAT pathways, enhancing robust tissue regeneration.

sections.text: Nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) are open wounds in diabetic patients that are difficult to heal due to nerve damage, vascular ischemia and metabolic disorders caused by chronic hyperglycaemia, triggering foot tissue destruction and infection [1]. Up to 20% of DFU cases lead to major amputation and the five-year mortality rate after a DFU incident is 49.1% [2,3]. Therefore, DFU pose a major global health challenge. Almost 23% of patients, receiving standard care, have a nonhealing DFU at 12 months [4], driving an urgent need for pathophysiology targeted interventions. The pathological microenvironment of diabetic wound is a complex network composed of multiple factors such as immune microenvironment disorders, vascular lesions, and persistent infections [5,6]. The most prominent feature is chronic inflammation, characterized by the sustained high overexpression of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 [7,8]. This inflammatory state directly inhibits the proliferation and migration of fibroblasts and keratinocytes [9,10]. Meanwhile, impaired angiogenesis results in local hypoxia and inadequate nutrient supply, precluding the establishment of effective microcirculation to necessary for tissue repair [11]. This fragile microenvironment is highly susceptible to mixed infections [12,13]. And the biofilm formed by pathogens further endows them with strong antibiotic resistance and immune evasion, thereby perpetuating chronic infection [14,15]. Ischemia and hypoxia exacerbate local inflammation and infection, while persistent infection and inflammatory responses further damage angiogenesis and aggravate tissue ischemia. These critical pathological factors are interdependent, forming a self-perpetuating vicious cycle, ultimately leading to difficulty in wound healing. The complex pathological network associated with DFU poses multi-dimensional challenges to treatment strategies. Interventions targeting a single pathological aspect have achieved significant progress. Zhang et al. facilitated the diabetic wound healing through the administration of galectin-3, which serves to mediate angiogenesis [16]. Concurrently, Zeng et al. developed an injectable self-healing hydrogel capable of modulating the immune microenvironment by suppressing the overactivation of M1-like macrophages [17]. However, single therapies that target angiogenesis or immune regulation are insufficient to comprehensively address the complex and multifaceted pathological network. Consequently, intelligent responsive hydrogels that integrate multiple therapeutic functions have emerged as a significant trend in research [[18], [19], [20], [21]]. Cheng et al. developed an intelligent hydrogel incorporating a microenvironment feedback mechanism, capable of concurrently modulating both the immune and angiogenesis microenvironment [22]. Zhang et al. fabricated a hydrogel membrane exhibiting robust antibacterial and antioxidant properties, which facilitates the accelerated healing of infected wounds [23]. These studies represent a significant advancement in the pursuit of multifunctional design of dressings. However, their scope remains confined to the binary synergies of immune-vasculature and antiinfection-antioxidation. These have yet to accomplish the simultaneous sensing and synergistic regulation of the three fundamental pathological processes, including immune microenvironment imbalance, angiogenesis disorder and persistent infection, within a single therapeutic system. Natural antioxidant enzyme mimics, such as nanozymes with superoxide dismutase (SOD) or catalase (CAT) activity, can scavenge ROS [[24], [25], [26], [27]], but they lack antibacterial efficacy and cannot adapt to dynamic pH or ROS fluctuations. In recent years, metal-organic framework (MOF) has been widely explored in the nanoenzyme field [28]. Manganese (Mn) ions act as the active center of natural SOD [29]. And by mimicking natural Mn-based SOD, nanoenzymes with excellent SOD activity can be obtained [30,31]. To address the combined need for reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and antibacterial properties, multifunctional MOF is one of the feasible solutions at the current stage. Previous studies have demonstrated that Mn-doping of ZIF-8 creates a hierarchical mesoporous framework (Mn-ZIF-8) exhibiting tandem SOD and CAT activity [32], while releasing Zn2+ for bacterial membrane depolarisation. However, Mn-ZIF-8 alone cannot synchronise angiogenic cue release. Desferrioxamine (DFO), an iron chelator approved by FDA, stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and up-regulates vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) [33,34], but its clinical translation to wound healing is hampered by burst release [35]. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosome (UCMSC-exo) carries pro-regulatory miRNAs that accelerate re-epithelialization and modulate inflammatory response [36], but requires a protective matrix to maintain their bioactivity and controlled release in protease-enriched wounds [37,38]. At present, the synergistic effects of Mn-ZIF-8, DFO, and UCMSC-exo on diabetic wound remains to be investigated. In this study, a chitosan-based injectable glucose and ROS responsive hydrogel integrating desferrioxamine-loaded Mn-doping zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (DFO@Mn-ZIF-8) and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosome was designed (Exo/MOF@CPH) (Fig. 1). It achieves intelligent response and synergistic regulation of the complex pathological microenvironment of diabetic wounds. The sustained release of UCMSC-exo directly modulates macrophage polarization, transitioning local macrophages from dominant pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype to pro-reparative M2 phenotype, which remodels the immune microenvironment and supports tissue regeneration. The responsively released Mn-ZIF-8 exerts its enzyme-like catalytic activity, rapidly scavenges excessive ROS to alleviate oxidative stress, and simultaneously releases antibacterial substances to effectively eliminate pathogens, breaking the infection-inflammation vicious cycle. As infection resolves and the pH of the wound shifts to weakly acidic, inducing the synergistically release of DFO and Zn2+ from disintegrated Mn-ZIF-8 potently activate the HIF-1α signaling pathway, thereby driving substantial neovascularization and fundamentally improving blood supply and hypoxia. Validated by animal models of infectious diabetes, Exo/MOF@CPH demonstrates the capability to concurrently facilitate immune reconstitution, promote angiogenesis, and exert anti-infective effects. This approach effectively disrupts the detrimental "high ROS-infection-hypoxia" microenvironment, offering a potential intelligent strategy for the comprehensive treatment of DFU.Fig. 1Schematic diagram of intelligent-responsive hydrogel Exo/MOF@CPH promoting diabetes skin healing through microenvironment-responsive cascade drug release.Fig. 1

Methyl alcohol, Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; General-Reagent, Titan, Shanghai, China); Deferoxamine mesylate (DFO; MCE, New Jersey, USA); Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, Mn(NO3)2·4H2O, 2-methylimidazole (Aladdin, Shanghai, China); UCMSC-exo (Langfang Kangbao Huitai Biotechnology, Langfang, China); Chitosan (CS; Deacetylation degree ≥95%, Macklin, Shanghai, China), 4-carboxyphenylboronic acid; polyvinyl alcohol (4-CPBA, PVA; Aladdin, Shanghai, China); N-(3-Dimethylaminopropyl)-N′-ethyl carbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC; Aladdin, Shanghai, China); N-Hydroxysuccinimide (NHS; Aladdin, Shanghai, China); PrimeScript RT Master Mix (Takara, Beijing, China); qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (Yeasen, Shanghai, China); CD9 antibody (Selleck, USA); TSG101 antibody (Abmart, Shanghai, China); CD86 flow antibody and CD206 flow antibody (BioLegend, USA); IL-6, CD206, HIF-1α, CK14, Ki67, CD31, VEGF and α-SMA (AiFang biological, China).

As described previously [39], A solution with a molar ratio of Mn/(Mn + Zn) at 20% was prepared by dissolving 0.5 mmol of Mn(NO3)2·4H2O, 2 mmol of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, and 40 mmol of 2-methylimidazole in 20 mL and 80 mL methanol, respectively. The two solutions were mixed and stirred at room temperature for 5 h. The resulting product was collected by centrifugation at 12,000 g for 10 min at room temperature, washed twice with methanol. Mn-ZIF-8 was obtained after dried overnight in a vacuum oven at 60 °C. For comparison, ZIF-8 was synthesized using the same procedure without the addition of the manganese source. DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 was synthesized with the addition of DFO. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM; Talos F200X G2, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was used to analyze the morphology of the nanoparticles. TEM with energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectrometry was used to characterize the different morphology and structure of Mn-ZIF-8 nanocomposites. The particle size measurement (Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS)), zeta potential measurement were performed by Nanoparticle Size and Zeta Potential Analyzer (BeNano, Dandong Bettersize, China). The crystal structure was measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD; SmartLab SE, Rigaku, Japan) using a copper target. The valence states of different elements were determined by X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

The encapsulation efficiency (EE) and loading efficiency (LE) of DFO were determined by Ultraviolet-visible (UV-VIS) spectrophotometer. In brief, a standard curve for the complex of DFO and Fe3+ was established by UV-VIS spectrophotometer firstly. After the sample was incubated with FeCl3 for 1 h, the content of DFO was measured at 460 nm [40,41]. The EE and LE were measured by the following formula:EE (%) = (mass of added DFO - mass of remnant DFO) / (mass of added DFO) × 100LE (%) = (mass of added DFO - mass of remnant DFO) / (mass of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8) × 100

UCMSC-exo was provided by Kangbao Huitai Biotechnology Co., Ltd. To obtain UCMSC-exo, cells at passages 3 to 5 were cultured until reaching 80 - 90% confluence. Subsequently, the culture medium was discarded. The cells were washed three times with PBS and then incubated in a fresh medium supplemented with 10% exosome-depleted FBS for 24 - 48 h. The medium was then collected for exosome isolation via differential low-temperature ultracentrifugation. Briefly, the collected supernatant was first passed through a 0.22 μm filter to eliminate suspended cells and large debris. The filtrate was then centrifuged at 10,000×g for 30 min at 4 °C to further remove residual microvesicles and cell debris. Finally, the supernatant was ultracentrifuged at 100,000×g for 70 min at 4 °C to pellet the exosomes. The obtained exosome pellet was carefully resuspended in sterile PBS and stored at −80 °C for subsequent experiments. TEM (HT-7800, HITACHI, Japan) was used to analyze the morphology of the exosome. After being air-dried, the exosome solution was embedded in a TEM grid of a thin carbon layer. NanoSight NS300 was used for the nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) to evaluate the particle size of exosomes. As our previous research [42], a BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime, Jiangsu, China) was used to assess the concentration of exosomes. Exosome-related markers, including CD9 and TSG101, were detected using Western blot (WB) analysis.

Exosome Labeling and Tracking Kit with PKH67 (Beyotime, Jiangsu, China) was used to stain the isolated exosomes according to the instruction. The Raw 264.7 macrophages received 10 μg of the PKH67-labelled exosomes, which were then incubated for 0, 6, 12 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. After incubation, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. Then the cells were stained for cytoskeleton and nuclear staining with tetramethylrhodamine B isothiocyanate (TRITC) phalloidin for 30 min at room temperature and DAPI, respectively. Confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM; SP8, Leica, Germany) was used for visualization.

sections.section: Synthesis and characterization of chitosan grafted with phenylboric acid (CS-PBA)
sections.text: CS-PBA was synthesized as previous reports [43]. In brief, 1 g of chitosan powder was dissolved in 100 mL of ultrapure water while glacial acetic acid (final concentration of 0.3%) was added to fully dissolve chitosan. Then, 0.25 g of 4-CPBA, 0.7 g of EDC and 0.5 g of NHS were dissolved in 60 mL of DMSO. The solutions were mixed and the reaction lasted for 12 h. The mixture was dialysed using ultrapure water for 3 days, during which time the water was changed at least 8 times, and the CS-PBA was obtained by freeze-drying. The synthesis of CS-PBA was verified by fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and nuclear magnetic resonance hydrogen spectroscopy (1H NMR).

sections.section: Preparation and characterization of Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel
sections.text: 5 wt% CS-PBA solution and 15 wt% PVA solution were mixed in a 1:1 ratio to obtain CPH hydrogel. The preparation of the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel was adapted from the CPH method. Briefly, DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 (25 μg/mL) and UCMSC-exo (100 μg/mL) were added to the PVA solution prior to mixing with the CS-PBA solution. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to observe the pore structure of the hydrogels after freeze-drying. The pore sizes of different groups of hydrogels were calculated using ImageJ software (each group of samples contained at least 100 pores, obtained by random analysis of SEM images).

To assess the degradation ratio of the CPH hydrogel in vitro, equal volumes of gel samples were freeze-dried and the dry weight of each sample was recorded as W0. The samples were then placed in PBS (pH = 7.4) at 37 °C. At designed time points, the samples were collected and freeze-dried and the dry weight was recorded as Wt. The degradation ratio was calculated using the formula: Mass remaining ratio (%) = Wt/W0 × 100%. To monitor in vivo degradation, Indocyanine Green (ICG) dye was conjugated to the hydrogels. Then the hydrogels were inserted subcutaneously on the dorsal side. The mice were anesthetized and subsequently imaged using an IVIS Spectrum imaging system (PerkinElmer, MA, USA) with an excitation wavelength of 780 nm. The fluorescence intensity at predetermined time points was used to evaluate the degradation kinetics of the hydrogel.

The rheological characteristics of the CPH hydrogel were evaluated using a rheometer (Mars60, Haake, Germany). The stiffness of the hydrogel was assessed by a time sweep test, which was performed at 25 °C with a constant frequency of 1 Hz and 1% strain. A strain amplitude test was carried out to detect the critical strain point of the hydrogel, which was performed at a constant frequency of 10 rad/s at 25 °C (γ = 0.1% - 500%). Viscosity and shear stress were observed by increasing the shear rate from 0.1 s−1 to 500 s−1 at 25 °C in a logarithmic manner.

sections.section: In vitro cytotoxicity and hemolysis evaluation
sections.text: The cytocompatibility was evaluated following the CCK-8 method (Beyotime) and live/dead staining (Beyotime). HUVECs and L929 fibroblasts were cultured for evaluation. Then cell viability was measured on days 1, 3 and 5. The images were captured using fluorescence microscope (DMi8, Leica) after staining with Calcein/PI on day 3. Mouse anticoagulated whole blood was centrifuged (1500 g) to collect erythrocytes, washed with saline into 2% red blood cell suspension. The mixtures of hydrogel and suspension were incubated at 37 °C, then centrifuged at 3000 rpm. The absorbance of the supernatant (540 nm, water as control) was measured to calculate hemolysis rate.

5-ethynyl-2ʹ-deoxyuridine (EdU) staining was used to evaluate the impact of hydrogel on cell proliferation. HUVECs, L929 fibroblasts were co-cultured with hydrogels using transwell inserts for 24 h. The staining steps were done according to the Click-iT EdU Cell Proliferation Kit (Epizyme, Shanghai, China). The images were captured using fluorescence microscope. Scratch experiments and transwell assay were carried out to evaluate the effect of hydrogel on cell migration. HUVECs and L929 fibroblasts were seeded. When the cell confluence reached 90%, linear wounds were created and the dislodged cells were rinsed with PBS. Then the cells were co-cultured with hydrogels in the upper transwell chamber. The images were captured using light microscopy at 0 and 24 h. For the transwell assay, HUVECs were seeded in the upper transwell chamber (5 × 104 cells), while hydrogels were added to the lower transwell chamber. After 24 h of incubation, the membrane of the upper chamber was carefully wiped with a cotton swab to remove non-migrated cells, and the migrated cells in the lower chamber were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min. After staining with crystal violet, the migrated cells were observed using light microscope.

sections.section: In vitro evaluation angiogenesis of hydrogel
sections.text: Tube formation assay on HUVEC was performed. Matrigel (MCE, USA) was thawed at 4 °C and then added to 24-well plates and incubated at 37 °C to allow solidification. HUVECs were seeded on the matrigel and then co-cultured with hydrogels in transwell inserts. After 4 h of incubation at 37 °C under 5% CO2, tube formation was observed under a light microscope. Angiogenesis-related gene expression was determined by RT-qPCR. The primer sequences for these genes are listed in Table S2.

By applying 10 μL of a bacterial suspension (107 CFU/mL) onto the hydrogels and incubating for 8 h at 37 °C. A saline-suspended bacterial suspension served as a negative control. Afterward, 990 μL of saline was added, and ultrasonic shaking was used for 10 min to detach bacteria. Finally, 100 μL of the suspension was spread on agar plates for colony counting. Biofilm formation was observed by bacterial Live/Dead staining assay and crystal violet staining assay. In brief, hydrogels were soaked in bacterial suspension (106 CFU/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C. A bacterial viability kit (Beyotime, China) was used to stain live and dead bacteria, according to the instructions. Then, the samples were captured by a CLSM in 3D mode with a height of 50 μm in total and 2 μm for each slide. The bacterial suspension was co-cultured with hydrogels in 24-well plates at 37 °C for 48 h, changing the medium every 12 h. After discarding the supernatant, it was washed 3 times with PBS. 0.1% crystal violet solution (Beyotime, China) was added to each well and stained for 5 min at room temperature. Gently wash with PBS to ensure complete removal of excess crystal violet. After natural drying, 200 μL of 95% ethanol was added to dissolve the bound crystal violet and shaken for 15 min. The absorbance at 570 nm was determined using a microplate reader.

sections.section: Antioxidant and ROS-scavening properties of Mn-ZIF-8
sections.text: The total antioxidant properties of Mn-ZIF-8 were measured by using the T-AOC assay kit with ABTS method (Beyotime). The SOD and CAT activitiy of Mn-ZIF-8 were investigated by using the total superoxide dismutase assay kit with WST-8 (Beyotime) and the catalase assay kit (Beyotime) according to manufacturer instructions, respectively. DCFH-DA staining was used to evaluate the intracellular ROS content. RAW 264.7 macrophages and HUVECs in confocal petri dishes were con-cultured with hydrogels for 24 h. 100 μM H2O2 was added to the medium to induce oxidative stress for 1 h. Then the cells were incubated with 10 μM DCFH-DA solution for 1 h in the dark. The images were observed by CLSM.

sections.section: In vitro anti-inflammatory properties of hydrogels
sections.text: After RAW 264.7 cells attached, the medium was replaced with DMEM containing 1 μg/mL LPS for 24 h. Then the cells were co-cultured with the hydrogels using transwell inserts for 2 days. On day 2, RNA was extracted using RNA purification kit (EZBioscience, USA), followed by reverse transcription and RT-qPCR to assess pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory gene expression. The primer sequences for genes are listed in Table S2. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining was used to detect the expression of iNOS and Arg-1, which was performed on day 2. For flow cytometry analysis, cell suspensions were prepared and blocked in a 0.3% bovine serum albumin (BSA) solution, incubated with primary antibodies (including PE-CD86 and FITC-CD206) for 30 min, washed with fresh 0.3% BSA, and applied to flow cytometry analysis on an LSRFortessa flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, USA) to count at least 30,000 events.

sections.section: Healing and evaluation of S.a-infected diabetic wounds in mice
sections.text: 4-week-old C57BL mice were used to construct an infected diabetic wound model. Mice were continuously fed on a high-fat diet and streptozotocin (STZ) was used to induce diabetes by intraperitoneal injection. Mice were classified as diabetic when random blood glucose exceeded 16.7 mmol/L. Mice were anesthetized by inhalation of isoflurane gas. Full-thickness defective skin wounds with a round shape (10 mm in diameter) were created on the back, followed by the application of S. aureus suspension (100 μL, 107 CFU/mL) to the wound area. The next day wounds were covered with hydrogel dressings along with 3M Tegaderm film to remain hydrogel stationary. All mice were randomly divided into 4 groups: Control (only PBS treated), CPH, MOF@CPH, or Exo/MOF@CPH. All tissues were collected on day 3, 7, 10 and 14 and then stored at −80 °C. To monitor wound healing, mice were given standard anaesthesia before photography, then wound closure was measured using ImageJ software. On day 14, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and blood was collected via cardiac puncture. Blood samples were immediately subjected to routine blood analysis to assess potential systemic toxicity.

After mice were sacrificed, regenerated skin samples were collected on day 7 and 14. Skin samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by dehydration, embedding in paraffin, and preparation of 5 μm thick sections for Hematoxylin-Eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome (MT) staining. Major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys, were harvested on day 14, then fixed, dehydrated, embedded, sectioned and stained with H&E. IL-6, CD206, HIF-1α, CK14 and Ki67 were detected by immunohistochemical (IHC) method, and CD31, VEGF, and α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) were detected by IF method. The quantification of H&E, MT, IHC and IF was calculated by ImageJ software.

RAW 264.7 macrophages and HUVECs were seeded in 6-well plates. The cells were activated by LPS for 24 h. Cells were co-cultured with different hydrogels for 24 h. The cells were collected and lysed using RIPA (with PMSF) in an ice bath. The proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and then transferred to PVDF membrane. After blocking at 25 °C for 1 h, the PVDF membrane was incubated with specific primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. After overnight, the membranes were incubated with the secondary antibodies 1 h at 25 °C. Then The protein bands were visualized using an ECL detection kit and captured by a chemiluminescence imaging system.

The results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). All data were analyzed in more than three independent experiments. Differences between two groups were analyzed using a two-tailed, unpaired t-test. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Statistical significance was set at ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001.

sections.section: Preparation and characterization of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and UCMSC-exo
sections.text: Fig. 2A schematically outlines the one-pot method synthesis of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8. Firstly, the bimetallic Mn-ZIF-8 was obtained by replacing the zinc ions with manganese ions at a specific molar ratio during the synthesis of ZIF-8. The results of TEM showed that a dodecahedral rhombic structure was synthesized (Fig. 2B and C), and the EDX mapping analysis showed that zinc and manganese atoms were evenly distributed in the framework structure of Mn-ZIF-8. In addition, XPS analysis was carried out for characterization (Fig. 2F–H). The presence of Mn2+ and Mn4+ was indicated by the peaks of Mn2p3/2 (641.5 eV), N1s generated by metal-N bond (401.2 eV). These results confirmed the successful synthesis of Mn-ZIF-8.Fig. 2Characterization of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and UCMSC-exo. (A) The process of synthesis of Mn-ZIF-8. (B, C) TEM images and elements mapping of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8. (D) Particle diameter of Mn-ZIF-8 and DFO@Mn-ZIF-8. (E) Zeta potential of Mn-ZIF-8 and DFO@Mn-ZIF-8. (F-H) XPS analysis of Mn-ZIF-8. (I, J) XRD analysis of Mn-ZIF-8 and DFO@Mn-ZIF-8. (K) The isolation process of UCMSC-exo. (L) Identification of UCMSC-exo by NTA, and Western blot for CD9, and TSG101. (M) TEM images of UCMSC-exo. Scale bar = 500 nm (left), 50 nm (right). (N) Internalization of UCMSC-exo by RAW 264.7 macrophages after 12 h of incubation. Statistical data are presented as mean ± SD (∗p < 0.05). (n = 3).Fig. 2 According to the standard curve, after testing the cytotoxicity and tube-forming effect on HUVEC with different concentrations of DFO, as well as the encapsulation efficiency and loading efficiency (Figs. S1 and S2, Table S1), DFO could be loaded into the frameworks by either one-pot co-assembly or physical adsorption [44,45]. DLS results demonstrated that the diameter of the Mn-ZIF-8 was 105.22 nm (Fig. 2D), which gradually increased to approximately 192.15 nm following loading with DFO. The Zeta potentials of Mn-ZIF-8 and DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 were 31.45 mV and 27.76 mV, respectively (Fig. 2E). The decrease in zeta potential may be attributed to the coordination interaction between the negatively charged DFO and Zn2+ of the Mn-ZIF-8 backbone. Even though DFO was mainly encapsulated inside Mn-ZIF-8, it changed the electron distribution at the particle interface and reduce the surface positive charge density. The XRD patterns of ZIF-8, Mn-ZIF-8 and DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 revealed characteristic diffraction peaks that corresponded well with those of simulated ZIF-8 (Fig. 2I), indicating a high degree of structural similarity. Moreover, the main peak (011) of the Mn-ZIF-8 is shifted to the left compared with that of ZIF-8 (Fig. 2J), When Zn2+ (74 p.m.) is replaced by Mn2+ (83 p.m.), which has a larger ionic radius, the crystal spacing increases. According to the Bragg equation, the value of 2θ decreases for Mn-ZIF-8. Neither the Mn doping, nor the loaded DFO have broken the skeleton of ZIF-8. Fig. 2K shows the preparation process of UCMSC-exo. After the hUCMSCs were isolated from the umbilical cord tissue and cultured, the UCMSC-exos were harvested and purified from the hUCMSC supernatants, their morphology, size and surface protein markers were characterized. TEM results showed that UCMSC-exo exhibited homogeneous morphological features, with a slight depression on one side and a chalice-like or hemispherical structure (Fig. 2M), and had an average diameter of 103.70 nm. In addition, as shown in Fig. 2L, the size distribution of the UCMSC-exo was determined by NTA, and most of exosomes had a size range between 50 and 300 nm (82.2%). WB results showed that the expression levels of CD9 and TSG101 were significantly increased in the exo compared with hUCMSCs (Fig. 2L), which are used as marker protein for identifying the existence of exosomes [46]. Therefore, the successful isolation of UCMSC-exo was confirmed. Exosomes need to be internalized into the cell to achieve intercellular communication [47]. RAW 264.7 macrophages were co-cultured with PKH67-labelled UCMSC-exo for 12 h, with PKH67-labelled PBS as a control, and then fluorescence assay was used to observe the exosome internalization. As shown in Fig. 2N, no green fluorescence signal was observed in the control group, while the exosome group exhibited obvious green fluorescence after 12 h of co-culture. The images at different time points are shown in Fig. S3. The results showed that the amount of exosome internalized was significantly higher at 12 h than that at 6 h. The above results confirmed that RAW 264.7 macrophages could successfully internalize UCMSC-exo.

sections.section: Preparation and characterization of Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel
sections.text: Fig. 3A shows the preparation process of the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel. CS-PBA was synthesized by grafting PBA on the CS chain. The proton signals of the benzene ring in CS-PBA were determined and confirmed by 1H NMR (Fig. 3B). FTIR was employed to verify the C=C stretching vibration of the benzene ring of CS-PBA at 1538 cm−1 and the B-O stretching vibration at 1323 cm−1 (Fig. 3C), thus confirming the synthesis of CS-PBA [43]. The formation of the hydrogel was achieved through the chemical crosslinking of boronic ester bonds between boric acid groups of CS-PBA and hydroxyl groups of PVA. Fig. 3D shows the formation of the CPH hydrogel by mixing the CS-PBA solution and PVA solution. To form Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel, it only additionally requires the dispersion of UCMSC-exo and DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 into the PVA solution. The section structures of the CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel were observed by SEM (Fig. 3E and F), which showed uniform porous structures with a pore size of approximately 3.0 and 3.8 μm, respectively (Fig. 3G).Fig. 3Characterization of intelligent-responsive hydrogel Exo/MOF@CPH. (A) Schematic diagram. (B) 1H NMR analysis of CS-PBA. (C) FTIR spectrum of CS-PBA, CS, 4-CPBA. (D) Photographs of CS-PBA and PVA assembled into crosslinked d hydrogel. (E-G) SEM of hydrogels and aperture analysis. (H) Self-healing ability of the hydrogel. (I) Rheological test of the storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) of the hydrogel. (J) Step-strain measurement of the hydrogel. (K) Adhesion performance. (L) Shear-thinning test of the hydrogel. (M) Zn and Mn inon release behaviour. (N) DFO drug release behaviour. (O) Exosome release behaviour. Statistical data are presented as mean ± SD (∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001). (n = 3).Fig. 3 The self-healing and injectable capacities of the hydrogels were also macroscopically evaluated. Two independent hydrogel samples were contacted and then stretched to visually investigate the self-healing properties. The samples became an integrated one and could maintain an integrated shape after stretching, indicating excellent self-healing ability of the hydrogels (Fig. 3H). The self-healing ability of the hydrogel was further verified. When alternating high (500%) and low strains (1%) were applied, respectively, the hydrogel was able to recover structural stability in a short time with only slight modulus loss (Fig. 3J). The oscillation of G″ may be related to the breaking and reforming of dynamic boronic ester bonds, and hydrogen bonds in the hydrogel network [48]. As a consequence of the dynamic covalent and non-covalent bonds, the hydrogel displays a self-healing capacity. Adhesion performance was intuitively evaluated on porcine skins. As illustrated in Fig. 3K, the hydrogel maintained continuous skin adhesion without edge detachment under stretching, bending, and twisting, demonstrating reliable wound sealing. The modulus of the hybrid hydrogel was detemined by rheological tests (Fig. 3I). The energy storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) of the hydrogel was 5645 Pa, 1620 Pa, respectively. Subsequently, shear-thinning testing also confirmed that the hydrogel rapidly decreased in viscosity with increasing shear frequency, which enabled it to be effectively delivered to deep sites through syringes (Fig. 3L). To investigate the degradation behavior of hydrogel in different environments, the ionic concentration of the hybrid hydrogel dissolved in various solutions was tested by ICP-OES (Fig. 3M). After 4 days of testing, the cumulative release rate of zinc ions and manganese ions reached 76.5% and 82.1%, respectively, with the addition of 1 mM H2O2. More metal ions were released than the control group, indicating that the Exo/MOF@CPH has a release behaviour in response to the ROS environment. The DFO drug release behaviour of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 in acidic environments was also tested, with higher rates of DFO release in pH 6.0 and pH 5.0 environments compared to neutral environments (Fig. 3N). The degradation of hydrogel was also characterized (Fig. S4). Furthermore, the self-adaptive release of exosomes from Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel in response to the ROS concentration and the glucose concentration was investigated by using the BCA method under H2O2 and glucose (Fig. 3O). After 168 h (7 days) of incubation, the cumulative release of exosomes reached 87.56% at 3 mg/mL glucose with 1 mM H2O2. Without H2O2, the cumulative release dropped to 74.40%. It is noteworthy that at 24 h, the cumulative release rate was 37.50% at glucose solution alone. With the addition of the effect of H2O2, the rate increased to 59.37%, confirming that the boronic ester bonds are dual-responsive [49]. These data indicated that the hydrogel can not only regulate exosome release kinetics in response to different ROS and glucose concentrations, but also achieve on-demand exosome delivery.

sections.section: Evaluation of bioactivity and antibacterial activity of Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel in vitro
sections.text: To systematically evaluate the in vitro performance of the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel, its bioactivity (including cell proliferation, migration, and tube formation) and antibacterial activity were comprehensively assessed in the present study (Fig. 4A). The cytotoxicity of the hydrogel was assessed by Live/Dead staining. After incubated with HUVECs and L929 fibroblasts for 3 days at 37 °C, all groups revealed no significant cytotoxicity and the live cell rate ranged from 95.29% to 99.87% (Fig. 4B and C). The hemolysis ratio of Exo/MOF@CPH was less than 5% (Fig. S5), The hemolysis rate of the hydrogel is less than 5%, which also confirmed biocompatibility. Differentiated cell migration and oriented cell divisions contribute to wound re-epithelialization [50]. The role of hydrogels in promoting cell proliferation was evaluated by EdU staining and CCK-8 assay. The EdU staining demonstrated a progressive increase in green fluorescence across the control, CPH, MOF@CPH, and Exo/MOF@CPH groups over 24 h (Fig. 4F and G). This enhanced effect was attributed to the impact of DFO and the bioactive factors carried by UCMSC-exo. In addition, the CCK-8 assay further confirmed significantly increased cell proliferation in Exo/MOF@CPH treated cells (Fig. 4D and E). Subsequently, cell migration was assessed using scratch assay and transwell assay, as shown in Fig. 4H and J. Compared with the control group, the number of migrated HUVECs through the transwell chambers in the CPH, MOF@CPH, Exo@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH groups exhibited a gradual increase, and the scratch assay results showed the same trend (Fig. 4I–K).Fig. 4Evaluation of bioactivity and antibacterial activity of Exo/MOF@CPH. (A) Schematic diagram. (B, C) Live/Dead staining of hydrogel and statistical analysis. (D, E) CCK-8 assay of hydrogel. (F, G) EdU staining of hydrogel and statistical analysis. (H, I) Transwell assay images of HUVECs and statistical analysis. (J, K) Scratch assay images of HUVECs and L929 fibroblasts and statistical analysis. (L-N) Tube formation assay and statistical analysis. (O) Images of the remaining bacterial colonies of S. aureus and E. coli after different treatments. (P) Antibacterial ratios of hydrogels against S. aureus and E. coli. (Q) Confocal microscopy images of S. aureus biofilm. Scale bar = 100 μm. (R) Crystal violet staining images. Scale bar = 4 mm. (S) OD570 values of the biofilm solution. Statistical data are presented as mean ± SD (∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001). (n = 3).Fig. 4 Angiogenesis has a positive effect on wound healing in diabetic patients. In vitro tube formation assay on the matrigel revealed that both DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and UCMSC-exo significantly promoted tube structure formation, increasing vessel-like structures, node numbers, and tube lengths (Fig. 4L–N). RT-qPCR was used to assess the expression of angiogenesis-related genes in HUVECs, including HIF-1α, VEGFA, and ANGPT1 (Fig. S6). The HUVECs cultured on the MOF@CPH, Exo@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH samples showed higher gene expression compared with the control group, indicating a better angiogenic activity. While both MOF@CPH and Exo@CPH comparably upregulated HIF-1α and VEGFA, the Exo@CPH group demonstrated a significantly stronger capacity to upregulate ANGPT1 than the MOF@CPH group. ANGPT1 is a critical factor for vascular stabilization and maturation. This result indicates that UCMSC-exos exert broader pro-angiogenic effects besides the classic HIF-1α cascade. Ultimately, the Exo/MOF@CPH group achieved the highest overall gene expression, which aligns with the extensive endothelial tube networks observed in vitro. This functional enhancement suggests that the chemical stabilization of HIF-1α by DFO acts synergistically with the broad-spectrum biological regulation of exosomes to promote comprehensive vascularization. S. aureus and E. coli are major pathogens associated with chronic wounds. Avoiding infection is crucial for diabetic wound management, especially since diabetic patients are more susceptible to infection due to chronic inflammation. The antibacterial properties of the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel are mainly derived from the adhesion to bacteria of chitosan via electrostatic interactions with bacterial cell membranes and the dual metal ion sustained release of Mn-ZIF-8 [51]. To assess the antibacterial efficacy, the prepared samples were utilized for separate co-cultures with S. aureus, and E. coli. According to our previous method [52], the spread plate method was carried out. As shown in Fig. 4O, fewer bacterial colonies were observed on the agar plates of all experimental groups than those of the control group. The antibacterial rates of MOF@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH were 91.45%, 98.08% against S. aureus, and 97.04%, and 94.67% against E. coli, respectively (Fig. 4P). The biofilm inhibition efficacy of the hydrogel was further evaluated using biofilms. Biofilm characterization was performed using crystal violet staining and DMAO/PI staining. It was observed that the green fluorescence intensity was reduced in all experimental groups. Moreover, with the incorporation of Mn-ZIF-8, the proportion of green fluorescence further decreased, and the majority of fluorescence observed under the microscope was red fluorescence, which corresponds to dead bacteria (Fig. 4Q–S7). Crystal violet staining images of biofilms are presented, and the addition of Mn-ZIF-8 resulted in no dye adherence in the well (Fig. 4R). The same trend was observed in the results of OD570 values of the solution after dissolving the adsorbed dye with ethanol (Fig. 4S). In conclusion, the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel has a broad-spectrum antibacterial ability due to multicomponent contribution.

sections.section: Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of hydrogel
sections.text: Pathogen invasion activates the body's immune defence system, and a large number of immune cells are recruited to the wound and produce large amounts of ROS through respiratory bursts [53,54]. ROS production helps the body to clear pathogens, but excessive or sustained ROS can lead to oxidative stress [55]. The antioxidant capacity of hydrogels is mainly formed by Mn-ZIF-8. The total antioxidant capacity of Mn-ZIF-8 was first measured by ABTS·+ scavenging (Fig. 5B). The scavenging efficiency of ABTS·+ was concentration-dependent, as the ABTS·+ scavenging activity was significantly enhanced with increasing Mn-ZIF-8 concentration. This phenomenon can be attributed to the SOD-like and CAT-like enzyme activities of Mn-ZIF-8, which are derived from the homogeneous doping of Mn ions into the ZIF-8 framework, forming a redox pair of Mn2+/Mn4+. As shown in Fig. 5E and F, The SOD-like and CAT-like enzyme activities were determined by the kit method. Notably, when DFO was encapsulated into Mn-ZIF-8, the SOD and CAT enzyme activity units were reduced. It may be the coordination interaction between DFO and the metal nodes of Mn-ZIF-8 compresses the pore space, forming a pore blockage and hindering the binding of the substrate to the active center.Fig. 5Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of Exo/MOF@CPH. (A) Schematic diagram. (B) The antioxidant capacity of Mn-ZIF-8 by ABTS·+ scavenging. (C, D) Intracellular ROS images after DCFH-DA staining and statistical analysis. (E, F) The SOD-like and CAT-like enzyme activities of ZIF-8, Mn-ZIF-8, DFO@Mn-ZIF-8. (G) Representative flow cytometry images of CD86 and CD206 in Raw 264.7 macrophages with different treatments. (H, I) Quantification of CD86 or CD206 positive cells. (J) Representative immunofluorescence images of iNOS (M1 marker) and Arg-1 (M2 marker). (K) Relative expression of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory genes. Statistical data are presented as mean ± SD (∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001). (n = 3).Fig. 5 To further measure ROS scavenging ability of hydrogel at the cellular level. Cells were treated with H2O2 to induce oxidative stress in vitro. As shown in Fig. 5C, the RAW 264.7 macrophages untreated exhibited intense green fluorescence and suffered from abundant ROS accumulation and severe oxidative stress. By contrast, the green fluorescence intensity of the cells decreased after treatment with the MOF@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel (Fig. 5D). Under simulated oxidative stress conditions, the MOF-containing groups exhibited significant intracellular ROS scavenging capacity, whereas the Exo@CPH group showed limited direct antioxidant effects. This difference confirms the specific role of the Mn-ZIF-8 component in neutralizing oxidative stress within the composite system. The same trend was observed in HUVECs (Fig. S8). Therefore, the hydrogel was effective at scavenging ROS and protecting cells from oxidative stress. Meanwhile, macrophages are phenotypically plastic and play a pivotal role in immune defense and wound repair by secreting inflammatory cytokines [56]. ROS in diabetic wound further promote the transformation of macrophages to pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotype [6], thus aggravating the development of inflammation and the damage of surrounding tissue. Next, we evaluated the modulatory effect of the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel on the phenotypic conversion of RAW 264.7 macrophages using flow cytometry to assess the expression of CD86 (an M1 marker) and CD206 (an M2 marker) (Fig. 5G). Most RAW 264.7 macrophages were polarized into the M1-like phenotype upon LPS stimulation by high CD86 expression. In both the MOF@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH groups, the proportion of M1-like macrophages was lower than that in the LPS-treated group (Fig. 5H). While the MOF@CPH hydrogel reduced pro-inflammatory markers by clearing ROS, it was less effective in promoting the M2 phenotypic switch alone. Meanwhile, the fully integrated Exo/MOF@CPH system demonstrated higher upregulation of anti-inflammatory markers compared to the Exo@CPH group (Fig. 5I). This comparison indicates that microenvironment modulation mediated by MOF assists in realizing the immunomodulatory potential of the UCMSC-exo. In contrast, the proportion of M2-like macrophages was the highest in the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel group, which increased from 5.62% to 9.41% relative to the LPS-treated group (Fig. 5I). It was notable that the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel promoted more macrophage differentiation to M2-like cells than the MOF@CPH. Additionally, the immunofluorescence staining for the M1 marker iNOS and the M2 marker Arg-1 was performed (Fig. 5J). RT-qPCR analysis was carried out to indicate that the mRNA expressions of IL-1β, iNOS, TNF-α, Arg-1, IL-10 (Fig. 5K). Collectively, the above findings confirm that the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel exerts robust antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, which derive from the synergistic effect of the ROS-scavenging activity of DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and the M2 macrophage polarization-promoting capacity of UCMSC-exo.

sections.section: In vivo wound healing evaluation of the infected diabetic wound model
sections.text: The in vivo experimental design was shown in Fig. 6A. To evaluate the wound healing effect of the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel in vivo, we first established a STZ-induced diabetic mouse model. Subsequently, a full-thickness wound of 10 mm in diameter was constructed on the back of the mice and inoculated with S. aureus to cause infection. Then the mice in the experimental group were treated with hydrogels and treated with saline only as a control group. Then, the wound healing was observed at different time points. Weight and blood glucose levels were monitored throughout the healing process (Fig. S9). As shown in Fig. 6B, after 3 days of healing, the wounds were infected to varying degrees in all groups, macroscopically. Among them, the control group had the most purulent exudates on the wounds implying the most severe infection. Significantly, Exo/MOF@CPH accelerated the healing of diabetic wounds (Fig. 6C). In the in vivo evaluation with S. aureus infection, the addition of the MOF component contributed to the overall healing outcomes. The Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel achieved a higher wound closure rate (reaching 99.41% at day 14) and better histological repair compared to the Exo@CPH treatment alone. This observation suggests that the MOF aids in modulating the infected diabetic microenvironment, which facilitates the tissue regeneration process. At day 14, the wound closure rate reached 99.41%, while the control group had only 77.12%, indicating the difficulty of autologous healing alone.Fig. 6In vivo wound healing evaluation of the infected diabetic wound model. (A) Schematic diagram of the experimental design. (B) Representative images of wounds treated at 3, 7, 10 and 14 days. (C) Quantitative analysis of wound closure percentage. (D) Representative images of H&E and MT staining of wound tissue from on days 7, 14 post-treatment. (E) Quantitative analysis of granulation tissue thickness. (F) Quantitative analysis of inflammatory infiltration (the group with biggest area as the benchmark). (G) Quantitative analysis of epidermis thickness. (H) Quantitative analysis of collagen deposition. (I) Quantitative analysis of follicle. Statistical data are presented as mean ± SD (∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001). (n = 3).Fig. 6 Then, to further elucidate the changes in the wound tissue during the healing process, we performed H&E and MT (Fig. 6D). As shown in Fig. 6E, on day 7, the Exo/MOF@CPH group developed thicker granulation tissue compared to the control and MOF@CPH groups. This increased thickness reflects enhanced extracellular matrix deposition during the healing process. The control group exhibited the most severe inflammatory response with extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells (e.g., neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells). The MOF@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH groups had less severe wound inflammation, attributed to the antibacterial, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of hydrogel in the early stages of healing (Fig. 6F). After 14 days of healing, the thickness of the new epidermis showed a decreasing trend (Fig. 6G). The epidermal thickness of the Exo/MOF@CPH group was closely resembled that of normal skin tissue, whereas the control group had not been fully epithelialised, indicating that the hydrogel accelerated the process of re-epithelialization and wound healing. Collagen deposition dynamics during the late stage of wound healing were evaluated via Masson's trichrome staining. By day 14 of wound healing, granulation tissue was gradually replaced with a new collagen-enriched dermal matrix in all experimental groups. The proportion of newly formed collagen fibers reached approximately 60% in the MOF@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH groups (Fig. 6H). Skin appendages are integral to the biological and physiological functions of the skin [57,58], and the formation of scarring does not allow for the reconstruction of structures such as hair follicles and sweat glands, which leads to the permanent loss of these functions. Interestingly, the regeneration of skin appendages (hair follicles and sebaceous glands) was also further facilitated in the Exo/MOF@CPH group (Fig. 6I). This suggests that UCMSC-exo promotes the regeneration of skin appendages through a potential mechanism to achieve, hopefully, scarless wound healing. To further assess oxidative stress and inflammation during wound healing in S.a-infected diabetic mice. We performed IHC and IF analysis. In the early stage of wound healing, IL-6 recruits inflammatory cells to the wound site to remove necrotic tissues and pathogens and is therefore one of the major inflammatory mediators. However, prolonged IL-6 stimulation is detrimental to the shift of the immune microenvironment from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory state [59]. Therefore IL-6 was evaluated as an important biomarker of the inflammatory state of the wound (Fig. 7A). IL-6 positive areas were significantly reduced in the MOF@CPH, Exo@CPH, and Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel-treated groups (Fig. 7C). These findings confirmed that the hydrogels are effective in mitigating oxidative stress and reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory factors. This observation is consistent with the histological findings from wound H&E staining. IL-6 was used as an M1-like phenotype macrophage marker, thus indicating a reduction in the proportion of pro-inflammatory M1-like macrophages. Concomitantly, IHC experiments for CD206 were also conducted (Fig. 7D), which showed that the Exo@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH groups had the largest CD206 positive areas, implying the highest number of M2 macrophages. The result revealed a gradual increase in CD206 positive areas after hydrogel treatment, implying a gradual increase in M2 macrophages and a shift in macrophage phenotype towards M2. This suggests that the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel can alleviate ROS, modulate the inflammatory environment and reduce the immune response.Fig. 7IHC and IF analysis. (A) IHC of IL-6, CD206, HIF-1α, CK14 and Ki67. (B) IF of CD31, VEGF and α-SMA. (C-G) Quantitative analysis of IHC. (H, I) Quantitative analysis of VEGF fluorescence on day 7, and CD31 fluorescence on day 14. (J) Quantitative analysis of blood vessels from CD31 staining on Day 14. Statistical data are presented as mean ± SD (∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001). (n = 3).Fig. 7 After cutaneous injury, impaired blood perfusion and enhanced cellular metabolism result in local tissue hypoxia at the wound. This local hypoxia drives the upregulation of HIF-1α expression in various cells [60], subsequently triggering the secretion of the pro-angiogenic factor such as VEGF [61]. This cascade ultimately activates the proliferation and migration of endothelial cells, thereby facilitating neovascularization [62]. On day 7 of healing, HIF-1α was detected in the newly formed skin tissue by IHC, as shown in Fig. 7E, and the HIF-1α positive areas were increased in both the MOF@CPH and Exo@CPH groups compared to the control. Furthermore, the Exo/MOF@CPH treatment exhibited the highest HIF-1α expression among all groups. This observation aligns with the combined effects of DFO-mediated HIF-1α stabilization and the concurrent activation of the HIF-1α signaling pathway by the UCMSC-exo. Additionally, the expression levels of CD31 and VEGF were assessed via IF (Fig. 7B–H), and their expression patterns exhibited a consistent trend with that of HIF-1α. This was attributed to stabilization of HIF-1α by DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and activation of the HIF-1α signaling pathway by UCMSC-exos. CD31 is a canonical marker of vascular endothelial cells, and its expression positively correlates with the degree of angiogenesis. Subsequently, the vascular structures of the newly formed skin tissue were further assessed by IF staning for CD31 and α-SMA on day 14. As shown in Fig. 7B, while the control group exhibited few vascular structures, both the MOF@CPH and Exo@CPH groups showed a comparable increase in CD31-positive vessel density (Fig. 7I). This indicates that both DFO-mediated chemical intervention and exosome delivery independently stimulate early endothelial sprouting. A distinct difference was observed in vessel maturation (Fig. 7J). The Exo@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH groups presented blood vessels with noticeably larger lumens and denser coverage by α-SMA-positive smooth muscle cells compared to the MOF@CPH group. Ultimately, the Exo/MOF@CPH group demonstrated the highest overall vascular density and structural maturity, suggesting that combining the rapid chemical angiogenic trigger with broad biological reprogramming generates highly functional and stable neovascularization. CK14 is a common fibrillin in epidermal cells and can be used to evaluate the thickness of the newly formed epidermis. We performed IHC for CK14 in the epidermis of each group (Fig. 7A). Compared with the control group, CK14 secretion progressively decreased in the CPH, MOF@CPH, Exo@CPH, and Exo/MOF@CPH groups, accompanied by a reduction in epidermal thickness that approached that of normal skin (Fig. 7F). Excessive epidermal thickening is typically associated with uncontrolled cell proliferation and abnormal differentiation, representing an early hallmark of hypertrophic scar formation. Tissue regeneration was analyzed using the cell proliferation marker Ki67 (Fig. 7A). Hydrogel treatment significantly enhanced Ki67 expression (Fig. 7G). Compared to MOF@CPH, Exo@CPH and Exo/MOF@CPH exhibited upregulation of Ki67 expression, indicating the exosome-mediated promotion of dermal cell proliferation. Moreover, the biosafety of Exo/MOF@CPH was confirmed through histological staining of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney), which showed no adverse effects compared to the control group (Fig. S10). Blood routine indicators were also within normal ranges, confirming that caused no systemic toxicity during wound healing (Fig. S11). In vivo degradation kinetics of hydrogel was evaluated using IVIS imaging following subcutaneous implantation in mice (Fig. S12). The hydrogel degrades more rapidly in diabetic mice, while demonstrating a longer retention time in normal mice. This disparity in degradation rates provides direct in vivo experimental evidence for the hydrogel's responsive degradation and on-demand release properties in diabetic wounds.

sections.section: Potential mechanisms of wound healing in the infected diabetic wound
sections.text: To elucidate the mechanism by which hydrogels accelerate wound healing, we performed transcriptome sequencing on newly formed skin tissue at the defect site. Transcriptomic profiling was performed on the control, MOF@CPH, and Exo/MOF@CPH groups at 14 days of wound healing. Fig. 8A shows the overlap and specific distribution of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) obtained from the pairwise comparative analysis of these groups. Volcano plot analysis of DEGs showed that, relative to the control group, the Exo/MOF@CPH group had 1339 significantly downregulated genes and 1486 significantly upregulated genes (Fig. 8B). Heatmap analysis showed the normalized gene expression levels of genes associated with four biological functional categories: angiogenesis, inflammatory response, scar inhibition, and skin barrier function (Fig. 8C). Notably, relative to the control group, the Exo/MOF@CPH group exhibited significant upregulation of angiogenesis-related genes (e.g., Hif1a, Vegfa, Kdr), anti-inflammatory genes (e.g., Il10, Tgfb1), scar inhibition-related genes (e.g., Klf4, Col3a1), and skin barrier-related genes (e.g., Flg2, Eln). Some pro-inflammatory genes and pro-scar formation genes (e.g., Acta2) were downregulated.Fig. 8Transcriptomic sequencing analysis of newly formed skin tissue. (A) Venn diagram showing the number of differential genes between different groups. (B) Volcano plots of DEGs (|log2(FC)| > 1). (C) Cluster analysis heatmap of DEGs. (D, E) GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of upregulated DEGs. (F) GO enrichment chord diagrams. (G, H) GSEA analysis of the HIF-1 signaling pathway and VEGF signaling pathway. (I) WB of HIF-1α, VEGF, PI3K-Akt and JAK-STAT pathways. (J) Schematic diagram of the molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways of hydrogel.Fig. 8 DEGs upregulated in the Exo/MOF@CPH vs. Con group were used for gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (Fig. 8D). This analysis revealed that these DEGs were significantly enriched in key biological processes, including epidermal cell proliferation, wound healing, keratinization, sprouting angiogenesis, positive regulation of angiogenesis, extracellular matrix organization, and negative regulation of inflammatory response. This further confirms that the Exo/MOF@CPH can effectively accelerate diabetic wound healing by synergistically modulating epidermal cell proliferation, angiogenesis, cutaneous ECM remodeling, and inflammatory homeostasis. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel synergistically promotes the wound healing process via the activation of multiple key signaling pathways, including the HIF-1 signaling pathway, VEGF signaling pathway, PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, Ras signaling pathway, Rap1 signaling pathway, focal adhesion pathway, and regulation of actin cytoskeleton pathway (Fig. 8E). The HIF-1 pathway responds to hypoxia and works in concert with the VEGF pathway to promote vascular endothelial cell function and accelerate vascularization of the wound to improve oxygen supply. The JAK-STAT pathway is closely related to the inflammatory response [63,64]. Upregulated genes within this pathway (e.g., Il10) inhibit the expression of pro-inflammatory factors and facilitate the polarization of anti-inflammatory macrophages via activation of the JAK2-STAT3 axis. Meanwhile, the Cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway promotes the transduction of anti-inflammatory factor signals. In addition, PI3K-Akt, Ras, Rap1 signaling pathways are classical regulatory pathways for cell proliferation and migration. Activation of these pathways promotes the proliferation and migration of fibroblasts and epidermal cells to the wound area, accelerating the process of granulation tissue filling and epidermal re-epithelialization. We performed chord plot analysis for GO enrichment results to delineate the associations between GO enrichment terms and key genes in the Exo/MOF@CPH versus control groups (Fig. 8F). Consistent with these observations, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) results revealed that DEGs in the Exo/MOF@CPH group were significantly enriched in the HIF-1 and VEGF signaling pathways. And the core genes of these two pathways were predominantly upregulated. These findings further confirm that the Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel promotes the activation of the HIF-1 and VEGF signaling pathways, thereby contributing to enhanced neovascularization (Fig. 8G and H).

The primary objective of this study was to develop a glucose and ROS dual-responsive hydrogel (Exo/MOF@CPH) for the stage-specific sequential delivery of UCMSC-exo and DFO in diabetic wound healing. The hydrogel was designed to dynamically sense the elevated glucose and ROS levels inherent to diabetic wounds. Upon exposure to these local pathological triggers, the dynamic chemical linkages within the network undergo targeted cleavage, initiating an on-demand, responsive release of therapeutic payloads. In vitro results indicated that the integration of the Mn-ZIF-8 provided necessary nanozyme-like and antibacterial activities. This MOF effectively scavenged excessive ROS, thereby offering antioxidant protection to the exosomes. Following this initial detoxification, the sustained release of DFO and UCMSC-exo promoted several key cellular processes, including enhanced endothelial tube formation, increased proliferation and migration of fibroblasts and endothelial cells, and the polarization of macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. These in vitro findings were consistent with observations in a S. aureus-infected diabetic mouse model. The Exo/MOF@CPH hydrogel accelerated macroscopic wound closure, reduced bacterial burden, and improved histological outcomes, as evidenced by increased granulation tissue thickness and organized collagen deposition. Collectively, these results demonstrate that modulating the pathological microenvironment enhances the therapeutic efficacy of cell-free systems in chronic wounds. The transition from traditional cell-based treatments to cell-free therapies represents a crucial paradigm shift in diabetic wound management. Stem cell therapies possess the remarkable ability to dynamically sense the injured microenvironment and secrete a continuous supply of growth factors to orchestrate tissue repair[[65], [66], [67]]. However, while direct cell transplantation offers robust biological benefits, its clinical translation is hindered by poor cellular survival in the hostile, highly oxidative diabetic wound bed, along with inherent risks of immune rejection and tumorigenesis [68]. Numerous studies suggest that the reparative effects of stem cells are mediated through paracrine effects rather than through differentiation and replacement following long-term implantation [69]. Exosomes exert comparable regenerative and immunomodulatory functions primarily through these paracrine mechanisms, yet as cell-free alternatives, they offer profound translational advantages [70,71]. They exhibit superior physicochemical stability, insignificant‌ immunogenicity, a complete absence of tumorigenic risk, and significantly easier storage and transportation [72]. Nevertheless, naked exosomes are highly susceptible to rapid clearance and proteolytic degradation when directly exposed to the protease-rich, inflammatory microenvironment of chronic wounds, thus necessitating a protective matrix with sustained-release capabilities to maintain their bioactivity [37,38]. The Exo/MOF@CPH system capitalizes on these cell-free therapeutic benefits. Furthermore, compared to conventional hydrogels that rely on passive degradation or single-stimulus triggers, which often suffer from premature drug leakage or insufficient on-demand release, this platform is engineered with a dual-responsive dynamic network. By integrating dynamic boronic ester bonds, the hydrogel maintains excellent structural stability in healthy tissues but achieves precise, localized degradation in response to the signature high-glucose and ROS-rich microenvironment of diabetic wounds. This establishes a sequential therapeutic paradigm: microenvironment clearance followed by synergistic regeneration. Rather than merely drug delivery system, the Mn-ZIF-8 acts as an early-stage vanguard to clear bacterial biofilms and pathological ROS, thereby creating a permissive biological niche that maximizes the subsequent angiogenic and immunomodulatory functions of the exosomes. The precise coordinated therapeutic mode of Exo/MOF@CPH relies on its excellent retention capabilities and internal biochemical compatibility. The sustained release of exosomes and MOF is governed by a dual retention mechanism. Physically, the dense and interwoven polymer network of the hydrated hydrogel provides substantial steric hindrance, thus preventing burst diffusion [73]. Chemically, the PBA groups within the hydrogel network form dynamic, reversible covalent bonds with native cis-diols. Unmodified exosomes are naturally enveloped with a dense glycocalyx abundant in sialylated glycoproteins [74,75], which present plentiful surface cis-diols. These diols form strong interactions with PBA groups, thereby establishing a highly specific exosome immobilization system. Crucially, the local microenvironment modulated by the MOF actively maintains the structural and functional integrity of exosomes. The nanozyme-like catalytic activity of Mn-ZIF-8 rapidly clears oxidative stress without disintegrating into massive, toxic bursts of metal ions. This temporal release gap, coupled with the antioxidant protection afforded by the MOF, effectively protects the stable exosomal lipid bilayer and cargo from oxidative damage before their release into the wound. While the macroscopic tissue regeneration demonstrates a clear synergistic effect, it is important to distinguish the specific mechanistic contributions of the drug molecule and the biological component to rule out functional redundancy. DFO and exosomes drive angiogenesis through distinct yet highly complementary pathways. The released DFO provides a rapid pharmacological priming by directly inhibiting prolyl hydroxylases, leading to the stabilization and accumulation of HIF-1α in the endothelial cells [76,77]. Concurrently, the exosomes orchestrate a much broader and more sustained biological reprogramming [71]. By delivering a diversity of functional miRNAs and proteins, the UCMSC-exo activates extensive signaling networks, prominently including the PI3K-Akt and JAK-STAT pathways, which drive robust cell proliferation, migration, and M2 macrophage polarization. This complementary integration of rapid targeted chemical intervention and broad-spectrum biological regulation maximizes the therapeutic outcome without competitive interference. Despite these highly promising therapeutic results, we acknowledge several limitations in the current study that deserve future fundamental investigation. First, although our transcriptomic and protein-level analyses robustly identified the activation of key regenerative pathways, the precise in vivo causal relationships remain to be definitively proven. Future studies employing pathway-specific pharmacological inhibitors or genetic knockdown models are essential to provide the gold-standard causal validation of these molecular mechanisms. Second, while biological functional assays verified the preservation of exosome bioactivity, direct multi-omics tracking post-release, such as miRNA-sequencing of the residual cargo, would provide a deeper, more granular understanding of how the encapsulation and microenvironmental changes specifically alter the exosomal molecular profile. Third, STZ-induced mouse model with a single S. aureus infection cannot fully replicate the chronic, polymicrobial, and neuropathy-associated nature of clinical DFU. Finally, although our 14-day observation window is consistent with the standard evaluation timeframe widely adopted in contemporary diabetic wound healing research, extended pharmacokinetic tracking is undoubtedly mandatory to comprehensively evaluate terminal scar collagen remodeling and the ultimate physiological clearance of the nanomaterials. Looking forward, intelligent hydrogels for diabetic wound management are expected to evolve from basic stimuli-responsive matrices into integrated, closed-loop theranostic platforms. Future designs should incorporate continuous biochemical sensing capabilities to monitor critical wound biomarkers in real time, such as pH, glucose, and protease levels. This feedback could then precisely calibrate on-demand therapeutic dosing. Furthermore, enhancing the spatiotemporal programmability of these matrices represents a crucial research trend. Advanced fabrication techniques, including 3D bioprinting, can generate anisotropic architectures that mimic the native ECM, enabling the compartmentalized delivery of multiple agents to distinct tissue layers. Additionally, integrating external triggers could provide non-invasive control over release kinetics to match specific healing phases. Ultimately, by merging bio-responsive materials with advanced manufacturing and bioelectronics, subsequent generations of intelligent dressings will likely become highly adaptive devices, capable of continuously responding to the dynamic physiological variations of individual DFU.

Considering the limitations of traditional dressings for DFU, which typically possess a singular function, this study introduces an intelligent treatment strategy of "intelligent response - synergistic regulation". By constructing a multifunctional integrated platform (Exo/MOF@CPH) based on a glucose and ROS dual-responsive chitosan hydrogel, which loads DFO@Mn-ZIF-8 and UCMSC-exo, synergistic intervention on multiple critical pathological processes including infection, oxidative stress, and angiogenesis disorders was achieved. The results demonstrate that Exo/MOF@CPH not only effectively clears bacteria and neutralizes excessive ROS but also continuously releases bioactive components that significantly promote angiogenesis. Consequently, this process transforms the pathological microenvironment impeding healing into a healing-friendly microenvironment conducive to tissue regeneration. This strategy enables the adaptive regulation of dynamic wounds through a single platform and offers a novel perspective with potential for clinical translation in the management of complex chronic wounds like DFU.
