title: Microalgae extracellular vesicles-loaded dual antioxidative and anti-inflammatory hydrogel system for wound healing and peripheral nerve repair in diabetes
abstract: Chronic wound healing and peripheral nerve repair in diabetes remain a major clinical challenge due to persistent oxidative stress, inflammation, and impaired tissue regeneration. Here, we developed a multifunctional hydrogel, mEVs@TAgel, for the synergistic delivery of microalgal extracellular vesicles (mEVs) from Haematococcus pluvialis and tannic acid (TA) to address these barriers. mEVs are rich in astaxanthin and functional proteins that target mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, while TA itself exhibits intrinsic antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. The hydrogel exhibits excellent injectability, tissue adhesion, and sustained release of mEVs. In vitro, mEVs@TAgel significantly reduced ROS levels by activating the Nrf2 signaling pathway, enhanced mitochondrial function in keratinocytes and Schwann cells, and drove M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization via suppression of NF-κB signaling. In diabetic mice, treatment with mEVs@TAgel accelerated full-thickness wound closure, promoted re-epithelialization, angiogenesis, and collagen remodeling, and reduced scar formation through early Col 3 deposition and an improved Col 3/Col 1 ratio. Notably, in a sciatic nerve injury model, mEVs@TAgel enhanced functional recovery, axonal regeneration, remyelination, and muscle preservation. Long-term biosafety evaluations showed no systemic toxicity or inflammatory side effects. Altogether, mEVs@TAgel represents a safe and potent platform that coordinately mitigates oxidative stress, inflammation, and tissue damage, offering a promising strategy for diabetic wound and nerve repair. •mEVs@TAgel was developed for synergistic delivery of microalgal extracellular vesicles (mEVs) and tannic acid (TA).•mEVs target mitochondrial dysfunction, while TA provides antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities.•mEVs@TAgel reduced ROS levels by activating the Nrf2 pathway and promoted macrophage polarization through NF-κB suppression.•In diabetic mice, mEVs@TAgel accelerated full-thickness wound closure and reduced scar formation.•In a sciatic nerve injury model, mEVs@TAgel promoted axonal regeneration, remyelination, and muscle preservation. mEVs@TAgel was developed for synergistic delivery of microalgal extracellular vesicles (mEVs) and tannic acid (TA). mEVs target mitochondrial dysfunction, while TA provides antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. mEVs@TAgel reduced ROS levels by activating the Nrf2 pathway and promoted macrophage polarization through NF-κB suppression. In diabetic mice, mEVs@TAgel accelerated full-thickness wound closure and reduced scar formation. In a sciatic nerve injury model, mEVs@TAgel promoted axonal regeneration, remyelination, and muscle preservation.

sections.text: The impaired healing of chronic skin wounds and peripheral nerve injuries in individuals with diabetes mellitus represents a major clinical challenge, imposing substantial physical, psychological, and economic burdens on patients and healthcare systems worldwide [1,2]. Despite the development of numerous therapeutic strategies, current treatments are often limited by incomplete efficacy, safety concerns, or inability to address the multifactorial nature of diabetic tissue repair [3,4]. Therefore, there is an urgent need for safe and effective approaches that can simultaneously target the interconnected pathophysiological barriers in diabetic wound healing. Skin wound repair proceeds through a well-orchestrated sequence of overlapping phases: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling. In diabetes mellitus, this process is severely disrupted due to a confluence of metabolic and vascular dysfunctions. Notably, hyperglycemia exerts direct toxicity on neurons, making diabetic neuropathy one of the earliest and most prevalent complications, significantly contributing to the formation of diabetic foot ulcers [5]. Concurrently, elevated glucose levels impair immune cell function, leading to persistent and exaggerated local inflammation [6,7]. Furthermore, diabetic wounds are characterized by microvascular damage and diminished angiogenic capacity, resulting in poor perfusion, inadequate nutrient delivery, and tissue hypoxia [8,9]. This hypoxic environment is further exacerbated by high oxygen consumption during prolonged inflammatory responses. Hypoxia not only sustains inflammation but also promotes the overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), creating a vicious cycle of oxidative stress and tissue injury [9,10]. Mitochondria, as both primary sources and key targets of ROS, lie at the center of this pathological cascade, with mitochondrial dysfunction contributing critically to delayed healing and impaired regeneration of both skin and nerve tissues. In recent years, microalgae have emerged as promising bioresources with broad applications in agriculture, industry, and biomedicine [11]. Among them, Haematococcus pluvialis (HP) is particularly notable for its ability to accumulate high levels of astaxanthin (AST) under environmental stress [12,13]. AST is a potent antioxidant capable of scavenging ROS and modulating inflammatory pathways, including suppression of key pro-inflammatory mediators such as COX-2, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β [14,15]. Given its capacity for sustained oxygen evolution and controlled release of AST, HP holds significant potential for promoting tissue regeneration in complex wound environments, including diabetic wounds [9]. However, the therapeutic application of whole microalgae is hindered by their relatively large size, which limits cellular uptake and biodistribution. To overcome this limitation, extracellular vesicles (EVs)—nanoscale, membrane-bound particles secreted by cells—have gained increasing attention as natural carriers for intercellular communication across diverse organisms [[16], [17], [18], [19]]. Recent research has proven that EV-based strategies are particularly suitable for tissue regeneration, especially in diabetic wounds [20]. Microalgal EVs offer several advantages over mammalian cell-derived EVs, including higher production yields, lower immunogenicity, and reduced manufacturing costs [21]. Among various EV sources, Haematococcus pluvialis-derived EVs (mEVs) are particularly attractive for diabetic wound therapy. Unlike most plant-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs), mEVs naturally encapsulate AST, eliminating the need for additional engineering in diabetic wound healing formulations [22]. EVs derived from bacteria [23], plants [24], and bovine milk [25], many of which exhibit therapeutic potential [[26], [27], [28]], and recent studies have successfully isolated extracellular vesicles from microalgae (mEVs) [[29], [30], [31], [32], [33]]. Notably, G. Adamo et al. reported preliminary evidence of antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities in EVs derived from Tetraselmis chuii [34]. Nevertheless, systematic investigation into the therapeutic functions of mEVs, particularly those from Haematococcus pluvialis, remains limited. To address the multifaceted challenges of diabetic wound and nerve repair, advanced biomaterials with tailored functionalities are essential. Multifunctional hydrogels have been widely explored for wound management due to their biocompatibility, tunable mechanical properties, and capacity for localized delivery of therapeutics [35]. Injectable, self-healing, and tissue-adhesive hydrogels offer minimally invasive application and conform well to irregular wound geometries, ensuring close contact with damaged tissue and reducing the risk of detachment [36,37]. Tannic acid (TA), a naturally occurring polyphenol abundant in plants such as oak and sumac, serves as a versatile building block for hydrogel design. Its rich phenolic content enables diverse noncovalent interactions—including hydrogen bonding, ionic coordination, and hydrophobic effects—facilitating physical crosslinking with hydrophilic polymers without the need for harsh chemical linkers [38,39]. Beyond structural utility, TA exhibits intrinsic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and biodegradable properties. Previous studies, including work by Ahmadian et al., have shown that TA-based hydrogels effectively mitigate oxidative stress and accelerate wound closure [40], highlighting their promise as functional wound dressings. In this study, we developed a novel composite therapeutic system by isolating mEVs from Haematococcus pluvialis and encapsulating them into a tannic acid-based hydrogel, forming mEVs@TAgel (Scheme 1). We hypothesized that this multifunctional platform would synergistically enhance diabetic tissue repair through several complementary mechanisms: (i) scavenging ROS and restoring mitochondrial function in keratinocytes and Schwann cells via activation of the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway; (ii) promoting the transition of macrophages from the pro-inflammatory M1 to the reparative M2 phenotype by suppressing NF-κB signaling; (iii) accelerating re-epithelialization and angiogenesis; (iv) improving collagen deposition and remodeling to minimize scarring; and (v) facilitating functional recovery in diabetic peripheral nerve injury, specifically in the sciatic nerve. Our findings demonstrate that mEVs@TAgel effectively overcomes multiple pathological barriers in diabetic wound healing and nerve regeneration, providing a safe, integrated, and biomimetic strategy for the treatment of complex diabetic complications.Scheme 1Schematic illustration of microalgae extracellular vesicles-loaded dual antioxidative and anti-inflammatory hydrogel system for wound healing and peripheral nerve repair in diabetes.

Carboxymethyl chitosan (CMCS), oxidized sodium alginate (OSA), polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), and tannic acid (TA) were individually dissolved in deionized water to prepare 5% (w/v) CMCS, 5% (w/v) OSA, 10% (w/v) PVA, and 2% (w/v) TA aqueous solutions. The TAgel hydrogel was formed via dynamic crosslinking by mixing equal volumes of the four precursor solutions under gentle stirring at room temperature. To fabricate mEVs@TAgel, purified mEVs were first resuspended in the OSA solution (5% w/v) at a concentration of 2 mg/ml. This mEV-laden OSA solution was then mixed with equal volumes of CMCS, PVA, and TA solutions under gentle stirring to form the composite hydrogel with uniformly encapsulated mEVs at a final concentration of 1 mg/ml. The injectability of the hydrogels was evaluated by loading the pre-gel solution into a syringe and extruding it through a needle. The microstructure of the hydrogels was examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SU-8010, Hitachi, Japan), both immediately after gelation and following 21 days of degradation under physiological conditions. Rheological properties, including storage modulus (G′), loss modulus (G″), and shear stress, were measured using a rotational rheometer (MCR302, Anton Paar, Austria) equipped with a parallel-plate geometry to assess the mechanical stability and viscoelastic behavior of the hydrogels. UV-Vis-NIR absorption spectra of mEVs, TAgel, and mEVs@TAgel were recorded using a spectrophotometer (UV-2600, Shimadzu, Japan). Swelling and degradation behaviors were evaluated in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH = 8.0) at 37 °C using a gravimetric method. Briefly, hydrogel samples were weighed at predetermined time intervals to monitor changes in water content and mass loss over time. For in vitro release studies, mEVs@TAgel was incubated in PBS (pH = 8.0) at 37 °C, and the release medium was gently refreshed at designated time points. Released mEVs were quantified using a standard protein assay or nanoparticle tracking analysis, and cumulative release profiles were plotted accordingly.

All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with protocols reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhejiang University (approval number: ZJU20250027). Five-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratories (Beijing, China) and acclimatized under standard laboratory conditions for one week. To induce diabetes, mice were fed a high-fat, high-glucose diet for 6 weeks, followed by intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (STZ; 60 mg/kg/day, Sigma, USA) for four consecutive days. Three days after the final injection, blood glucose levels were measured using a glucometer (Roche, Switzerland). Mice with non-fasting blood glucose levels ≥16.7 mM sustained over 10 consecutive days were considered successfully diabetic and included in the study. Diabetic mice were then randomly assigned to four treatment groups (n = 3 per group): Blank, TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel. Under anesthesia, a full-thickness excisional wound (1 cm in diameter) was created on the dorsal skin of each mouse using a sterile biopsy punch. Treatments were administered by direct injection into the wound bed, followed by coverage with sterile medical dressings. To maintain therapeutic efficacy, treatments were repeated every two days. Wound tissues and surrounding skin were harvested at predetermined time points (days 12, 30, and 70 post-injury) for histological analyses.

sections.section: Diabetic sciatic nerve injury model and treatment
sections.text: A partial sciatic nerve crush injury model was selected for this study. In complete transection or full-crush models, the damage is often severe and irreversible. In contrast, the partial injury model preserves a portion of healthy nerve fibers. This model better mimics the progressive nature of diabetic peripheral neuropathy and allows for the evaluation of pro-regenerative effects. To ensure consistency and reproducibility, all surgeries were performed by the same experienced researcher using standardized surgical instruments. Following the establishment of the diabetic mouse model as described above, animals were randomly assigned into four experimental groups (n = 3 per group): Blank (control), TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel. Under anesthesia, the right sciatic nerve was exposed via a lateral mid-thigh incision and carefully separated from the surrounding biceps femoris muscle through blunt dissection. A standardized partial nerve injury was induced by gently crushing one-third of the sciatic nerve diameter using ultrafine forceps. Immediately after injury, 50 μL of the respective treatment, PBS (Blank), TAgel, mEVs, or mEVs@TAgel, was injected directly into the site of injury to ensure close contact with the damaged nerve. The muscle and skin layers were then sutured sequentially. Postoperatively, all mice received standard care and were housed under controlled conditions with free access to food and water for four weeks. At the end of the four-week period, functional recovery was assessed through nerve conduction velocity testing and gait analysis. Subsequently, the injured sciatic nerves and ipsilateral gastrocnemius muscles were harvested at day 28 for further histological, molecular, and biochemical evaluations.

Data from at least three independent experiments are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Differences between groups were assessed using one-way or two-way ANOVA, followed by appropriate post hoc tests for multiple comparisons. The effect size was reported as eta-squared (η2). Statistical significance was defined as: ns (not significant), ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. All analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.2.0.

sections.section: Isolation, characterization, and content analysis of mEVs
sections.text: Haematococcus pluvialis (HP), a type of unicellular algae, has significant economic and research implications due to its ability to accumulate astaxanthin (AST) under stress conditions [41,42]. Under nutrient-rich conditions, HP cells proliferate rapidly and appear green due to chlorophyll content (G-HP). As nutrients are depleted and light exposure increases, the growth rate of HP cells declines, leading to the gradual accumulation of AST. With continued AST accumulation, the HP cells exhibit a distinct red coloration (R-HP). (Fig. 1A–C). UV-vis-NIR absorption spectra confirmed the transformation from G-HP to R-HP. During this process, the chlorophyll peak at approximately 680 nm (green arrow) diminished significantly, while the AST peak at approximately 470 nm (orange arrow) increased markedly (Fig. 1D). To isolate mEVs, the supernatant was obtained through centrifugation at 4000 g to separate R-HP from the culture medium. This was followed by microfiltration using a 0.22 μm filter to remove cell debris and large vesicles, and ultracentrifugation at 100,000 g was performed to collect the mEVs. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images revealed that isolated mEVs were spherical core-shell nanoparticles with a lipid bilayer structure, characteristic of typical extracellular vesicles (Fig. 1E). This confirms their identity as mEVs. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements indicated that the size distribution of mEVs predominantly ranged from 40 nm to 200 nm, with a peak at 58.8 nm (Fig. 1F). The morphology and size range are consistent with the typical characteristics of extracellular vesicles.Fig. 1Isolation, characterization, and content analysis of mEVs@TAgel. (A) Schematic illustration of the process for isolating mEVs from R-HP cultures. Images of the culture and morphology of (B) G-HP and (C) R-HP. (D) UV-vis-NIR absorption spectra of G-HP and R-HP cultures. (E) TEM images of mEVs. (F) Size distribution of mEVs. (G) HPLC chromatogram of AST in mEVs. (H) Precursor, peptides, protein groups, and proteins identified in mEVs. (I) EggNOG functional classification of proteins identified in mEVs. (J) KEGG pathway analysis of proteins in mEVs. GO analysis of (K) biological processes, (L) cellular components, and (M) molecular functions associated with proteins in mEVs. HPLC analysis showed a significant enrichment of AST in the mEVs (Fig. 1G). Proteomic analysis revealed a total of 909 precursors, 868 peptides, which were grouped into 336 protein groups and identified as 442 proteins (Fig. 1H). The top 10 most abundant proteins in mEVs were primarily involved in energy metabolism, antioxidant defense, and stress response (Table S2). Functional annotation of the mEVs proteome using the EggNOG database revealed that the most abundant functional category was energy production and conversion. Other categories associated with cell metabolism, such as carbohydrate transport and metabolism, lipid transport and metabolism, and coenzyme transport and metabolism, were also enriched (Fig. 1I). KEGG pathway analysis showed significant enrichment in several metabolic pathways. The most enriched pathways included carbon metabolism and photosynthesis. Additionally, other notable pathways such as glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, peroxisome, oxidative phosphorylation, glutathione metabolism, and pyruvate metabolism were also identified (Fig. 1J). Gene ontology (GO) analysis was performed to categorize the proteins based on their involvement in various biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions. The most significantly enriched biological processes were metabolic process, cellular process, and primary metabolic process. Notably, the electron transport chain was also significantly enriched, suggesting the involvement of mEVs in mitochondrial functions (Fig. 1K). The most significantly enriched cellular components were cellular anatomical entity, organelle, and intracellular organelle (Fig. 1L). The most significantly enriched molecular functions were catalytic activity, binding, and structural molecule activity. Oxidoreductase activity, electron transfer activity, proton transmembrane transporter activity, and ATP hydrolysis activity coupled to transmembrane movement of substances were notably enriched, reflecting the involvement of mEVs in redox reactions and electron transport processes (Fig. 1M). The abundant AST and protein composition of mEVs strongly suggest their potential functions in antioxidant activity and regulation of cellular mitochondrial energy metabolism. Notably, proteomic analysis revealed enrichment of electron transport chain proteins, oxidoreductases, and proton transmembrane transporters (Fig. 1K–M) - functions essential for mitochondrial homeostasis. Moreover, AST's mitochondrial accumulation makes mEVs a naturally organelle-targeted platform to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction. Unlike nonspecific synthetic antioxidants, mEVs combine multi-component antioxidant activity with intrinsic mitochondrial tropism, providing a physiologically grounded strategy to restore mitochondrial function in diabetic wound healing.

Tannic acid (TA), a polyphenolic polymer, is more accessible and cost-effective compared to dopamine. Its catechol groups can adhere to the surfaces of various materials through chemical or physical interactions (such as hydrogen bonds, electrostatic forces, π-π stacking, and hydrophobic interactions), bestowing hydrogels with superior adhesive properties [[43], [44], [45]]. Additionally, TA possesses antioxidative, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial qualities [40,46]. To enhance the properties of the skin dressing, TA solution was combined with carboxymethyl chitosan (CMCS), oxidized sodium alginate (OSA), and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) to form a hydrogel. The TAgel was synthesized using a direct mix method, followed by the incorporation of mEVs to obtain mEVs-loaded TAgel (mEVs@TAgel) (Fig. 2A). Specifically, dynamic covalent Schiff base bonds form between the amino groups (–NH2) of CMCS and the aldehyde groups (–CHO) of OSA upon mixing. Concurrently, catechol and galloyl groups on tannic acid (TA) engage in multiple hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl (–OH), carboxyl (–COOH), and amino groups of CMCS, OSA, and PVA. Moreover, hydrophobic interactions and π–π stacking among TA molecules further stabilize the three-dimensional (3D) network (Fig. S1). Collectively, these dynamic covalent and reversible physical crosslinks yield a robust three-dimensional (3D) network structure. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images revealed that both TAgel (Fig. 2B) and mEVs@TAgel (Fig. 2C) displayed 3D porous network structures, indicating that the incorporation of mEVs cannot broken the structure of TA gel. The presence of fluorescent small particles within mEVs@TAgel resulted from the incorporation of mEVs, which were stained with DiO (Fig. 2D). At a concentration of 0.5% TA, the gelation time is approximately 2 min, considered an optimal operational timeframe (Fig. 2E).Fig. 2Synthesis and characterization of mEVs@TAgel. (A) Schematic illustration of the preparation process for mEVs@TAgel using TA, CMCS, OSA, PVA, and mEVs. SEM images of (B) TAgel and (C) mEVs@TAgel. (D) Confocal microscopy image of mEVs@TAgel, highlighting the distribution of mEVs within the gel network. (E) Photographs of the gelation time, adhesion, and injectable properties of mEVs@TAgel. (F) Rheological properties of mEVs@TAgel, including storage modulus, loss modulus, and shear stress (n = 3). (G) UV-vis-NIR absorption spectra of TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel. (H) Water uptake capacity of TAgel and mEVs@TAgel over 3 h (pH = 8.0, n = 3). (I) Mass remaining percentage of TAgel and mEVs@TAgel over 21 days (pH = 8.0, n = 3). SEM images of (J) TAgel and (K) mEVs@TAgel after 21 days. (L) Release profile of mEVs from mEVs@TAgel over 21 days (pH = 8.0, n = 3). The adhesive properties of mEVs@TAgel were demonstrated by its ability to remain firmly attached to the dry skin even under dynamic mechanical deformation, such as changes in finger joint angle, indicating excellent adhesion and ductility. Notably, the hydrogel exhibited robust tissue adhesion on wet skin, maintaining stable attachment even when the joint angle was dynamically adjusted from 180° to 90° - demonstrating reliable adhesion under physiologically relevant, dynamic conditions characteristic of diabetic wound sites (Fig. S2). Furthermore, the hydrogel exhibited immediate and robust adhesion, capable of supporting a 200 g weight without detachment (Fig. S3A). Quantitative shear adhesion tests revealed an adhesive strength of approximately 20 kPa at room temperature (25 °C), which increased to 27 kPa at physiological temperature (37 °C), highlighting enhanced interfacial bonding under body-relevant conditions (Fig. S3B). Moreover, the mEVs@TA hydrogel could be readily injected into various predefined molds and retained structural integrity over time (Fig. 2E). It extruded smoothly through a standard injection syringe and rapidly self-recovered its gel structure post-injection, demonstrating excellent injectability (Fig. S4). Rheological analysis showed that the storage modulus (G′) of mEVs@TAgel was higher than the loss modulus (G″), indicating a gel-like behavior with excellent mechanical stability. The shear stress required to deform the gel also increased with time, suggesting enhanced structural integrity (Fig. 2F). Moreover, viscosity decreased progressively with increasing shear rate, confirming the pronounced shear-thinning behavior of the mEVs@TA hydrogel (Fig. S5). As shown in Fig. S6 and G' > G″ indicates a viscoelastic solid state at 1% strain; however, G'' > G′ at 100% strain, signifying structural failure. Upon returning to 1% strain, both moduli recover to their initial values, and this recovery is maintained over two consecutive cycles, demonstrating the robust self-healing capability of the mEVs@TA hydrogel. UV-vis-NIR spectra of mEVs@TAgel exhibited characteristic absorbance peaks corresponding to both mEVs and TAgel (Fig. 2G). The addition of mEVs did not significantly alter the water absorption and retention properties of the gel (Fig. 2H). The mass remaining percentage of TAgel and mEVs@TAgel was investigated over a period of 21 days at pH 6.0. Both materials exhibited significant mass loss over time, indicating degradation. The mass loss was more pronounced in the initial stages, with both TAgel and mEVs@TAgel losing approximately 60% of their mass within the first week. After this initial rapid degradation, the rate slowed down, and by day 21, both materials retained only about 10% of their original mass (Fig. 2I). After 21 days, SEM images showed significant degradation of both TAgel (Fig. 2J) and mEVs@TAgel (Fig. 2K). The remaining structure in the degraded mEVs@TAgel appeared to be composed primarily of PVA, known for its slow degradation rate and contributing to the residual framework observed in the SEM images [47]. Furthermore, the cumulative release of mEVs was quantified by immersing mEVs@TAgel in a PBS solution (Fig. 2L). It was observed that mEVs@TAgel could rapidly release the loaded mEVs during the first 3 days, followed by a gradual release of the remaining mEVs at a reduced rate over the subsequent 18 days. In summary, the synthesis and characterization of mEVs@TAgel demonstrated its potential as a versatile and functional material for various biomedical applications, particularly in wound healing and drug delivery systems.

sections.section: Effects of mEVs@TAgel on oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and Nrf2 pathway in skin keratinocytes
sections.text: To explore the wound healing potential of mEVs@TAgel at the cellular level, we investigated its effects on skin-related cells. Human immortalized keratinocytes (HACAT cells) were selected for testing due to their crucial roles in skin healing, particularly in the context of diabetes mellitus [48]. A cell model of high glucose-induced damage was established, demonstrating that a glucose concentration of 50 mmol/L effectively impaired the cellular activity (Fig. 3A). The effective concentration of mEVs was assessed using the CCK-8 assay, which indicated that 25 μg/mL significantly enhanced cell proliferative activity. Increasing the mEVs concentration beyond this threshold did not yield a notable increase in cell activity (Fig. 3B), leading to the selection of this dose for subsequent experiments. The effects of different TA concentrations were also evaluated using the CCK-8 assay, showing that TA alone did not effectively stimulate cell proliferation (Fig. S7A). Live/Dead staining revealed that neither the TA hydrogel nor the mEVs@TA hydrogel induced cytotoxicity in HaCaT cells, demonstrating the favorable biocompatibility of both formulations (Fig. 3C). Furthermore, colocalization analysis demonstrated that mEVs were internalized by HACAT cells and localized near mitochondria and the nucleus (Fig. 3D). To gain insight into the internalization mechanism, we performed a preliminary investigation using specific endocytosis inhibitors. Treatment with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) markedly inhibited mEVs uptake, while Dynasore and Pitstop 2 also showed moderate inhibitory effects. In contrast, 5-(N-ethyl-N-isopropyl)amiloride (EIPA) and Brefeldin A (BFA) exhibited negligible inhibition (Fig. S8). These results suggest that mEVs internalization primarily occurs via lipid raft-mediated endocytosis, as well as clathrin- and caveolae-dependent pathways. To assess the antioxidant capacity of mEVs@TAgel, intracellular ROS levels were measured. Treatment with TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel successfully scavenged ROS induced by high glucose or H2O2, with mEVs@TAgel exhibiting the most pronounced antioxidant effect (Fig. 3E, F and S9). Given the enrichment of mitochondrial proteins and AST in mEVs (Fig. 1), we next assessed the direct impact of mEVs@TAgel on mitochondrial function using JC-1 staining. Mitochondrial function was evaluated using JC-1 staining, which measures mitochondrial membrane potential [49]. TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel all increased the aggregates/monomers ratio, indicating improved mitochondrial function compared to the blank group. Notably, mEVs@TAgel showed superior efficacy compared to TAgel or mEVs alone (Fig. 3G and H). To further assess mitochondrial function, intracellular ATP production ability was evaluated. TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel all increased ATP production, with mEVs@TAgel showing the strongest effect (Fig. S10). These results are consistent with the JC-1 analysis, further confirming that mEVs@TAgel restores mitochondrial function. The Nrf2 pathway is a central cellular defense mechanism that enhances antioxidant capacity and preserves mitochondrial function during oxidative stress. Therefore, we hypothesized that mEVs@TAgel confer protection by activating this pathway [49]. Herein, immunofluorescence staining and Western blot analysis were used to investigate Nrf2 pathway activation. NRF2 nuclear translocation was significantly enhanced in cells treated with TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel, with the most pronounced effect observed in the mEVs@TAgel group (Fig. 3I). Western blot analysis revealed no significant differences in NRF2 and Keap1 expression among groups, whereas NQO1 and HO1 protein levels were significantly upregulated in the TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups compared to the blank group. Notably, NQO1 and HO1 expression was highest in the mEVs@TAgel group (Fig. 3J–N). We speculate that during this regulatory process, a slight conformational change in Keap1 may lead to NRF2 nuclear translocation, which could explain the lack of significant changes in the overall expression levels of these two proteins. Nevertheless, the marked upregulation of NQO1 and HO1 sufficiently demonstrates the synergistic antioxidant effects of TAgel and mEVs. A wound healing assay was performed to evaluate the effects of mEVs@TAgel on cell migration, and the migrated area was quantified, confirming the enhanced migratory capacity of mEVs@TAgel-treated cells (Fig. 3O and P). In summary, mEVs@TAgel enhances diabetic wound healing in vitro by activating the Nrf2 pathway, which alleviates oxidative stress and improves mitochondrial function, ultimately promoting keratinocyte migration (Fig. 3Q).Fig. 3Effects of mEVs@TAgel on oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and Nrf2 pathway in HACAT cells. (A) Cell viability of HACAT cells treated with different concentrations of glucose (n = 5). (B) OD values of HACAT cells treated with different concentrations of mEVs for 24 h (n = 5). (C) Live/dead staining of cells treated with different materials for 24 h. (D) Colocalization analysis of mEVs and mitochondria after 12 h of incubation. (E) ROS generation in different groups. (F) Quantification of ROS-positive cells (n = 4). (G) JC-1 staining. (H) Quantification of the aggregates/monomers ratio (n = 4). (I) NRF2 staining. (J) Western blot analysis of NRF2, Keap1, NQO1, and HO1 protein expression. β-actin was used as a loading control. (K-N) Relative expression levels of (K) NRF2, (L) Keap1, (M) NQO1, and (N) HO1 normalized to β-actin (n = 3). (O) Scratch assay of HACAT cells treated with different materials. (P) Quantification of migrated area. (Q) Schematic diagram illustrating the mechanism of the Nrf2 pathway. Control group was cultured under normal conditions; Blank, TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups were treated with high glucose (HG, 50 mM). Ordinary one-way ANOVA showed significant treatment effects in all parameters except for NRF2 and Keap1 in Western blot assays (η2= 0.7451-0.9235, all p < 0.001). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001.

sections.section: Effects of mEVs@TAgel on oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and migration in Schwann cells
sections.text: Diabetes is associated with multiple complications, among which diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) represents a major clinical challenge. Characterized by peripheral nerve axonal degeneration and demyelination, DPN involves Schwann cell dysfunction as a central pathological event [50,51]. Schwann cells, the principal glial cells in the peripheral nervous system, play a crucial role in neural development, supporting structural integrity and maintaining functionality. They also facilitate neural recovery following injuries by forming a protective myelin sheath around axons and providing essential neurotrophic support [52,53]. In this study, we employed RSC96 cells, a well-established model for Schwann cells, to investigate the therapeutic effects of mEVs@TAgel. To establish a high-glucose-induced cellular damage model, various concentrations of glucose were tested. As shown in Fig. 4A, a concentration of 50 mmol/L was identified as sufficiently effective in inducing cellular damage, significantly reducing cell viability compared to the control group. The optimal concentration of mEVs was determined using the CCK-8 assay. Treatment with 25 μg/mL mEVs significantly enhanced cellular proliferation (Fig. 4B), while higher concentrations did not yield further improvements. The effects of different TA concentrations were also evaluated, revealing that TA alone did not effectively promote cell proliferation (Fig. S7B). Live/dead staining confirmed that none of the materials tested exhibited cytotoxic effects on Schwann cells, ensuring the safety of the treatments. Similarly, both the TA hydrogel and the mEVs@TA hydrogel exhibited no cytotoxicity toward RSC96 cells, further supporting the biocompatibility of these hydrogel systems (Fig. 4C). Colocalization analysis demonstrated that mEVs were efficiently internalized by RSC96 cells and localized near mitochondria and the nucleus (Fig. 4D). Notably, Schwann cells exhibited significantly higher uptake efficiency than keratinocytes within 12 h, revealing cell type - dependent differences in endocytic activity. This may be related to the high metabolic activity of Schwann cells, which are glial cells in the peripheral nervous system. This localization suggests that mEVs may directly interact with key cellular organelles, potentially modulating their functions.Fig. 4Effects of mEVs@TAgel on oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and migration in RSC96 cells. (A) Cell viability of RSC96 cells treated with different concentrations of glucose (n = 5). (B) OD values of RSC96 cells treated with different concentrations of mEVs for 24 h (n = 5). (C) Live/dead staining of cells treated with different materials for 24 h. (D) Colocalization analysis of mEVs and mitochondria after 12 h of incubation. (E) JC-1 staining. (F) ROS generation in different groups. (G) Scratch assay of RSC96 cells treated with different materials. (H) Transwell assay of RSC96 cells treated with different materials. (I-L) Quantification of the (I) aggregates/monomers ratio (n = 4), (J) ROS-positive cells (n = 4), (K) migrated area (n = 3), and (L) migrated area (n = 5). Control group was cultured under normal conditions; Blank, TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups were treated with high glucose (HG, 50 mM). Ordinary one-way ANOVA showed significant treatment effects in all parameters (η2= 0.7284-0.9524, all p < 0.001). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. Mitochondrial function was also assessed using JC-1 staining, and the results showed that mEVs and mEVs@TAgel significantly increased the aggregates/monomers ratio, indicating improved mitochondrial function compared to the blank group (Fig. 4E–I). Notably, mEVs@TAgel showed superior efficacy in enhancing mitochondrial function than mEVs alone, also suggesting a synergistic effect between TAgel and mEVs. To further assess mitochondrial function in Schwann cells, intracellular ATP levels were evaluated. Consistent with the results in HaCaT cells, the ATP levels were enhanced in the TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups, and the mEVs@TAgel group exhibited the strongest effect (Fig. S11). As mitochondria are a major source of ROS, intracellular ROS levels were then assessed. High glucose levels significantly increased ROS production, but treatment with TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel successfully scavenged these ROS (Fig. 4F–J). Among the treatments, mEVs@TAgel exhibited the most pronounced antioxidant effect, effectively reducing cellular ROS generated by elevated glucose levels. Cell migration is a critical aspect of Schwann cell function, particularly in the context of neural repair. Scratch assays were performed to evaluate the migratory capacity of RSC96 cells. High glucose compromised the migration ability of RSC96 cells; however, exposure to mEVs@TAgel restored this capacity to levels comparable to the control group (Fig. 4G–K). Similarly, transwell assays indicated that the migration potential of RSC96 cells improved after treatment with mEVs@TAgel (Fig. 4H–L). These findings suggest that mEVs@TAgel can enhance the migratory capacity of Schwann cells, potentially promoting neural recovery in diabetic peripheral neuropathy. In summary, mEVs@TAgel effectively reduced oxidative stress, improved mitochondrial function, and enhanced migration in RSC96 cells. These results highlight the therapeutic potential of mEVs@TAgel in mitigating the detrimental effects of high glucose on Schwann cells, thereby offering a promising approach for the treatment of diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

sections.section: Effects of mEVs@TAgel on macrophage polarization, inflammation responses, and NF-κB pathway regulation in macrophages
sections.text: Diabetic wounds are characterized not only by impaired neural function but also by dysregulated inflammatory responses. Macrophages, as key regulators of inflammation, exhibit remarkable plasticity that allows them to modulate tissue repair by translation between pro-inflammatory (M1) and anti-inflammatory (M2) phenotypes [54,55]. The initial phase is predominantly characterized by pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages [56], but this stage is brief and transitions into a subsequent phase dominated by anti-inflammatory macrophages, such as M2 macrophages, which facilitate the integration of implants and tissue regeneration [[57], [58], [59]]. To further investigate the impact of mEVs@TAgel on macrophage polarization and immune response regulation, Raw 264.7 cells were utilized in this study. First, we labeled mEVs with Dio to observe their uptake by macrophages. The results showed that macrophages extensively internalized mEVs within 12 h (Fig. 5A), laying the foundation for the immunomodulatory effects of mEVs. Fluorescence imaging revealed that treatments with TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel effectively reduced intracellular ROS levels induced by high glucose (Fig. 5B and C). Among these treatments, mEVs@TAgel demonstrated the highest efficacy in minimizing ROS levels, indicating its potential to mitigate oxidative stress associated with inflammation.Fig. 5Effects of mEVs@TAgel on macrophage polarization and inflammation responses, and NF-κB pathway regulation in Raw 264.7 cells. (A) Fluorescence images of cellular uptake of mEVs by Raw 264.7 cells. (B) Bright-field, fluorescence, and merged images of intercellular ROS. (C) Statistical data of the percentage of ROS-positive cells (n = 5). (D-E) Immunofluorescence staining of (D) M1 macrophages (CD68+CCR7+ cells) and (E) M2 macrophages (CD68+CD163+ cells) in different groups. (f-g) Statistical data of the percentage of (F) M1 macrophages, (G) M2 macrophages, and (H) the M2/M1 ratio (n = 4). (I) Heatmap of relative expression of pro-inflammatory genes (IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα) and anti-inflammatory genes (Arg1, CD206, and IL-10) measured by qRT-PCR. (J) Western blot analysis of the protein expression (p65, p-p65, and β-actin) of the NF-κB pathway. (K-L) Statistical data of the relative expression of (K) p65 and (L) p-p65 (n = 3). Control group was cultured under normal conditions; Blank, TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups were treated with high glucose (HG, 50 mM). Ordinary one-way ANOVA showed significant treatment effects in all parameters except for p65 (η2= 0.8818-0.98, all p < 0.01). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. In investigating the populations of M1 and M2 macrophages following various treatments, specific markers were employed: CCR7 for M1 macrophages and CD163 for M2 macrophages, relative to the total macrophage population identified by CD68 (Fig. 5D and E). Immunofluorescence staining results demonstrated that TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel significantly reduced the proportion of M1 macrophages while concurrently increasing the population of M2 macrophages, with mEVs@TAgel exhibiting the most pronounced effect (Fig. 5F and G). This was accompanied by a significant increase in the M2/M1 ratio in the mEVs@TAgel groups compared to other groups (Fig. 5H). This shift in macrophage polarization highlights the therapeutic potential of mEVs@TAgel in promoting an anti-inflammatory environment. Furthermore, the study evaluated the expression of various pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory genes in macrophages subjected to different treatments. The findings consistently indicated that the application of TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel resulted in a significant down-regulation of pro-inflammatory genes, including IL-6, IL-1β, and TNFα. In contrast, anti-inflammatory genes such as Arg1, CD206, and IL-10 were markedly up-regulated following these treatments, especially in the mEVs@TAgel groups (Fig. 5I). Previous research has indicated that AST derived from HP can enhance the expression of low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein-1, which can bind to and inhibit p65, p-c-Jun, and NF-κB, thereby preventing the activation of the JNK and NF-κB pathways. This inhibition promotes M2 macrophage polarization [60]. Therefore, we further measured the expression of p65 and p-p65, which are related to the activation of the NF-κB pathway. The results showed that TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel could effectively inhibit the expression of p65, with mEVs and mEVs@TAgel showing more effective inhibition than TAgel alone (Fig. 5J–L). These results indicate that both TAgel and mEVs exhibit certain anti-inflammatory effects. However, regarding inflammation associated with macrophages, the anti-inflammatory effect of mEVs is greater than that of TAgel, and their combination exerts a more potent anti-inflammatory effect. Treatment with mEVs@TA gel significantly reduced p-p65 levels, indicating suppression of NF-κB pathway activity. These results suggest that the anti-inflammatory effects of mEVs@TAgel may be mediated by inhibition of the NF-κB signaling pathway.

sections.section: mEVs@TAgel accelerates diabetic wound healing in a full-thickness skin defect model
sections.text: Angiogenesis plays a vital role in wound healing by facilitating the delivery of nutrients and oxygen. To evaluate the pro-angiogenic potential of mEVs@TAgel, tube formation assays were performed on human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). A cell model of high glucose-induced damage was established, demonstrating that a glucose concentration of 50 mmol/L effectively impaired the angiogenesis activity (Fig. S12). The effective concentration of mEVs was assessed using the CCK-8 assay, which indicated that 25 μg/mL significantly enhanced the angiogenesis activity of HUVECs (Fig. S13). Tube formation analysis conducted in this study revealed that mEVs@TAgel treatment counteracted the reductions in nodes, junctions, meshes, branches, and total length caused by high glucose (Figs. S14 and S15). Treatment with mEVs@TAgel effectively reversed these impairments, demonstrating its angiogenic capacity at the cellular level. Motivated by promising in vitro findings indicating that the mEVs@TA hydrogel possesses robust ROS-scavenging properties, enhances cell migration and angiogenesis, and promotes macrophage polarization, we established diabetic mouse models to investigate its effects on diabetic wound healing at the animal level. The mice were randomly divided into four groups: Blank, TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel. Full-thickness skin wounds (1 cm in diameter) were created on the dorsal side of each mouse. The wounds in the TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups were injected with their respective materials and subsequently covered with medical bandages. Digital images were captured every two days to assess the progression of wound healing (Fig. 6A). By day 12, it was observed that the wounds in the mEVs@TAgel group had fully closed, while those in the other groups remained unhealed (Fig. 6B). A summary and analysis of the changes in wound area over the 12-day period was conducted. The results indicated that the healing rate in the mEVs@TAgel group significantly outperformed that of the other conditions, as the wound areas were markedly reduced in this group compared to the others at nearly every observation point (Fig. 6C and D). To provide a more detailed assessment of the healing outcomes for each group, we visualized the microstructure of the wound areas at day 12 using hematoxylin-eosin (H&E), Masson, and immunofluorescence staining (Fig. 6E–G). In the mEVs@TAgel group, complete re-epithelialization was achieved by day 12, whereas the wounds in the other groups remained partially exposed to varying extents (Fig. 6E–F, H-I). Moreover, the wounds in both the TAgel and mEVs@TAgel groups exhibited significantly thicker granulation tissue (Fig. 6E–F, J). The presence of blood vessels was identified using the vascular marker CD31. Notably, the mEVs@TAgel group demonstrated the highest number of blood vessel formations compared to the other groups (Fig. 6G–K).Fig. 6mEVs@TAgel accelerates diabetic wound healing in a full-thickness skin defect model. (A) Schematic illustration of the experimental design. (B) Wound images in different groups at days 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12. (C) Pattern graphs of wound areas at different time points. (D) Quantitative analysis of wound area over time (n = 3). Two-way ANOVA indicated a significant effect of treatment (η2 = 0.067, p < 0.0001). (E) H&E and (F) Masson's trichrome staining of wound tissues on day 12. (G) Immunofluorescence staining of CD31+ endothelial cells. (H–K) Histomorphometric and fluorescence quantification (n = 3): (H) wound length, (I) re-epithelialization percentage, (J) granulation tissue thickness, and (K) CD31/DAPI fluorescence intensity. Ordinary one-way ANOVA showed significant treatment effects in all parameters (η2= 0.9285-0.9686, all p < 0.001). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. However, murine skin exhibits a notably pronounced contraction during wound healing, which differs significantly from the human skin healing process. To minimize the confounding effects of this contraction, we established an alternative healing model. Specifically, after creating a full-thickness skin defect, we fixed a ring-shaped splint of comparable size around the wound margin to mechanically restrain skin contraction. Additionally, we included a commercially available, market-approved wound-healing gel (a medical trehalose-based repair gel) as a positive control to evaluate the relative advantages of mEVs@TAgel (Fig. S16). Its core functional component, trehalose, is known to form a protective hydration layer and exert mild antioxidant activity, representing a standard clinical strategy for moisture retention and wound protection. Macroscopic observations revealed that the use of the anti-contracture splint substantially slowed the overall wound healing rate, extending the process to more than 16 days. Notably, by day 16, wounds in the mEVs@TAgel group had achieved complete closure, whereas the other groups still exhibited residual unhealed areas of varying sizes (Fig. S16A and B). The wound closure curves further confirmed that mEVs@TAgel not only outperformed both the standalone TAgel and mEVs groups, but also demonstrated significantly superior healing efficacy compared to the commercial gel, with statistically significant differences (Fig. S16C). Histological analysis by H&E staining showed that the control group still exhibited full-thickness tissue defects, while the TAgel, mEVs, and commercial gel groups displayed moderately thick granulation tissue capable of supporting wound repair, although re-epithelialization remained incomplete. In contrast, only the mEVs@TAgel group achieved complete re-epithelialization (Fig. S16D). Quantitative analysis of re-epithelialization length and granulation tissue thickness revealed that both mEVs and the commercial gel promoted faster re-epithelialization compared to TAgel alone (Fig. S16E). Conversely, in terms of granulation tissue formation, TAgel performed comparably to mEVs@TAgel and significantly better than the mEVs group, with all treatment groups outperforming the control (Fig. S16F). These findings collectively suggest that during in vivo wound healing, TAgel primarily provides structural support and promotes the formation of robust granulation tissue, while mEVs contribute not only to granulation tissue development but also significantly accelerate re-epithelialization. The synergistic interaction between TAgel and mEVs results in a healing outcome that surpasses that of the commercial gel, highlighting the therapeutic potential of the combined formulation on diabetic wounds.

sections.section: mEVs@TAgel promotes M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization and modulates the inflammatory response in diabetic wounds
sections.text: Transforming the immune landscape within wound beds is critical for improving the healing process, particularly through the polarization of M1 macrophages to M2 macrophages, which exerts a long-lasting anti-inflammatory effect [61]. In vitro results have demonstrated that mEVs@TAgel play a significant role in macrophage polarization. Moreover, this treatment not only inhibits the expression of pro-inflammatory genes but also enhances the expression of anti-inflammatory genes, thereby fostering a more favorable environment for healing (Fig. 5). To further elucidate the impact of mEVs@TAgel on the regulation of inflammation in vivo, immunofluorescence staining was employed (Fig. 7A and B). The identification of different macrophage populations was achieved using the M1 marker, CCR7, and the M2 marker, CD163, both measured relative to the overall number of macrophages indicated by CD68 (Fig. 7A). The findings were consistent with the in vitro results, demonstrating a noteworthy reduction in the percentage of M1 macrophages within the mEVs@TAgel treatment group compared to the other groups. Conversely, a significant increase in the percentage of M2 macrophages was observed in the mEVs@TAgel group relative to the others (Fig. 7C), accompanied by a significant increase in the M2/M1 ratio (Fig. S7). In addition to assessing macrophage polarization, the levels of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory factors were evaluated through immunofluorescence staining (Fig. 7B). The results revealed a down-regulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNFα across the TAgel, mEVs, and mEVs@TAgel groups, with the mEVs@TAgel group exhibiting particularly low signals for these cytokines (Fig. 7D–E). Additionally, the administration of mEVs@TAgel significantly increased the expression of anti-inflammatory factors, Arg1 and IL-10 (Fig. 7F–G). Collectively, these findings underscore the impressive capability of mEVs@TAgel to alleviate inflammation associated with macrophage activity, suggesting its potential utility in enhancing wound healing outcomes.Fig. 7mEVs@TAgel promotes M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization and modulates the inflammatory response. (A) Immunofluorescence staining of M1 macrophages (CD68+CCR7+) and M2 macrophages (CD68+CD163+). (B) Immunofluorescence staining of pro-inflammatory factors (IL-6 and TNFα) and anti-inflammatory factors (Arg1 and IL-10). (C) Statistical data of the percentage of M1 macrophages and M2 macrophages (n = 3). Two-way ANOVA indicated a significant effect of treatment (η2 = 0.8664, p < 0.0001). (D-G) Quantification of relative fluorescence intensity normalized to DAPI (n = 3): (D) IL-6, (E) TNFα, (F) Arg1, and (G) IL-10. Ordinary one-way ANOVA showed significant treatment effects in all parameters (η2= 0.8689-0.9767, all p < 0.001). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001.

sections.section: mEVs@TAgel mitigates pathological scarring and promotes collagen remodeling
sections.text: Wound healing progresses beyond the inflammatory phase into the remodeling stage, during which excessive scar formation impedes skin regeneration [62]. Persistent inflammation and dysregulated immune responses are key drivers of pathological scarring [54,62,63]. To evaluate the anti-scarring efficacy of the engineered mEVs@TAgel hydrogel, in vivo wound healing was monitored over a 70-day period, with scar tissue analyzed at multiple time points (Fig. 8A). Digital imaging revealed marked differences in scar area reduction across treatment groups. While both TAgel and mEVs alone showed moderate scar attenuation compared to the blank control, the mEVs@TAgel group exhibited the most pronounced improvement. Notably, significantly smaller scars were observed in the mEVs@TAgel group as early as day 30, with this effect sustained through day 70 (Fig. 8B). Quantitative analysis confirmed these observations, demonstrating significantly reduced scar areas in the mEVs@TAgel group at all assessed time points (Fig. 8C). Histological evaluation using H&E and Masson's trichrome staining provided further insight into structural tissue remodeling. By days 30 and 70, the mEVs@TAgel group displayed a more organized scar architecture and improved dermal reconstruction compared to other groups (Fig. 8D and Fig. S18). The scar atrophy index—a metric reflecting the extent of scar remodeling—was lowest in the mEVs@TAgel group (Fig. 8E), indicating that the regenerated skin in this group closely resembled the surrounding normal tissue in morphology and structure.Fig. 8mEVs@TAgel mitigates pathological scarring and promotes collagen remodeling. (A) Schematic illustration of the experimental timeline. (B) Scar images after different treatments on days 30, 50, and 70. (C) Scar area quantification (n = 3). Two-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of treatment (η2 = 0.828, p < 0.0001). (D) H&E staining of scar tissues on days 30 and 70. (E) Scar atrophy index (%), with significant treatment effect (η2 = 0.6475, p < 0.0001). (F-H) Immunofluorescence staining of Col 1 and Col 3. (I,L) Mean fluorescence intensity for Col 1 (n = 3), with significant treatment effect (η2 = 0.407, p < 0.0001) and time (η2 = 0.289, p < 0.0001). (J,M) Mean fluorescence intensity for Col 3 (n = 3), with significant treatment effect (η2 = 0.626, p < 0.0001) and no significant time effect (η2 = 0.0394, p = 0.2488). (K,N) Col 3/Col 1 ratio (n = 3), with significant treatment effect (η2 = 0.473, p = 0.0005) and no significant time effect (η2= 0.0396, p = 0.3588). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. Further investigation into extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling revealed distinct collagen dynamics. Immunofluorescence staining for Collagen 1 (Col 1) and Collagen 3 (Col 3) was performed on days 12, 30, and 70. The mEVs@TAgel group promoted a more disorganized, reticular, skin-like arrangement of Col 1, resembling native dermal architecture, whereas Col 1 in the other groups exhibited predominantly parallel alignment, characteristic of fibrotic scarring (Fig. 8F–H). Quantitative analysis of mean fluorescence intensity revealed that Col 1 levels gradually increased over time in the blank, TAgel, and mEVs groups. In contrast, the mEVs@TAgel group exhibited high Col 1 expression as early as day 12, with no significant change thereafter (days 30 and 70; Fig. 8I–L). This early upregulation of Col 1 likely provides essential structural support during initial tissue repair, consistent with the accelerated wound closure observed in this group. Col 3 fluorescence intensity remained relatively stable over time within each group, with the mEVs@TAgel group maintaining the highest levels throughout (Fig. 8J–M), suggesting that Col 3 deposition is primarily driven by early therapeutic intervention and remains largely unchanged in later stages of healing. Analysis of the Col 3/Col 1 ratio showed significantly higher values in both the mEVs and mEVs@TAgel groups compared to the blank and TAgel groups (Fig. 8K–N), indicative of a more regenerative ECM profile. Although the mEVs group exhibited a slight downward trend in the ratio over time, the mEVs@TAgel group showed a modest upward tendency, though neither trend reached statistical significance. In summary, these findings highlight the ability of mEVs@TAgel to effectively modulate collagen composition and spatial organization, thereby promoting regenerative healing and minimizing scar formation. This regulatory function is likely attributable to the mEVs, particularly in influencing the proportion of Col 3. Overall, the mEVs@TAgel hydrogel demonstrates superior anti-scarring efficacy by reducing scar formation, improving dermal architecture, and favorably regulating ECM dynamics. These results underscore its great potential as a promising therapeutic strategy for mitigating scarring in diabetic wound repair and other challenging wound-healing contexts.

sections.section: mEVs@TAgel promotes functional recovery and nerve regeneration in diabetic sciatic nerve injury
sections.text: Beyond its effects on skin repair, we next investigated whether mEVs@TAgel could promote nerve regeneration in diabetic peripheral neuropathy. This hypothesis was motivated by its protective effects on Schwann cells observed in vitro (Fig. 4). To evaluate the therapeutic potential of mEVs@TAgel in diabetic peripheral nerve injury, we established a sciatic nerve injury model in diabetic mice. The right sciatic nerve was exposed and subjected to a standardized incomplete injury using microsurgical instruments (Fig. 9A). Following injury, the site was treated with the respective formulations, and the wound was closed. Functional recovery was assessed one month post-injury by gait analysis to calculate the Sciatic Function Index (SFI) [51] (Fig. 9B and C). The mEVs@TAgel group exhibited significantly higher SFI scores compared to the blank control group at 30 days (Fig. 9D), and outperformed both the TAgel and mEVs groups, indicating superior restoration of motor function. The electromyography (EMG) signals were recorded to assess the amplitude and latency of the compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs). In the control group, a robust and well-defined CMAP was observed, indicating normal nerve conduction. In contrast, the blank group exhibited significantly reduced CMAP amplitude and prolonged latency, reflecting impaired nerve function following injury. Treatment with TAgel and mEVs showed some improvement in CMAP amplitude compared to the blank group, but the latency remained prolonged, suggesting partial recovery of nerve conduction. Notably, the mEVs@TAgel group displayed the most significant recovery in both CMAP amplitude and latency, closely resembling the profile of the control group (Fig. S19), indicating effective restoration of electrophysiological function. Histological evaluation of the injured nerves via H&E and Masson's trichrome staining revealed that the mEVs@TAgel group exhibited significantly improved nerve fiber architecture compared to the other groups, with more intact fascicular organization and reduced pathological alterations (Fig. 9E and F). To assess axonal regeneration and remyelination, immunofluorescence staining was performed for neurofilament (NF), myelin basic protein (MBP), and S100β—key markers of axonal integrity and Schwann cell activity [51]. The mEVs@TAgel group showed significantly enhanced NF expression (Fig. 9G), increased MBP fluorescence intensity (Fig. 9H), and upregulated S100β signal (Fig. 9I), suggesting robust axonal regrowth and myelination. Quantitative analysis confirmed significantly higher mean fluorescence intensities for all three markers in the mEVs@TAgel group relative to other groups (Fig. 9J–L).Fig. 9mEVs@TAgel promotes functional recovery and nerve regeneration in diabetic sciatic nerve injury. (A) Schematic illustration of the experimental design. (B) Representative footprints from the left (control) and right (experimental) hindpaws in different groups. (C) Formula for calculating the Sciatic Function Index (SFI). (D) Statistical analysis of SFI scores (n = 3). One-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of treatment (η2 = 0.8337, p = 0.0018). (E-H) Histological and immunofluorescence staining of sciatic nerves at day 28 post-injury: (E) H&E, (F) Masson's trichrome, (G) NF, (H) MBP, and (I) S100β. (J-L) Quantification of mean fluorescence intensity: (J) NF, (K) MBP, (L) S100β. Treatment had a significant effect across all markers (η2 = 0.8579-0.9358, all p < 0.001; n = 3, one-way ANOVA). (M–Q) Assessment of gastrocnemius muscle atrophy and fibrosis: (M) representative muscles, (N) H&E, (O) Masson's trichrome staining. (P) Relative wet weight (η2 = 0.8549, p = 0.001) and (Q) collagen area percentage (η2= 0.7517, p = 0.0084), both showing significant treatment effects (n = 3, one-way ANOVA). Data are mean ± SD. ns, p > 0.05, ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001. Given that sciatic nerve injury leads to downstream muscle atrophy [64], we evaluated gastrocnemius muscle recovery. Gross morphological observation revealed severe atrophy in the right gastrocnemius of the blank group, with only modest improvement in the TAgel and mEVs groups. In contrast, the mEVs@TAgel group displayed substantial recovery, with muscle size nearly comparable to the contralateral uninjured side (Fig. 9M). Histological analysis (H&E and Masson's trichrome) further demonstrated improved myofiber organization and reduced fibrotic deposition in the mEVs@TAgel group (Fig. 9N and O). Consistently, the mEVs@TAgel group showed a significantly higher relative wet weight of the gastrocnemius muscle compared to the blank and TAgel groups (Fig. 9P), indicating effective preservation of muscle mass. Quantification of collagen area percentage revealed a significantly lower fibrotic burden in the mEVs@TAgel group compared to the blank control, with no significant differences among the other groups (Fig. 9Q), further supporting its anti-fibrotic and regenerative effects. In summary, mEVs@TAgel treatment significantly enhances functional recovery, promotes axonal regeneration and remyelination, mitigates muscle atrophy, and reduces fibrosis in a diabetic sciatic nerve injury model. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of mEVs@TAgel as a promising strategy for the treatment of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. A comprehensive biosafety evaluation is essential to ensure the biocompatibility and systemic safety of therapeutic materials prior to clinical translation. To evaluate the long-term safety of mEVs@TAgel, a comprehensive assessment was conducted 70 days post-treatment. Histological examination of major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys, revealed no significant pathological alterations in any treatment group compared to the control group. All tissues exhibited normal architecture, with no signs of inflammation, necrosis, or organ damage (Fig. S20A). Hematological parameters, including white blood cell count (WBC), red blood cell count (RBC), hemoglobin (HGB), hematocrit (HCT), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), red cell distribution width (RDW), and platelet count (PLT), were within normal physiological ranges and showed no significant differences among groups, indicating no adverse effects on hematopoiesis or systemic homeostasis. Serum biochemical markers such as alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) remained at normal levels across all groups, suggesting preserved liver and kidney function (Fig. S20B). Furthermore, serum concentrations of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α showed no significant elevation in the mEVs@TAgel group relative to controls (Fig. S21). Collectively, these results demonstrate that mEVs@TAgel exhibits excellent biocompatibility and does not induce systemic toxicity or inflammatory responses over the 70-day observation period, supporting its favorable long-term biosafety profile.

While our study offers a novel hydrogel system (mEVs@TAgel) for diabetic wound healing and peripheral nerve repair, it is important to acknowledge its inherent limitations. Specifically, although mEVs@TAgel exhibited desirable properties comparable to reported TA-based hydrogels, a direct comparison of adhesive properties between TAgel and mEVs@TAgel was not performed in this study. Therefore, the specific impact of mEVs incorporation on the mechanical and adhesive properties of the TA hydrogel matrix remains to be quantitatively determined. Future side-by-side characterization of both formulations will clarify whether mEVs loading affects the hydrogel system. This system promotes tissue regeneration through multiple mechanisms, including activation of the Nrf2 pathway in keratinocytes, protection of mitochondrial function in keratinocytes and Schwann cells, and inhibition of the NF-κB pathway in macrophages. Although both our in vitro and in vivo results demonstrate these therapeutic effects, the detailed molecular mechanisms by which mEVs@TAgel regulates diabetic wound and nerve healing in vivo remain to be fully elucidated. Transcriptomic or proteomic analysis of wound and nerve tissues would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying pathways, which should be considered in the future. Moreover, macrophage polarization and inflammatory markers were analyzed only on day 12 after treatment. Since the inflammatory response is most active during the early phase of wound healing (days 2-8), additional time points (e.g., days 3 and 7) are needed to fully understand how mEVs@TAgel regulates inflammation over time. In addition, although we demonstrated that mEVs localized near mitochondria and improved mitochondrial function in keratinocytes and Schwann cells, similar validation in macrophages has not yet been performed. Future studies should include mitochondrial co-localization and functional assays in macrophages to further elucidate the impact of mEVs@TAgel on mitochondrial function in these cells. Only in vitro degradation data over 21 days are available in this study; in vivo degradation of mEVs@TAgel was not assessed. Future studies should include in vivo implantation experiments to evaluate the long-term degradation behavior of the hydrogel.

In this study, we successfully isolated and characterized microalgal extracellular vesicles (mEVs) derived from Haematococcus pluvialis, which are rich in astaxanthin and functionally active proteins involved in antioxidant defense and mitochondrial energy metabolism. These mEVs were effectively incorporated into a tannic acid-based hydrogel (TAgel) to form a multifunctional composite biomaterial, mEVs@TAgel, which demonstrated excellent mechanical stability, adhesion, biodegradability, and sustained mEVs release. In vitro, mEVs@TAgel significantly alleviated oxidative stress, enhanced mitochondrial function, promoted cell migration in both skin keratinocytes and Schwann cells, and modulated macrophage polarization toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype by suppressing the NF-κB pathway. These effects were attributed to the synergistic actions of astaxanthin-enriched mEVs and the antioxidative, anti-inflammatory properties of tannic acid. In diabetic wound healing models, mEVs@TAgel accelerated wound closure, promoted robust granulation tissue formation, enhanced re-epithelialization, and stimulated angiogenesis. Notably, it effectively modulated the inflammatory microenvironment by promoting M1-to-M2 macrophage transition and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. Furthermore, mEVs@TAgel significantly improved collagen remodeling, reduced scar formation, and promoted regenerative healing with a more skin-like extracellular matrix architecture. In a diabetic sciatic nerve injury model, mEVs@TAgel treatment led to superior functional recovery, enhanced axonal regeneration and remyelination, mitigated muscle atrophy, and reduced fibrosis. Importantly, long-term biosafety evaluation revealed no systemic toxicity or organ damage, underscoring its excellent biocompatibility. While this study presents compelling evidence for the therapeutic potential of mEVs@TAgel, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the diabetic wound environment is multifactorial, and although our model addresses hyperglycemia-induced impairment, it does not incorporate other clinically relevant factors such as bacterial infection or ischemia, which could influence treatment outcomes. Second, the sample sizes in animal experiments were relatively small, which may limit the statistical power and generalizability of the results. Third, all in vivo studies were conducted in rodent models; future validation in larger animal models with skin and nerve physiology more comparable to humans would strengthen translational relevance. Finally, while the 70-day observation period provides valuable long-term safety data, even longer-term studies may be warranted to fully assess durability and potential late effects. Despite these limitations, the robust efficacy and favorable safety profile of mEVs@TAgel support its further development as a novel regenerative therapy for diabetic complications.
